cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm an HR Manager. My team handles everything from recruiting to onboarding to benefits — kind of the full spectrum for a company our size.
v.Q2: Just over two years. I joined when the company was around 55 people.
v.Q3: We're a B2B SaaS company, so squarely in tech. We're at about 85 employees right now and growing, I think we expect to cross 100 sometime in the next year.
v.Q4: We use BambooHR as our core HRIS — it handles employee records, time off, onboarding checklists, and some performance stuff. And then we have Gusto on top of it for payroll, because BambooHR's payroll offering wasn't available in all the states we operate in when we set things up. So it's two tools, which isn't ideal but it's what we've got.
v.Q5: That was about a year and a half ago, maybe closer to 18 months. It was a fairly focused evaluation that took maybe two months total.
v.Q6: Honestly, not much. We were mostly on spreadsheets and some manual processes. We had a basic ADP account for payroll but nothing that you'd call a real HRIS.
v.Q7: The main driver was that we were scaling fast enough that the manual approach was breaking down. Onboarding new hires was taking too long, time-off tracking was a mess of email threads, and I couldn't give leadership any reliable headcount data without building a spreadsheet from scratch every time. I think we also had a near-miss on a payroll error that made the CEO finally agree we needed real infrastructure. And we were starting to hire in more states, so multi-state payroll compliance became a real concern.
v.Q8: We'd gone fully remote, which meant we were suddenly hiring people anywhere in the US, and that made state-by-state compliance a much bigger issue than it had been when everyone was in Seattle. There was also some investor pressure around getting our HR operations cleaned up as part of a broader maturation push ahead of a fundraise.
v.Q9: ADP was painful to use — the interface felt like it was designed in 2005, customer support was really slow, and it wasn't giving us any of the self-service features employees expected. People couldn't even look up their own pay stubs without calling me. And the reporting was basically nonexistent. I wanted employees to be able to handle basic stuff themselves so I could focus on more strategic work.
v.Q10: We looked at BambooHR, Rippling, Gusto, and briefly at Lattice for the performance side. Rippling and BambooHR were the two we got deepest with.
v.Q11: It had to have solid multi-state payroll support, or at least a clear path to it. Employee self-service was non-negotiable — I needed people to be able to access their own information. And it had to integrate with our ATS, which at the time was Greenhouse. Price ceiling was also a factor; we couldn't spend more than roughly $15,000 a year at our size.
v.Q12: Our VP of Finance had budget authority and was involved in the final call. My HR coordinator was in some of the demos and gave input on usability. But I drove the whole evaluation — I built the comparison matrix, managed the vendor conversations, and made the final recommendation to the VP of Finance, who signed off.
v.Q13: We switched. We moved to BambooHR as the core HRIS, and layered Gusto in for payroll.
v.Q14: BambooHR won on usability and price. The employee experience was just cleaner and more intuitive than what we saw from ADP, and the implementation was straightforward enough that my small team could handle it without external consultants. It was also within budget. Rippling was actually more impressive in terms of features — especially the IT and device management stuff — but it was priced higher than we were ready for, and honestly felt like a bit more platform than we needed at 60 people.
v.Q15: Rippling lost on price and complexity — it felt like more than we needed and the sales process was a little aggressive in a way that turned me off. Gusto we actually did bring in for payroll because it handled our multi-state situation better than BambooHR's payroll module did at the time, so it wasn't fully rejected. Lattice we realized was really more of a performance tool and didn't solve the core HRIS gap we had.
v.Q16: BambooHR is genuinely easy to use, for both HR and employees. Time-off management is smooth, onboarding workflows are solid, and the reporting for basic headcount and turnover metrics is good enough for what we need most of the time. Employees actually use the self-service features, which is all I wanted.
v.Q17: The two-tool situation is the main thing. Having BambooHR and Gusto as separate systems means I'm still reconciling data across platforms more than I'd like. And BambooHR's performance management module feels a little basic — it works, but it's not as flexible as I'd want as we start thinking about more structured review cycles.
v.Q18: The fragmentation between BambooHR and Gusto is my biggest frustration. It's a moderate frustration — nothing is catastrophically broken — but every payroll cycle I'm doing a manual check to make sure changes I made in BambooHR actually made it over to Gusto correctly. That's time I shouldn't have to spend, and it's a source of low-level anxiety every month.
v.Q19: We've grown by about 25 people, which has made compensation management more of a priority. I'm also thinking about a real performance review process now rather than the informal thing we've been doing, so the performance module requirements have gotten more serious. And I think I'd want a single platform if we went back to market — the two-tool setup made sense then but feels like the wrong architecture now.
v.Q20: I think we're somewhere around $15,000 to $20,000 combined for BambooHR and Gusto. I don't have the exact number in front of me but that's roughly the range.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. It's not a huge line item and we do get real value from it. But I think if we consolidated to one platform, we might get better value for similar or lower spend.
v.Q22: If seamless payroll sync between the two systems was just built in and reliable? Probably worth $5,000 to $10,000 a year to us in time savings and reduced risk of payroll errors.
v.Q23: I'd say it's somewhat likely we at least evaluate our options in the next six months. The two-tool situation has been on my mind and if we cross 100 employees, I think that becomes the trigger to revisit. Not a certainty, but I wouldn't rule it out.
v.Q24: Integration is still the biggest headache for most people I talk to in similar roles — nothing talks to each other cleanly, and that creates manual work that nobody budgeted for. And I think there's a real gap between what vendors promise in demos and what the day-to-day experience actually looks like once you're live. That trust gap is something the whole industry has a problem with.

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm an HR Manager. My official title is actually People Operations Manager, but the function is HR. I'm the only dedicated HR person at the company right now, which at our size is a stretch, to put it mildly.
v.Q2: I've been here four years. Long enough to have lived through two different tool evaluations and more than a few reorgs.
v.Q3: We're a technology company — we build enterprise data infrastructure software, so kind of a B2B enterprise tech play. We're at about 310 employees right now. We've been growing in that slow and steady way, adding maybe 40 to 50 people a year, which sounds manageable until you're the only HR person managing all of the onboarding.
v.Q4: BambooHR is our main system — it covers the core HRIS, time off, onboarding, and we use their performance management module even though I have a complicated relationship with it. For payroll, we actually use ADP Run, which predates my involvement in the tooling decisions. And benefits are administered through a broker that uses their own portal. So technically we have three different systems, and they do not talk to each other in any meaningful way, which is a constant source of frustration for me.
v.Q5: About 14 months ago. We ran a pretty thorough evaluation — I want to say it took about 10 or 12 weeks from initial research to final decision. I've actually been through two evaluations at this company, but the most recent one is the one that's fresh.
v.Q6: We had BambooHR in place already — the question was whether to stay with it, upgrade within the BambooHR ecosystem, or switch to something else entirely. ADP Run was also already there for payroll. So this was less of a greenfield evaluation and more of a should-we-rebuild-our-stack conversation.
v.Q7: The primary trigger was hitting the point where BambooHR felt like it was starting to strain at our size. We were around 260 employees when we started the evaluation and some things that had worked fine at 150 were showing cracks. The performance management module in particular — I was getting a lot of complaints from managers that it wasn't flexible enough for how we do reviews. We also had a new VP of Engineering come in who started asking for workforce analytics I simply couldn't produce with the tools I had. And honestly, there was some internal pressure from our operations team to think more seriously about whether we had the right infrastructure to scale to 500 people without adding HR headcount, because that was on the table. So it was a combination of tool capability gaps, evolving leadership expectations, and a forward-looking scaling concern.
v.Q8: We had formalized our hybrid work model — we'd been loosely hybrid since coming back from the pandemic, but we actually codified it into a policy, which meant we needed better tooling around things like tracking in-office days, equity in how we handled time off for remote versus on-site employees, and more structured manager training workflows. The hybrid formalization made some of BambooHR's lighter-weight features feel inadequate. There was also a broader digital transformation initiative at the company level that HR was supposed to be part of, and the state of our tooling made it hard to tell that story credibly.
v.Q9: The lack of any real integration between BambooHR and ADP was a significant pain point. Every payroll cycle, I was manually exporting from BambooHR and importing into ADP, which is exactly the kind of work that should be automated but wasn't. I was also deeply frustrated with BambooHR's reporting — you can kind of pull basic stuff, but anything nuanced requires custom reports that take forever to build and don't always give you what you asked for. And the performance review cycle management was genuinely difficult. Setting up multi-step review cycles with different forms for different employee populations was not something BambooHR handled gracefully, and I spent an embarrassing amount of time managing that process in spreadsheets alongside the tool.
v.Q10: We looked seriously at Lattice, Rippling, Workday — which we very quickly ruled out as being way too enterprise for us — and we took a hard look at whether just staying with BambooHR and adding some point solutions on top was the right move. I also had a conversation with Culture Amp but that was more on the engagement and performance analytics side rather than a core HRIS replacement.
v.Q11: Payroll integration was the first gate — I was not willing to continue the manual export-import routine, so either the platform had to handle payroll natively or it had to have a certified, bidirectional integration with ADP. The second gate was real performance management flexibility — I needed configurable review cycle templates, not a rigid one-size-fits-all flow. And the third was scalability credibility — I needed to see evidence that the platform worked well for companies in the 300 to 700 range, not just case studies about 50-person startups. Implementation support mattered a lot too, given that I was going to be standing this up alone.
v.Q12: Our CFO had budget authority and was looped in on cost comparisons, though he trusted my judgment on the HR-specific functionality. The VP of Engineering, who had been the one asking for better analytics, was an informal stakeholder — I shared the shortlist with him and he gave feedback, but he wasn't in the formal decision. And our CEO did a brief review of the finalist before we signed. So I was the primary recommender and did all the evaluation work, but the CFO had sign-off power and the CEO did a gut-check review. It wasn't a full committee, but it wasn't purely my call either.
v.Q13: We stayed with BambooHR. I know that might be surprising given everything I described, but the switching cost analysis came back in BambooHR's favor when we factored in implementation risk, retraining 300-plus employees on a new system, and the cost differential. We did add Lattice as a separate performance and engagement layer, which was a meaningful addition.
v.Q14: The decision to stay came down to risk-adjusted cost. Switching a 300-person company to an entirely new HRIS, with one HR person managing it, during a period where we're also trying to maintain growth — that's a significant operational risk. BambooHR isn't perfect, but our employees knew how to use it, the data was already in it, and the incremental improvements we could get from switching didn't outweigh the disruption cost. Adding Lattice for performance and engagement was a kind of compromise solution — it addressed the most acute pain point without blowing up the whole stack. Rippling was the most compelling alternative, but the implementation scope felt like a part-time job in itself.
v.Q15: Rippling lost primarily on implementation complexity and the sense that I would be undertaking a massive project without sufficient internal support to execute it well. The platform is genuinely impressive, but standing it up across HR, IT, and payroll as a solo HR person felt unrealistic. Workday was immediately eliminated — it's priced and scoped for companies much larger than ours, and the implementation timeline they quoted was laughable for our situation. Culture Amp was interesting but it's a specialist tool and didn't address the HRIS or payroll integration problems. Lattice, which we ultimately did adopt as a point solution, was rejected as a full HRIS replacement for the obvious reason that it doesn't do HRIS — but it won in its lane.
v.Q16: BambooHR is reliable for the basics — employee records are clean, time-off management works, the employee self-service portal is genuinely good and reduces a lot of inbound questions. And the onboarding workflow builder, while not the most sophisticated thing I've ever seen, is solid enough that I can build a reasonable new hire experience without a lot of manual intervention. Lattice has been a meaningful upgrade for performance management and engagement surveys — that addition solved the most visible pain point from our evaluation.
v.Q17: The ADP integration is still not what I need it to be — we got a slightly better data sync set up after a lot of back and forth with BambooHR support, but it's still not fully automated and I still have eyes-on-it anxiety every payroll cycle. And the reporting in BambooHR, even now, is kind of surface-level. I can get headcount and turnover, but anything involving comp analysis, tenure distribution by function, or promotion velocity — I'm building that myself. At 310 employees, that's a real gap.
v.Q18: The payroll-to-HRIS sync situation is still my biggest frustration, and I'd characterize it as significant. It's not severe in the sense that payroll isn't running or people aren't getting paid, but the amount of manual oversight and reconciliation it requires of me personally is significant given that I'm a team of one. Every pay period I'm doing a manual audit pass to make sure nothing got dropped in the handoff between systems. That's time and cognitive load that I genuinely cannot afford, and it feels like a problem that should have been solved by the industry years ago.
v.Q19: We've added about 50 people since the evaluation, which has made compensation benchmarking a more urgent need — we're competing for engineering talent in a tough market and I need better data to support comp conversations. I'm also starting to think about succession planning and skills mapping in a way that I wasn't before, because our engineering leadership has been asking about workforce planning. And I think my expectations around AI-assisted features have genuinely shifted — a year ago I wasn't thinking about it at all, but now I'm curious what tools are doing with AI for things like policy generation or HR question answering, because that could actually move the needle for a solo HR person.
v.Q20: Across BambooHR, Lattice, and ADP Run, I think we're somewhere in the $50,000 to $100,000 range annually. I don't own all the contracts directly — ADP in particular is managed partly by Finance — but that's my best estimate of the aggregate spend.
v.Q21: I'd say somewhat yes, but with reservations. Lattice I feel good about — we're getting real value there. BambooHR is adequate for the price. ADP I think we're probably overpaying for what we get out of it, and if I could replace it with something more modern and better integrated, I would.
v.Q22: If I had a truly automated, reliable, bidirectional payroll sync — where changes in BambooHR propagated to payroll without me babysitting it — I think that's conservatively worth $10,000 to $25,000 annually to us. Probably on the higher end when you factor in the risk reduction in addition to the time savings.
v.Q23: I'd say it's somewhat likely that we re-enter evaluation mode, maybe not within six months but within the year. The trigger would probably be hitting 350 employees or getting a new head of HR above me — either of those things would create the organizational appetite to take on a larger-scope platform change. Right now, somewhat unlikely to switch in the next six months, but the trajectory is pointing toward another evaluation sooner rather than later.
v.Q24: I think the core challenge is that most platforms are still not actually integrated — they sell you on the vision of a unified system and then the reality is a lot of middleware and manual reconciliation. That gap between the demo and the lived experience is I think the defining frustration for HR professionals right now. And for people in a solo or small-team HR function, the administrative burden of managing and maintaining these tools can actually rival the administrative burden the tools were supposed to eliminate. There's also an emerging challenge around AI — vendors are all announcing AI features but it's hard to know what's real versus marketing, and making a wrong bet on an AI-forward platform that doesn't deliver is a real risk.

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: Sure. I'm a Director of People Operations. So I oversee everything from onboarding and benefits administration to compliance and employee relations for our firm.
v.Q2: I've been here just about four years now, so I'd say in that three-to-five-year range.
v.Q3: We're in financial services — specifically a registered investment advisory firm based out of Chicago. And we're sitting at around seventy-five employees right now. We've been pretty stable at that size for the last couple of years, which is actually somewhat intentional. We're not in a growth-at-all-costs mode.
v.Q4: We're primarily on Gusto. It handles payroll, benefits administration, and some basic HR record-keeping for us. We do supplement it with a standalone performance management tool — we use Lattice for that — but Gusto is the core system of record for us on the people operations side.
v.Q5: That was roughly a year and a half ago, so I'd put it in the one-to-two-year range.
v.Q6: At that point we were using a combination of ADP Run for payroll and a very basic HRIS — honestly it was closer to a glorified spreadsheet system that a prior HR person had set up in Namely. The integration between those two was essentially nonexistent, and everything was more manual than it needed to be.
v.Q7: There were a few things layered together. The most immediate trigger was honestly our ADP contract renewal coming up — that gave us a natural opening to ask whether we were getting value. But beyond that, I had just moved into this director role about six months prior, and I came in with fresh eyes on the toolset. What I saw was a lot of manual reconciliation between payroll and our HRIS records, and our benefits open enrollment was this incredibly painful process every year where we were manually entering elections from a broker spreadsheet. We were also struggling with compliance documentation — in financial services, you need solid audit trails, and our previous setup did not give us that with any reliability. So it was really a combination of the contract renewal moment, my own new-leadership perspective, and some genuine operational pain points that were causing real risk.
v.Q8: I think the regulatory environment in financial services was — and continues to be — a factor. Our compliance team was raising concerns about how we were tracking and documenting things like Form I-9s and employment verifications, and there was a recognition that our people operations infrastructure needed to be tighter. There was also some pressure from our CFO around administrative efficiency. Nothing dramatic, but there was a general sense that we were running a people function that looked like it belonged to a fifteen-person firm, not a seventy-five-person firm.
v.Q9: Yes, and I'd say the biggest one was the total lack of integration between payroll and HR data. Every time we had a compensation change or a status change, I or someone on my team had to manually update it in two or three places. That's just an invitation for error. The other major frustration was reporting — ADP Run's reporting was functional but not particularly useful for the kinds of workforce analytics questions our leadership was starting to ask. And benefits administration was just painful. Open enrollment felt like a project that consumed weeks of bandwidth every year for a team our size. I knew there had to be a better way.
v.Q10: We looked seriously at Gusto, Rippling, and Paychex Flex. We also took a brief look at Zenefits — or Zenefits rebranded as TriNet Zenefits at that point — but we didn't get very deep into that evaluation.
v.Q11: A few things were non-negotiable for us. First, it had to handle both payroll and benefits administration in one platform — we were done with the two-system problem. Second, it needed to have solid compliance documentation features, particularly around I-9 management and audit trails, given our regulatory environment. Third, the implementation support had to be real and hands-on — we're a small HR team and we couldn't afford to self-implement something complex. And honestly, price was a factor. We weren't looking for an enterprise system, and we weren't going to spend six figures on something for a company our size.
v.Q12: So it was primarily me driving the evaluation, but I needed sign-off from our CFO, who was very focused on the cost side of the equation and wanted to understand the ROI argument. Our head of IT was looped in for a fairly brief review around data security and SSO requirements. And our CEO was kept informed but was largely deferring to me and the CFO. So I was the primary recommender — I did all the demos, built the comparison, and made the recommendation — but the CFO had formal approval authority on the budget.
v.Q13: We switched. We moved to Gusto, which we've been on since then.
v.Q14: Gusto stood out on a few dimensions. The unified payroll and benefits experience was genuinely seamless compared to what we had, and it was clearly built for companies at our scale — it didn't feel like we were using a watered-down enterprise product or a tool meant for five-person startups. The pricing was transparent and fair, which mattered a lot to our CFO. And honestly, the implementation experience was really positive. Their onboarding support was attentive and they helped us migrate our data without it being a disaster. The platform itself is also just easy to use, which matters when I'm asking managers to self-serve certain things without a lot of training.
v.Q15: Rippling was interesting and honestly more powerful than Gusto in some ways, but it felt like a lot of platform for what we needed, and the pricing structure was more complex. I also had some concerns about whether the implementation would be heavier than our team could absorb. Paychex Flex felt dated to me — the UX was not great, and it reminded me too much of what we were trying to move away from with ADP. And TriNet Zenefits, the brief look we took at it, just didn't inspire confidence. The product felt like it was still finding itself after the rebrand, and the sales process was a little disorganized, which made me nervous about support post-sale.
v.Q16: Gusto does payroll really well — it's reliable, the tax filings are handled automatically, and I have never had a payroll run that I had to chase down or correct because of a platform error. Benefits administration is also genuinely better than what we had. Open enrollment is still work, but it's manageable work, not a crisis. And the employee self-service experience is good — our employees can access their pay stubs, update their own information, and manage their benefits elections without coming to me for every little thing.
v.Q17: Reporting is still a gap. I can get the basics out of Gusto, but anything more sophisticated — headcount analysis, turnover trend reporting, compensation band analysis — I'm still doing in spreadsheets. That's frustrating for a team that wants to be more strategic. The HRIS functionality is also pretty thin if I'm being honest. It's fine for a system of record, but there's no real performance or engagement infrastructure built in, which is why we're still paying separately for Lattice. And I think the compliance documentation features, while better than ADP, still leave something to be desired for a regulated industry like ours.
v.Q18: I'd say the reporting limitations are my biggest frustration, and I'd rate it as moderate to significant. It's not a daily crisis, but it comes up repeatedly when leadership asks me for data that I know should be readily available from our HR system and isn't. I end up spending time pulling and manipulating data that should be a few clicks. It undermines my ability to present people data in a credible, timely way to our executive team, and in financial services, credibility with data really matters.
v.Q19: The expectation around people analytics has gone up considerably, both from our leadership and honestly from my own professional standards. When I first evaluated tools, getting off the manual-reconciliation treadmill was the goal. Now that we've solved that baseline problem, I'm more focused on what I can actually do with the data we're collecting. There's also been more interest from our compliance team in having tighter documentation around certain HR processes, which I think Gusto handles adequately but not exceptionally.
v.Q20: Between Gusto and Lattice, I think we're in the range of twenty to thirty thousand dollars annually. Gusto is the larger piece of that.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes, I'd say. Gusto is reasonably priced for what it does, and payroll and benefits administration running smoothly has real value. But I do think there's a gap between what we're paying and what we're getting on the analytics and HRIS side. So the value story is partial — strong on the operational basics, weaker on the strategic tools I'd want.
v.Q22: If Gusto had genuinely strong reporting and workforce analytics built in, something that would eliminate the spreadsheet work and let me present meaningful people data to leadership with a few clicks, I think that's worth somewhere in the five-to-ten-thousand-dollar range annually to us. Maybe a bit more if it saved meaningful time across the team.
v.Q23: Probably not within six months. I'd say somewhat unlikely. We're not in a place organizationally where a migration would be welcome right now, and Gusto is stable even if it's not perfect. I think the next evaluation cycle is more likely twelve to eighteen months out, depending on how our needs evolve.
v.Q24: I think the most common frustration I hear from peers is that most tools are still making you choose between something that's easy and something that's capable. The user-friendly platforms often lack depth, and the powerful platforms have implementation and usability overhead that small HR teams can't absorb. There's also a lot of conversation around data — people want better workforce analytics but they don't want to pay for a separate analytics layer on top of an already adequate HRIS. And in regulated industries like mine, compliance tooling is still not where it needs to be in most of these mid-market platforms.

Q4: Point Solution Layered on Core Platform

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: Sure, I'm a Director of HR. So my scope covers the full employee lifecycle — everything from recruiting and onboarding through performance management, total rewards, and eventually offboarding. I'm the most senior HR person at the company, which in practice means I'm both the strategist and the person doing the detailed work, which is kind of the nature of the role at a company our size.
v.Q2: I've been here just over two years now. I came in when we were around ninety people and we've grown pretty substantially since then, which has made it a busy two years, to say the least.
v.Q3: We're a B2B SaaS company — so, technology industry, specifically enterprise software. We're at about one hundred and eighty employees right now. We're fully distributed, so we have people across multiple states, which creates a certain kind of complexity that you don't deal with in a single-location company. We've grown from under ninety to one hundred and eighty in about two years, which is significant from an HR infrastructure standpoint. Every new state we hire in is a new compliance obligation, and that reality shapes a lot of how I think about our tooling.
v.Q4: We're on Rippling as our primary platform, and it really does function as our central system of record across HR, payroll, IT device management, and app provisioning. We also use Greenhouse for applicant tracking — that's one piece Rippling hasn't displaced for us because we're pretty heavily invested in our Greenhouse workflows and integrations. But for everything post-offer, Rippling is the engine.
v.Q5: That evaluation happened about eighteen months ago, so I'd call it in the one-to-two-year range. It was a fairly intense evaluation — we ran it over about three months — and it was one of the bigger infrastructure decisions I've made here.
v.Q6: When I kicked off the evaluation, we were using Gusto for payroll and benefits, and we had BambooHR as our HRIS. They weren't integrated in any meaningful way, so we were running two separate systems that required a lot of manual synchronization. For recruiting, we already had Greenhouse. So the core problem was the Gusto-plus-BambooHR combination — it had served us well when we were fifty people, but at eighty to ninety employees and growing fast, the seams were starting to show in ways that were becoming operationally painful.
v.Q7: There were honestly several things converging at once, which is usually what it takes to actually get a tool evaluation off the ground in a company like ours. The most immediate pressure was multi-state payroll complexity. We had just crossed into our eighth or ninth state and Gusto, while fine for straightforward payroll, was creating friction every time we had a new state setup — tax registration, workers' comp, state-specific leave policies. My team was spending a meaningful amount of time managing those edge cases manually. The second major driver was onboarding. We were onboarding sometimes five or six people in a week and our onboarding process was this patchwork of Gusto tasks, BambooHR tasks, manual IT provisioning, and Slack channel invites that my admin coordinator was orchestrating by hand. It was fragile and inconsistent. Third — and this one was more forward-looking — I was getting increasing pressure from our VP of Engineering and our CFO to give them better workforce data. Headcount forecasting, cost-per-hire, compensation analysis by department and level. Neither Gusto nor BambooHR gave me the reporting infrastructure to do that credibly. And fourth, honestly, Gusto's benefits brokerage experience had become a pain point. We had outgrown the self-service broker model and needed something with more hands-on support for a team our size.
v.Q8: Yeah, I think there were two broader forces at play. The first was the remote-first operating model. We had fully committed to being distributed, and that has real infrastructure implications — particularly around IT provisioning and app access management. Every time we hired someone, we were manually provisioning a laptop, manually setting up their software stack, and hoping nothing fell through the cracks. We knew that model wasn't going to scale, and when I started looking at platforms that could tie HR and IT together, Rippling stood out specifically because of that capability. The second broader factor was the general investor environment at the time. We had just closed a Series B and there was real pressure to demonstrate operational efficiency as we scaled. Our CEO and CFO were thinking carefully about how we build the people infrastructure for a two-hundred-plus person company, and that conversation gave me the organizational mandate to make a meaningful platform investment. That kind of air cover from leadership is, I think, what actually allows a real evaluation to happen rather than just a wishful-thinking exercise.
v.Q9: The frustrations were pretty concrete. With BambooHR, the reporting was limited and the automation capabilities were minimal. I could store employee records, but I couldn't do much intelligent work with the data. Every time I needed a headcount report or a tenure analysis, I was exporting to a spreadsheet and building it manually, which felt like a waste of time and also introduced data integrity risk. With Gusto, the multi-state complexity I mentioned was a constant friction point, and the benefits administration experience was something employees complained about — the enrollment interface wasn't intuitive, and the carrier connectivity wasn't always reliable. We had a couple of situations where elections didn't transmit correctly to carriers, and fixing those was a time-consuming process that involved a lot of back-and-forth with Gusto support. I also want to be honest that the integration between BambooHR and Gusto was essentially nonexistent in any automated sense. We had a Zapier workaround that was fragile and broke periodically, and when it broke, no one always noticed right away, which meant data drift between the two systems. That is not a comfortable place to be when you're responsible for payroll accuracy.
v.Q10: We seriously considered Rippling, Deel — mostly for the global angle, which we thought we might need sooner than we did — Justworks, and we also took a look at TriNet as a PEO option, which ended up not being the right fit for us structurally. Rippling was the one that made it to a formal demo and pilot stage.
v.Q11: Yes, and this was something I was very deliberate about defining before we started vendor conversations, because otherwise you end up getting sold on features you don't need. My table-stakes list had four things on it. First, unified payroll and HRIS in a single platform — I was not going to repeat the two-system problem. Second, strong multi-state payroll handling, including automated tax registration support, because I knew we were going to keep adding states. Third, meaningful onboarding automation — I needed a tool that could trigger provisioning workflows, send the right documents, and create a consistent experience without my coordinator manually orchestrating everything. And fourth, a credible integration story with Greenhouse, because that was a non-negotiable anchor in our tech stack. Any tool that couldn't connect to Greenhouse cleanly was off the list immediately. Security compliance — SSO, SOC 2 certification — was also a quiet requirement that my IT team flagged as mandatory.
v.Q12: So I was the primary driver and ultimate recommender on this decision. I ran all the demos, managed the vendor relationships, and built the evaluation framework. My IT Manager was deeply involved on the device management and app provisioning side of the Rippling evaluation — that was a meaningful chunk of the value proposition and he needed to validate it technically. Our CFO was involved at two specific points: she reviewed the pricing proposals and gave final budget approval, and she also had a strong point of view on the PEO-versus-platform question, which is why we ultimately landed on a platform rather than going the TriNet route. Our CEO was looped in for the final recommendation meeting but was largely trusting me and the CFO on this one. So the structure was really: me as primary recommender, CFO with approval authority, IT as a functional stakeholder on a specific module, and CEO as informed executive sponsor.
v.Q13: We switched — we moved from the Gusto-plus-BambooHR combination to Rippling. That was about eighteen months ago and it was a significant migration, but one that I think we made the right call on.
v.Q14: Rippling won primarily because it was the only platform that genuinely unified HR, payroll, and IT in a way that felt native rather than bolted together. The device management and app provisioning capability was something no other vendor in our consideration set could match — and for a fully remote, engineering-heavy company, that was a significant operational advantage. When a new engineer starts, their laptop ships automatically, their GitHub and Jira and Slack and Google Workspace access gets provisioned through Rippling workflows, and my IT manager doesn't have to do anything manually. That kind of end-to-end automation is genuinely valuable at our velocity. The onboarding workflow builder was also meaningfully better than anything else we saw. The Greenhouse integration worked as advertised. And honestly, the Rippling team ran a very good sales process — they were responsive, they brought in a solutions engineer who understood our specific multi-state complexity, and the demo was configured to our actual use cases rather than generic feature walkthroughs. That kind of attentiveness matters when you're evaluating a platform you're going to live with for years.
v.Q15: Justworks was genuinely a good product for what it is, but it's fundamentally a PEO, and we didn't want to co-employ our workforce — we wanted to own our HR infrastructure. So that was a structural mismatch, not a feature complaint. Deel we looked at because we thought global hiring was imminent, but at the time of the evaluation we didn't have any international employees and Deel's domestic payroll and HRIS capabilities were, at that point, thinner than Rippling's. It felt like a company that was very strong on the global contractor and international payroll side but hadn't fully built out the core domestic HRIS features we needed. TriNet, similarly, was the PEO concern — the co-employment model and the loss of direct carrier relationships on benefits wasn't something our CFO was willing to accept. And the pricing structure at our headcount was hard to justify. So Rippling was really the only one that hit all our criteria at the same time, which made the final decision less agonizing than I expected.
v.Q16: Rippling does the core operational things really well. Payroll is reliable, multi-state is handled smoothly, and I don't think about it much, which is the goal. Onboarding automation is genuinely excellent — we've built flows that handle provisioning, document collection, benefits enrollment kickoff, and manager notifications, and the whole thing runs without my team needing to babysit it. The IT management module has been a major win with our engineering organization. And the reporting, while not perfect, is meaningfully better than what we had before — I can pull headcount snapshots, comp summaries, and tenure reports without a spreadsheet gymnastics session.
v.Q17: A few areas. The performance management module is pretty underpowered — we tried to use it for our review cycle and ended up going back to a combination of Lattice forms and manual processes because Rippling's performance tooling just doesn't have the depth we need for calibration and review workflows. Benefits administration is functional but the employee experience during enrollment is still not as polished as I'd like — there are places where the UI is confusing for employees and we get a lot of the same questions during open enrollment that I'd hoped we'd eliminate. And customer support response times have gotten slower as the company has grown, which is something I've heard from other Rippling users too — the quality of support you get seems to correlate with your contract size.
v.Q18: I'd say the support experience is my biggest current frustration, and I'd rate it as significant. When something goes wrong — and things do go wrong occasionally, like a payroll discrepancy or a benefits carrier sync issue — the time it takes to get a knowledgeable person on the phone or chat has degraded noticeably compared to the early days of our contract. I end up escalating through multiple channels to get resolution on things that should be simple. For a company that's running payroll for one hundred and eighty people, support responsiveness isn't a nice-to-have. It's a trust issue. And I think that frustration is amplified because one of the reasons I chose Rippling over alternatives was the quality of the sales-side engagement, and I feel like the post-sale support experience doesn't always match that initial impression.
v.Q19: Two things have shifted meaningfully. First, performance management has become a bigger priority than I anticipated. When we were growing fast, just getting people onboarded and paid correctly was the headline. Now that we're a bit more mature, our leadership is asking harder questions about how we develop people, run calibration cycles, and tie compensation decisions to performance data in a defensible way. Rippling can't really serve that need, so I'm carrying a second tool relationship with Lattice that I didn't plan for. Second, AI capabilities are now part of the conversation in a way they genuinely weren't eighteen months ago. I'm getting asked by our CHRO — well, we don't have a CHRO, but our CEO who functions in that capacity — whether our HR tools are using AI in meaningful ways. And I don't have a great answer for that right now, which signals to me that the next evaluation cycle will probably have an AI dimension that this last one didn't.
v.Q20: Between Rippling and Lattice and Greenhouse, I'd estimate we're spending somewhere in the range of eighty to one hundred thousand dollars annually on people ops and recruiting infrastructure. Rippling is the largest line item, probably in the fifty-to-sixty-thousand range. It's meaningful spend for a company our size, and I feel that accountability.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. The operational value of having unified payroll, HR, and IT provisioning is real and I can articulate it. But the support quality decline and the performance management gap make me feel like we're leaving value on the table. So it's not a strongly enthusiastic yes — it's more like a cautious yes with an asterisk.
v.Q22: If Rippling had a genuinely responsive, dedicated support model — like a named customer success manager who knows our account and can actually resolve issues rather than triaging them — I think that's worth somewhere in the ten-to-twenty-five-thousand-dollar range annually in avoided cost, given the time my team spends managing around support gaps. And honestly, the risk mitigation value of knowing payroll and compliance issues will be resolved quickly is hard to put a number on but it's real.
v.Q23: Not within six months — I'd say very unlikely to switch that quickly. The switching cost and implementation effort for a platform like Rippling is meaningful, and we're too operationally dependent on it right now to absorb a migration without significant risk. But I'd say I'm in a watching mode. If the support situation doesn't improve, or if a competitor demonstrates meaningfully better performance management capability integrated with core HR and payroll, I could see myself initiating an evaluation in the twelve-to-eighteen-month timeframe.
v.Q24: I think there are a few themes that resonate pretty universally among HR leaders at companies our size. One is the platform consolidation tension — every vendor is trying to be a platform, but most of them are still better at some things than others, so you end up either accepting gaps or running multiple tools in parallel. Neither is ideal. A second theme is the expectation inflation around analytics — leadership at most companies now expects HR to show up to the table with data-driven insights, but the tools don't always make that easy for a two-person HR team without a dedicated analyst. And third, I think the compliance burden for distributed or multi-state companies has genuinely increased, and a lot of tools that were built for simpler operating models are still catching up. The patchwork of state-level leave laws, pay transparency requirements, and benefits mandates is a real operational weight that I think the software industry has been slow to fully absorb.

Beyond that, we had a genuine scaling problem — we were going to be hiring aggressively for the plant and for the engineering organization, and the existing infrastructure couldn't support that volume without significant manual overhead. Benefits administration was a particular pain point because we were managing elections through the broker almost entirely by hand, and the error rate was unacceptable. And ADP Workforce Now, while functional, felt like a lot of cost for what we were actually using. I also had a strong personal view that our people data needed to live in a modern system so that I could build workforce analytics capabilities over time, and Paylocity as configured was not going to support that vision.
v.Q8: We were coming off a significant contract win in the defense sector that was driving the headcount growth, so there was real urgency from our CEO and board to scale the workforce without operational breakdowns. There was also increasing attention to ITAR compliance and workforce documentation requirements that come with defense contracts — having clean, auditable HR records was not optional. That compliance pressure was a real accelerant for the technology investment.
v.Q9: The manual benefits administration was probably the sharpest pain. We had situations where employee elections weren't making it to carriers on time, which meant coverage gaps, which meant employee relations issues that were entirely avoidable. ADP Workforce Now was also generating a lot of reporting complaints from our finance team — they couldn't get clean headcount and labor cost data without our HR team manually running and exporting reports. v.Q10: We considered Rippling, Paycom, and Paycor. We also had a brief conversation with UKG given that we were already using their time and attendance product, to understand whether the full UKG suite made sense for us.
v.Q11: I had a clear list going in. The platform had to handle payroll and HRIS natively in one system — no integrations required to connect the two. It needed to support both hourly and salaried pay structures, because our plant floor and our professional workforce are meaningfully different. Benefits administration had to be electronic and carrier-connected — no more manual election processing. And I needed a system that could produce clean, timely labor and headcount reports for finance without my team running manual exports. Those were the baseline requirements. Implementation support was also non-negotiable — I didn't have the bandwidth to self-implement something at our scale.
v.Q12: As CPO, I had the authority to make this decision within a defined budget, but I chose to involve a few key stakeholders. Our CFO was aligned on the budget and was a vocal advocate for improving the financial reporting we got out of payroll. Our VP of Operations was consulted because any system change affecting plant floor employees has operational risk, and I needed his buy-in on the change management plan. Our IT Director did the security review. So I was the decision-maker, but I ran a collaborative process to make sure I had the right stakeholders bought in before we contracted.
v.Q13: We switched to Rippling. That was roughly two years ago and we've been building on the platform since then.
v.Q14: Rippling stood out on a few dimensions that mattered specifically to us. The platform architecture — the idea that HR, IT, payroll, and eventually other business systems could all talk to each other natively — felt like the right infrastructure bet for a company that was going to keep growing and getting more complex. The benefits administration functionality was genuinely better than what we'd seen elsewhere, and their carrier connectivity story was credible. I also thought the user interface was the most modern in our consideration set, which mattered for employee self-service adoption across a workforce that isn't all desk workers. And Rippling's implementation team was organized and responsive, which after the chaos of what we were replacing, felt like a significant green flag.
v.Q15: Paycom had good functionality but the employee self-service experience felt designed for an older generation of software interaction — it wasn't intuitive enough for what I was trying to accomplish culturally. Paycor was a reasonable option and the price was competitive, but their implementation story was weaker and their integration capabilities felt more limited. We were already dependent on other systems — our UKG time and attendance, for instance — and I needed clean integrations. UKG's full-suite pitch was appealing in theory, but their HR and payroll platform felt heavyweight for our size and the licensing costs at our headcount were harder to justify when we didn't need everything they were selling.
v.Q16: Rippling runs payroll reliably, which sounds like a low bar but after what we came from, it genuinely isn't. Benefits administration is markedly better — enrollment errors are rare now and employees can self-serve their elections without calling HR. The reporting for finance has improved substantially. And the onboarding workflows we've built in Rippling have meaningfully improved the new hire experience for our professional workforce. My team spends far less time on administrative orchestration than they used to.
v.Q17: The time and attendance functionality for hourly workers is not where it needs to be, which is why we're still running UKG separately for the plant floor. That dual-system situation creates some of the same integration friction we were trying to escape from. I also think Rippling's compensation management features are limited — we're doing a lot of our comp analysis in spreadsheets still, which is not ideal when you're trying to build a sophisticated total rewards program. And the performance management module, which we've tested, is too lightweight for what I'd want to deploy company-wide.
v.Q18: The inability to fully unify the hourly workforce management with the professional workforce management is my biggest operational frustration, and I'd call it significant. I have two sources of truth for workforce data, and reconciling them for reporting purposes costs my team time every single payroll cycle. It was a known compromise when we chose Rippling, but it hasn't gotten better, and as we continue to grow the plant floor workforce, that gap is widening rather than narrowing.
v.Q19: I think our compensation strategy sophistication has increased significantly. Two years ago we needed basic comp structures to be codified and managed. Now I'm building salary bands, running market data analyses, and trying to connect comp decisions to performance outcomes in a defensible, auditable way. Rippling supports parts of that, but not all of it. And the plant floor population has grown as a proportion of our total headcount, which makes the time and attendance integration gap more painful than it was when we first implemented.
v.Q20: Between Rippling and UKG for time and attendance, I'd estimate we're in the range of ninety to one hundred and twenty thousand dollars annually. Rippling is the larger piece. It's a meaningful line item and I track it closely.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. The baseline operational value is real and defensible. But the fact that I'm paying for two systems to manage one workforce is a persistent irritant. If I could truly consolidate, I think I'd be getting better value at a similar or lower total cost.
v.Q22: If Rippling could replace UKG for our plant floor and give me a single system for the entire workforce, the direct licensing savings alone would be in the twenty-to-thirty-thousand-dollar range annually, and the time savings from eliminating manual reconciliation would be worth at least that much again in staff hours. So I'd put the value of solving that problem somewhere north of twenty-five thousand dollars annually, probably higher when you factor in the risk reduction and the leadership time we spend managing around the gap.
v.Q23: Not within six months — I'd say somewhat unlikely in that timeframe. The switching cost and change management burden for a three-hundred-plus-person manufacturing workforce is significant. But I'd say I'm more open to evaluating alternatives in the twelve-to-twenty-four-month range than I was a year ago, particularly if a vendor can make a credible case for unified hourly and salaried workforce management.
v.Q24: I think the core tension that most HR leaders in manufacturing or similarly complex operating environments face is that the modern HR platforms are built around the knowledge-worker experience and haven't fully solved for mixed workforce models. The hourly and salaried gap is real and expensive. Beyond that, I think there's a universal frustration with the fragmentation of the HR tech stack — everyone has a platform claim but almost everyone is still running two or three tools to cover their actual needs. And for companies in regulated industries, the compliance documentation and audit trail expectations are increasing faster than most platforms are keeping pace with.

v.Q1: Sure. I'm an HR manager at a mid-size tech company based in Austin. I sit within the broader HR function and I kind of own a mix of generalist responsibilities — onboarding, policy, and some employee relations work.
v.Q2: I've been here just under three years, so I'd say in that one-to-three-year band honestly.
v.Q3: We're in technology — specifically B2B SaaS. And we're sitting at around three hundred and twenty employees right now, so solidly in that two-fifty to five hundred range.
v.Q4: We use BambooHR as our core HRIS. Payroll actually runs through a separate provider — we use Paylocity for that — and then benefits administration is handled through BambooHR's benefits module, though honestly it's a bit limited and we supplement it with our broker's portal.
v.Q5: That was roughly a year and a half ago, so I'd put it in the one-to-two-years-ago window.
v.Q6: We were already on BambooHR at that point, but we were looking at whether to replace it or expand around it. So the prior tool was BambooHR itself — we were questioning whether it still made sense for where we were heading.

The biggest driver was that our reporting capabilities felt really limited — we had grown to a point where people leaders were asking for workforce analytics and BambooHR just couldn't give us what we needed without a lot of manual exports. I think the second thing was that our payroll and HRIS were completely disconnected, so every pay cycle involved a lot of manual reconciliation that was time-consuming and honestly error-prone. And then our contract with our benefits broker was also coming up for renewal, so there was a natural window to think about whether we wanted a more integrated solution overall.
v.Q8: We had just wrapped up a pretty significant hiring push the year before, so our headcount had jumped meaningfully and the HR team had also grown. I think leadership was starting to expect more from HR in terms of data and strategic input, and our tools weren't keeping up with that expectation. There was also a broader digital transformation initiative happening across the company — the engineering and ops teams were modernizing their tooling and HR felt a little left behind.
v.Q9: The reporting thing I mentioned was a big one. But honestly, the onboarding workflow in BambooHR also felt pretty clunky — we had a lot of manual steps that didn't feel scalable. And the mobile experience was not great for employees, which I heard about frequently. Our integrations with Slack and with our ATS were also not as clean as we wanted — data was going in through workarounds rather than native connections.
v.Q10: We looked at Rippling, Lattice — though Lattice was more on the performance side — and we did a demo with Workday just to understand where we'd be in a couple of years. We also re-evaluated BambooHR's newer modules to see if upgrading our plan would get us where we needed.

v.Q15: Rippling was genuinely impressive but felt like it had more complexity than we needed at our size, and the pricing was meaningfully higher all-in. Lattice wasn't really a full HRIS play so it was more of a partial solution. So for all the alternatives, it came down to cost or scope mismatch.

v.Q19: We've started having more conversations about compensation benchmarking and pay equity, and I don't have a clean way to run that analysis in BambooHR. I also think our people leaders are asking for more manager-facing dashboards than they were eighteen months ago. Getting true integration without enterprise-level pricing is the core tension I hear from peers.

v.Q1: Sure. I'm a Director of HR at a manufacturing company headquartered in the greater Cincinnati area. I oversee all HR operations — which honestly covers a pretty wide scope given the size of our team — including payroll, compliance, benefits, and some talent acquisition.
v.Q2: Coming up on five years now. I joined when we were a much smaller organization and I've grown with the company through a pretty significant expansion period.
v.Q3: We're in manufacturing — specifically precision metal components, primarily for automotive and aerospace customers. We have just under seven hundred employees right now across three facilities in Ohio and one in Indiana.
v.Q4: Our main platform is Rippling. We use it for HR, payroll, and benefits administration. We also have a separate time-and-attendance system — Kronos, which is now UKG — because our shop floor workers need something purpose-built for shift and overtime tracking. So Rippling is the core but it's not our only tool.
v.Q5: That was about fourteen months ago, so within the last twelve to eighteen months. We completed the implementation of Rippling roughly a year ago, so the evaluation happened before that.
v.Q6: We were running on ADP Workforce Now. That had been in place for several years before I even arrived. It was deeply embedded but also deeply frustrating, which is kind of how those legacy systems tend to go.
v.Q7: There were several things pushing us toward evaluation at once. First, we had added two new facilities in about eighteen months, which roughly doubled our headcount, and ADP's configuration for multi-location compliance was a nightmare — we had different state tax setups, different shift differentials, and it all required constant manual intervention from my team. My team at the time was just two people including me, so we were drowning. Second, the cost of ADP at our scale had crept up significantly with each contract renewal and we genuinely felt like we weren't getting more value — just more invoices. Third, our CFO had flagged payroll processing errors in back-to-back quarters and put pressure on me to fix it. That was really the forcing function that elevated the conversation from "maybe someday" to "we need to act now." And finally, we had acquired a smaller shop in Indiana and the idea of onboarding them onto ADP was just not appealing given all the existing problems.
v.Q8: Manufacturing as an industry has gotten a lot more focused on workforce compliance in recent years — I think OSHA requirements and state-level wage-and-hour laws have gotten more complex, and our legal team was flagging that our record-keeping in ADP wasn't audit-ready in a way that felt safe. So compliance risk was genuinely elevated. And honestly, from a talent competition standpoint, we were trying to position ourselves as a more modern employer to attract skilled tradespeople, and having a clunky HR portal that employees hated wasn't helping. We also had some investor visibility — we're private equity backed — and they were asking questions about operational efficiency that put HR processes under a microscope we weren't used to.
v.Q9: Where do I start. The ADP self-service portal for employees was so confusing that we'd get multiple calls per week from hourly workers who couldn't access their paystubs or update their direct deposit. That was a real-time drain on my team. Reporting was another one — getting a custom headcount report out of ADP felt like it required a PhD in their specific data model, and half the time the exports were formatted in ways that didn't load cleanly into Excel. Benefits open enrollment was also particularly painful — we basically ran it ourselves through manual spreadsheets because the ADP enrollment module had configuration limits we kept hitting. And new hire onboarding had about eleven manual steps that all lived in different systems, so something almost always fell through the cracks.
v.Q10: We looked at Rippling, Paycom, Paylocity, and UKG Pro — we already had a relationship with UKG on the time-and-attendance side so that made them an interesting option. We also had one conversation with Ceridian Dayforce but it felt out of scope for our size pretty quickly.
v.Q11: Multi-state payroll had to be fully supported — that was the hardest gate. We needed native support for Ohio and Indiana tax compliance without custom configuration workarounds. Second, it had to integrate with UKG Dimensions, our time-and-attendance system, because we were not replacing that. IT also required SOC 2 compliance documentation before any tool got past the security review. And honestly, the employee self-service interface had to actually be usable by hourly workers who aren't sitting at a desk all day — that was more of a qualitative gate but it mattered a lot.
v.Q12: I led the evaluation and I was the primary recommender. Our CFO had budget approval authority and was closely involved in the pricing discussions — probably more than most CFOs I've worked with. Our VP of Operations weighed in on the time-and-attendance integration requirements because that touched his team's workflows. And IT had a formal security review checkpoint. So it was HR plus Finance plus IT plus Ops, with me doing the day-to-day evaluation work and the CFO making the final call on spend.
v.Q13: We switched. We moved to Rippling and completed the full migration about twelve months ago.
v.Q14: Rippling won on a few things. The implementation experience was the most structured of any vendor we saw — they had a dedicated implementation manager and a clear project plan that actually had milestone dates in it, which matters a lot when you're running a small HR team and can't dedicate months to a bad rollout. The UKG integration worked out of the box, which was validated during the proof-of-concept stage. And I think the self-service interface was genuinely the cleanest — we had a few hourly supervisors look at it during the demo and they could navigate it without training, which was not true of Paycom or Paylocity in the same demos. The pricing landed in a competitive place after negotiation. I think the combination of those factors made it feel like the lowest-risk path to actually solving our problems.
v.Q15: Paycom had a very slick sales process but when we got into the technical details of the UKG integration, it was not native — it would have required a middleware layer that our IT team didn't want to manage. That was disqualifying. Paylocity was honestly close and I think a different CFO might have gone that direction, but their implementation timeline was longer and their dedicated implementation support felt lighter than Rippling's. UKG Pro was interesting given the existing relationship, but the product for HR and payroll felt like it had been bolted onto their time-and-attendance core rather than built cleanly, and the pricing was the highest of the group. Ceridian we ruled out early — it was clearly oriented toward larger enterprises and the contract terms were not flexible enough for our situation.
v.Q16: Rippling does payroll really well for our multi-state setup — the tax filings run without the manual intervention we used to do constantly in ADP. The employee self-service adoption has been surprisingly high even among our hourly workforce, which I attribute to the mobile app being genuinely functional. And the automation for onboarding has probably saved my team four or five hours per new hire compared to what we were doing before. The benefits administration module also handles open enrollment much more cleanly than anything we had access to previously.
v.Q17: The reporting and analytics layer is good but not great at our level of complexity. I can get standard reports easily, but when I need to do things like track headcount variance across facilities by job classification over a rolling twelve months, I'm still exporting to Excel. I'd also say the HR support response time has slowed down noticeably compared to what we experienced during implementation — I get the feeling the team that helped us onboard was much more attentive than the ongoing support tier.
v.Q18: Honestly, it's the support degradation. During implementation we had a great experience — responsive, knowledgeable, proactive. Post go-live, support tickets have taken two to three business days for anything that isn't a P1 payroll issue. For a team of three managing seven hundred employees, that lag is significant. I'd call the frustration level moderate to significant — it hasn't caused a major incident yet but it's created a few close calls around benefits enrollment deadlines that made me very uncomfortable.
v.Q19: We're likely adding a fifth facility in the next eighteen months, which means another state and probably another hundred employees. So scalability is more top-of-mind than it was when we made the original decision. I'm also getting more pressure from our PE owners for workforce cost analytics — things like cost-per-head by department and overtime trend analysis — and I need a better reporting layer to answer those questions without a lot of manual work. And I'll be honest, I'm starting to think more about succession planning and performance management features, which we don't really have a clean solution for yet.
v.Q20: I think we're in the one-hundred-to-two-hundred-fifty-thousand range when you combine Rippling and our UKG contract, though those are two separate line items. Rippling alone is probably in the hundred-to-one-fifty range annually.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. The time savings on payroll alone justify a significant portion of it. But the support quality declining post-implementation makes me feel like we're not getting full value, and that's something I'm actively tracking.
v.Q22: If they fixed the support tier — meaning genuine priority routing and faster resolution times — I'd estimate that's worth somewhere in the ten-to-twenty-five-thousand-dollar range annually in avoided risk and avoided staff time spent on workarounds. Maybe more if you factor in the compliance risk associated with slow response on a benefits or payroll issue.
v.Q23: Not within six months — the switching cost at this point is too high and we're still under contract. I'd say somewhat unlikely in the near term. But I'll be honest: if the support quality doesn't improve, and if the reporting gaps become more painful as we add the fifth facility, I could see re-evaluating at the next contract renewal. So let's say unlikely now but I'm paying close attention.
v.Q24: In manufacturing specifically, I think the core tension is that most HR software is designed for white-collar, desk-based workforces and it struggles with the realities of hourly, shift-based, multi-location environments. Compliance complexity — OSHA, state wage-and-hour law, multistate tax — is genuinely hard and most platforms handle it at a surface level. And then the broader challenge I hear from peers across industries is that HR teams are being asked to do more analytics and strategic work without getting any more headcount to do it, and the tools still require too much manual effort to produce insights that should be automatic by now.

And the reporting layer was just not there — I couldn't produce a headcount-by-department-by-level view without pulling raw data and building it myself in Sheets. For a people function that was supposed to be strategic, that was untenable.
v.Q8: We had just closed a Series B, which meant there was board-level visibility into our hiring plan and headcount forecast. Investors at that stage expect your people function to have real operational rigor — they're looking at whether your HR infrastructure can support the growth trajectory they're funding. So there was external accountability that elevated the urgency. We were also in the early stages of establishing a compensation philosophy and salary banding framework, and I needed a system that could actually hold and surface that data in a way that managers could use. The informal spreadsheet environment we had inherited was not going to work for where we were headed.
v.Q9: The international capability gap was the most acute frustration because it had an active business impact — we had a candidate in London we were trying to close and no clean path to employing them. Beyond that, the absence of workflow automation was painful. Every change — a promotion, a location update, a benefits change — required a manual update in three different places, and there was no audit trail. For a company that was going to keep growing, that was a compliance exposure we couldn't afford to ignore. The employee self-service experience in Gusto also felt dated compared to what our engineers expected from their internal tools — there was a constant cultural dissonance between the modern developer tooling we used everywhere else and the HR portal, which felt like it was built for a different era.
v.Q10: We evaluated Rippling, Deel — primarily for the international employment angle — HiBob, and we did a lighter-touch review of Lattice as a potential full-suite play. We also looked at whether upgrading our Gusto plan would get us close enough to avoid a full migration.
v.Q11: International employment support — either native or through a tight EOR partnership — was non-negotiable. SSO and SCIM provisioning were required by our Head of Engineering who also ran IT. I needed a real API so that we could build connections with our finance system and our ATS. And honestly, the product had to feel modern — I know that's qualitative, but at a developer tools company, I was going to face internal scrutiny if I implemented something that felt ten years behind. Those were the filters that really shaped the shortlist.
v.Q12: I was the primary evaluator and the main recommender. Our CEO had final approval on spend at this level — we're still a stage where I don't have unilateral budget authority above a certain threshold. Our CFO was involved in reviewing the pricing and assessing the total cost of ownership, including implementation. And our Head of Engineering reviewed the technical security posture. I'd describe my role as driving the decision end-to-end and presenting a recommendation with a clear rationale, rather than being one vote among many.
v.Q13: We switched fully to Rippling and decommissioned Gusto. The migration took about eight weeks from contract signing to payroll running cleanly on the new platform.
v.Q14: Rippling stood out on a few dimensions that mattered specifically to our context. The platform architecture — the way it handles device management and app provisioning alongside HRIS and payroll — resonated with our engineering leadership in a way no other vendor could match. It felt like it was built by people who understood how tech companies actually operate. The international story, while not perfect, was further developed than HiBob's at the time and the EOR pathway through their network was credible. The API depth was also real — our engineering team actually pulled the documentation during the evaluation and confirmed we could build the integrations we needed. And I think the implementation scoping was more precise than what we got from Deel, which felt like they were still figuring out their mid-market motion. The overall combination of technical credibility and product breadth made Rippling the obvious choice for our specific profile.
v.Q15: Deel was a serious contender for the international capability but their HR and payroll product for domestic employees felt secondary — it was clearly an EOR company adding HRIS rather than the reverse, and for a team where domestic payroll was the majority of the load, that mattered. HiBob had a genuinely beautiful interface and strong engagement features, but the payroll component was not native in the US market at the time — it required a separate payroll integration that added complexity I didn't want. Lattice was interesting but they were really a performance and engagement layer, not a full HRIS, so it was comparing apples to oranges. And Gusto — I looked at whether the premium plan would close the gaps, but the API limitations and international immaturity were structural, not tier-based, so upgrading wasn't going to solve the core issues.
v.Q16: Rippling does the unified platform story really well in practice — the fact that onboarding triggers payroll setup, device provisioning, app access, and benefits enrollment through one workflow is genuinely transformative compared to what we had before. Payroll runs without drama, which is the baseline expectation but not something I take for granted after the fragmented setup I inherited. The Ashby integration for ATS-to-HRIS handoff is clean. And the employee experience — the mobile app, the self-service portal — consistently gets positive feedback in our engagement surveys, which matters to me.
v.Q17: The performance management module within Rippling is pretty thin — it's why we run Lattice separately, which I'd ideally like to consolidate. Compensation management features, specifically salary banding and total rewards modeling, aren't robust enough for the framework I'm trying to build out. And international support — which was a key buying criterion — has been fine for Canada but getting more complex employees in the UK on a clean direct employment model has required more manual work than I expected.
v.Q18: The compensation management gap is my biggest current frustration. I'm trying to build a structured total rewards framework — salary bands, equity refresh logic, bonus modeling — and Rippling's native compensation tools don't support that level of sophistication. I'm doing that work in a combination of Sheets and a point solution called Pave, which is fine but it means my compensation data lives outside my system of record. I'd call it a moderate-to-significant frustration — it's not blocking operations, but it's limiting the strategic work I was hired to do.
v.Q19: Compensation infrastructure has become a much higher priority than it was when I first evaluated — there's been a lot of external pressure on pay transparency and equity, and our employees are paying attention. I also didn't fully anticipate the analytics needs that would come from our board wanting workforce cost reporting on a quarterly basis. And I think my appetite for AI-assisted features has grown — things like intelligent compensation benchmarking, or draft policy generation, that didn't feel essential two years ago now feel like real differentiators.
v.Q20: Across Rippling, Lattice, Ashby, and Pave, I think we're in the fifty-to-one-hundred-thousand range annually. Rippling is the largest component, probably around forty to fifty thousand of that.
v.Q21: Strongly yes for Rippling specifically. The operational leverage it gives a six-person people team managing nearly two hundred employees is genuinely hard to put a price on. I feel somewhat more neutral on the full stack cost when I add in all the point solutions we're running alongside it.
v.Q22: If Rippling had robust native compensation management — real salary banding, equity modeling, total rewards statements — I could probably eliminate Pave and reduce the manual Sheets work my team does. I'd estimate that's worth somewhere in the ten-to-twenty-five-thousand range annually between the tool cost savings and the time savings, though the strategic value of having it all in one system is honestly harder to quantify.
v.Q23: I don't think we'll switch from Rippling in the next six months — very unlikely. But I do think we'll evaluate replacing some of the point solutions around it. If a competitor launched a credible compensation management module that integrated cleanly, I'd pay attention to it. The core platform is sticky though.
v.Q24: I think the platform consolidation versus best-of-breed tension is the central challenge for people in my role right now. Everyone wants fewer tools and cleaner data, but the all-in-one platforms haven't fully closed the gap on specialized functionality. So you're constantly choosing between integration simplicity and capability depth. The other big theme is that AI promises are outrunning AI delivery — every vendor is claiming AI features that are either superficial or still in beta, and it's genuinely hard to separate signal from noise in demos. And finally, I think the expectation that people teams produce board-level analytics is here and not going away, and most tools still require too much manual effort to meet that bar.

We were adding a couple of new plan options — a dental and a vision upgrade — and Gusto's benefits tools felt clunky for managing the enrollment. On top of that, we had some manual process pain around onboarding documentation. Everything was being done in a mix of Gusto, email, and DocuSign, and there was no clean flow to it. Those two things together made us want to at least look around and see if there was something that handled both better.
