v.Q1: I'm a Director of People Operations. I oversee everything on the people side — HR policy, compliance, benefits, and I've been the lead on managing the workforce restructuring we've been going through over the past several months.
v.Q2: Six years. Long enough that I've seen two CEOs, three rounds of hiring, and now a significant reduction in force.
v.Q3: We're in professional services — legal and compliance consulting, specifically. We peaked at around eight hundred employees but we're now closer to five hundred and eighty after the restructuring. And honestly that number might still move a bit before things stabilize.
v.Q4: Gusto is our primary platform. It handles payroll and benefits administration. We do have a separate HRIS — we use HiBob for core employee records and people analytics — so it's not fully unified. Those two systems are integrated but I wouldn't call it seamless. We also use Greenhouse for recruiting, though recruiting activity has slowed significantly given where we are in the business cycle.
v.Q5: The most recent evaluation was about fourteen months ago. We were exploring whether to consolidate our stack — specifically whether something could replace both Gusto and HiBob in one platform. We didn't end up switching, but it was a real evaluation, not just a casual look.
v.Q6: Same setup as today — Gusto for payroll and benefits, HiBob for HRIS. So we went into the evaluation already on that split-stack model and were questioning whether it was the right long-term architecture for us.
v.Q7: The primary driver was the integration friction between Gusto and HiBob. Every time there was an employee change — a promotion, a compensation adjustment, a termination — we had to make updates in both systems and verify that they were in sync. That sounds manageable until you're doing it at scale across six hundred-plus employees and a small HR team, and then it becomes a real operational drag. We were also approaching the renewal window for one of the contracts, which made it a natural evaluation point. And honestly, I was curious whether there was a platform that could do what both tools do, but in one place, without the integration overhead. There was also a push from our CFO to get better visibility into total compensation and benefits spend, which our current setup wasn't surfacing cleanly. So the triggers were really: integration pain, contract renewal timing, a consolidation goal, and a finance-driven need for better cost reporting.
v.Q8: At the time we started the evaluation, we hadn't yet anticipated the scale of the restructuring that was coming. But there was a general sense that the business was heading into a more uncertain period — client demand was softening, and leadership was starting to talk about cost discipline more explicitly. So there was an organizational pressure to demonstrate that the people function was running efficiently and that we weren't overspending on tools. That context made the consolidation argument even more appealing — fewer vendors, simpler contracts, potentially lower cost. And in professional services broadly, there was increasing regulatory complexity around employment — remote work across state lines, pay transparency laws starting to roll out — and we wanted to make sure whatever platform we were on could keep up with that compliance landscape.
v.Q9: The data reconciliation between Gusto and HiBob was probably the loudest frustration. When the two systems disagreed about something — and they did, more often than I'd like to admit — figuring out which was the source of truth was tedious and sometimes genuinely stressful, especially around payroll close. The benefits administration in Gusto is functional but the employee experience during open enrollment is pretty basic — employees found it confusing and we got a lot of questions that a better self-service experience should have answered. And reporting was a challenge — I had to pull from two different systems and reconcile them in a spreadsheet to answer even basic workforce questions. None of these were catastrophic failures, but together they created a lot of low-grade friction that consumed my team's time constantly.
v.Q10: We looked seriously at Rippling, Paylocity, and Bamboo — I mean BambooHR. We also had an exploratory conversation with UKG but that pretty quickly felt like it was sized for a much larger company than us.
v.Q11: It had to have native payroll and HRIS in the same platform — that was the whole reason we were looking, so anything that was HRIS-only or payroll-only didn't make the cut. Strong benefits administration was required, and specifically I wanted to see a better open enrollment experience than what we had. It needed to integrate with Greenhouse because we weren't looking to replace our ATS. And we had a fairly firm budget ceiling — we were not going to spend more per employee per month than our current combined spend on Gusto and HiBob, or at least not significantly more without a very clear ROI case.
v.Q12: I was the primary driver — I owned the evaluation process, ran all the demos, and built the recommendation. Our CFO was involved on the cost side; she was actually the one who had originally asked whether we could consolidate to save money, so she had a stake in the outcome. Our CEO was kept informed but wasn't hands-on in the evaluation. IT was looped in to review the security documentation for any platforms we were seriously considering. And I got feedback from a couple of department heads who were heavy users of the HR system. So the structure was really me as primary recommender, CFO as financial gatekeeper, and CEO as final sign-off.
v.Q13: We stayed with our current setup — Gusto and HiBob. We didn't switch. The evaluation led to a decision to renew rather than migrate.
v.Q14: The renewal decision came down to timing and risk, more than enthusiasm. By the time we got deep into the evaluation, we were starting to get signals that the business was going to go through some significant changes — and committing to a major platform migration right before a potential restructuring felt like the wrong call. The cost of switching — not just licensing but implementation time, data migration, retraining a team that was already going to be stressed by org changes — didn't justify the operational benefit we'd get from a consolidated platform. Gusto and HiBob, for all their friction, are tools my team knows well. So we negotiated a better rate on our renewals and decided to live with the integration overhead for another contract cycle. It wasn't the most exciting decision but I think it was the right one given the circumstances.
v.Q15: Rippling was actually quite compelling — the platform breadth was impressive and the automation story was strong. cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

Total headcount is around 190 people right now, so we're in that 101 to 250 bucket. Those two don't have a particularly deep native integration, which creates some friction for us, but that's the setup we're working with. v.Q7: The primary driver was a capability gap with JazzHR specifically. As our hiring volume increased for clinical roles — physical therapists in particular are in really high demand and you're competing hard for them — we needed more sophisticated sourcing and pipeline management tools than JazzHR was giving us. The candidate-facing application experience was also a genuine problem. We'd see drop-off in the application funnel and we heard directly from candidates that the process felt clunky. In healthcare recruiting you cannot afford to lose a qualified PT candidate because your application portal is frustrating. So capability gap was the main thing. Beyond that, the manual handoff between JazzHR and Gusto was creating administrative overhead. When someone was hired, data had to be re-entered manually into Gusto, which was error-prone and time-consuming for our onboarding team. We were hoping to find something that either integrated better or consolidated those functions. And there was a cost element too — JazzHR's pricing tier we were on wasn't cheap for what we were getting, and when the contract renewal came up it felt like a natural time to reassess.
v.Q8: Honestly, the healthcare labor market context was a huge factor. Physical therapy has been dealing with a significant shortage of practitioners — the demand for outpatient PT has gone up considerably post-pandemic while the pipeline of graduating therapists hasn't kept pace. That means recruiting has become a real competitive differentiator for organizations like ours. Leadership was paying close attention to our time-to-fill metrics and our offer acceptance rates, and there was clear pressure from the CEO and our operations leadership to make sure our recruiting infrastructure was not a limiting factor. So while the immediate trigger was the JazzHR contract renewal, the broader context was that talent acquisition had become a strategic priority for the organization in a way it maybe hadn't been historically. I also think our HR director at the time had been building a case internally for investing in better people technology, and this evaluation was partly the fruit of that advocacy.
v.Q9: The biggest frustrations were on the ATS side. The mobile experience for candidates was poor, which matters a lot when you're recruiting clinical staff who aren't sitting at desks all day — they're applying on their phones, often between patients. And the collaboration features for hiring managers were weak. When a clinic director wants to give feedback on a candidate, the system wasn't making that easy, which meant I was chasing feedback via email and text. Those were the core frustrations. On the Gusto side, honestly, my frustrations were lower — it mostly worked for what it was supposed to do, though the lack of integration with our ATS was a constant nuisance.
v.Q10: We seriously evaluated Workable, Greenhouse, Lever, and Rippling. We also had an initial look at Jobvite but didn't get deep into it. And we briefly looked at whether Gusto's own recruiting module could serve our needs, but it wasn't robust enough for what we needed.

Third, structured interview kits and hiring manager collaboration tools — our clinic directors are not power users of HR technology, so whatever we chose needed to make it easy for them to participate in the process without a steep learning curve. They didn't have formal vote weight but their feedback shaped our final recommendation meaningfully. IT was not heavily involved — our infrastructure is relatively simple and the security questions were handled at the contract review stage.

The candidate experience was genuinely clean — the application flow was mobile-friendly, the communication templates were easy to configure, and it just felt like a more modern experience than what we'd had. The hiring manager portal was intuitive enough that our clinic directors could actually use it without me having to handhold them through every step, which was a real test for us given that population. Reporting was better than JazzHR — I could get source tracking and pipeline metrics out of the box without needing to build custom reports. And the pricing was honest and reasonable for our size — it was competitive with what we were paying for JazzHR without feeling like we were buying a lot of features we'd never use. I think the other factor was that Workable's implementation support during the sales process felt attentive to our specific context. They clearly understood healthcare recruiting and the dynamics around clinical roles, which built confidence.
v.Q15: Greenhouse was probably the strongest product we looked at, honestly. The structured hiring approach is well-designed, and the analytics are genuinely excellent. But it felt like a level of sophistication our organization wasn't ready for. The implementation was going to take longer, the configuration overhead was meaningful, and our clinic directors — who are not especially tech-forward — would have struggled with it. The price was also higher, and I couldn't build an ROI case that justified the premium given our current scale. Lever was interesting but their focus felt very much oriented toward tech company hiring — the product messaging, the integrations they led with, the sales rep's framing — it all felt designed for a startup talent team, not a clinical healthcare operator. I didn't feel like they deeply understood our world. Rippling was compelling as a unified platform — I see the vision — but the payroll migration risk was something our CFO was not willing to take on at that moment. Moving both our ATS and our payroll system at the same time felt like too much operational risk. So we kept Gusto and changed just the ATS. Jobvite just didn't get far enough into our process to have a detailed rejection reason — it felt heavier and more complex than we needed.
v.Q16: Workable has been a meaningful improvement for us on the recruiting side. v.Q17: The integration between Workable and Gusto is still not where I want it. And Workable's reporting, while better than JazzHR, still doesn't give me the kind of predictive analytics or benchmarking against healthcare-specific hiring norms that I'd find valuable.
v.Q18: The integration friction between the ATS and Gusto is my biggest frustration, and I'd describe it as moderate. It's not causing payroll errors or compliance issues — it's more of a process inefficiency that costs my team time and creates risk of data inconsistencies. When I think about the promise of having connected systems, we're not fully there, and that's frustrating because it was actually one of the things I was trying to solve in the last evaluation.
v.Q19: Our headcount has been pretty stable, so it's not a growth story. But I think the expectations around recruiting analytics have evolved. Leadership wants a more sophisticated read on our talent pipeline — cost per hire, diversity metrics in the funnel, quality of hire over time — and the tools I have are not set up to easily answer those questions. I also think there's a growing expectation around AI-assisted sourcing that I'm starting to hear about from peers in healthcare TA. I haven't fully evaluated what's out there, but I'm aware that some platforms are building sourcing intelligence that could be meaningful for finding passive PT candidates, and I want to make sure my stack isn't falling behind on that front.
v.Q20: Across Gusto, Workable, and the other ancillary tools, I'd estimate we're in the $20K to $50K range annually. I don't have the exact number in front of me, but that's my best approximation.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. For Gusto specifically, I think the value is solid. Workable is reasonable for what it delivers. But given the integration gaps I'm still dealing with, I sometimes feel like we're paying for two systems and getting less than the sum of their parts.
v.Q22: If I'm thinking about a truly seamless integration between our ATS and Gusto — eliminating the manual handoff, syncing candidate-to-employee data automatically, and supporting our clinical onboarding workflow — I'd put that value somewhere in the $5K to $10K range annually. That's a combination of the time savings for my team and the reduced risk of data errors during the onboarding process. It's not a transformational number, but it's meaningful.
v.Q23: I'd say very unlikely within six months. We just completed a significant ATS transition not that long ago, and the organization doesn't have the appetite for another change so quickly. That said, I think we'll probably do a more structured review of our full TA tech stack sometime in the next year or two — especially as AI capabilities in recruiting tools mature and I need to decide whether what we have is still competitive.
v.Q24: In healthcare specifically, I think the top frustration is that most HR and TA tools are designed for white-collar knowledge worker environments and don't translate well to clinical settings. The workflows assume everyone has a company email, sits at a computer, and has time to engage with HR portals during their workday. That's just not the reality for bedside or clinic staff. Beyond the healthcare-specific piece, I think the broader challenges that most Directors in my function would name are: fragmentation of the tech stack — too many tools, not enough native integration — and the increasing expectation from leadership that TA should be delivering data-driven insights that most of our tools aren't built to easily provide. And then there's the AI question, which is both an opportunity and a source of uncertainty. Everyone is being told AI will transform recruiting, but it's not always clear which platforms are delivering something real versus just rebranding existing features.

v.Q7:
There were honestly several things converging at the same time, and I think it's worth walking through each of them because they each played a role. The most immediate trigger was that our benefits renewal was coming up, and for the first time we were considering switching benefits carriers. And once we started that conversation with our broker, it became clear that doing it while staying on Paychex was going to create a really painful manual re-enrollment process. Our broker essentially told us that a lot of the platforms she worked with had much cleaner carrier integrations and that switching HR software at the same time as switching carriers might actually be less painful than staying on Paychex and trying to patch things together.

The second factor was that I had just gone through the most painful open enrollment of my career on Paychex — it took me and my colleague almost three weeks of back-and-forth with employees to get everyone enrolled correctly because the employee-facing portal was confusing and we had a lot of people who ended up in the wrong elections. That caused real problems and real stress for people, and I knew we couldn't do that again.

The third factor was more of a slow burn — we had been remote-first for a while by that point, and managing HR admin for a distributed team across nearly twenty states on a system that had essentially no employee self-service was becoming really unsustainable. Something as simple as an employee updating their address required them to email me, and then I'd have to go into the system and do it manually. That kind of thing adds up.

And then the fourth piece was a compliance concern that had been raised by our auditors. We had some documentation gaps around I-9 records and employee acknowledgment of policy updates, and our prior system had no real document management capability. So compliance was also on the list.
v.Q8:
I think the broader organizational context was really about us reaching a maturity point where we needed to operate more like a professionally run organization and less like a scrappy advocacy group. We'd been around for over a decade and we'd grown to a size where the informal systems — the spreadsheets, the email chains, the broker phone calls — were starting to create liability and inefficiency. Our Executive Director had made a few comments about wanting the People function to be more strategic and less administrative, and I think she understood that some of that meant investing in better tools.

There was also a grant funding piece that's kind of specific to nonprofits. We'd received some capacity-building funding from a foundation that was explicitly earmarked for operational infrastructure improvement. That created a budget window that we knew was time-limited — we had roughly eighteen months to spend it on things like software and organizational development. So the evaluation happened partly because the money was there in a way it usually isn't. In a nonprofit context, discretionary tech budget is rare, so when that window opened, we moved on it.

And I think there was also just a broader awareness in the nonprofit sector that remote-first was becoming permanent, not temporary, and that the tools that worked for in-office teams didn't necessarily translate well. We heard from peers at other organizations who were going through similar transitions, and that peer conversation was actually part of what put certain tools on our radar.

v.Q12:
So the decision structure was actually a little bit layered. I led the evaluation — I did all of the initial research, built out our comparison matrix, ran the vendor demos, and made the recommendation. My direct manager, who is our VP of Operations, was involved in reviewing my recommendation and had some input on the finalist decision. Then our Executive Director and our CFO both had to sign off on the budget, because it represented a meaningful annual commitment for us. Our CFO had specific questions about the payroll processing reliability and the multi-state compliance piece, because those were areas where she was going to feel any failure acutely. The employee self-service portal was also clearly the most user-friendly of the options we saw. I remember doing a usability walkthrough with my office manager and she said something like, 'I could figure this out without any training,' which was meaningful given that she's not particularly tech-forward. Price was also a factor — Gusto came in at a meaningfully lower cost than Rippling for our headcount and use case. And multi-state payroll was handled well. The implementation support was responsive and honest, which I appreciated — they didn't oversell what the platform could do.

I think the thing that sealed it was that several peers at other nonprofits had positive experiences with Gusto specifically in the nonprofit context. That social proof from similar organizations was genuinely reassuring.
v.Q15:
For Rippling, the primary reason was cost — it was significantly more expensive for our headcount, and the additional capabilities it offered beyond what we needed felt like we'd be paying for features we'd never use. The IT and device management pieces, for instance, are great if you have an IT team to leverage them, but we don't. I also thought the implementation complexity was higher than what we could realistically manage with a three-person people ops team. I think Rippling is a genuinely strong platform but it's optimized for a different kind of company than ours.

For Namely, the main issues were a combination of concerns about the company's stability — I had read some things at the time about leadership changes and customer churn — and the fact that their benefits administration module felt less polished than Gusto's during the demo. The demo experience itself was also less impressive. The sales rep was a little disorganized and we had a technical issue during the walkthrough that didn't get resolved in the session. I know that's not necessarily indicative of the product, but it does shape your impression of how the company operates. And given that we were trusting this platform with payroll and benefits for seventy-five people, confidence in the vendor matters a lot.
v.Q16: Gusto does payroll and benefits really reliably, which sounds like a low bar but actually wasn't something we could take for granted with Paychex. Employee self-service works — people can find their own pay stubs, update their address, download their W-2, and do basic profile maintenance without needing to email me. v.Q18: I think my biggest frustration is the data fragmentation between Gusto and Lattice. v.Q23: I'd say we're somewhat likely to consider it within the next six months, though I want to be honest that switching costs are a real concern for me. I think switching likelihood is somewhere between neutral and somewhat likely — we'd probably consider it seriously if a platform emerged that clearly did what Gusto does on payroll and benefits while also providing more HRIS depth and better analytics, at a price point that works for a nonprofit budget.
v.Q24: I think the challenge that resonates most universally with People Ops practitioners at our scale is the fragmentation problem — almost everyone I talk to is running at least two or three systems that don't communicate well, and the manual overhead of bridging those gaps is a consistent tax on small teams. The people function is being asked to operate more strategically — to inform workforce planning, to analyze engagement and retention, to do compensation equity analysis — but the tools that small and mid-size organizations can afford are often still built around transactional HR. There's a real gap between what leadership expects from people data and what most systems at our price point can actually deliver. And I think for nonprofits specifically there's a unique challenge around budget justification — you're constantly competing with program spending for resources, and it can be genuinely hard to quantify the ROI of better HR infrastructure in the same way you can measure the impact of a program dollar.

v.Q7:
There were honestly several things happening at once. The biggest driver was that Justworks had this very rigid benefits structure, and as we'd scaled and our employee population had become more diverse in terms of needs — like we had people in multiple states, we had employees asking about HSA options and more flexible health plan tiers — the platform just couldn't flex with us. That was probably the loudest pain point.

Beyond that, the reporting capabilities were basically nonexistent. I mean, I would export data to spreadsheets and build my own reports, which is fine when you're 80 people, but at 250-plus employees, that process was eating up hours every week. And when leadership started asking me for headcount trend data or cost-per-hire breakdowns tied to compensation data, I just didn't have the infrastructure to pull that together cleanly.

And then there was the integration issue. We had moved to Greenhouse for recruiting, and there was just no clean handoff between the ATS and our HR system. Every time we made a hire, it was a manual data re-entry situation, which introduced errors and wasted time. That friction point kept coming up in conversations with our finance team too, because they needed accurate headcount and payroll data and were often getting stale numbers.

So I'd summarize it as: benefits limitations, terrible reporting, and integration failures all kind of converging at the same time.
v.Q8: Yeah, I think the shift to fully remote was a big one for us. We had gone fully remote during the pandemic and had never really gone back, and that meant we were hiring across a lot more states than we used to. So all of a sudden we had multi-state payroll compliance requirements that Justworks wasn't handling particularly elegantly. There was also this broader conversation happening at the executive level about building out a more sophisticated people analytics function, and part of that conversation was recognizing that the tooling we had wasn't going to support that ambition. I think there was also just some pressure from our CFO to get better visibility into people costs as a percentage of overall spend, which pushed the conversation forward internally.
v.Q9:
Definitely. The one that frustrated me the most on a day-to-day basis was the manual work. In Justworks, anytime there was a life event change, a benefit election update, a new hire onboarding — it all required me to manually touch multiple systems and cross-check everything. It felt like I was spending more time administering data than actually doing strategic HR work. And as a solo HR person, that's a real problem because there's nobody else to absorb the administrative load.

Support was also a frustration. When I had questions or something was broken, the support experience felt slow and impersonal. I'd submit a ticket and wait, and sometimes the answer I got back didn't even fully address what I'd asked. That erodes trust pretty quickly when you're responsible for making sure 300 people get paid correctly.

And I think a quieter frustration was just the employee self-service experience. The interface that employees used felt dated, and I kept getting questions from employees about things they should have been able to find or do themselves in the platform. That added to my inbound volume in ways that were totally avoidable.
v.Q10: We seriously looked at Gusto, Rippling, and TriNet. We also briefly looked at Namely, but I eliminated that one pretty quickly in the early stages. So the real finalists were Gusto and Rippling, with TriNet staying in the conversation for a while because of their PEO model, which some of our leadership found appealing initially.
v.Q11: Yes, absolutely. For me, multi-state payroll compliance was non-negotiable — we needed a platform that handled tax registration and filings across states without requiring me to manage that separately. Integration with Greenhouse was also a hard requirement, because I wasn't willing to give up our ATS and I needed that handoff to be automated. And we had a price ceiling roughly around the $50,000 annual range, so anything that was going to come in dramatically above that was going to face a lot of internal resistance. I also personally required a real self-service employee portal, because reducing my inbound HR questions was a genuine strategic priority given that I'm solo.
v.Q12: So I was the primary driver of the evaluation — I built the RFP framework, ran the demos, and put together the recommendation. But the final call required sign-off from our CFO and our CEO. Our CFO was specifically focused on total cost of ownership and the payroll compliance piece, and our CEO wanted to make sure whatever we chose could scale with the company without requiring us to rip and replace again in two years. IT was loosely in the loop on security and SSO requirements but wasn't a heavy voice in the final decision. I'd characterize my role as primary recommender — I had strong influence, but the CFO effectively had veto power on cost grounds.
v.Q13: We switched. We moved from Justworks to Gusto, which we're still on today.
v.Q14:
Honestly, Gusto stood out primarily on the price-to-value equation and the implementation experience. Rippling had a lot more horsepower in terms of automation and integrations, but it came in at a meaningfully higher cost, and the implementation was going to be more involved, which felt risky for a solo HR person with no dedicated implementation support internally.

Gusto's Greenhouse integration was clean enough to satisfy my requirement, the employee self-service interface was noticeably more modern than what we'd had, and the multi-state payroll handling was solid. The demo experience was also better — I felt like the Gusto team actually understood what a company at our size and structure needed, whereas the Rippling pitch felt like it was calibrated for a company with a bigger IT and HR team than ours.

And then TriNet, I pushed back against the PEO model because I felt like it created a layer of dependency that would limit our flexibility as we grew and eventually wanted to bring more HR functions in-house. So that was more of a strategic fit issue than a pure feature issue.
v.Q15:
Rippling — great product, genuinely impressive automation depth, but the cost was higher than we could justify given our current needs, and the implementation complexity felt like it required more internal IT bandwidth than we had. I also thought some of the more advanced features were things we weren't going to use for at least another year or two, so we'd be paying for capability we weren't ready to leverage.

TriNet — the PEO model was the core issue. I wasn't comfortable with the idea of co-employment and the limits it placed on our employer brand and our ability to fully own the employee experience. Our CEO also had concerns about what happens when you want to exit a PEO relationship — the transition costs and complexity scared us off.

Namely — I eliminated this one early. The product felt dated, the demo was underwhelming, and when I looked at user reviews and talked to a few peers who'd used it, the support reputation was not great. It just didn't make the cut on basic capability grounds.
v.Q16: Gusto handles payroll reliably, which sounds basic but is genuinely the most important thing. Multi-state tax filings happen automatically, I almost never have to think about it. The benefits open enrollment flow is also pretty smooth — employees can do most of it themselves without me having to hand-hold, which was a big improvement over what we had. And the onboarding checklists feature has been helpful for making new hire setup more consistent.
v.Q17: The reporting and analytics piece is still not where I need it to be. I can pull standard payroll reports, but anything custom requires exporting to a spreadsheet and building it myself, which is kind of exactly what I was doing before. And the Greenhouse integration, while functional, is not as seamless as I'd like — there's still some manual cleanup required on the data that flows through. I've also found that as we've approached 300-plus employees, Gusto starts to feel a little bit like it's stretching at the seams. Some of the workflow customization options just aren't there.
v.Q18: The biggest frustration is definitely the analytics and reporting limitations. I have a CFO who asks me regularly for things like headcount by department with loaded cost per head, or turnover trend data broken out by tenure band, and I can't produce those reports from Gusto without a lot of manual work. Every time that request comes in, I'm spending two or three hours in spreadsheets that should be taking me fifteen minutes. I'd call the intensity of that frustration significant — not severe enough that I'm actively looking to rip out Gusto, but significant enough that it comes up in almost every leadership conversation I have about HR data.
v.Q19: The biggest shift is that leadership is now expecting much more from a people analytics standpoint than they were a year and a half ago. There's a lot more pressure to quantify the HR function — show ROI on recruiting spend, track offer acceptance rates against market benchmarks, model out headcount scenarios for the next planning cycle. None of that was on the radar when I was doing the Gusto evaluation. And I think there's a growing expectation around AI-assisted features — I'm getting asked about things like automated job description generation and interview scheduling optimization, which is not something I even thought to ask about when I was evaluating tools eighteen months ago.
v.Q20: For Gusto specifically, I think we're in the $40,000 to $45,000 per year range when you factor in our headcount and the plan tier we're on. If you roll in Greenhouse and the other adjacent tools, we're probably closer to $80,000 to $90,000 all-in across the HR tech stack.
v.Q21: For Gusto on its own, I'd say somewhat yes — the payroll reliability and benefits administration justify the cost, but the reporting gaps make me feel like we're not getting full value. If I'm being honest, we're paying a mid-tier price for what feels like a slightly below mid-tier analytics experience.
v.Q22: If Gusto had genuinely robust people analytics built in — like real configurable dashboards, turnover modeling, compensation benchmarking, the whole thing — I think that would be worth somewhere in the $10,000 to $20,000 range annually to us, partly in direct time savings and partly in the value of the decisions we'd be able to make faster. So I'd say in the $10K to $25K band.
v.Q23: Probably not in the next six months — I'd say somewhat unlikely. The switching costs are real, and I don't have the bandwidth as a solo HR person to run another evaluation right now. But I'd say if the analytics gap doesn't get addressed in the next twelve to eighteen months, either through a Gusto product improvement or a third-party add-on, I'll probably start looking more seriously. So not imminent, but I wouldn't say I'm fully locked in long-term either.
v.Q24: I think the number one thing most people in my position would point to is the fragmentation problem. You've got an ATS over here, an HRIS over there, a payroll system somewhere else, and you're constantly stitching them together manually or through integrations that half-work. The dream of a truly unified platform that doesn't sacrifice depth in any one area is still pretty elusive, especially for companies in that 200 to 500 employee range where you've outgrown SMB tools but you're not big enough to justify enterprise pricing. I also think the analytics gap is industry-wide — most HR leaders I talk to are still building their reporting in spreadsheets, which feels crazy given how sophisticated other business functions have gotten. And honestly, AI is now becoming a conversation topic in every vendor pitch, but most people aren't sure yet which AI features are genuinely useful versus just marketing noise.

v.Q1: I'm a director of Talent Acquisition. I oversee our full recruiting function and I also have some oversight of the HR ops side as it intersects with hiring — onboarding, offer letter workflows, headcount planning, that kind of thing.
v.Q2: I've been here just under three years. So right at the edge of that one-to-three-year band, almost tipping into three-to-five.
v.Q3: We're in facilities management and commercial real estate services — so kind of a mix of field operations and corporate staff. I know that doesn't fit neatly into the usual tech or healthcare buckets. We're at about 190 employees right now, so in that 101 to 250 range. We have a hybrid setup where the corporate team is mostly in our Chicago office a few days a week, but we have field staff distributed across several Midwest markets.
v.Q4: We're on Rippling as our primary platform. It handles payroll, benefits, device management for our corporate staff, and we use the Rippling ATS module for recruiting. We do have a couple of point solutions layered in — we use LinkedIn Recruiter separately, and we have a background check vendor that plugs into Rippling via an integration — but Rippling is genuinely our system of record for most things.
v.Q5: That was about two and a half years ago, so I'd put it in the two-to-three-year range. I had just joined the company and the evaluation was already in motion, but I came in early enough to shape it meaningfully.
v.Q6: The company was on ADP Workforce Now for payroll and benefits, and they were using a completely separate applicant tracking system — Breezy HR. So there were essentially two systems that didn't talk to each other, and a lot of manual handoff work between recruiting and HR ops.
v.Q7:
The disconnection between ADP and Breezy was a constant source of friction. Every time we made a hire, someone had to manually enter the new employee into ADP, and the error rate was not trivial — we had a few payroll issues that stemmed directly from data entry mistakes during that handoff. That was the most acute pain point.

Beyond that, ADP Workforce Now felt extremely heavy and complex relative to our size. I mean, it's built for much larger organizations, and the support model reflected that — our account rep was hard to reach and the ticketing system was slow. For a 150-person company with a small HR team, it felt like overkill in all the wrong ways.

And then on the Breezy side, the ATS was just too lightweight for what we needed as we were trying to scale recruiting. Reporting was thin, and there was no real structured interview workflow capability. So both systems were kind of failing us simultaneously, which made the case for switching pretty compelling.
v.Q8: We were pushing toward a more structured hybrid model post-pandemic, and that meant we needed better device management and access control for employees coming in and out of the office — which is something Rippling was uniquely positioned to help with, honestly. There was also a broader digital transformation initiative happening at the executive level, where the COO wanted to consolidate vendor relationships and reduce the number of point solutions we were managing. That created organizational appetite for a platform that could do more things in one place.
v.Q9: The manual data entry and the errors it caused were the biggest operational frustration. But I think the thing that affected me most directly as a TA director was the complete lack of recruiting visibility. In Breezy, I had no meaningful pipeline analytics — I couldn't see time-to-fill by department, source-of-hire breakdowns, or offer-to-acceptance ratios without exporting everything and building it manually. When I was trying to make the case to leadership for additional recruiting resources, I had no clean data to support that conversation. That was genuinely painful.
v.Q10: We seriously evaluated Rippling, Paylocity, and Bamboo HR. We also had a brief conversation with Paychex Flex but that didn't go very far — it felt too similar to the ADP model we were trying to move away from.
v.Q11: Unified payroll and ATS in one platform was the top requirement — I wasn't willing to maintain two separate systems again. We also needed solid multi-state payroll support because we operate across Illinois, Ohio, and Wisconsin. And we had a requirement around background check integration because our field operations roles have specific compliance requirements around screening. Anything that couldn't meet those three criteria didn't make it into the real consideration set.
v.Q12: I was the primary recommender. Our CFO was involved primarily on cost and payroll accuracy grounds, and our COO had the final sign-off authority because it was framed as a broader operational transformation initiative. IT was involved specifically to evaluate the device management and SSO components of Rippling, which was actually a bigger part of the conversation than I initially expected. I'd say it was HR plus Finance plus Ops plus IT — a fairly broad committee, but with the COO effectively holding the final vote.
v.Q13: We switched to Rippling. Fully moved off ADP and Breezy and consolidated onto the Rippling platform.
v.Q14:
Rippling won primarily because of the unification story. The fact that payroll, HR, IT, and recruiting could all live in one place with a single employee record was genuinely compelling for us — it addressed the core problem we had. The device management piece was also a real differentiator that the other platforms couldn't match, and our COO latched onto that as a reason to move forward.

I also think the Rippling implementation team was strong. They were organized, had a clear migration plan, and the data migration from ADP went more smoothly than I expected. That execution confidence during the sales process gave us some trust that the transition wouldn't be a disaster. BambooHR felt a bit lighter weight and I wasn't sure it would hold up as we continued to grow. Paylocity was competitive on payroll but didn't have the ATS depth we wanted.
v.Q15:
BambooHR — I think it's a strong product for companies that have separate, best-in-class tools for everything and just need a clean HRIS core, but for us, the ATS capability wasn't robust enough and the IT management piece was nonexistent. It felt like it would have left us still running two systems.

Paylocity — solid payroll, genuinely competitive pricing, and the support reputation was good. The thing that knocked it out was that the recruiting module felt bolted on rather than native, and when I pushed them on ATS analytics during the demo, the answers were vague. For me, that was a disqualifying gap.
v.Q16: Rippling does the unification piece very well — having one employee record that flows through payroll, benefits, IT provisioning, and recruiting has genuinely reduced errors and manual work across the board. Workflow automation is also a strength — we have automated onboarding sequences that trigger device provisioning and system access at the same time as the HR onboarding tasks, and that kind of choreography would have been impossible before. Payroll runs reliably and the compliance support for our multi-state footprint has been solid.
v.Q17: The ATS module is where I feel the most friction. Rippling's recruiting functionality has improved, but it still doesn't feel as mature as a purpose-built ATS. Structured interviewing and scorecard workflows are functional but not particularly flexible, and the candidate-facing experience is kind of basic compared to what you'd get from a dedicated tool like Lever or Greenhouse. For roles where candidate experience really matters, I sometimes feel like we're at a disadvantage.
v.Q18: The ATS candidate experience limitation is my biggest ongoing frustration. Specifically, the careers page customization is very limited — we can't really create a branded, compelling application experience that reflects who we are as a company. For a facilities management company that's competing against tech and healthcare employers for corporate talent, employer brand presentation really matters and I feel like Rippling holds us back a bit there. I'd call it moderate to significant frustration — it's not enough to trigger a full platform switch, but it comes up regularly.
v.Q19: Employer branding has become a much bigger priority than it was when we evaluated two and a half years ago — we've had some turnover at the manager level and we're being much more intentional about how we attract and retain corporate talent. And honestly, AI features are now on our radar in a way they weren't before. I'm curious about AI-assisted screening and candidate communication tools, but Rippling's current AI capabilities in the recruiting module are pretty limited.
v.Q20: I believe we're spending somewhere in the $55,000 to $70,000 range annually for Rippling, depending on which modules you include. That's a meaningful step up from what we were spending on ADP and Breezy combined, but the consolidation and time savings have justified it in our CFO's view.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. The operational efficiency gains are real, especially on the IT and payroll side. But I'm a little less convinced on the ATS value relative to what we're paying when I compare it to what a dedicated recruiting platform could offer at maybe a fraction of the incremental cost.
v.Q22: If Rippling had a genuinely polished, customizable employer branding and careers page experience built in — something that could compete with a dedicated employer brand platform — I'd estimate that's worth somewhere in the $5,000 to $10,000 range annually in direct tool savings plus the brand value of better candidate conversion.
v.Q23: Not within six months — I'd say very unlikely in that timeframe. The switching costs from Rippling are significant and the operational gains have been real. That said, if a best-in-class ATS were to come along with a clean Rippling integration, I might lobby internally to add it as a point solution rather than replace the core platform.
v.Q24: I think the tension between consolidation and depth is the defining challenge right now. Every vendor is pitching a platform approach, but the reality is that the all-in-one platforms often sacrifice depth in specific areas — recruiting, analytics, whatever — and that forces HR leaders to choose between operational simplicity and functional excellence. That's a frustrating tradeoff. I also think recruiter workload and time-to-fill pressure are real across industries, and tools haven't fully solved the AI promise yet — there's a lot of hype but the practical automation gains for most recruiting teams are still pretty incremental.

ADP Run was fine for what it did but felt like it was built for a smaller company than we were at that point.
v.Q7:
There were a few distinct triggers, and they kind of piled up in a way that made the decision feel urgent.

The first one was what I'd call a compliance wake-up call. We had gotten some feedback during an internal audit that our employee record-keeping was inconsistent — some records had gaps, some acknowledgment documents weren't being tracked properly, and the version of Namely we were running had some configuration issues that were creating data integrity problems. For a company operating in regulated industries, that's not a minor issue. That pushed the conversation from 'we should probably look at new tools eventually' to 'we need to move on this now.'

The second trigger was headcount growth. We had grown from about 270 to 360 employees over the prior eighteen months, and the manual processes that had been good enough at 270 were breaking down at 360. Specifically, onboarding was becoming a real pain point — we were doing so many things manually, and the error rate and time investment were climbing.

And then honestly, there was a new CHRO who came in about six months before the evaluation kicked off. She had a strong point of view on what a modern HR function should look like, and she was not impressed with the tooling she inherited. So there was some leadership pressure to professionalize the function, which included getting on a better platform.
v.Q8: The shift to hybrid was a meaningful contextual factor. We'd gone hybrid in 2021 and were still sorting out what that meant for our workforce in terms of systems and process. Some of the workflows we'd built in Namely assumed everyone was in an office, and they just didn't translate cleanly to a distributed team. I think there was also a broader recognition in our industry — professional training — that if you're going to deliver training on workforce effectiveness to clients, you probably need to actually model good workforce practices internally. There was some reputational dimension to getting our people ops house in order that went beyond just operational efficiency.
v.Q9:
The biggest operational frustration was onboarding. In the setup we had, getting a new employee properly set up required my team to touch six or seven different systems manually, in a specific sequence, with no automation connecting any of it. New hire paperwork would go into Namely, then payroll setup had to be entered separately into ADP Run, then benefits enrollment happened through a completely separate portal that the employee had to be manually invited to. If any one of those steps was missed or delayed, the downstream consequences could be significant — someone not getting paid correctly on their first check, or not having benefits active on their start date.

I also want to flag the reporting frustration, because it's related. When our CHRO asked me for a headcount report broken out by employment type, tenure, and department, I had to pull data from three systems and reconcile it in a spreadsheet. That kind of request should take minutes, not hours. And the fact that it took hours meant I was producing that kind of analysis less frequently than leadership needed it, which limited our ability to have data-informed conversations about workforce planning.
v.Q10: We seriously evaluated BambooHR, Lattice — specifically because they had expanded into HR and onboarding at the time — and we also looked at UKG Ready, which some of our board advisors had referenced. We briefly considered Workday, but it was clearly oversized for us in terms of implementation complexity and cost. So the real finalists were BambooHR and UKG Ready, with Lattice being eliminated in a middle round.
v.Q11: We had a few hard requirements. The first was configurable onboarding workflows with e-signature capability built in — not a third-party add-on, actually built in. After the manual onboarding nightmare we'd had, that was truly non-negotiable. The second was a reliable integration or native sync with Paychex, because our CFO was not willing to move payroll systems at the same time as the HRIS — she wanted to separate the risks. And the third requirement was strong employee self-service functionality, because I wanted to get my team out of the business of answering routine questions about PTO balances and benefits elections that employees should be able to answer themselves. Anything that couldn't demonstrate all three of those in a live demo didn't advance.
v.Q12: This was a reasonably collaborative decision process. I was the primary evaluator and built the scoring rubric and led all the vendor conversations. Our CHRO was involved in the finalist demos and held final approval authority — she made the call ultimately. Our CFO was a key voice on budget and anything touching payroll integration, and she had informal veto power on cost grounds. We also had our IT director review the security documentation and SSO requirements for each finalist, which narrowed things slightly. And I involved two members of my HR ops team in the demos because they'd be the day-to-day users, and I wanted their input on usability. So I'd call it HR plus Finance plus IT plus CHRO as the decision committee, with me as primary recommender and the CHRO as final decision-maker.
v.Q13: We switched. We moved off Namely and onto BambooHR about two years ago, and that's where we are today. ADP Run was kept in place temporarily during the transition and then migrated to Paychex later — that was a separate project.
v.Q14:
BambooHR won on a combination of usability, implementation confidence, and price-to-value. When I'm being really honest, the employee self-service experience in BambooHR is genuinely intuitive — the interface is clean, employees actually use it without being forced to, and that was validated by reference checks I did with other HR directors who had implemented it. That matters a lot to me because tool adoption is often where these implementations fall apart.

The onboarding workflow builder was also strong in the demo — we could map out our specific sequence of tasks and assign them to different people and see how they'd flow, which was exactly what we needed after the manual onboarding chaos we'd had.

And BambooHR had a documented Paychex integration that had apparently been in place for a while, which satisfied our CFO's risk concern about not disrupting payroll. UKG Ready had a better compliance and workforce management feature set, I'll give them that, but the implementation timeline they quoted was significantly longer, the cost was higher, and honestly the complexity felt like more than we needed. I think UKG Ready is a great product for a manufacturing or hourly workforce environment, but for our salaried-heavy population it was overkill.

Lattice got cut because even though their performance management product is genuinely excellent, the HR and onboarding modules felt immature relative to what BambooHR offered, and they couldn't match the Paychex integration requirement cleanly.
v.Q15:
UKG Ready — too complex, too expensive for our size, and the implementation timeline was going to be disruptive. I also had concerns that the configuration burden would require ongoing IT involvement that we didn't have the bandwidth for. It's a strong platform, but it felt like it was built for a company with a dedicated HRIS administrator or a bigger IT function than ours.

Lattice — the performance management piece is excellent, and I genuinely like what they've built there, but the HR core and onboarding modules were not mature enough at the time we evaluated. The Paychex integration was also not well-documented, which introduced risk. I think they've continued to build out the HR platform since then, so I might revisit them in a future evaluation, but they weren't ready at the time we needed them to be.

Workday — this one was basically eliminated at the criteria-setting stage. The implementation costs alone for a company our size would have been prohibitive, and the complexity of the configuration process requires dedicated internal resources we just don't have. I've worked with Workday at a previous employer that was much larger, and it's an impressive system in the right context, but that context is not a 380-person professional services company.
v.Q16: BambooHR does employee self-service genuinely well — the adoption rate on our team is high, and I get far fewer routine questions from employees than I did before. The onboarding workflow builder has worked as intended, and new hire setup is dramatically less manual than it was. The time-off tracking and approval workflows are clean and reliable, which sounds basic but was actually a persistent problem with Namely. And the UI is approachable enough that managers who aren't power users can figure out what they need without a lot of training.
v.Q17:
The performance management module in BambooHR is where I feel the most friction. It's functional for basic review cycles, but it doesn't support the kind of continuous feedback and goal-tracking workflows that our CHRO is now pushing us toward. We've basically had to build a parallel process in a separate tool because BambooHR's performance features can't accommodate what we need. That fragmentation is frustrating because it defeats some of the purpose of having a unified HRIS.

Reporting is also still a gap. I can pull standard reports easily enough, but the moment I need something cross-functional or trend-based, I'm still exporting to spreadsheets. And the Paychex integration, while functional, requires occasional manual reconciliation that I wish was fully automated.
v.Q18: The performance management gap is my biggest frustration, and I'd rate it as significant. We're now running BambooHR for core HRIS and a completely separate tool for continuous feedback and goal-setting, and my team is spending real time managing the seams between those two systems — making sure manager information is consistent, making sure org chart changes are reflected in both places, that kind of thing. It creates confusion for employees and extra work for my team, and it's starting to erode some of the efficiency gains we got from moving to BambooHR in the first place. Our CHRO asks me fairly regularly why we can't do everything in one place, and honestly I don't have a great answer for her.
v.Q19: The biggest shift is around performance management and employee development. Two years ago, our CHRO was mostly focused on getting the operational foundation right — reliable payroll, clean records, functional onboarding. That work is largely done now. The agenda has moved toward talent development, succession planning, and a more continuous performance culture, and BambooHR isn't well-positioned for that next chapter. I've also started hearing more about AI-assisted HR features — things like sentiment analysis on engagement survey responses or predictive attrition modeling — and I'm genuinely curious whether those capabilities will mature enough to be useful in our context within the next year or two. That wasn't even a real conversation when we were evaluating last time.
v.Q20: For BambooHR specifically, I believe we're in the $35,000 to $45,000 per year range. When you add in the Paychex contract and the separate performance management tool we've layered in, the total HR tech spend is probably closer to $90,000 to $100,000 annually. That's across multiple vendors, which is part of why a consolidated solution is becoming more attractive again.
v.Q21: For BambooHR on its own, I'd say somewhat yes — the core HRIS value is there and the price is fair for the size we're at. But when I look at the total stack cost including the add-ons we've needed to compensate for BambooHR's gaps, the overall number is harder to justify. I'd rather pay a bit more for a platform that did more things well than pay a mid-tier price for the core and then keep adding point solutions.
v.Q22: If BambooHR had a genuinely capable continuous performance management and goal-tracking module built in — something that could replace the separate tool we're paying for and running — I think that's worth somewhere in the $15,000 to $20,000 range to us, between the direct cost savings on the point solution and the time my team would reclaim from managing two systems. So I'd put it in that $10K to $25K band.
v.Q23: Within six months, probably not — I'd say somewhat unlikely in that specific timeframe. But I think a twelve-to-eighteen-month horizon is where the conversation starts to get real. Our CHRO has been hinting at wanting a more holistic platform review, and if the performance management gap continues to create friction, I think there's a reasonable chance we'll be in evaluation mode again within the next year or so. I'm keeping an eye on a few platforms that have been expanding their feature sets, and I'd say I'm in active monitoring mode rather than active evaluation mode right now.
v.Q24:
I think the fundamental tension that most people ops leaders are navigating is between breadth and depth. The platforms that promise to do everything tend to do several things at a mediocre level, and the point solutions that do one thing excellently create integration and data consistency problems. Neither model is fully satisfying, and most of us are managing some version of that tradeoff every day.

Compliance complexity is also something I hear about constantly — multi-state employment, classification rules, evolving leave laws — and the platforms haven't kept pace particularly well with how fast the regulatory environment is moving, especially for companies with hybrid or distributed workforces.

And I think there's a real challenge around change management that doesn't get enough attention. Even if you pick the right platform, getting employees and managers to actually adopt it and use it consistently is hard, and most vendors underprepare their customers for that part of the journey. The tool is only as valuable as the adoption rate, and that's a people problem more than a technology problem, honestly.

cat.Q5: More than 24 months ago (24+ mo to 24+ mo)
cat.Q21: Somewhat no / not really reasonable

v.Q1: Sure. I'm a manager in Talent Acquisition. So my focus is really on the recruiting side of the house — sourcing candidates, managing our ATS pipeline, coordinating interviews, and working pretty closely with hiring managers across our clinical and administrative departments.
v.Q2: I've been here about three years now, so I'd say in that one-to-three-year range, closer to the upper end.
v.Q3: We're in healthcare — specifically outpatient behavioral health services, which has its own set of compliance and hiring quirks that make tool selection a bit more complicated than it might be in other sectors. We have around 180 employees right now, so solidly in that 101-to-250 range. And we've been growing kind of steadily, which is part of why we started paying more attention to our tooling.
v.Q4: We're primarily on Rippling. It handles payroll, benefits administration, and device management, and we also use their ATS module for recruiting. Honestly, it covers most of what we need under one roof, which was a big part of the appeal when we switched.
v.Q5: That was about a year and a half ago, so I'd put it in the one-to-two-year range.
v.Q6: We were using Paychex for payroll and benefits, and then a separate tool called JazzHR for recruiting. So they were completely siloed — no real connection between the two, which was a constant source of friction for us.
v.Q7: There were really a few things that kind of stacked up at the same time. The biggest one was the integration failure between our recruiting tool and payroll. Every time we made a hire, someone — usually me or our HR coordinator — had to manually re-enter all the candidate data from JazzHR into Paychex. It was tedious and error-prone, and we'd had a couple of payroll issues that traced back to that manual entry step. That was frustrating enough on its own, but we were also growing, and I think our leadership recognized that the way we were doing things wasn't going to scale. We'd hired about 30 people over the prior 18 months and we could feel the strain. And then there was just a general capability gap — JazzHR was fine for basic tracking but it didn't give us the kind of reporting or pipeline visibility I needed to have real conversations with our clinical directors about hiring timelines. So it was really a combination of manual process pain, the integration gap, and the sense that we needed something more robust as we grew.
v.Q8: Healthcare recruiting is genuinely tough right now, and I think that context pushed us to be more intentional about our tools. There's a real shortage of licensed behavioral health clinicians in most markets, and we needed every efficiency advantage we could get to reduce time-to-hire and not lose candidates to competitors. Also, our state had updated some credentialing and background check requirements for certain clinical roles, so making sure our onboarding and compliance workflows were airtight became a bigger priority. I think the broader pressure to do more with a lean HR team also played into it — we're a three-person team supporting close to 180 employees, so any manual process we can automate is genuinely valuable.
v.Q9: Beyond the manual data entry issue I already mentioned, the reporting in JazzHR was pretty limited. I couldn't easily pull time-to-fill by department or show offer acceptance rates over time without doing a lot of spreadsheet work. And on the Paychex side, the support experience was honestly not great — long hold times, inconsistent answers. So we were hoping a new platform would give us better analytics out of the box, stronger integration between recruiting and HR functions, and a more responsive support model.
v.Q10: We seriously looked at Rippling, BambooHR — which also has an ATS add-on — and Paylocity. We did demos with all three and got pricing from each.
v.Q11: Yes, and we were pretty clear about this going in. The tool had to have native payroll and a built-in or tightly integrated ATS — we didn't want to be stitching together point solutions anymore. It also needed to support benefits administration since we were managing that in Paychex and wanted to consolidate. And honestly, it had to have a mobile app because a good chunk of our clinical staff don't sit at desks, so they need to access pay stubs, request time off, and complete onboarding on their phones. Those were real must-haves, not just nice-to-haves.
v.Q12: Our VP of HR was the main decision-maker and she had final sign-off. I was the primary recommender — I led all the demos, built the comparison matrix, and presented a recommendation to her. Our CFO was also looped in because of the cost involved, and she essentially had veto power on the budget. IT wasn't really involved since we're not a large tech organization, so the evaluation was mostly HR-driven with Finance holding the purse strings.
v.Q13: We switched — we moved to Rippling and left both Paychex and JazzHR behind.
v.Q14: Rippling really stood out on the integration story. Everything we needed was genuinely native — payroll, benefits, the ATS, device management, even the employee app — and the data flowed between modules without any manual steps. That was the core problem we were trying to solve, and Rippling addressed it more convincingly than the other options. The demo was also really well done. The Rippling rep understood our healthcare context and showed us specific workflows for onboarding clinical staff that mapped pretty closely to what we actually do. BambooHR felt a little lighter on the payroll side, and Paylocity felt like it was built for companies bigger than us — the implementation scope and pricing reflected that. Rippling hit the right balance of capability and accessibility for a company our size.
v.Q15: BambooHR was actually a close second. The interface was really clean and the HR core was solid, but their payroll module felt less mature than Rippling's, and I wasn't confident their ATS would give us the reporting depth I needed. The price was attractive, I'll give them that. Paylocity was eliminated fairly early — the implementation timeline they quoted was something like three to four months, which felt really long for our situation, and the pricing was noticeably higher. It also felt like their sweet spot was companies with 500-plus employees, and some of the features they were pitching us on were things we just didn't need yet. It felt like paying for complexity we hadn't earned.
v.Q16: The unified experience is genuinely as good as advertised. When I move a candidate to hired status in the ATS, the onboarding workflow kicks off automatically, the payroll record gets created, and benefits enrollment is triggered — it's a really smooth handoff and it saves us a lot of time. The employee app is also well-received by our clinical staff. And the reporting is significantly better than what we had before.
v.Q17: The ATS is honestly the weakest part of the platform for us. It's functional, but it feels like a secondary product compared to the payroll and HR modules. The candidate experience for applicants isn't great — we've had a few comments that the application flow feels clunky on mobile. And the sourcing tools are pretty thin. I end up supplementing with LinkedIn Recruiter and doing a lot of manual work to manage those pipelines. I kind of wish there was a stronger integration with external job boards built in.
v.Q18: The candidate-facing experience in the ATS is my biggest frustration right now. We work hard to build a positive candidate experience because we're competing for clinical talent in a tight market, and I think the application flow in Rippling's ATS undercuts that a bit. It's not terrible, but it's not modern either. I'd call it a moderate frustration — it hasn't caused me to start looking at other tools, but it's something I notice and think about regularly.
v.Q19: We've grown since we implemented Rippling, and I think our analytics needs have matured. I want deeper dashboards — things like offer acceptance trends by job type, source-of-hire attribution, and turnover by tenure band. Those weren't things I was thinking about 18 months ago, but now that the basics are solid, I'm ready to go deeper on the data side. AI-assisted screening tools are also something I'm starting to pay attention to that weren't really on my radar before.
v.Q20: I think we're somewhere in the $20,000 to $50,000 range annually, when you account for the per-employee fee across all the modules we're using.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. The value is real — we've reduced manual work significantly and payroll errors are basically gone. But I think there's room to question whether the ATS module justifies its share of the cost given the limitations I mentioned. So it's not a strong yes, more of a qualified one.
v.Q22: If they genuinely improved the candidate-facing ATS experience — better mobile application flow, more modern design, cleaner communication templates — I'd say that's worth something in the $5,000 to $10,000 range annually to us, maybe on the lower end of that. It's not a make-or-break issue, but in healthcare recruiting every edge matters.
v.Q23: Probably not within six months — I'd say somewhat unlikely. The switching cost and disruption would be significant, and honestly the platform does enough well that I'm not in active exploration mode. But I wouldn't say it's completely off the table if a better ATS option emerged that also had strong payroll integration.
v.Q24: I think the biggest challenge is that most platforms are either great at the HR and payroll side or they're built around recruiting, but very few do both really well. For TA folks like me who sit at the intersection, that gap is a constant frustration. And I think there's a growing expectation around AI — for sourcing, screening, scheduling — that most platforms haven't caught up to yet. The tools are still pretty manual in a lot of ways that feel solvable.
