cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm a senior manager in People Operations.
v.Q2: Five years this past spring, so I'm right at that five-to-ten-year mark.
v.Q3: We're in education — specifically online professional development and credentialing for K-12 educators. Headcount is around six hundred and fifty right now, and it's been pretty flat for the past two years. We're not in a growth mode at the moment.
v.Q4: BambooHR is our core system. We run HR data and some benefits administration through it, and then we use ADP for payroll separately. So it's not a fully unified stack, but BambooHR is the primary system of record.
v.Q5: That was about fourteen months ago, so within the last twelve to eighteen months. It was a fairly thorough evaluation.
v.Q6: We were using an older version of Paylocity as our HRIS, and a separate benefits platform through our broker. Paylocity had been in place since before I joined.
v.Q7: The main push was that Paylocity felt increasingly misaligned with how our team actually worked. The UX was dated and employees were constantly frustrated with self-service tasks — things like updating direct deposit or accessing their documents felt unnecessarily complicated. Beyond that, our benefits broker was pushing us toward a more integrated benefits admin experience. And honestly, the Paylocity contract renewal was coming up and the pricing increase they proposed didn't feel justified given the experience we were having. So capability gaps, employee experience problems, and cost concerns all layered on top of each other.
v.Q8: We had become primarily remote during the pandemic and never fully returned to office, so our employee base is now spread across about thirty states. That created more compliance complexity than Paylocity was helping us manage gracefully. And I think there was also a broader moment in the education sector where organizations like ours were having to do more with tighter budgets, so finding tools that made our small team more efficient was a real priority.
v.Q9: Yes — the self-service experience in Paylocity was genuinely painful. Employees submitted IT tickets about HR tasks on a regular basis, which is a sign something is very wrong. Reporting was also a frustration; pulling even basic headcount reports required our HR coordinator to spend significant time in the system. And the benefits open enrollment module was clunky enough that we were supplementing it with paper packets, which just shouldn't happen in a fully remote organization.
v.Q10: We seriously evaluated BambooHR, Rippling, and Paycom. I also looked at Workday at a high level but ruled it out very quickly as too enterprise for where we are.
v.Q11: Clean, intuitive employee self-service was non-negotiable — we'd suffered enough from bad UX. We also required solid multi-state compliance support given our remote footprint. And we needed a tool that my team of three could realistically administer without a dedicated HRIS specialist. If it required heavy IT involvement to maintain, it was out.
v.Q12: I led the evaluation and made the formal recommendation. Our CFO had final budget approval and was specifically focused on total cost of ownership. Our VP of Finance also weighed in on the payroll integration requirements. It was a fairly small decision committee — I'd say I was the primary recommender with exec sign-off required.
v.Q13: We switched to BambooHR.
v.Q14: BambooHR won on employee experience and administrative simplicity. The self-service interface is genuinely intuitive — employees figured it out without training, which was a big deal for us. The reporting tools were meaningfully better than what we had, and the implementation timeline was realistic for a team our size. It also came in at a price point our CFO could approve without a long negotiation.
v.Q15: Rippling had strong automation and IT integration features, but felt like more complexity than we needed given that we're not in a growth phase and don't have a large IT team to leverage those capabilities. Paycom had a good payroll story but the demo experience was honestly not great — the implementation consultant felt very scripted and couldn't answer specific questions about our multi-state setup confidently. That raised concerns. Workday was simply too enterprise in scope and cost for an organization our size.
v.Q16: Employee self-service is genuinely excellent — we almost never get HR-related IT tickets anymore, which was a meaningful shift. The performance management module is clean and our managers actually use it. And for a team of three, the administrative burden is manageable in a way it wasn't before.
v.Q17: The ADP integration is imperfect — we still have some manual reconciliation in payroll that I thought we'd eliminate. And BambooHR's compensation management tools are pretty basic; as we've tried to build more structured pay bands, the system doesn't support that well natively.
v.Q18: The payroll integration gap is the biggest frustration, and I'd call it moderate in intensity. It's not catastrophic, but every pay cycle my coordinator spends time on reconciliation that shouldn't be manual. For an organization that specifically chose BambooHR partly to reduce manual work, that's a meaningful disappointment.
v.Q19: Honestly, our needs haven't shifted dramatically — we're stable in headcount and our model hasn't changed much. I think the one area where I'm paying more attention is compensation benchmarking; the market has been volatile enough that having better comp data tools integrated would be valuable. And I'm starting to think more about what AI-assisted HR tools actually look like in practice.
v.Q20: Combined between BambooHR and ADP, I think we're in the fifty-to-one-hundred-thousand-dollar range annually, probably closer to seventy-five.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. BambooHR feels fairly priced for what it delivers. The ADP spend is where I'd push back a little — I'm not sure we're getting proportional value there given the integration friction.
v.Q22: A seamless, truly native payroll integration that eliminated that reconciliation work? I'd say that's worth ten to fifteen thousand dollars a year to us, accounting for the coordinator time saved and the reduced error risk.
v.Q23: No, not within six months. We're not in a place organizationally where a switch makes sense right now, and switching costs are real. I'd say very unlikely in that window.
v.Q24: I think the core challenge is that integration promises consistently exceed integration reality — vendors sell you on a connected ecosystem and you end up with more manual work than you expected. For People Ops leaders at organizations our size, there's also a real tension between wanting sophisticated tools and not having the team capacity to implement and maintain them. And in education specifically, budget constraints mean you're always making tradeoffs that private-sector HR teams don't face in the same way.

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm a director of Talent Acquisition. My team handles full-cycle recruiting — everything from sourcing and screening through offer negotiation and onboarding handoff. I've been a director for about four years across a couple of companies now.
v.Q2: Just under two years, so I'm in that one-to-three-year band.
v.Q3: We're a technology company — enterprise SaaS, specifically compliance and risk management software. We have about eighty employees right now. I know that probably sounds like a lot of recruiters for a company that size, but we're structured as a centralized TA function that also supports sourcing strategy and employer brand, not just requisition management. Headcount has been pretty stable; we went through a period of aggressive hiring two years ago and then pulled back, and now we're in a kind of steady-state mode.
v.Q4: Gusto is our core platform for payroll and benefits. On the TA side, we use Lever as our ATS, which integrates with Gusto for onboarding hand-off. So we've got two primary systems plus a few point solutions — Greenhouse Sourcing, LinkedIn Recruiter, and a couple of assessment tools — but Gusto and Lever are the backbone.
v.Q5: About eight months ago. We looked specifically at payroll and benefits platforms — not the ATS side, which we'd already refreshed. So this was squarely the Gusto evaluation and whether we should stay or move.
v.Q6: We were already on Gusto — so this was a renewal evaluation, not a first-time purchase. We were asking whether Gusto still made sense for where we were going or whether we should migrate to something else.
v.Q7: The core trigger was a combination of things. Our Head of People had some concerns about whether Gusto's benefits administration could handle the complexity we were adding — we were expanding our benefits package pretty meaningfully to stay competitive in the talent market, and there were questions about whether Gusto could support some of the voluntary benefits and supplemental coverage options we wanted to offer. There was also a push from our CFO to do a formal cost-benefit review at contract renewal rather than just auto-renewing. And honestly, there was some internal conversation about whether we'd benefit from tighter integration between payroll and HR data, since we were doing some manual bridging between Gusto and Lever that felt inefficient.
v.Q8: The talent market in our sector had been really competitive, and we'd lost a few candidates at the offer stage where compensation and benefits were cited as a factor. That created internal urgency to upgrade our total compensation strategy, which put pressure on our benefits infrastructure. There was also a board-level conversation about operational efficiency — we had grown our headcount fairly quickly and there was a sense that our HR infrastructure needed to mature to match. And I think the general conversation in the tech industry about AI capabilities in HR tools was starting to surface; a couple of our team members were asking why our tools didn't have more intelligent features.
v.Q9: From a TA perspective, the onboarding handoff between Lever and Gusto was the most visible friction point. When a candidate accepted an offer, there was a meaningful amount of manual data transfer happening that created delays and occasionally errors in the new hire setup. That was a real frustration for my team because it reflected poorly on the candidate experience right at the moment when we most want to impress a new employee. The broader People team also flagged that Gusto's reporting on benefits utilization and cost trends was pretty thin, and that made it hard to evaluate whether our benefits spend was landing with employees or not.
v.Q10: We looked at Rippling, Justworks, and TriNet as alternatives to Gusto. I also did some initial research on Deel because we had a couple of international contractors and wanted to understand the landscape, but Deel didn't make it to a formal demo for the core payroll evaluation.
v.Q11: Yes. We needed a native integration with Lever — that was a hard line for me specifically. v.Q8:
Yeah, I think the Series C context is worth expanding on because it wasn't just about having money to grow — investors were asking us specific questions about hiring efficiency metrics and HR infrastructure during diligence conversations. There was a real sense that if we were going to be taken seriously as a company at our next stage, we needed to have HR operations that looked like a company operating at a higher level. So there was some board-level pressure, I think, to professionalize the people stack.

And then more broadly in fintech at the time, there was a lot of competition for talent — engineers, compliance specialists, product people — and the candidate experience we were delivering was not where it needed to be. Candidates would fall through the cracks, communication was inconsistent, and in a competitive talent market, that costs you offers. So the broader talent market environment made fixing our tooling feel more urgent than it might have otherwise.
v.Q9:
The biggest one on my side specifically was the reporting. Namely's analytics were really shallow — I could pull basic headcount reports, but if I wanted to look at time-to-fill by department, offer acceptance rates by recruiter, or pipeline conversion by source, I was building those in spreadsheets manually. In a fast-growth environment, you need to be able to look at that data in real time, not spend two hours every Friday pulling it together.

The other major frustration was the candidate experience side. Our careers page through Namely looked dated, the application flow had too many steps, and mobile experience was genuinely poor. I had candidates tell me directly that the application process felt clunky, and in fintech especially, where we're hiring tech-savvy people, that's a real signal.

And then the onboarding workflow — new hires were getting five or six separate emails from different systems, none of it was branded, and the sequence of tasks was confusing. We had new hires showing up on day one who hadn't completed their I-9 or hadn't set up direct deposit because the instructions weren't clear. That's not a great first impression.
v.Q10: We looked at Rippling, Workday, Lattice combined with a separate ATS, and we briefly evaluated Deel because we were anticipating some international hiring. We also had an initial conversation with HiBob but kind of ruled them out early. So the real final consideration was between Rippling and Workday, with Lattice as kind of a wild card option.
v.Q11: Definitely. We had a pretty explicit list. First, it had to have a native ATS or a genuinely deep integration with Greenhouse — not just a basic data sync, but actual workflow integration. Second, it needed strong background check workflow management, preferably native or through a tight Checkr integration, because of our compliance requirements. Third, it had to have solid audit trail functionality for I-9 and employment eligibility — that was non-negotiable given our regulatory environment. And honestly fourth, the candidate-facing experience had to look modern — a careers page that could be customized and a mobile-friendly application flow. Those were the things that had to be there for us to even have a serious conversation.
v.Q12: So the core decision group was me, our Head of People — who is a VP — our CFO, and our Head of IT Security. I was the primary recommender and the one doing most of the hands-on evaluation, running demos, talking to references, building the comparison. The Head of People had final sign-off authority on the HR side and was really the executive sponsor of the project. The CFO had to approve the budget, and given we were talking about a meaningful spend increase, that conversation took a few cycles. And IT Security got involved because Rippling specifically — and Workday too — were asking for fairly deep integration access to our identity management stack, so IT wanted to do their own security review before we signed anything. So it was HR plus Finance plus IT Security, with the Head of People as the ultimate decision-maker, but the CFO could have effectively vetoed it on cost grounds.
v.Q13: We switched. We moved to Rippling, left Namely behind entirely, and ran Greenhouse in parallel for a transition period before migrating into Rippling Recruiting fully.
v.Q14:
Rippling won primarily on the unified platform story and the automation capabilities. The pitch that one platform could handle HRIS, payroll, benefits, and recruiting — and that workflows could span all of those systems automatically — was really compelling given what we had experienced with Namely and Greenhouse running as silos.

The device and IT management layer was actually a real differentiator too, which I didn't fully anticipate going into the evaluation. Our IT Security lead got excited about it because it meant we could automate provisioning and deprovisioning as part of the onboarding and offboarding workflow, which was something we'd been doing manually and getting wrong regularly.

On the recruiting side specifically, the workflow automation was meaningfully better than what Namely had, and the onboarding flow — the way it handed off from offer acceptance to new hire tasks to payroll setup — was genuinely smooth in a way that Workday, honestly, was not able to match at our size and budget. Workday felt like it was built for a company twice our size and would have required a significant implementation investment that we weren't positioned to make.

Price-to-value was also a factor. Rippling's pricing for our size was more competitive than Workday's by a significant margin, and the implementation timeline was realistic for what we needed.
v.Q15:
Workday was too enterprise for where we were. The implementation would have required a third-party implementation partner, the timeline we were quoted was six to nine months, and the per-seat cost was substantially higher. For a company our size trying to move fast, that wasn't a real option even if the product is objectively powerful.

The Lattice option kind of fell apart because Lattice isn't really an ATS or a full HRIS — it's a performance and engagement tool, so we would have still needed a separate payroll and recruiting solution. That was actually a worse fragmentation problem than what we already had.

HiBob we ruled out pretty early. Honestly the ATS story just wasn't there, and the payroll integration options felt more like partnerships than native capabilities, which gave us less confidence in the reliability of the data flow.

Deel we kept in the conversation longer than expected, but ultimately they were stronger on the international and contractor side than on the domestic full-time employee experience. We're primarily US-based with some international ambition, but our immediate need was domestic full-time hiring at scale, and Rippling was just more purpose-built for that.
v.Q16: Rippling does the automation story really well — the workflow builder is genuinely powerful, and the way we can trigger actions across different parts of the platform based on an event, like an offer being accepted or a termination being initiated, saves my team a lot of manual work. Onboarding in particular has gotten dramatically better. New hires have a clear, sequenced set of tasks, everything is in one place, and we rarely have people showing up on day one without their paperwork done. The payroll accuracy has also been very consistent, which sounds like a low bar but was genuinely not the case with Namely.
v.Q17: The recruiting module — Rippling Recruiting — is still not where I need it to be for a team hiring at our pace. The pipeline reporting is limited, the sourcing integrations are thin compared to what a dedicated ATS like Greenhouse or Lever offers, and the candidate communication tools are pretty basic. I sometimes feel like the recruiting product is a few years behind the rest of the platform. I've also heard from my recruiters that the search and filter functionality in the candidate database is frustrating to use at scale. And honestly, the careers page customization is still pretty rigid — I can't do everything I want from a branding standpoint.
v.Q18: The biggest frustration is the recruiting analytics. I need to be able to slice pipeline data in a lot of different ways — by department, by recruiter, by source, by role level — and right now Rippling Recruiting doesn't give me that without me going into a spreadsheet or building a custom report that takes forever to set up. I would characterize the frustration level as significant. It affects how I run weekly pipeline reviews, it affects how I talk to the Head of People about recruiting performance, and it affects how quickly we can identify bottlenecks in the hiring process. It's not a nice-to-have — it's genuinely impeding how I manage the function.
v.Q19: The biggest shift is that we've grown, so the scale of everything we're doing is just higher — more requisitions open at once, more complex org structures, more states we're operating in from a compliance standpoint. I also think my expectations around analytics and data have genuinely evolved. When we made the Rippling decision two years ago, I would have said reporting was important but not critical. Now I would put it in the must-have column. And there's also more expectation from leadership that I can tell a data story about talent — pipeline health, time-to-fill trends, offer acceptance rates — in a way that connects to business outcomes. So the analytics gap that was a frustration before has become a more acute need.
v.Q20: I think we're in the range of $100K to $250K annually, all in across the Rippling platform including the different modules. I don't have the exact contract number in front of me but that's roughly where I'd estimate it sits.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. I think the core HR, payroll, and automation value is solid relative to the cost, but the recruiting module specifically feels like it's pulling down the overall value calculation for me given how much of my job depends on it performing well.
v.Q22: If Rippling's recruiting analytics were genuinely as good as what a best-in-class standalone ATS provides, and I could get real-time pipeline reporting, source attribution, and recruiter performance dashboards without manual work — I think that's worth somewhere in the $10K to $25K range annually to us, maybe toward the higher end of that. When I think about the time my team spends compensating for the gap right now, and the decision speed we'd gain, that's a real number.
v.Q23: I'd say somewhat unlikely in the next six months. The switching costs are real, and the core platform does enough things well that I wouldn't want to blow that up. But I'm not going to say never — if the recruiting analytics don't improve meaningfully in the next cycle, I think there's a real conversation to be had about whether we go back to a best-of-breed ATS approach even if it means reintroducing some fragmentation.
v.Q24: I think the number one thing is the tension between platform consolidation and best-in-class functionality. Every all-in-one platform promises you that you can replace five tools with one, and the operational efficiency of that is real, but the tradeoff is that individual modules — especially things like ATS or analytics — are rarely as strong as the dedicated point solution would be. So you're constantly negotiating between simplicity and capability. And then the second big one is data — HR teams are being asked to be more data-driven, to tell stories with numbers, to connect people metrics to business outcomes, and honestly the reporting in most of these mid-market platforms is still not there. You end up living in spreadsheets even when you're paying for a quote-unquote modern platform.

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm a Director of People Operations.
v.Q2: Just over five years. I came in as a senior HR manager and moved into the director role about two years ago.
v.Q3: We're in retail — specialty retail, specifically. We operate a chain of brick-and-mortar stores across the Midwest and Southeast, with our corporate headquarters in Columbus, Ohio. Headcount is around 750 right now, so solidly in the 500-to-1,000 range.
v.Q4: We're primarily on Rippling for core HR, payroll, and benefits. We also use a separate workforce scheduling tool for store-level hourly employees because Rippling's scheduling capabilities aren't really built for retail shift management at our scale. But Rippling is the system of record.
v.Q5: That was about two years ago, roughly.
v.Q6: We were on ADP Workforce Now. Had been on it for years before I joined, honestly. It was deeply embedded but also deeply frustrating.
v.Q7:
The primary driver was the ADP support experience — it had become genuinely unacceptable. Resolution times were long, we'd get bounced between service reps who didn't know our account, and payroll errors were taking weeks to correct. That's not something you can tolerate when you have hourly workers depending on accurate, timely paychecks.

The second driver was that our HR team had grown — I had added several new people ops specialists — and ADP's user experience made training new staff really difficult. The UI is honestly archaic. And we were doing a lot of manual work that we knew should be automated, like onboarding paperwork, benefits enrollment reminders, and offboarding checklists.

So it was poor support, manual process burden, and a UX that was slowing down my team. Those three things together made the case.
v.Q8: Retail has been going through a lot of pressure on labor costs and turnover, and our CFO was asking harder questions about HR efficiency. There was a general push across the company to modernize operations, and HR was expected to be part of that. So there was some top-down pressure to get our house in order from a systems standpoint.
v.Q9: The benefits enrollment process in ADP was a nightmare every open enrollment season. Employees couldn't navigate it easily on a phone, and we'd get hundreds of support requests from store staff who couldn't complete enrollment. We also had no good visibility into benefits participation rates or cost trends. Those were the operational pain points I most wanted to solve.
v.Q10: We looked at Rippling, Ceridian Dayforce, and UKG Ready. Those were the three we got to a full demo and pricing stage.
v.Q11: It had to handle multi-state payroll reliably — we operate in about twelve states, so that was non-negotiable. It needed a solid mobile experience for store employees who don't sit at desks. And it needed to be able to handle hourly wage configurations, shift differentials, and overtime rules correctly out of the box. Those were the hard minimums.
v.Q12: It was me, our CFO, and our VP of Store Operations. I led the evaluation and made the recommendation. The CFO controlled the budget approval, and the VP of Store Operations had to sign off because his teams are the primary end users. I'd call myself the primary recommender with CFO sign-off required.
v.Q13: We switched to Rippling.
v.Q14: Rippling's implementation timeline and the quality of their implementation support were genuinely better than the alternatives. Ceridian and UKG both had longer implementation windows and felt more like big-enterprise deployments. Rippling also had a cleaner mobile experience for employees, which mattered a lot for our store workforce. The automation capabilities — especially around onboarding — were meaningfully more modern. And the pricing was more competitive for our size than Ceridian.
v.Q15: Ceridian Dayforce is a strong product but it felt more suited to a company larger than us, and the implementation cost was higher than we were comfortable with. UKG Ready was actually a closer call — the scheduling module was better for retail, but the overall UX and the support model weren't as compelling as Rippling's, and a few peer references I checked came back mixed on their service quality post-sale.
v.Q16: Payroll runs cleanly and on time. The onboarding automation has reduced our manual paperwork significantly. Benefits enrollment is much more navigable for employees, and we've seen participation rates go up. The employee self-service experience is genuinely better than ADP — store employees can update their information, view pay stubs, and request time off without calling HR.
v.Q17: The scheduling piece is the obvious gap — we had to bring in a separate tool for that, which creates some integration overhead. I also think the reporting on workforce trends — turnover by store, tenure distribution, overtime spend by location — requires more manual configuration than it should. It's not impossible, but it's not as intuitive as I'd like.
v.Q18: The scheduling integration gap is probably the most operationally painful thing. We're running two systems and syncing data between them, and when something goes wrong — a punch that doesn't sync, a schedule change that doesn't flow into payroll correctly — it takes time to untangle. I'd characterize the frustration as moderate. It's manageable but it's a recurring source of noise for my team.
v.Q19: Honestly, our headcount has been pretty stable, so the growth pressure isn't what it was. What's changed is that we're more focused on retention now — reducing turnover, understanding what drives people to leave. So I need better workforce analytics and engagement data than I had on my radar two years ago.
v.Q20: I'd estimate somewhere in the $100K to $250K range annually for Rippling plus the scheduling tool we have layered on.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. It's a meaningful improvement over what we were paying for ADP with far more frustration, so I think the value equation is better. But I want to get more out of the analytics side before I'd call it a strong yes.
v.Q22: If the scheduling integration were native and reliable, I think that's worth somewhere in the $10K to $25K range, factoring in the cost of the separate scheduling tool we're paying for and the time my team spends managing the sync issues.
v.Q23: Very unlikely in the next six months. Switching at our size is a serious undertaking, and we're not at a breaking point. I'd want to see how Rippling's roadmap evolves on the analytics and scheduling front before I'd seriously entertain an evaluation.
v.Q24: In retail specifically, the hourly workforce experience is chronically underserved by the major HR platforms. Most of these tools are designed for a salaried office worker, and when you try to apply them to shift-based, high-turnover, multi-location environments, the seams show pretty quickly. I think the broader challenge is that HR platforms are still not as good at the intersection of workforce management and HR data as the industry needs them to be.

Q4: Point Solution Layered on Core Platform

cat.Q5: More than 24 months ago (24+ mo to 24+ mo)
cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm a Director of People Operations. I'm the only person on the HR side of the house, so I wear a lot of hats — everything from recruiting support to compliance to benefits to the day-to-day HR admin functions.
v.Q2: Coming up on two years. I joined when the company was around 55 people and we're now just under 90, so I've been here through a period of meaningful growth.
v.Q3: We're a B2B SaaS company — we build data infrastructure tooling, so pretty squarely in tech. Headcount is around 85 right now. We're fully distributed across the US, with a small cluster of folks in Austin where the founders are based, but otherwise everyone works remotely.
v.Q4: BambooHR is our HRIS and the center of everything. For payroll we actually run through Gusto because BambooHR's payroll product felt limited for what we needed when we set things up. And benefits are administered through a broker with a separate benefits portal. So technically it's a few tools, but BambooHR is the system of record for employee data.
v.Q5: That was about 18 months ago. Shortly after I joined, honestly — I came in and the tools we had were not set up in a way that could scale, so one of my first projects was to evaluate what we were actually using and whether it made sense.
v.Q6: We had a patchwork situation. The founders had set up Gusto early on for payroll and it had kind of organically become the de facto employee database too, even though it's not really designed for that. There was no actual HRIS. Offer letters were Word documents in a Google Drive folder. I think I'm kind of giggling because it's funny in retrospect, but at the time it was just a lot of manual work.
v.Q7:
The most immediate thing was that we had no real HRIS, which meant there was no single source of truth for employee data. Every time I needed to pull together org chart information, tenure data, or a headcount report, I was cobbling it together from Gusto, a spreadsheet, and whatever was in our ATS at the time.

We were also growing steadily, and without proper onboarding workflows, every new hire was kind of a manual project for me. I was spending probably a third of my time on onboarding administration that should have been systematized. And as a solo HR person, that's time I can't get back — every hour I spend on manual admin is an hour I'm not spending on anything strategic.

Compliance was also a real concern. We had employees in seven states at that point, and I was doing a lot of manual tracking to make sure we were staying current on state-specific requirements. That's the kind of thing that keeps you up at night when you're the only HR person.
v.Q8: I think the remote-first model was a big factor. In a fully distributed company, the HR tools are kind of the connective tissue — they're how employees experience the company in a tangible way, beyond Slack and Zoom. And our tools at the time were not giving anyone a good experience. There was also a general push from our CEO to build more people infrastructure ahead of a planned growth phase, so there was top-level support for investing in this area.
v.Q9:
Gusto as a pseudo-HRIS was genuinely painful. The org chart functionality was basically nonexistent, document management was limited, and there were no structured onboarding workflows. New hires would get a Gusto invite for payroll and then I'd have to manually email them a checklist of other things to complete, which felt unprofessional for a tech company that expects polish.

I also had no good way to track PTO across the company consistently. Different managers were tracking it in different ways, and it was creating equity issues — some employees felt like they could take unlimited time because no one was tracking it formally, and others felt constrained. Getting that into a real system was a priority.
v.Q10: I looked at BambooHR, Lattice, and Rippling. I also did a brief exploratory call with Personio, which is more of a European-focused platform, but I ruled them out quickly once I understood their US payroll story wasn't fully mature at the time.
v.Q11: It had to have real onboarding workflow functionality — not just a task checklist but actual sequencing, e-signature, and document management built in. It needed to work for a remote-only workforce, so a good employee self-service experience was essential. And I needed it to either handle PTO tracking natively and well, or integrate seamlessly with Gusto for payroll since I knew switching payroll systems at the same time would be too much to manage.
v.Q12: It was primarily me, with our CEO signing off on the budget. Our Head of Engineering also had a point of view because he manages the largest team and was feeling the most pain from the lack of onboarding structure. But I'd say I was the sole decision-maker on the selection itself — the CEO just needed to approve spend above a certain threshold, and he trusted my recommendation.
v.Q13: We added BambooHR as our HRIS while keeping Gusto for payroll. So it was more of an addition than a full replacement, and we've maintained that setup since.
v.Q14:
BambooHR honestly just fit where we were. The onboarding workflow builder was exactly what I needed — I could set up templated onboarding experiences by role type and everything flowed in a logical sequence. The employee self-service experience felt right for a remote team, and the UI was clean enough that I felt confident employees would actually use it without me having to hold their hand.

Price was also a real factor. At 85 people with a solo HR function, I have a limited budget to work with, and BambooHR's pricing was accessible in a way that Rippling wasn't — Rippling wanted me to take on more modules than I needed, and the overall cost was higher than I could justify at the time.

I also think the customer support experience during the sales process was genuinely good with BambooHR. They were patient, they understood the small-team context, and the implementation felt manageable for one person to own.
v.Q15:
Rippling was compelling from a platform breadth standpoint, but it felt like buying a lot more than I needed. The IT management and device provisioning features are great if you have an IT team, but I don't — I'm People Operations, and I wasn't going to own those workflows. The per-employee cost was also higher, and the implementation felt more complex than one person could reasonably manage.

Lattice is a strong product but it's really positioned around performance management and engagement. It's not really an HRIS at its core, so it would have left the employee record and onboarding problem unsolved.

Personio I ruled out quickly — their US presence and US payroll integration story wasn't mature enough at the time for me to feel confident.
v.Q16: BambooHR does onboarding really well for us — it's genuinely transformed how new hire experiences look. PTO tracking is clean and consistent, and the employee directory and org chart give us a shared source of truth that we didn't have before. The reporting on basic HR metrics — headcount, tenure, turnover — is easy to pull and good enough for what leadership asks me for on a regular basis.
v.Q17: The performance management module is honestly not great. We tried to run a review cycle through BambooHR and it felt clunky — the templates were rigid, the manager experience was confusing, and I ended up getting a lot of support tickets from people who couldn't figure out how to complete their sections. I'm kind of patching that with a Google Forms process right now, which isn't ideal. I also think their compensation management tooling is pretty limited for a company that wants to do structured pay bands.
v.Q18: Performance management is the biggest frustration by far. Running a semi-annual review cycle is a significant operational lift for me, and the BambooHR tooling doesn't reduce that lift — it might actually add to it because of how much configuration and cleanup is required. I'd call the frustration level significant. It's one of the highest-visibility things I do all year, and I'm doing it with a tool that wasn't built for it.
v.Q19: When I chose BambooHR, performance management was kind of an afterthought — we were so early-stage that we didn't have formal review cycles yet. Now that we're closer to 90 people, it's a real expectation from employees and from the CEO. So that's the biggest shift. I've also started thinking more seriously about compensation benchmarking and pay equity, which I couldn't even contemplate two years ago, and BambooHR doesn't help me there.
v.Q20: Between BambooHR and Gusto, I'd estimate we're in the $20K to $50K range annually. It's not a huge number in absolute terms, but it's meaningful relative to our overall HR budget.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes — but I think the value is more concentrated in BambooHR than in Gusto at this point, and I wonder sometimes if consolidating would be worth it.
v.Q22: If BambooHR had a genuinely good performance management module — one that worked intuitively for managers and didn't require me to do extensive training and handholding every review cycle — I think that's worth maybe $5K to $10K annually, when I factor in my time and the cost of the workarounds we currently use.
v.Q23: I'd say I'm somewhere between neutral and somewhat likely to at least consider it. The performance management gap is real enough that I've already started poking around at Lattice again and looking at what Culture Amp offers. I'm not committed to switching, but I'm not locked in either. If our next review cycle goes badly again, I think that tips me into a more active evaluation.
v.Q24: For solo HR people at small companies, the challenge is that most tools are either too simple — they're really just digital filing cabinets — or too complex and priced for teams that have multiple HR staff to manage them. There's a gap in the market for something that's genuinely full-featured but designed to be run by one person without a lot of overhead. And I think the AI conversation is starting to matter more too — people are asking why their HR system can't help them draft job descriptions or flag compliance risks automatically, and most platforms aren't really there yet.

v.Q1: Sure. I'm a Director of Talent Acquisition. I oversee recruiting strategy, vendor relationships, and the tooling stack we use to find and hire people across the company.
v.Q2: I've been here just under three years, so I'd say in the one-to-three year band, closer to the upper end of that.
v.Q3: We're a technology company — B2B SaaS, specifically. And we're sitting right around 380 employees right now, so solidly in that 251 to 500 range. We've been growing pretty aggressively over the last two years, which honestly is a big part of why tooling conversations keep coming up.
v.Q4: We're primarily on Rippling. It's our core platform for HR, payroll, and benefits administration. We also use Greenhouse on top of it for ATS functionality, because Rippling's native recruiting module wasn't quite where we needed it to be when we evaluated things. So it's kind of a two-platform setup, but Rippling is the system of record.
v.Q5: That was roughly 18 months ago, so within the last two years. It was a pretty focused evaluation — we had a clear trigger and moved through it relatively quickly compared to other software decisions I've been part of.
v.Q6: We were on BambooHR for core HRIS and payroll, and we had Lever as our ATS. So two separate tools, and neither one was really talking to the other in any meaningful way.
v.Q7: There were honestly several things converging at the same time. The biggest one was scaling pain — we had gone from about 180 employees to over 280 in roughly 14 months, and BambooHR was just not keeping up with what we needed operationally. Onboarding was almost entirely manual, and with the volume of new hires we were processing, that was becoming a real bottleneck. The integration between BambooHR and Lever was fragile. Offer data wasn't flowing cleanly, we had duplicate records, and the recruiting team was spending a lot of time on data hygiene instead of actually recruiting. There was also a payroll reliability issue — we had two payroll runs that had errors in the same quarter, and that got the CFO's attention very quickly. And then I think the third factor was that our IT team was pushing hard for a single-platform vendor that could handle device management and app provisioning alongside HR, which pointed pretty clearly toward a platform like Rippling.
v.Q8: We had just closed a Series B, and with that came a lot of pressure from the board to scale the team efficiently and show that we could hire without blowing up our HR overhead ratio. So there was real investor pressure behind the urgency. And I think broadly in the tech hiring market at that time, there was a lot of movement around consolidating the HR tech stack — that conversation was happening at a lot of companies our size. We weren't doing anything unusual, but the pressure to have a cleaner, more automated setup felt very real.
v.Q9: The manual onboarding workflow was probably the single biggest frustration. In BambooHR, every new hire required a checklist of manual steps across five or six different systems — sending equipment requests to IT, setting up Okta, getting them into Slack and Jira, all of that was entirely disconnected. We also had no meaningful reporting out of the recruiting side. Lever had its own analytics, but nothing was consolidated with our HRIS data, so headcount planning was basically happening in spreadsheets. And honestly the candidate experience during onboarding was a little embarrassing for a company that was trying to sell itself as a tech-forward employer.
v.Q10: We seriously looked at Rippling, Workday — which we pretty quickly took off the table — Lattice's HR product, and Deel, mostly because we had a few international contractors at that point. Rippling and Deel were the real finalists.
v.Q11: Absolutely. IT provisioning integration was non-negotiable — the tool had to be able to trigger device and app setup at the point of hire, not as a separate manual process. We also required a clean integration with whatever ATS we ended up keeping or adopting. Payroll had to be native — we weren't interested in a tool that outsourced payroll to a third party. And we had a soft price ceiling around $30 to $35 per employee per month all-in, because anything above that was going to be a hard conversation with finance.
v.Q12: Our VP of People had final sign-off authority — I was the primary recommender and ran the evaluation process end to end. Our CTO was involved specifically on the IT provisioning side, and he had strong opinions about the device management piece. Finance reviewed the pricing proposals and flagged a few contract terms. So it was HR plus IT plus Finance, with the VP of People making the final call based on my recommendation.
v.Q13: We switched. We moved to Rippling and migrated off BambooHR and Lever — well, we kept Greenhouse actually, because Rippling's ATS wasn't strong enough. So we switched our HRIS and payroll to Rippling.
v.Q14: Rippling stood out primarily because of the IT provisioning story. That was genuinely differentiated — no other vendor we looked at could do what Rippling does with device lifecycle and app provisioning natively within the same platform. The onboarding workflow automation was also meaningfully better than anything else we saw. You could build a workflow that triggers across HR, IT, and finance simultaneously at the point of offer acceptance, and that was very compelling for us. The demo was strong. Their implementation team had clearly done a lot of fast-growing tech company deployments, so they understood our context. And honestly, the per-seat pricing at our employee count was competitive enough that finance didn't push back hard.
v.Q15: Workday was off the table within the first week — it's built for companies with 1,000-plus employees and a dedicated HRIS team, and we had three people in HR at the time. v.Q1: I'm a Director of People Operations. My team handles everything from onboarding and HR compliance to compensation benchmarking and employee experience — pretty broad scope for a company our size, honestly.

We have about 215 employees. Most are full-time, and the team has been pretty stable in size for the last year or so.
v.Q4: Our primary platform is Rippling. We use it for core HRIS, payroll, benefits administration, and time and attendance. We also run 15Five separately for performance and engagement because Rippling's native performance tools don't meet our needs, but Rippling is definitely the center of gravity for the people operations function.
v.Q5: That evaluation was about two years ago. So I'd put it in the one-to-two-year window. It was actually a fairly long evaluation — I think we spent close to five months on it, which felt like a lot at the time but turned out to be worth it.
v.Q6: We were using ADP Workforce Now for payroll and had BambooHR as our HRIS. They were technically integrated, but the integration was unreliable enough that we kind of stopped trusting it and were manually reconciling employee data between the two systems on a monthly basis. It was a mess.
v.Q7: So there were really four things converging. First, the integration failure between ADP and BambooHR was genuinely unsustainable — when you're running a people operations team and you can't trust your own system of record, that's a foundational problem. Second, we had shifted to a fully remote model and our workforce was now spread across 23 states, and ADP's multi-state compliance handling at our tier of service was not keeping pace. We'd had two instances of late tax filings that the ADP team had to fix retroactively, and that created real anxiety for our finance team. Third, we were adding a lot of benefits complexity — we had moved to a multi-carrier benefits setup and neither BambooHR nor ADP was handling the enrollment and reconciliation work without a lot of manual intervention. And then the fourth thing was honestly just a leadership change — we brought in a new CFO who came from a company that used a more modern, consolidated platform, and she pushed pretty hard for a re-evaluation.
v.Q8: The remote shift was the biggest macro factor. We had gone from a single-office company in Austin to fully distributed essentially overnight, and the operational model for HR had to change with it. We needed tooling that was genuinely built for distributed workforces, not tools that had added remote features as an afterthought. There was also some pressure within our own client base — we do HR consulting, so our credibility partly depends on being seen as operationally sophisticated. Running on a fragmented stack was inconsistent with how we wanted to position ourselves externally.
v.Q9: The reconciliation burden was the most time-consuming frustration — I think my team was spending close to 20 hours a month just keeping data aligned between ADP and BambooHR. That's an enormous amount of wasted capacity. Beyond that, the employee self-service experience in BambooHR was okay but not great, and for a remote team where HR can't just walk over to someone's desk, self-service quality really matters. And I'd say the benefits administration in ADP was clunky enough that we were fielding a disproportionate number of enrollment support questions from employees because the interface was genuinely confusing.
v.Q10: We evaluated Rippling, Paylocity, Paycom, and Zenefits — which I think was rebranding to Trinet HR Platform at that point. We also had a demo with HiBob, which a few people on my team had pushed for because of the employee experience focus.

We'd lived that experience and didn't want to go back. Multi-state payroll compliance had to be native and strong, not bolted on. And we required a genuinely modern employee self-service mobile experience, because a remote workforce that's on mobile a lot needs that to work well. We also had a soft ceiling on pricing around $28 to $32 per employee per month.
v.Q12: I ran the full evaluation process and was the primary recommender. Our CFO had strong involvement — she reviewed all pricing proposals and had a veto on anything that exceeded budget. For us, that wasn't just a technical preference — it was a direct solution to the core problem we'd been experiencing. The multi-state compliance handling was clearly best in class among the options we evaluated. And I thought the employee experience layer in Rippling was significantly more modern than what Paylocity or Paycom were showing. The mobile app in particular looked and felt like something employees would actually use, which matters a lot for a distributed team. And you know, the implementation support was strong — we had a dedicated implementation manager who had done remote-first company deployments specifically, which gave us confidence.
v.Q15: Paylocity has a decent product, but when we dug into the architecture, payroll and HRIS are still separate modules that sync — it's not truly unified. I really liked the HiBob team and the product vision, but it wasn't the right fit for where we were.

v.Q17: Compensation management and benchmarking are genuinely weak in Rippling. v.Q19: Compensation and total rewards tooling has become much more critical as we've stabilized headcount and shifted focus from growth to retention. v.Q20: Across Rippling and 15Five, I'd estimate we're somewhere in the $75K to $95K range annually. So I'd put us in that $50K to $100K band.

v.Q22: If Rippling built a genuinely strong compensation management module — with salary banding, market benchmarking integrations, and structured merit cycle workflows — I think that's worth $15K to $20K annually to us, when you factor in the 15Five and compensation consulting costs we might be able to reduce, and the time savings for my team during merit season.
v.Q23: No, I don't think we'd switch in the next six months. I'd say very unlikely in that window. Neither path is clean, and I think most Directors and VPs of People are navigating that tension constantly. And I'd add that the compensation management and pay equity space specifically feels underserved for mid-market companies — there are point solutions, but nothing that's fully native in a modern HRIS platform in a way that's actually usable for a team of our size.

And third, I think the contract renewal was coming up anyway, so the combination of the reliability issues, the manual process pain, and the timing of the renewal created a natural window to say, okay, let's look at what's out there. It would have felt irresponsible not to evaluate at that point.

Honestly, yes. I needed a payroll and HR platform that could keep pace with that regulatory environment rather than one that was always a step behind.

There was also a broader conversation at the board level about operational efficiency. We're not growing headcount rapidly right now — we're in a more stable phase — but the board was very focused on ensuring that our back-office infrastructure could scale if we did decide to add sites or acquire a smaller practice. v.Q10: We looked at Gusto, Paychex Flex, Rippling, and we had a demo with Paylocity as well. We also had a brief conversation with Namely, but I think they didn't quite make it to the serious consideration stage — they came up in initial research but we didn't go deep on them.

We also required a benefits administration module that could connect directly to our broker, or at minimum had strong EDI support for carrier connections. The manual reconciliation problem we had with ADP was something we were not willing to replicate.

And I'd say a credible implementation and customer support model was a requirement — not a nice-to-have. Given the disruption that a payroll migration causes in a healthcare org, I needed to know we would have a dedicated resource or at least a structured onboarding program, not just a knowledge base and a chat bot.
v.Q12:

He wasn't evaluating the HR features, but he had a veto right on anything that didn't meet our security requirements.

That mattered to me because benefits enrollment is one of those high-visibility HR moments where the technology either builds goodwill with employees or frustrates them.

The pricing was also more transparent than some of the competitors. Paylocity, for example, had a very opaque quoting process and the total cost of ownership was hard to pin down until late in the evaluation. Gusto's pricing model was cleaner and the per-employee cost landed well within our budget parameters.

v.Q15:

v.Q24:
I think the fundamental tension most HR leaders at mid-size companies face is that the tool market is bifurcated. You have lightweight SMB tools that are easy to use and affordable but run out of capability as you scale, and you have enterprise platforms that have all the features but are priced and architected for organizations much larger than yours. And most of us in the two-to-five-hundred-employee range are sitting right in the middle of that gap, constantly making tradeoffs.

On top of that, the pace of change in what HR technology is expected to do has accelerated — everyone's talking about AI, predictive analytics, skills-based hiring — and it's genuinely hard to evaluate whether those capabilities in current platforms are real and mature or whether they're marketing features that sound good in a demo and don't hold up in practice. I think that skepticism combined with the switching cost reality means a lot of HR leaders are staying put on tools that are good enough rather than risking a disruptive migration for uncertain upside.

Q4: Point Solution Layered on Core Platform

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats
