v.Q21: Somewhat yes — but it's getting less so over time. When I look at the total spend across those tools and then think about how much manual work we're still doing, the value equation feels less compelling than it did two years ago. I think if we were getting strong analytics and a modern employee experience, I'd say yes, clearly. But right now I'm paying for a collection of tools that each do their specific thing adequately and don't really add up to a coherent platform.
v.Q22: If BambooHR had genuinely strong workforce analytics and compensation equity reporting built in — the kind of thing where I could run a multi-variable equity analysis in twenty minutes instead of a day — I think that would be worth somewhere in the ten to twenty-five thousand dollar range to us annually. When I factor in the time my team spends on manual reporting work and multiply that by our fully loaded cost, we're probably losing close to that in productivity already.
v.Q23: I'd say consideration is likely — I'm honestly already in a kind of passive monitoring mode where I'm keeping an eye on what's out there. Switching in the next six months specifically, I'd say somewhat unlikely. The timing needs to be right, and right now I'm focused on a compensation review cycle that's going to take most of my bandwidth for the next quarter. But I think there's a realistic chance I re-open a formal evaluation within the next twelve to eighteen months, especially if the analytics gap continues to be painful.
v.Q24: I think the number one challenge is that the market has fragmented so much that you're almost always stitching together a stack rather than running on one true platform, and the integration between those tools is never as seamless as the vendors claim. Every integration has edge cases and failure modes that you only discover after you've signed the contract. The second big challenge is that the analytics and reporting capabilities across most SMB-focused HR tools are genuinely not good enough for what modern HR teams are being asked to deliver. Boards and CFOs want workforce data that can inform strategy, and most tools are still optimized around administrative accuracy rather than insight generation. And I think there's a real challenge around the pace of change — AI capabilities, remote and hybrid compliance complexity, new state-level laws — the platforms that were built even four or five years ago are struggling to keep up, and it creates real risk for HR leaders who are being held accountable for compliance in environments their tools weren't designed for.

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm a manager in HR. My role is a little bit of everything — employee relations, benefits administration, compliance, and some recruiting when we have openings. In healthcare at our size, you wear a lot of hats and you kind of have to be comfortable with that.
v.Q2: Coming up on six years. So definitely in the five-to-ten-year band. I've seen a lot of change here, which I guess gives me a pretty long lens on how our HR needs have evolved.
v.Q3: We're in healthcare — specifically we're an outpatient behavioral health clinic group. We operate three clinic locations here in the greater Columbus, Ohio area. Our headcount is right around seventy-five people, and honestly it's been pretty flat for the past couple of years. We went through a phase of growth about three years back and then things stabilized, which has actually been a welcome change after a pretty chaotic stretch.
v.Q4: We use Gusto as our primary platform — it handles payroll, basic HR records, and benefits administration. We also use a separate credentialing and licensing management tool because in behavioral health, every clinician has a set of licenses and certifications that have to be tracked and renewed on specific cycles, and Gusto doesn't do anything useful there. So that's a parallel system we run. For recruiting, when we do it, we've been using Indeed and just managing things kind of manually through a shared spreadsheet, which I know isn't ideal.
v.Q5: About fourteen months ago. So within the last twelve to eighteen months — I'd put it solidly in the within-the-last-twelve-months to one-to-two-years range. It was a fairly structured evaluation, not just a conversation.
v.Q6: We were on Gusto, same as now. So this was an evaluation of whether to stay on Gusto or move to something else, not a greenfield selection. We'd been on Gusto for a few years at that point.
v.Q7:
There were a few things that came together pretty close in time. The most immediate trigger was a compliance issue — not a major one, but significant enough to get our Executive Director's attention. We had a situation where we weren't properly tracking mandatory continuing education credits for some of our licensed counselors, and when one of our payers did a credentialing audit, it created a stressful few weeks. Our credentialing tool at the time was pretty basic, and Gusto obviously wasn't helping with that at all. That conversation naturally expanded into a broader question of whether our HR technology was fit for purpose in a regulated clinical environment.

The second motivator was that I had taken on benefits administration more formally about a year prior, and I was finding Gusto's benefits features more limited than I needed. Managing open enrollment manually through Gusto's interface, trying to reconcile carrier invoices, dealing with qualifying life event paperwork — it was all more manual than I expected for a platform that's supposed to handle this stuff. I had two HR coordinators spending significant time each month just on benefits reconciliation, which felt wrong.

And the third thing was honestly a conversation I had with a peer at another behavioral health organization at a regional HR conference. She had switched her organization to a different platform and was describing how much easier compliance tracking had become. That planted a seed that maybe we were just used to the friction and hadn't stopped to ask whether it had to be this way.
v.Q8:
Yes, definitely. The healthcare compliance environment has been getting more complex, not less. Ohio has been updating some of its behavioral health licensing requirements, and there's been federal movement around mental health parity regulations that creates documentation requirements we weren't fully prepared for. I think there was a general sense at the leadership level that our administrative infrastructure needed to get more rigorous, and that included our HR technology.

Also, we were coming out of a period where we'd had some staff turnover that I think was partly driven by burnout and workload — which is extremely common in behavioral health — and leadership was interested in doing more with employee experience and wellbeing as a retention strategy. There was an expectation that HR should be doing more proactive work in that area, which required tools that could support things like engagement tracking and manager-employee check-ins, none of which Gusto does. So the scope of what we were asking HR technology to do was expanding even as our headcount was staying flat.
v.Q9:
Quite a few, honestly. Benefits administration was probably the loudest pain point in terms of day-to-day frustration. Gusto is okay for simple benefits setups, but we have a fairly complex benefits package because we're competing for licensed clinicians who have options — we offer multiple medical plan options, we have a dental and vision plan, an HSA, and some supplemental coverage. Managing all of that through Gusto was more error-prone than I was comfortable with, and I was spending real time each month chasing down discrepancies between what Gusto showed and what the carriers were billing.

The second frustration was the absence of any meaningful HR analytics. I couldn't pull a turnover report that broke down voluntary versus involuntary departures by department or tenure band. I couldn't see compensation positioning by role relative to our own salary bands. Everything that required any analysis meant exporting to a spreadsheet, and by the time I'd done the analysis, I wasn't sure the data was current.

And the third thing was the absence of any structured performance management capability. We had been doing annual reviews through a Google Form process, which is, I think we can all agree, not ideal. I wanted something that could support structured check-ins and goal tracking, especially given that we were trying to do more around retention and manager development.
v.Q10: We looked at BambooHR pretty seriously — they were actually the frontrunner for a while. We also had conversations with Paycor, which a couple of other healthcare organizations in our network were using. And we looked at Zenefits, which I know has gone through some changes, but they came up in our initial research. Those were the three we got to some version of a demo with.
v.Q11: We had some clear lines. Benefits administration had to be genuinely strong — not just payroll with benefits bolted on, but a real enrollment workflow with carrier connections and reconciliation support. That was probably the hardest filter because it eliminated a few tools pretty quickly. We also needed some form of performance management — even if it wasn't sophisticated, it needed to be built in rather than requiring yet another integration. And we needed the vendor to have demonstrated experience with healthcare clients specifically, because I didn't want to be explaining what credentialing is to a customer success rep. We also had a budget ceiling — I'd done some benchmarking and knew what comparable organizations were paying, and I was not going to recommend something that doubled our per-employee HR tech spend.
v.Q12: The decision was primarily mine to recommend, with final approval from our Executive Director, who is also our de facto People leader in terms of organizational authority. Our Director of Finance was involved because any new contract above a certain threshold requires her sign-off, and the budget conversation was real. I also looped in one of our senior clinical managers who I trust to give me honest feedback on the employee experience side of things — she sat in on one of the BambooHR demos and gave me her impressions of how the self-service features would land with our clinical staff. So it was a small group, but it wasn't just me deciding in isolation. I was clearly the primary recommender and did all the heavy lifting on the evaluation.
v.Q13: We stayed with Gusto. It was not the outcome I necessarily expected going in — I had gone into the evaluation fairly open to switching — but when we got to the end, the case for switching wasn't strong enough to justify the disruption and the cost increase.
v.Q14:
The honest answer is that it was less about Gusto standing out and more about the alternatives not clearing the bar in the ways that mattered most.

But specifically on Gusto — the payroll reliability has been excellent and that matters enormously in our environment. We have clinical staff who are paid on a combination of salary and productivity-based compensation, and payroll errors create a level of distrust with clinicians that is very hard to repair. Gusto has never made a payroll error in six years, which is something I can't say lightly.

We also got a better sense during the evaluation of some Gusto features we hadn't been using — there were some HR document management and e-signature capabilities that I hadn't activated, and when I set those up during the evaluation period, it actually reduced some of the paper-based friction we'd been dealing with. So part of the decision was recognizing that we hadn't fully utilized what we were already paying for.

And finally, the switching cost in a clinical environment is real. Migrating payroll history, re-enrolling employees in a new benefits system mid-year, and retraining staff who were already comfortable with Gusto's self-service — the disruption risk felt higher than the potential upside, given that none of the alternatives were clearly superior on the dimensions that mattered most to us.
v.Q15:
BambooHR was the hardest rejection because I genuinely liked the product. The employee experience is much better than Gusto's, the HR features are richer, and the performance management module seemed like it would actually get used. But when we got into the details of benefits administration, it became clear that they rely on a third-party broker integration model that would have meant our current broker needed to support a specific connection, which she didn't. Setting up a new broker relationship at the same time as implementing a new HRIS felt like too many moving parts. That one genuinely stung.

Paycor was interesting because they have strong healthcare experience and a credentialing module — which is something I actually need. But the pricing was significantly higher than what we're paying now, and when I ran the numbers on a per-employee basis, it was hard to justify for a seventy-five-person organization. It's more of an enterprise healthcare product than we need right now. Their implementation timeline was also quoted at about three months, and I didn't have the bandwidth to manage a three-month implementation project while keeping everything else running.

Zenefits — honestly, the product had improved from what I'd heard about it a few years prior, but the brand reputation in healthcare was a concern. Some of the people I spoke with in my professional network had hesitations, and in a compliance-sensitive environment, vendor trust matters more than it might in other industries.
v.Q16: Gusto is genuinely reliable on payroll, and I want to give that credit because it's not a small thing. Tax filings are handled automatically, direct deposit works without issues, and the year-end W-2 process is about as painless as I've experienced anywhere. The employee self-service features for basic things — checking pay stubs, updating personal information, downloading tax documents — are clean enough that I don't get a lot of HR tickets for those tasks. And the onboarding flow for new hires is decent. It's not exciting, but it works.
v.Q17: The performance management gap is still very real. We ended up implementing a lightweight check-in process using a Google Form and a calendar reminder system, which is not sustainable as a long-term approach. Benefits administration is still more manual than I want — I'm still doing monthly carrier reconciliation by hand. And the reporting really is just not there for an organization that's trying to be more data-informed about our workforce. I know I keep coming back to that, but it's a persistent friction point.
v.Q18: The benefits reconciliation process is my biggest operational frustration right now and I'd describe the intensity as significant. Every month I or one of my coordinators has to manually compare what Gusto shows as enrolled employees against what each carrier is billing us. In a perfect world those would match. In practice, there are almost always discrepancies — someone had a qualifying life event, someone was terminated mid-month, someone's dependent turned twenty-six — and resolving those discrepancies requires logging into the carrier portals, comparing line by line, and sometimes calling carrier representatives. We probably spend close to eight to ten hours per month on this across my team, and it's the kind of work that is low-value but high-risk, because if you miss something, you're either overpaying premiums or, worse, someone finds out their coverage lapsed because the enrollment didn't sync correctly. In healthcare, that second scenario is not something I'm willing to let happen.
v.Q19: A few things have become clearer since we went through the evaluation. The compliance complexity in behavioral health has continued to increase — Ohio Medicaid has rolled out some new documentation requirements for our credentialed providers that I'm now tracking manually alongside everything else. I think I've also become more serious about the performance and engagement side of HR than I was eighteen months ago. We had two good clinicians leave in the past year for organizations that they described as more supportive in terms of manager relationships and career development, and I think better tooling for structured conversations could have helped there. And honestly, the time I spend doing manual work in Gusto is time I'm not spending on things that actually require my expertise, and that's starting to bother me more than it used to.
v.Q20: Across Gusto and our credentialing tool, I think we're in the five to twenty thousand dollar range annually. Gusto is the majority of that.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes on the payroll side. Less so when I think about the totality of what we're getting. The manual work my team does that should be automated — if I assign an hourly cost to that — probably erodes the apparent cost savings of using a lower-priced tool. So it's reasonable on paper but less so when you account for the true cost of ownership.
v.Q22: If Gusto had automated carrier reconciliation — something that could directly compare our enrollment data to carrier billing and flag discrepancies automatically — I think that would be worth somewhere in the five to ten thousand dollar range annually. When I think about the staff hours we spend on it and the risk of errors, that feels like a conservative estimate honestly.
v.Q23: I'd say consideration is somewhat likely within the next six months — I'm at the point where the benefits reconciliation frustration and the performance management gap are both bad enough that I'm mentally ready to look again. Switching within six months is probably somewhat unlikely just because of the timing relative to our benefits renewal cycle, which I don't want to disrupt. But I could see a formal evaluation happening in the fall, honestly.
v.Q24: I think one of the most common challenges for HR managers in mid-sized organizations is that the tools built for small businesses stop being adequate well before you can afford the tools built for large enterprises. There's a gap in the market right now where you're a hundred people and you need real benefits administration and real analytics and some version of performance management, but everything at that capability level is priced and scoped as if you have an IT team and a six-month implementation runway. The second big challenge, especially in healthcare and other regulated industries, is that compliance requirements are evolving faster than most HR platforms update their features. And I think there's a real challenge around the employee experience expectations gap — employees today expect their HR portal to feel like the consumer apps they use every day, and most HR platforms, especially in the SMB space, are genuinely behind on that.

Q4: Point Solution Layered on Core Platform

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: Sure. I'm a Director of HR at a professional services firm based in Chicago. I've been in this role for a little over three years now, and I oversee the full HR function — everything from recruiting and onboarding through benefits administration and employee relations.
v.Q2: I think it's just about four years total, so slightly longer than I've been in the director seat.
v.Q3: We're in professional services — specifically management consulting and advisory work, primarily for mid-market clients. And we're sitting right around 190 employees right now, so comfortably in that 101 to 250 range.
v.Q4: We're primarily on Rippling now. It handles our HRIS, payroll, and benefits administration, and we also use a couple of the add-on modules — specifically their device management piece, which matters a lot for us given how we handle client-sensitive data. So honestly it functions as a pretty unified platform for us at this point.
v.Q5: That evaluation was roughly two years ago, so it would've been in the first half of my tenure as director. I had inherited the prior setup and fairly quickly started questioning whether it was the right fit for where we were headed.
v.Q6: We were using ADP Workforce Now for payroll, and separately we had BambooHR handling the HRIS side — employee records, PTO, performance stuff. They weren't integrated in any meaningful way, and that was a core part of the problem.
v.Q7:
There were honestly several things converging at once. The biggest one was the integration failure I just mentioned — running ADP and BambooHR separately meant our data was constantly out of sync. Someone would get a salary change in ADP and it would take days or longer to reflect accurately elsewhere. That created real compliance risk for us, and in a consulting environment, we are held to a pretty high standard around process integrity. So that was the primary driver.

Beyond that, we were growing at a steady clip — not explosive growth, but adding somewhere between 15 and 20 people a year — and the manual overhead of keeping two systems aligned was starting to consume a disproportionate amount of my team's time. I also had a new CFO come on board who was pushing for more consolidated spend reporting, and he had questions about what we were actually paying for HR tech and whether we were getting value. That created a kind of executive-level pressure to rationalize what we had. And then honestly the ADP contract was coming up for renewal, and that felt like a natural moment to ask whether we should just rethink the whole stack.
v.Q8: I think the broader shift toward digital operations in professional services was real context for this. Clients were increasingly expecting their advisors to model good operational hygiene, and internally we had a digital transformation initiative underway that was touching every function. HR wasn't exempt from that pressure. There was also a general expectation from our partners and leadership that we would modernize infrastructure to support a hybrid-capable workforce, even though we are primarily in-office — we wanted the optionality.
v.Q9:
Absolutely. The reporting situation was really painful. Between BambooHR and ADP, I couldn't pull a single coherent headcount or compensation report without manually reconciling two exports in a spreadsheet. That felt embarrassing, honestly, for a function my size. We had eleven people on the HR team and we were still doing this manually.

Beyond reporting, the onboarding experience was fragmented — new hires were touching three or four different systems in their first week, which created a bad first impression. And benefits enrollment was a separate workflow altogether that felt completely disconnected from everything else. My team was spending real time just being system coordinators rather than doing anything that looked like strategic HR work.
v.Q10: We looked seriously at Rippling, Workday — though we pretty quickly determined it was oversized for us — Paylocity, and TriNet as a kind of PEO alternative. We also took a brief look at Lattice but that was more of a performance-focused play and didn't really address the full stack problem.
v.Q11: Yes, I was pretty firm on a few things. First, native payroll — I wasn't interested in another integration where payroll lived in a separate system. Second, it had to support benefits administration with carrier connections, not just record-keeping. Third, we needed SSO and strong role-based permissions because of our client data obligations. And fourth, honestly, it had to have a credible implementation track record for companies our size. I'd heard too many stories about platforms that sold well and then had terrible go-live experiences.
v.Q12: The CFO was involved from the start, primarily around cost and contract terms. Our head of IT had a seat at the table because of the device management and security requirements. And I brought in two of my senior HR managers to evaluate usability and workflow fit. Ultimately I was the primary recommender — I drove the evaluation, built the scorecard, and presented the recommendation — but the CFO had final sign-off authority on anything above a certain spend threshold, which this cleared.
v.Q13: We switched. We moved to Rippling, which meant deprecating both ADP and BambooHR and consolidating onto a single platform.
v.Q14:
Rippling stood out primarily because of the unification story — the fact that HRIS, payroll, benefits, and IT management all lived in one data model was genuinely differentiated at our size point. Paylocity was a reasonable payroll platform but the HRIS piece felt like an afterthought, and the IT management capability wasn't there at all. Workday was frankly oversized — the implementation complexity and cost were not appropriate for 190 people. TriNet as a PEO had some appeal but I didn't want to give up direct employer control over our HR processes, especially for a consulting firm where workforce strategy is a meaningful part of how we differentiate ourselves.

With Rippling, the demo experience was also notably better — their sales team actually understood our specific context, which I appreciated. And the pricing, while not the lowest, felt defensible when I modeled out what we were spending across two systems plus the labor cost of reconciling them manually.
v.Q15: Workday — too enterprise, too expensive, and the implementation timeline was going to be six to nine months minimum. Not right for a firm our size. Paylocity — solid payroll, but the HRIS and benefits modules felt underdeveloped, and they couldn't do IT management at all, which was a requirement for us. TriNet — the PEO model itself was the problem. Ceding employer-of-record status and having less flexibility on benefits design was a nonstarter for our leadership. And Lattice — genuinely wasn't in the running for the full stack, it was more of a curiosity on the performance management side.
v.Q16: Rippling does the unification piece really well, and that continues to be its primary value for us. The fact that a new hire flows through one workflow and lands correctly in payroll, benefits, and IT provisioning simultaneously is genuinely something my team appreciates every single week. Reporting has improved substantially — I can pull headcount, compensation, and turnover data in one place without a spreadsheet reconciliation. And the employee self-service experience is clean and modern, which reduces the volume of routine questions my team fields.
v.Q17: The performance management module honestly leaves a lot to be desired. We've been managing performance cycles through a kind of workaround in Rippling, and it's not purpose-built for what we need. I've been eyeing dedicated performance tools as a potential addition. Customer support has also been inconsistent — when something is routine it's fine, but when we hit something complex or time-sensitive, getting a knowledgeable person on the line is harder than it should be.
v.Q18: I think the biggest frustration right now is the support experience. When we have a payroll issue that needs to be resolved before a run closes, the ticket-based support model is not adequate. I'd characterize that as a significant frustration — it's not so bad that I'm ready to blow up the platform, but it's a recurring source of stress for my team and it erodes confidence in the system over time.
v.Q19: Performance management has become a more prominent need — when we adopted Rippling we were okay with a lighter-weight approach, but as we've grown and as expectations from employees around career development have increased, I feel the gap more acutely. I've also developed stronger expectations around analytics — I want predictive retention signals, not just historical headcount data.
v.Q20: I believe we're somewhere in the $50,000 to $100,000 range annually, all in across the Rippling modules we use.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. It's defensible when I think about what we were spending across two disconnected systems and factor in the labor savings. But I wouldn't say I feel like we're getting exceptional value — it's more like appropriate value.
v.Q22: For a genuinely improved support model — dedicated account management, faster resolution on payroll-critical issues — I think that's worth somewhere in the $10,000 to $25,000 range to us. That's real time and stress it would recover.
v.Q23: I'd say somewhat unlikely for the full platform, but I'm actively evaluating adding a dedicated performance management tool alongside Rippling. A full replacement isn't on my near-term agenda — the switching cost is real and I don't have the organizational appetite for it right now.
v.Q24: I think the biggest challenge is the tension between wanting an all-in-one platform and the reality that no single platform is best-in-class across every module. You end up either accepting mediocrity in certain areas to preserve integration simplicity, or you add point solutions and reintroduce the integration headaches you were trying to escape. That tradeoff doesn't have a clean answer, and I think most HR directors at companies our size are navigating that constantly. The other challenge I hear consistently is support quality at scale — vendors grow their customer base and support doesn't scale with it.

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm a Senior Manager in People Operations. I'm based in Atlanta and I support a healthcare organization that operates across a few states.
v.Q2: Coming up on three years. I joined right before things got complicated with our restructuring, which was interesting timing.
v.Q3: Healthcare. We operate outpatient behavioral health clinics, so it's a pretty regulated environment. Right now we're around 320 employees, though we were closer to 400 a year and a half ago before the restructuring.
v.Q4: We're on Rippling now. It covers HRIS, payroll, and benefits. We also use a separate credentialing tool because of our clinical staff requirements, but for the core HR stack it's Rippling.
v.Q5: That was roughly a year and a half ago, so within the last two years. It overlapped directly with the start of our restructuring, which shaped the evaluation a lot.
v.Q6: We were on Paycom. Had been for a couple of years before I arrived, I think.
v.Q7: Honestly, the restructuring was the main trigger. We were reducing headcount, which meant a wave of offboarding, and Paycom's workflows for terminations and final pay compliance across multiple states were genuinely difficult to manage. Healthcare is heavily regulated, and multi-state final pay rules vary a lot — California especially is brutal if you get it wrong. Beyond that, the cost structure on Paycom didn't make sense as we shrank. We were paying a per-employee rate that was calibrated for a larger workforce, and it felt punitive given the circumstances. So it was a combination of compliance risk and cost pressure at the same time.
v.Q8: The hybrid shift had created some operational complexity too. We had a mix of clinical staff who were on-site and administrative staff who were remote, and the tool we had wasn't handling that split workforce cleanly. There was also a broader push from our executive team to reduce vendor count across the organization, and HR tech was on the list.
v.Q9: Yes. Multi-state payroll compliance was the biggest pain point — I mentioned that. But I'd add that the reporting in Paycom was hard to use. Getting a clean headcount report by location or employment type required way too many steps. And the self-service experience for employees was clunky enough that we got a steady volume of basic questions that should have been self-solvable. That stuff taxes a team that was already going through a stressful period.
v.Q10: We looked at Rippling, Paylocity, and briefly at Gusto, though Gusto felt a bit underpowered for our compliance needs pretty quickly.
v.Q11: Multi-state payroll was non-negotiable — had to be built-in and reliable, not bolted on. We also needed strong offboarding workflows because of where we were at. And I wanted something where benefits administration wasn't a separate product that required a separate login. Those were kind of the gates.
v.Q12: Our CFO and controller were involved on the cost and contract side. Our VP of HR — I report to her — had final approval. I drove the evaluation day to day, scored the vendors, ran the demos with my team, and made the recommendation. So I was the primary recommender with the VP as the formal approver.
v.Q13: We switched. Moved from Paycom to Rippling.
v.Q14: Rippling's multi-state payroll compliance automation was the main reason — it genuinely handled the complexity of our clinical and administrative workforce across different states. The offboarding workflows were solid and configurable. I also liked that it was a single platform with a real data model underneath everything, not a patchwork. Paylocity was competitive but felt like it had more of a traditional payroll DNA and less of the modern HR ops sensibility I was looking for. And honestly, the Rippling implementation team during the sales process was responsive and specific, which gave me confidence.
v.Q15: Gusto — too SMB-focused, didn't have the compliance depth we needed for healthcare across multiple states, and their customer support model felt too light for our risk profile. Paylocity — it was a close second honestly, but the UX felt dated compared to Rippling and the integration story across modules was less cohesive. That mattered to me because I didn't want to recreate the fragmentation problem we were solving.
v.Q16: Payroll accuracy and compliance across states has been solid — that was the core problem we were solving and it's held up. The employee self-service experience is genuinely good, and we've seen a reduction in routine questions to our team. Onboarding workflows are flexible and we've built out some good automations there.
v.Q17: The analytics are still not quite where I need them. I can get the data out but building dashboards that are meaningful for our restructuring conversations takes more manual work than it should. Also, benefits carrier connectivity has had some reliability issues — occasionally eligibility files don't transmit cleanly and we have to manually intervene.
v.Q18: The benefits carrier file issues are the most acute frustration. When an employee's coverage doesn't update correctly because of a transmission error, that's a compliance and employee relations problem simultaneously. I'd call that a significant frustration — it's not constant but when it happens it's a fire drill. It's the one area where I feel like Rippling has underdelivered relative to what was sold to us.
v.Q19: Our workforce has continued to shrink, so I'm now thinking more about rightsizing the cost of our HR tech stack. I'm also more focused on retention analytics — understanding which clinical staff are attrition risks matters a lot more now that we're smaller and every departure is meaningful. That kind of workforce intelligence wasn't really on my radar two years ago.
v.Q20: I think we're in the $50,000 to $100,000 range right now, though that's come down from what it was when we were larger.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. The compliance value is real and I can justify the core spend. But some of the module pricing feels high for features that aren't fully baked yet — analytics especially.
v.Q22: If the benefits carrier connectivity worked flawlessly — no manual interventions, clean EDI transmissions every time — I think that's worth somewhere in the $5,000 to $10,000 range annually in recovered time and reduced compliance risk exposure.
v.Q23: I'd say somewhat unlikely. We just came out of a transition and another one right now would be too disruptive given everything else the organization is managing. I'm more focused on making Rippling work better for us than on replacing it.
v.Q24: I think the top challenge is that these platforms were mostly built for growth scenarios, and a lot of HR teams right now are managing flat or declining workforces. The offboarding, restructuring, and cost-optimization use cases aren't as well-supported as the hire-fast, onboard-fast use cases. There's also a real gap in how well these tools support compliance in highly regulated industries — healthcare especially. It's not enough to have payroll that works for tech companies.

v.Q1: I'm a Director of People Operations. I'm based in Boston, and our company is a registered investment advisory firm, so we sit within financial services. I have a team of seven and I report directly to our COO.
v.Q2: I've been here about two and a half years. The company was in a pretty different place when I joined — we were around 95 people — and we've grown significantly since then.
v.Q3: Financial services — specifically registered investment advisory and wealth management. We're at about 215 employees today. Two years ago we were under a hundred, so you can see why the HR infrastructure conversation has been pretty active.
v.Q4: We're primarily on BambooHR for our HRIS — employee records, onboarding, PTO, performance. Payroll runs through Paychex Flex, which predates my time here and is kind of a legacy situation. Benefits administration is handled through a combination of our broker's portal and some manual BambooHR tracking. So it's kind of a split stack, which I'll be honest, is something I'm actively thinking about changing.
v.Q5: That was about eighteen months ago. We had crossed the hundred-person threshold and the tools we had at the time were starting to show real strain.
v.Q6: We had Namely at the time. It was the system that had been put in place before I joined, and it was trying to do HRIS and payroll together but not doing either particularly well.
v.Q7:
Growth was the primary driver, full stop. We had been adding 25 to 35 people per year and the Namely setup that worked fine at 70 employees was buckling under the weight of actually operationalizing HR at scale. Onboarding was taking too long because too much of it was manual or required my team to intervene at every step. The performance review cycles were being tracked in separate spreadsheets because the Namely module wasn't configurable enough for what our leadership wanted.

We also had a compliance trigger. As a registered investment advisory firm, we have SEC and FINRA obligations that touch our HR data, and I was increasingly uncomfortable with our audit trail capabilities in Namely. If we ever needed to demonstrate that we had properly documented a hiring decision or a disciplinary action, I wasn't confident we could do that cleanly. That was a significant escalation factor that got the COO and our General Counsel involved. And then there was just general frustration — my team was doing a lot of workarounds that I knew weren't sustainable as we kept growing.
v.Q8: There was some investor-level interest in our operational maturity — we had brought on a strategic investor and they asked some pointed questions about our people infrastructure. That created a kind of indirect board pressure to demonstrate that HR was professionalized. In financial services generally, I think there's an increasing regulatory expectation around HR documentation and auditability, and that's only intensified. Those macro dynamics reinforced what we were already feeling internally.
v.Q9:
Definitely. The audit trail issue I mentioned was the most serious one — it kept me up at night a little, honestly. Beyond that, Namely's reporting was surface-level at best. I couldn't do meaningful workforce analytics without exporting data and doing my own analysis. For a firm where the COO wants quarterly workforce reviews, that was a real gap.

The candidate experience during onboarding was also problematic. We recruit a lot of credentialed financial professionals who have high expectations, and our onboarding process looked embarrassingly manual compared to what some of them were used to at larger institutions. New hires would sometimes comment on it, which reflects poorly on us as an employer brand.

And integration was a chronic problem — Namely didn't connect cleanly with our ATS, which was Greenhouse at the time, and so the handoff from recruiting to onboarding was always a manual data re-entry exercise.
v.Q10: We seriously evaluated BambooHR, Rippling, and HiBob. We also had initial conversations with UKG Ready but fairly quickly determined it was more implementation complexity than we needed.
v.Q11: I had a few firm requirements. First, a robust audit log and document management capability — this was non-negotiable given our regulatory environment. Second, I needed a clean API or native integration with Greenhouse, our ATS. Third, the performance management module had to be genuinely configurable, not just a checkbox feature. And fourth, I needed the vendor to have a credible customer base in financial services or similarly regulated industries — I wanted references I could call who would understand our context.
v.Q12: The COO had final approval authority. Our General Counsel reviewed the security and compliance documentation for each vendor and had an informal veto on anything she wasn't comfortable with from a regulatory standpoint. I drove the full evaluation — built the RFP framework, ran all the demos, managed the reference calls, and synthesized the recommendation. Two of my People Ops managers also participated in demos specifically to evaluate usability from a day-to-day operations perspective.
v.Q13: We switched. We moved to BambooHR, and separately retained Paychex for payroll because the COO wanted to sequence the transition and not change payroll processors at the same time.
v.Q14:
BambooHR won primarily on usability and time-to-value. For a team my size doing a platform migration while also managing rapid growth, the implementation complexity of Rippling was a real concern. I felt like Rippling was asking me to make a bigger organizational investment — more configuration, more IT involvement, a steeper learning curve — than I could realistically manage at that moment. BambooHR's onboarding was straightforward and my team was productive in it within weeks.

The audit trail and document management capabilities in BambooHR were genuinely strong, and they had solid financial services references. HiBob was actually a close contender — I liked their engagement and culture features a lot — but their compliance documentation was lighter and some of their financial services clients were primarily European, which made the regulatory parallels less relevant for us.

I'll be honest that the payroll gap was a conscious tradeoff I accepted. At the time, getting the HRIS right felt more urgent than consolidating payroll.
v.Q15: Rippling — I genuinely liked the platform and still think it's sophisticated, but the implementation scope felt too ambitious given our operational bandwidth during a growth phase. My IT resources are limited, and Rippling's full deployment requires more IT involvement than we could give it. HiBob — the product is excellent for culture and engagement, but the compliance and audit capabilities weren't as robust as BambooHR's, and the US financial services reference pool was thin. UKG Ready — we eliminated them quickly because the implementation complexity and contract structure felt disproportionate for a 215-person firm. They're built for companies that are bigger than us.
v.Q16: BambooHR does employee records and document management really well — I trust the audit trail and our General Counsel has been satisfied with the documentation structure. Onboarding workflows are clean and configurable, and we've built out a fairly comprehensive new hire experience in the platform. The reporting for standard HR metrics is accessible and I can get the data I need for our COO's quarterly reviews without a lot of manual extraction.
v.Q17: The payroll disconnect is honestly becoming more of a problem as we've grown. Running HRIS in BambooHR and payroll in Paychex means manual data synchronization and reconciliation that I thought we could live with and increasingly cannot. Benefits administration is also weak — we're essentially using BambooHR as a record of truth but the actual enrollment and carrier management happens outside of it, which creates data integrity risk. And I feel like the platform hasn't kept pace with where the market is going on analytics and workforce intelligence.
v.Q18: The payroll-HRIS disconnect is my biggest frustration, and I'd call it significant and building. Every time we process payroll there is a reconciliation step where someone on my team is cross-checking BambooHR data against Paychex to catch discrepancies — salary changes, new hires, terminations. It's error-prone and it's a productivity drain. As we've grown from 150 to 215 people, the frequency and complexity of those reconciliations has increased. I'm honestly a little surprised we haven't had a more serious payroll error yet, and I don't want to wait until we do to act on it.
v.Q19: Payroll integration has gone from a nice-to-have to a must-have — that's the biggest shift. When I made the BambooHR decision I thought we could manage the split stack, and at 130 people maybe we could. At 215 and growing, we can't. I've also developed much stronger requirements around compensation management and total rewards visibility, because we're competing with larger financial institutions for talent and I need to be able to run sophisticated comp analyses quickly. And AI-assisted features have started to matter more to me — I want intelligent automation on things like document generation and basic employee inquiries.
v.Q20: Across BambooHR and Paychex combined, I think we're spending somewhere in the $50,000 to $100,000 range. I'd want to pull the actual invoices to give you a precise number but that's my general sense.
v.Q21: Somewhat no, honestly. For what we're actually getting — a split stack with manual reconciliation overhead — I don't think the value equation is strong. I think we could get meaningfully more value from a unified platform at a similar or modestly higher price point.
v.Q22: If the payroll-HRIS reconciliation problem were solved — meaning a native payroll integration that eliminated the manual step entirely — I'd put that at $10,000 to $25,000 in recovered staff time annually, plus the risk reduction value of fewer payroll errors, which is harder to quantify but real.
v.Q23: Yes, I'd say I'm somewhat likely to formally re-evaluate within the next six months. The payroll situation has become the forcing function I didn't have eighteen months ago. I'm not in crisis mode, but I'm in planning mode, and I've already started having informal conversations with a couple of vendors. It's a real evaluation on the horizon.
v.Q24: I think the dominant challenge for People Ops leaders at growth-stage companies is that the tool decisions you make at a hundred people rarely hold at two hundred, and the cost and disruption of re-platforming is disproportionate to the size of the organization. You end up in this cycle of evaluating, switching, stabilizing, and then finding out in eighteen months that you've outgrown the new thing too. The market doesn't have a great answer for that middle-market tier that needs enterprise-grade compliance and data integrity without enterprise-level implementation complexity and price. That gap is real, and I think most people in my position feel it.

cat.Q21: Somewhat no / not really reasonable

v.Q1: Sure. I'm the Chief People Officer, so that's C-suite, and my function is HR broadly — I oversee everything from recruiting through compensation, HRIS, and employee experience.
v.Q2: I've been here about three and a half years, so I'd put myself in the three-to-five bucket.
v.Q3: We're in the professional employer organization and workforce management space, so I usually say "Other" because it doesn't fit neatly into most dropdown categories. We're at about 190 employees right now, which puts us solidly in that 101-to-250 range, and honestly we've been moving fast — we were under 130 people two years ago.
v.Q4: Our main platform is Gusto. We use it for payroll, benefits administration, and a lot of the core employee data stuff. We also layer in Lattice for performance and Greenhouse for recruiting, so it's not truly a single-platform environment, but Gusto is the system of record for pay and benefits.
v.Q5: That was about 14 months ago, so just inside the last 12 months is not quite right — I'd call it one to two years ago, honestly.
v.Q6: At that point we were already on Gusto, but we were also carrying a separate ADP Workforce Now instance that a legacy business unit had been using before I joined. So it was really a mixed environment — Gusto for the newer headcount and ADP for maybe 40 or 50 people from the old structure.
v.Q7: There were honestly several things happening at once. The biggest driver was just that the dual-platform situation had become operationally painful — we were reconciling payroll across two systems every pay period and the error rate was climbing. So manual process pain was a big one. Beyond that, we had hit a scaling inflection point where the HR team had grown to the point that we needed real workflow automation — approvals, onboarding checklists, things that Gusto kind of does but not robustly. And we had a CFO who was pushing hard on cost transparency, so there was internal pressure to consolidate spend and get better reporting on total comp and headcount costs. I'd also say benefits renewal was coming up and our broker was encouraging us to look at whether our platform could handle the complexity of our new plans, which it could not do well at the time.
v.Q8: Yeah, I think the broader context was that we were in a pretty aggressive growth mode — we had done two small acqui-hires and added a remote-first engineering team, so suddenly we had people in twelve states when we used to be concentrated in two. That multi-state compliance complexity was a real forcing function. You know, I also think there was a board-level conversation about operational maturity — the idea that if we're going to raise a Series C we need to look like a scaled company, and that includes having HR infrastructure that reflects that.
v.Q9: The reporting was genuinely bad on both systems, which was maddening when I was trying to build anything resembling a workforce analytics story for the board. I mean, I was pulling CSVs and building pivot tables in Google Sheets, which is not a great look when you're a CPO. The integration story was also broken — Gusto and our ATS didn't talk to each other in any real-time way, so new hire data had to be entered manually in multiple places. And the employee self-service experience was clunky enough that we were fielding basic benefits questions that employees should have been able to answer themselves.
v.Q10: We looked at Rippling, Namely, Paylocity, and we had a demo with Paychex Flex. We also briefly considered TriNet but ruled it out pretty quickly because it's a PEO model and that wasn't the direction we wanted to go.
v.Q11: Absolutely. Multi-state payroll support was non-negotiable given where we had gotten to geographically. Native integration with Greenhouse was a hard requirement — I was not going to manage another broken ATS handoff. And we needed a self-service portal that was actually usable on mobile, because a significant chunk of our workforce is not sitting at a desk. SSO was also a requirement that IT pushed on us, and honestly I agreed with it from a security standpoint.
v.Q12: It was a small committee. I was the primary decision-maker and budget holder. Our CFO had sign-off authority because the annual contract value crossed a threshold that required his approval. Our IT director weighed in heavily on the security and SSO requirements. And I brought in two people from my HR team — our head of benefits and our HRIS manager — as the operational evaluators who actually went deep on feature testing. So the final call was mine, but it wasn't made in a vacuum.
v.Q13: We stayed with Gusto and eliminated the ADP instance. So technically it was a renewal and a consolidation rather than a switch to something entirely new. We also added some Gusto modules we hadn't been using.
v.Q14: Honestly, the decision came down to a few things. Gusto had meaningfully improved its multi-state support since we first signed on, and the pricing for our headcount tier was still very competitive against what Rippling and Paylocity were quoting us. The Greenhouse integration had been built out since we last evaluated it, so that box got checked. And I think there was also a switching cost argument — my team already knew Gusto, our employees were used to it, and the disruption of migrating everything mid-growth-phase felt like a real risk. Rippling was the closest competitor, and I think if we'd been starting fresh I might have gone there, but the value of continuity mattered in our situation.
v.Q15: Rippling was genuinely close, but the implementation timeline they quoted us was longer than we could absorb given our hiring pace, and the price point was notably higher. Namely felt like it was built for a slightly different company profile — more traditional, more office-centric — and the UX felt dated compared to what we were seeing elsewhere. Paylocity had strong payroll bones but the benefits administration piece felt bolted on rather than native, and their demo left some open questions about the Greenhouse connector. Paychex Flex was out pretty fast — it's really built for a different market than ours, and the account management model they described sounded like we'd be calling a call center when we had issues, which I'm not willing to do.
v.Q16: Gusto does payroll execution really well — it's reliable, the tax filing is handled cleanly across all our states, and the employee-facing pay stub experience is genuinely good. Benefits open enrollment has also gotten better. The UX is clean enough that our HR team isn't constantly hand-holding employees through it.
v.Q17: Reporting and analytics is still the sore spot. I can get basic data out of it, but if I want anything that requires cross-referencing headcount trends with comp data or turnover cohorts, I'm still going to a spreadsheet. The workflow automation for things like promotion approvals and role changes is also pretty limited — it exists, but it's not flexible enough for how we operate. And as we've grown, I've started feeling the ceiling on things like compensation band management and org chart tooling.
v.Q18: The analytics gap is my biggest frustration, and I'd call it significant — not severe enough to make me want to rip and replace right now, but significant. Every time I'm prepping a board deck or trying to answer a question from my CFO about headcount cost trends, I'm doing manual data work that I really should not have to do at this point. It slows me down, it introduces the possibility of error, and it frankly makes the HR function look less sophisticated than it is. I've looked at adding a standalone people analytics tool, but that just adds another integration problem.
v.Q19: We've added about 50 more people since the last evaluation, and we now have employees in 17 states, which adds compliance complexity. I'm also much more focused on compensation equity and band management than I was before — we did a pay equity audit this year that surfaced some issues, and I need tooling that helps me manage that proactively. And honestly, the expectation around AI-assisted insights has shifted — I'm now expecting any serious platform to give me something smarter than a static dashboard.
v.Q20: For Gusto specifically, we're in the $50,000 to $100,000 range annually when you include all the modules and per-employee fees. If you add Lattice and Greenhouse on top, total HR tech spend is probably pushing $150,000 or so.
v.Q21: For Gusto, I'd say somewhat yes — it's reasonable for what it does on the payroll and benefits side. But I feel like I'm leaving value on the table because I'm not getting the analytics and workflow depth that I'd want at this price point.
v.Q22: If Gusto built out a real people analytics capability — configurable dashboards, comp band tracking, turnover cohort analysis — I'd probably value that at somewhere in the $10,000 to $25,000 range annually, because it would effectively replace a standalone tool I'd otherwise have to buy and the analyst time I'm currently spending.
v.Q23: I'd say it's somewhat unlikely in the next six months — we have too much operational momentum right now and I don't want to run a platform migration during a growth phase. But I'd be lying if I said it wasn't on my radar for the 12-to-18-month window.
v.Q24: I think the core tension everyone in my position is wrestling with is that the mid-market is genuinely underserved. You've got SMB tools that are easy but shallow, and enterprise tools that are deep but require an implementation team and cost a fortune. Most of us are sitting in this 100-to-500 person band trying to get enterprise-grade analytics and workflow capability at SMB-friendly pricing, and nobody has fully cracked that. Compliance complexity as teams go distributed is also a real shared pain point — multi-state, some international, contractor versus employee classification. And I'd say the integration fragmentation problem hasn't been solved — everyone claims to have an open API and a marketplace, but the reality of getting your ATS, your HRIS, your payroll, and your performance tool to actually share clean data in real time is still harder than it should be.

Q4: Point Solution Layered on Core Platform

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: Sure, I'm VP of Talent Acquisition. So I oversee all recruiting for the company — that includes sourcing strategy, recruiter capacity, employer brand, and our tech stack as it relates to finding and hiring people. I sometimes bleed into onboarding and early employee experience conversations as well, just because I think the handoff from offer acceptance to day 30 really matters for retention.
v.Q2: I've been here just under two years — I'd call it in the one-to-three-year range. I came in specifically to build out a more structured recruiting function because the company had been doing ad hoc hiring for a while and needed to get serious about talent infrastructure.
v.Q3: We're a B2B SaaS company, so squarely in technology. We build workflow automation software for mid-market professional services firms — think accounting firms, consulting shops, that kind of buyer. Right now we're at about 215 employees, so we're in the 101-to-250 band. When I joined we were at 150, so it's been a meaningful growth period — I'd guess we've added close to 70 people in the last 18 months, which is pretty intense for a company our size.
v.Q4: We use a few tools but Gusto is the anchor for payroll and benefits. On the recruiting side, we use Lever as our ATS — I brought that in when I joined because we had basically nothing before. We also use Calendly for interview scheduling, which sounds simple but it's saved us a lot of back-and-forth. And then we have a separate tool, Culture Amp, for engagement surveys and onboarding feedback. So it's not all one system — I'd describe it as loosely coupled, with Gusto as the HR system of record.
v.Q5: The most significant evaluation cycle I was personally involved in was roughly 16 or 17 months ago, so I'd put that in the one-to-two-year bucket. We've done smaller point-solution evaluations since then — like when we were shopping for the engagement survey tool — but the big platform evaluation was about 16 months back.
v.Q6: When I first arrived, the company was using Gusto for payroll and benefits — that had been in place since the early days. For recruiting, there was essentially no structured ATS — people were tracking candidates in a shared Google Sheet, which, you know, is fine when you're 20 people, but completely untenable when you're trying to run 15 open roles at once. So when we kicked off the broader platform review, it was partly about validating whether to stick with Gusto or move everything to a more integrated platform, and partly about solving the ATS problem specifically.
v.Q7: There were really four distinct triggers that came together at roughly the same time, which is why it felt urgent. The first was pure scaling pressure — we had just closed a Series B and the board had approved a headcount plan that called for adding about 60 people over the next 12 months. Trying to do that with our existing tooling was not realistic. The second was what I'd call a candidate experience problem — we were getting feedback through our offer stage that the process felt disorganized, and we lost a couple of good candidates to competitors who were just faster and more communicative. That's painful when you're competing for engineering talent with companies that have much stronger employer brands than we do. Third was the integration gap — Gusto and whatever loose recruiting process we had were completely disconnected, so new hire data was being manually re-entered at every step, and we were getting errors on things like start dates and offer letter details because of that manual handoff. And fourth, honestly, was that I was a new VP who wanted to put my own stamp on the function and build it properly. I think that's a real trigger that doesn't get talked about enough — new leadership brings a fresh look at the toolset and a mandate to improve it.
v.Q8: Yeah, I think the broader context here was really the hiring market dynamics of that period. We were trying to hire senior engineers and product people in a market where everyone was competing for the same candidates, and the time-to-offer was a real competitive differentiator. There was a sense that if our process had too much friction — slow scheduling, disorganized communication, clunky DocuSign flows — we'd lose people to companies that had invested in a smoother experience. And from a company-wide perspective, there was a digital transformation push happening — our CEO had come from a more operationally mature company and had a strong view that we needed to get our internal systems up to a standard that matched where we wanted to go. So HR tech was kind of part of a larger modernization effort that included finance, IT, and sales ops as well. That tailwind made it easier to get budget approved for a more comprehensive evaluation.
v.Q9: From the recruiting standpoint, the absence of a real ATS was the dominant frustration — I mean, you can't run a disciplined hiring process out of a spreadsheet when you're doing volume recruiting. But beyond that, the integration between whatever we had and Gusto was essentially nonexistent, and that caused downstream payroll errors that our finance team was very unhappy about. I think we had three separate instances in a four-month window where a new hire's first paycheck was wrong because of a data entry mistake somewhere in the handoff. That's a terrible first impression for a new employee and it was causing real internal friction. On the Gusto side specifically, the benefits experience was okay but not great — employees didn't feel like they had a clear window into their total comp package, and during open enrollment we got a lot of inbound questions that suggested the self-service experience wasn't doing enough of the heavy lifting.
v.Q10: So we evaluated along two tracks — one was whether to consolidate onto a single HR and payroll platform, and the other was evaluating standalone ATSs on the assumption that we'd keep Gusto for payroll. On the platform consolidation side, we looked seriously at Rippling and did a deep-dive demo with Workday — though Workday got eliminated pretty quickly once we saw the implementation requirements and pricing for our size. On the ATS side, we looked at Lever, Greenhouse, and Ashby. We also had a brief conversation with Rippling's recruiting module as part of their platform pitch.
v.Q11: For the ATS piece, we had a few non-negotiables. It had to have a native integration with Gusto or a robust API — I was not going to solve the data handoff problem with another manual workaround. It needed structured interview kits and scorecards because I was trying to bring more rigor to our interview process and I needed the tool to enforce that. And it needed to have a candidate-facing experience that I wouldn't be embarrassed to put in front of someone we were trying to recruit — good email communication templates, a clean careers page builder, easy scheduling links. On the platform side more broadly, SSO through Okta was a hard IT requirement. And I had an implicit price ceiling — I needed to stay under what felt like a reasonable per-employee per-month cost given our Series B budget constraints.
v.Q12: The decision structure was pretty clear. I was the primary recommender and the one doing all the evaluation work — demos, reference calls, feature scoring. Our CEO had final sign-off because anything over a certain contract value threshold required his approval, and he was also personally interested in the employer brand piece of the ATS. Our Head of Finance was involved primarily on pricing and total cost of ownership — she wanted to understand the multi-year cost implications before we committed. And our IT manager weighed in specifically on the SSO and data security requirements. I'd say I was functionally the decision-maker in terms of which tool to recommend, but it required alignment from three other people before we could move forward. The CEO's involvement was actually helpful — it accelerated the internal approval process because he was already bought in by the time I brought the final recommendation.
v.Q13: We made a split decision. We stayed with Gusto for payroll and benefits — we evaluated Rippling as a full replacement but ultimately decided the switching cost and implementation risk wasn't worth it given that Gusto was handling payroll reliably. And we separately purchased Lever as our ATS, which was a new tool for the company. So it was a renewal on the payroll side and a net-new purchase on the recruiting side.
v.Q14: For Gusto, the main reason we stayed was that it was doing the core job reliably and the switching cost was real. We'd had some integration issues but they were traceable to our lack of an ATS, not to Gusto itself. The pricing was also favorable — when we benchmarked it against what Rippling was quoting us for equivalent functionality, Gusto came out meaningfully cheaper for our headcount tier. And honestly, my HR generalist knew Gusto well, and asking her to learn a whole new system while also onboarding 60 people felt like adding unnecessary risk. For Lever specifically — and this was the more contested decision — it won on a combination of the candidate experience quality, the Gusto integration, and the interview kit functionality. Greenhouse was a strong second, and I know a lot of people in my network swear by it, but Lever's UX felt slightly more modern and the implementation support they offered was better matched to a small TA team like ours. Ashby was interesting — it has some very smart analytics features — but it felt like it was built for a more sophisticated recruiting operation than we were ready to be yet.
v.Q15: Workday was eliminated basically on the first pricing call — it's just not designed for a company our size, and the implementation timelines they described were measured in months, not weeks. I think Workday is a great product for a 2,000-person company, but for us it would have been buying a jet when we need a reliable commuter car. Rippling was genuinely competitive and I want to be fair about that — the platform consolidation pitch is compelling, and the idea of having IT, HR, and payroll all in one place is attractive in theory. But a few things worked against them: the implementation complexity for a migration mid-growth-phase, the price premium relative to keeping Gusto plus adding Lever, and some concerns our IT manager raised about the security configuration options. Greenhouse I liked and I think it's an excellent ATS, but Lever's sales process was frankly better — they moved faster, the account executive was more responsive, and they offered us a more tailored onboarding package. Sometimes the buying experience itself signals how the vendor relationship will go, and Lever felt like they wanted our business more. Ashby, as I mentioned, was eliminated mostly because it felt like we'd be buying ahead of our operational maturity — I want to grow into something like that, but it wasn't right for where we were.
v.Q16: Gusto does payroll and tax compliance well — I mean, it just runs, and for a lean HR team that's genuinely valuable. The direct deposit setup is painless, the year-end tax stuff is handled without drama, and the benefits carrier connections are solid. Lever has transformed our recruiting operation — candidate communication is structured, our interviewers are using scorecards consistently for the first time, and I can actually see pipeline velocity data that tells me where we're losing candidates. The combination of those two with the integration between them has cut our new hire data errors to basically zero, which was one of the core problems we were trying to solve.
v.Q17: On the Gusto side, the HR management features beyond payroll feel thin for where we are now. Things like headcount planning, org chart visualization, and anything resembling workforce analytics are pretty basic. I find myself wanting more from the HRIS layer — there's not much structure for managing job levels, compensation bands, or performance data. Lever is good but the reporting customization has some frustrating limits — I can get the standard pipeline metrics but building custom reports for specific role families or hiring manager performance takes more work than it should. And the handoff from Lever into onboarding still has some gaps — the new hire doesn't really get a structured digital onboarding experience from either tool.
v.Q18: I'd say my biggest frustration is the lack of a coherent onboarding workflow that bridges recruiting and HR. Right now, when someone accepts an offer in Lever, there's still a somewhat manual process to get them set up in Gusto, assign their equipment through IT, get their accounts provisioned, and give them a structured first-week experience. We've cobbled together a checklist approach, but it's not automated, it's not trackable in a single place, and it creates dropped balls — especially when we're onboarding multiple people in the same week. I'd call that a significant frustration, not quite severe, but it's something that adds real overhead to my team and creates an uneven new hire experience, which I care about a lot from an employer brand standpoint.
v.Q19: A few things have shifted meaningfully. We're now hiring in more markets — we've added people in Canada for the first time, which introduces international payroll complexity that Gusto doesn't fully handle, so we've been supplementing with a separate PEO arrangement for those hires, and that's a friction point. We've also become much more focused on internal mobility and career pathing as a retention tool, and neither Lever nor Gusto really helps me with that. And I think my expectations around analytics have matured — when I started this role I was happy just to have a pipeline dashboard, but now I want to be able to correlate hiring source with 90-day retention, or look at interview-to-offer conversion by hiring manager, and that kind of analysis requires more than what my current stack offers natively.
v.Q20: Gusto is probably in the $40,000 to $60,000 range annually for our headcount, including all the benefits admin fees. Lever is another $25,000 or so. Culture Amp is maybe $15,000. So all-in on the HR and TA tech stack, I'd estimate we're in the $80,000 to $100,000 range — maybe a bit over, honestly, when you add up the smaller point solutions.
v.Q21: I think it's somewhat yes — we're getting real value, especially from Lever, which has materially changed how we recruit. But I feel like the stack is maybe 10% more expensive than it should be given some of the gaps that still exist. I'd expect more for what we're paying in aggregate, particularly on the onboarding and analytics side.
v.Q22: If someone built a seamless, automated onboarding workflow that connected Lever through to Gusto to IT provisioning, gave the new hire a structured portal, and tracked completion status in one place — I'd say that's worth somewhere in the $10,000 to $25,000 range annually for us. Maybe toward the higher end of that, because I'd probably be able to reduce some of the HR coordinator time that's currently going into manual onboarding logistics, and the downstream retention value of a better early experience is real even if it's harder to quantify.
v.Q23: I'd say I'm somewhat likely to be in evaluation mode within the next 6 months, particularly around the payroll and HRIS side given the international complexity we're starting to face. I wouldn't call it very likely, because I just went through a cycle not that long ago, but the Canada situation is a legitimate forcing function and I'm not satisfied with the PEO workaround as a long-term solution. I'd say the switching likelihood is neutral to somewhat likely — I'm watching the market and I'm open to it if the right platform makes a compelling case.
v.Q24: I think the number one challenge is that the tools are designed in silos and the real life of a candidate-turned-employee doesn't happen in silos. The handoff from recruiting to onboarding to payroll to benefits to performance — each of those handoffs is a place where data gets lost, the employee experience degrades, and the HR team has to do manual work to compensate. Everyone claims to solve this with integrations, but the integrations are never as good as the native experience, and you end up paying for five tools and a lot of your own time to make them talk to each other. I also think the analytics story across the board is undersold and underbuilt — we're in 2024 and most HR leaders are still pulling Excel exports to answer basic questions about their workforce. There's a real opportunity for a tool to genuinely own the analytics layer and become indispensable on that basis alone. And then I'd add that the mid-market pricing model is often misaligned with how fast companies at our stage actually grow — you sign a contract at 150 people and six months later you're at 200, and the per-seat cost creep adds up in ways that feel punitive when you're growing fast and already stretched on budget.

Q4: Point Solution Layered on Core Platform

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm VP of People Operations.
v.Q2: Just under four years, so I'd say in the three-to-five-year range.

v.Q4: BambooHR is our primary platform — we use it for HRIS, onboarding, and time tracking. Payroll we run through a separate connection to ADP RUN, which BambooHR feeds data into. Benefits is handled through a broker portal that's kind of its own thing.
v.Q5: That was about 18 months ago, so right on the edge of the one-to-two-year window.
v.Q6: We were on Paycor at the time — they handled payroll, HR, and benefits in one bundle. It had been in place for a few years before I got involved in the decision.
v.Q7: The biggest driver was that we had grown from around 140 to 190 employees in about 14 months, and Paycor was struggling to keep up with our needs in a few specific ways. The onboarding workflows were rigid and couldn't handle the variability we have in store roles versus corporate roles — the experience was too generic. We were also hitting the contract renewal window, which felt like a natural checkpoint to ask whether we were in the right system. And honestly, our store managers were complaining about the time-tracking module constantly — it wasn't built for hourly retail workers and the clock-in experience was clunky.
v.Q8: We had opened five new store locations in 18 months and we were planning three more. That kind of physical expansion creates a lot of HR process volume — new location setup, new manager onboarding, compliance for different state labor laws. The existing system wasn't built for that kind of distributed growth.
v.Q9: The reporting in Paycor was really frustrating — I could never get clean turnover reports by location, which is kind of critical in retail. The onboarding experience for store associates was also bad — lots of paper, not mobile-friendly, and the completion tracking was unreliable. We were losing track of whether new hires had actually finished their compliance training.
v.Q10: We looked at BambooHR, Rippling, UKG Ready, and Paycom. We started with a longer list but those were the four we actually demo'd.
v.Q11: Mobile-friendly self-service was non-negotiable — most of our store associates don't have company email or a desktop. We needed solid time and attendance for hourly workers. And we needed location-level reporting because I manage HR outcomes by store, not just company-wide.

Our Director of Retail Operations had input on the time and attendance piece specifically — she cared a lot about how store managers would experience the tool. v.Q13: We switched. We moved from Paycor to BambooHR, paired with ADP RUN for payroll.

The employee self-service experience on mobile was genuinely good, and the pricing was the most transparent of all the vendors we talked to. I also appreciated that the implementation process was clearly defined and not a massive project — we're a small People Ops team and I couldn't dedicate months to a migration.
v.Q15: Rippling felt overbuilt for what we needed — the IT device management and global payroll features were impressive but irrelevant to us, and the price reflected all that functionality we'd never use. UKG Ready had strong time and attendance but the HRIS side felt dated and the implementation timeline they quoted was longer than I wanted. Paycom had a good product but the sales process was pushy in a way that made me nervous about the post-sale relationship — I've heard that from other HR people too, so it wasn't just my experience.
v.Q16: BambooHR does onboarding really well for us — the e-signature workflows, the task assignments, the custom tracks by role type.
