v.Q13: We ended up staying with BambooHR. So technically a renewal, not a switch.
v.Q14: Honestly, the switching cost scared me more than anything else. We had a lot of historical data in BambooHR, and migration timelines from Rippling and Paylocity both looked like three to four months minimum. I also felt like BambooHR had improved their reporting a bit since we first implemented, and they offered us a better contract structure when I told them we were evaluating alternatives. So it was kind of a combination of inertia and a decent renewal offer.
v.Q15: Rippling was honestly really impressive but felt more complex than what I needed, and the implementation timeline was a concern. Paylocity felt very enterprise and the UI was dated — I just didn't love the experience. Namely had some good positioning for mid-market but I'd heard some things through my network about their support quality declining, so that made me nervous.
v.Q16: BambooHR does a good job with employee records and basic org management. The self-service portal is clean enough that employees actually use it, which is something I really value as a solo HR person. Time-off tracking is solid too.
v.Q17: The reporting is still my main complaint. And I still have no native payroll, so I'm still managing that ADP sync. At 700 people it's genuinely painful. I also think the performance management module is pretty weak.
v.Q18: The payroll integration with ADP. Every single payroll cycle I'm manually reconciling discrepancies, and it takes me easily two or three hours that I should be spending on something strategic. It's a significant frustration — probably a seven out of ten in terms of impact on my week.
v.Q19: We've added about fifty more people since then, so the scale problem is worse. I'm also being asked to produce more workforce analytics for leadership — things like turnover by department, time-to-fill trends — and I just can't do that efficiently in BambooHR right now.
v.Q20: Between BambooHR and ADP, I think we're somewhere in the $80,000 to $100,000 range annually. That's my rough estimate — I don't own the ADP contract directly.
v.Q21: Somewhat no. Given the manual effort I'm still putting in on top of what we pay, I don't think we're getting good value, especially at this headcount.
v.Q22: If someone solved the payroll integration problem natively, I'd say that's worth $15,000 to $25,000 a year to us easily, just in time saved and error reduction.
v.Q23: Yes, I think we'll consider it. I'd say somewhat likely to switch — I'm actively building the business case internally right now, so it's not just theoretical.
v.Q24: For people running HR solo at mid-sized companies, I think the biggest issue is that tools are either built for small businesses and don't scale, or they're built for enterprises and are way too complex and expensive for what we actually need. That middle ground is really hard to find. And the integration story between HR, payroll, and benefits is still a mess for most vendors — everyone claims they connect but in practice it's always duct tape.

cat.Q21: Somewhat no / not really reasonable

v.Q1: Sure, so I'm a VP of HR. I came up through talent acquisition but my scope now covers the full people function — compensation, HR business partnering, learning and development, and all the HR systems infrastructure. It's a pretty broad remit, especially given that I'm operating without a direct team right now, which is honestly a conversation in itself.
v.Q2: I'm coming up on two years. I joined at a pretty pivotal inflection point for the company — we were about 380 people when I came on board and the mandate was very explicitly to build the infrastructure to support doubling headcount.
v.Q3: We're a B2B SaaS company, so squarely in technology. And right now we're at around 820 employees globally, though the majority are in the US — I think it's about 680 US-based. We're headquartered in Austin but we are fully remote as an operating model, so people are distributed across thirty-plus states.
v.Q4: So BambooHR is our system of record for HR data — employee profiles, org structure, time off, performance reviews, that kind of thing. Payroll runs through Gusto right now, which is a bit of an odd pairing at our size but it predated me and nobody wanted to touch it when I first got here. Benefits are through Ease, which is a broker-connected platform. And then we use Greenhouse for recruiting separately. So it's genuinely four systems that kind of loosely talk to each other, and I think that setup is becoming increasingly untenable at our current scale.
v.Q5: The most recent formal evaluation was about twelve months ago. I had actually kicked off an informal scan even before that — probably about eighteen months ago — but the real structured evaluation with demos and a decision framework was about a year ago.
v.Q6: Same stack as now, honestly. BambooHR, Gusto, Ease, and Greenhouse. The evaluation was specifically about whether to consolidate onto a unified platform rather than continuing to patch together these four different systems.
v.Q7:
So there were really several converging factors that all kind of hit at once, which is what finally pushed me to put a real evaluation on the calendar rather than just continuing to complain internally about our tech stack.

The first and most significant was the headcount trajectory. We were growing at roughly thirty percent year over year, which meant I was onboarding somewhere between twenty and thirty people per month, and the manual lift involved in syncing data across four systems was genuinely unsustainable for one person. Every new hire meant manual entry in BambooHR, then in Gusto, then enrolling them in Ease, and then making sure Greenhouse got properly closed out. It sounds like it should take fifteen minutes but when you're doing it for twenty-five people and every system has its own quirks, it adds up to something like a full day and a half per month just on that one workflow.

The second factor was compliance. We'd expanded into several new states — I think we crossed into twelve new states in an eighteen-month period — and I was terrified about multi-state payroll compliance. Gusto is honestly fine for a small company but I wasn't confident it was giving us the compliance coverage we needed in states like California and New York where the regulatory environment is complicated.

And the third factor was executive pressure. Our CFO had started asking for workforce analytics that I just couldn't produce without a lot of manual work — things like cost per hire, span of control by department, turnover broken out by tenure cohort. I was exporting data from three different systems and stitching it together in Google Sheets, which is embarrassing frankly at this company size and certainly not scalable.
v.Q8:
Yeah, I think a few things. We'd just closed a Series C and our investors were explicitly asking about operational maturity, and I think our HR tech stack was one of the things that came up in that conversation as something that needed professionalization. There was also a broader conversation happening in our leadership team about digital transformation — we were modernizing our internal systems across the board, not just HR — so there was some top-down momentum behind the idea of upgrading infrastructure.

And honestly, within the HR tech space more broadly, there was a lot of noise around AI-powered features — things like predictive attrition, automated compensation benchmarking — and I was getting questions from our CEO about whether we were leveraging any of that. So I think the industry conversation around AI was also in the background as a motivator, even if it wasn't the primary driver.
v.Q9:
Definitely. The most acute frustration was the data integrity problem. Because I had four systems with no real-time sync between them, I was constantly finding discrepancies — employee records that hadn't been updated in one system when something changed in another, or pay data that didn't match what was in BambooHR. It was a confidence issue, not just an efficiency issue. When a leader asked me a question about their team, I wasn't always fully confident the answer I was giving them was accurate to the day.

Beyond that, BambooHR's performance review functionality had gotten really limiting for us. We'd tried to build something more sophisticated around continuous feedback and goal alignment, and the tool just wasn't flexible enough to support it. We ended up bolt-on a separate tool for that, which was just adding more complexity.

And Gusto — look, I don't want to be too negative about it because I think it's a solid product for companies under 200 people, but at 600-plus employees across thirty states, it really felt like we were asking it to do something it wasn't designed for. The reporting was minimal, the multi-state compliance support felt thin, and the lack of an HR system integration meant every payroll cycle involved some manual reconciliation.
v.Q10: So I did a pretty thorough market scan. The tools I evaluated seriously were Rippling, Workday, Ceridian Dayforce, and HiBob. I also had early conversations with Lattice and Culture Amp but those were more focused on the performance and engagement layers and didn't make it into the formal evaluation because I was prioritizing the core HRIS and payroll consolidation problem.
v.Q11: I had a pretty clear set of table stakes going in. First, it had to run payroll natively and have demonstrated compliance capability across all fifty states — not just the big ones. Second, it needed to have an open API or at minimum a native integration with Greenhouse, because our recruiting workflow wasn't going anywhere. Third, SSO was non-negotiable — our IT team wouldn't allow any new system that didn't support SAML-based SSO. Fourth, it had to be able to handle our org complexity, which included some international contractors in Canada and the UK even though they weren't on our primary payroll. And fifth, I needed real reporting — not just canned dashboards but configurable analytics I could build without a data team. Any vendor that couldn't check all five of those boxes pretty clearly was out of the running early.
v.Q12: So I was the primary decision-maker and primary recommender, but the final sign-off was a shared process. Our CFO had budget authority and was very engaged — she had specific questions about payroll accuracy and cost, and she came to two of the vendor demos, which surprised me honestly. Our VP of IT was involved from a security and integration standpoint, and he had a kind of veto power over anything that didn't pass his security review. And our CEO weighed in at the very end — not in the evaluation process itself but I gave him a final summary of my recommendation and he pushed back a little on Workday because of the implementation cost, which ultimately did factor into the outcome. So it was kind of a tripartite sign-off between me, the CFO, and the CEO, with IT as a gating function.
v.Q13: We stayed with BambooHR. So it was technically a renewal, not a switch, which honestly wasn't the outcome I had expected or recommended going in. I had built a recommendation for Rippling and it got to the finish line and then stalled out on cost and implementation timing concerns from the CFO and CEO.
v.Q14:
So I want to be honest that staying with BambooHR was not really a choice made on its merits — it was more of a default outcome after the preferred option fell through. What happened is that I built a business case for Rippling that I thought was genuinely strong, and when it got to final approval, our CFO was uncomfortable with the total implementation cost including the professional services hours, and our CEO was worried about the timing because we were heading into a product launch cycle and he didn't want a major systems migration happening at the same time.

So BambooHR won by attrition, essentially. We did renegotiate the renewal contract and added a few add-on modules — I think we added their engagement survey feature and upgraded our reporting tier — so it wasn't a pure status quo renewal, but the fundamental fragmentation problem I set out to solve was not solved.

I think BambooHR does genuinely have some things going for it — the UI is clean and employees tend to adopt it without a lot of friction, which matters in a remote environment where self-service is critical. But the reason it won was inertia and risk aversion, not because it was the best solution for where we're going.
v.Q15:
So Rippling was my actual recommendation and the reasons it was rejected were implementation cost and timing risk, not product concerns. The product was honestly the strongest fit for our profile — the unified data model, the built-in payroll, the IT and HR convergence story all resonated with me. But the ACV with implementation services came in around $180,000 and that was a hard number for our CFO at that moment.

Workday was the right answer if we were a 2,000-person company, but we're not there yet. The implementation complexity and the professional services dependency felt excessive for our current scale, and I think we'd outgrow BambooHR before we outgrow Workday's need to be heavily customized. So it was more of a maturity mismatch.

Ceridian Dayforce impressed me on compliance and payroll depth — honestly probably the strongest payroll engine I evaluated — but the HRIS layer felt clunky and the UX was dated. In a remote company where employees are self-sufficient or not at all, you can't afford to have a hard-to-use interface. I think it's better suited to a workforce that's more operational and less tech-savvy.

HiBob I really liked aesthetically and it had strong engagement and org visualization features, but the payroll story was a partnership-based integration rather than native, which didn't solve my core consolidation problem. And I'd heard from a few peers that their implementation support was inconsistent, which made me nervous given I was going to be flying solo through the migration.
v.Q16: BambooHR does a few things pretty well for us. Employee self-service is genuinely strong — people manage their own PTO requests, update their personal information, pull up their org chart, and they do it without much handholding, which I appreciate in a fully remote environment. The onboarding workflow builder is reasonably functional and I've built out some decent automated task sequences for new hires. And the time-off management is clean and relatively painless. Those are the things I'd say I'd actually miss if I moved.
v.Q17: The gaps are significant, honestly. Reporting and analytics is still the most pressing — I need workforce analytics that I can build on demand and right now I'm still exporting to Sheets for anything beyond a basic headcount report. The payroll fragmentation hasn't changed, so I'm still maintaining the Gusto relationship separately and dealing with reconciliation friction every cycle. And the compensation management capabilities are really thin — I can't run a proper compensation review cycle inside BambooHR without a lot of manual workarounds.
v.Q18: The compensation management gap is probably my single biggest frustration right now. We're doing our annual comp review cycle and I'm essentially running it in a combination of Google Sheets, Carta for equity, and BambooHR for base salary data, and getting all of those things to talk to each other coherently is a multi-week project every time. The fact that I'm a solo HR person managing compensation for 820 employees without a proper system to support it is genuinely stressful. I'd rate the frustration level as severe — it's the kind of thing that makes me question whether we made the right call staying put.
v.Q19: A few things have shifted. We've grown another 150 people since the evaluation, so the scale pressure is more acute. I've also started to get questions from our board about workforce planning — headcount forecasting by department, scenario modeling for different growth trajectories — and that's a capability I didn't even have on my requirements list a year ago but it's now something I actively need. And I think the AI conversation has evolved — I was somewhat skeptical of vendor AI claims a year ago, but I've seen enough credible demonstrations of things like anomaly detection in payroll and skills inference from job data that I'm now genuinely interested in platforms that have invested in that layer.
v.Q20: Across all four systems — BambooHR, Gusto, Ease, and Greenhouse — I think we're somewhere in the $200,000 to $240,000 range annually. BambooHR is probably $65,000 to $70,000 of that at our employee count, and Greenhouse is actually the biggest line item at somewhere around $90,000.
v.Q21: Somewhat no. The aggregate spend is defensible in isolation but the fact that I'm still spending significant personal time stitching these systems together manually means the true cost is higher than the line items suggest. If you factored in my time cost, which I think is a fair way to look at it, I don't think we're getting good value for the money.
v.Q22: For a genuinely functional compensation management module — one that could handle merit cycles, equity refresh, total comp statements, and integration with our equity platform — I'd say that's worth somewhere in the $25,000 to $40,000 per year range. That's a combination of the time I'd save, the errors I'd reduce, and frankly the peace of mind of not running comp for 800-plus people in a spreadsheet.
v.Q23: Yes, I'm already in early conversations with a couple of vendors. I'd say I'm somewhat likely to switch within six months — the constraints that blocked us last time were timing and cost, and I think I can address the cost concern with a more detailed ROI model, and the timing concern is less valid now that we're in a calmer operational period. So I'm actively working toward another formal evaluation, and I'd say this one has a higher probability of resulting in an actual switch.
v.Q24:
I think the honest answer is that the market is kind of fractured in a way that doesn't serve mid-market companies well. You have SMB tools that are intuitive and cheap but don't scale, and you have enterprise platforms that are powerful but require a full implementation team and a dedicated HRIS administrator to maintain — and most companies in the 300 to 1,000 employee range don't have either of those things. The genuine mid-market sweet spot, something that's sophisticated enough to handle real complexity but operable by a lean HR team, is genuinely hard to find.

I also think the integration story in this space is still largely broken. Everyone claims to integrate with everything, but the reality is usually a one-way sync with a twelve-hour delay and a bunch of edge cases that require manual intervention. And for a VP of HR who is also the only person in HR, that matters a lot.

And I guess I'd add that the AI narrative from vendors is getting ahead of the reality a bit — there's a lot of marketing around AI features that turn out to be fairly superficial when you get into a demo. I think the HR leaders who've been around for a while are getting a little fatigued by that gap between the promise and the product.

Q4: Point Solution Layered on Core Platform

cat.Q5: 6 to 12 months ago (6-12 mo to 6-12 mo)
cat.Q21: Somewhat no / not really reasonable

v.Q1: I'm a Director of People Operations. So my scope is the full employee lifecycle — HRIS, benefits, compliance, and some light talent development work. I have two people on my team reporting to me.
v.Q2: Just over four years. I joined as an HR manager and was promoted into the director role about eighteen months in.
v.Q3: We're in financial services — specifically a registered investment advisory firm. We have about 190 employees, and the headcount has been pretty steady for the last couple of years. We're not in growth mode right now, which actually changes what I look for in a tool compared to when we were scaling more aggressively.
v.Q4: We use BambooHR as our main HRIS. Payroll runs through Paychex Flex, which I inherited when I joined and have mixed feelings about. Benefits are administered through our broker's platform, which is Benecaid — it's not the most modern interface but our broker relationship is strong so we've stuck with it. So three systems total.
v.Q5: About fourteen months ago, so just over a year. It was a structured evaluation — I built out a requirements doc and we ran a formal RFP process.
v.Q6: The same stack we have today. BambooHR, Paychex, and Benecaid. The evaluation was really about whether to consolidate BambooHR and Paychex into a single platform, or potentially replace all three.
v.Q7:
The primary trigger was a compliance audit. We're a regulated firm and we had an external compliance review that flagged some data consistency issues between our HR system and our payroll records — things like job title mismatches and incorrect state designations on a handful of employee records. None of it was catastrophic but it was embarrassing and it highlighted the risk of maintaining two separate systems with manual syncing.

The second factor was that Paychex Flex's contract was coming up for renewal and I genuinely didn't love the product. The interface is clunky and their support response times had deteriorated. So the renewal was a natural trigger to ask whether we should look around.

And the third factor was that my team was spending a meaningful amount of time on what I'd call administrative maintenance tasks — keeping records consistent across systems, manually pulling data for reporting — and I wanted to get that time back for work that was actually higher value.
v.Q8: In financial services specifically, there's always a regulatory compliance lens on everything, and we'd seen some changes in state-level wage and hour regulations that made me want more confidence in our payroll platform's compliance tracking. There was also a general push from our COO to reduce operational risk and improve audit readiness, and our HR systems were identified as an area where tighter controls would be beneficial.
v.Q9:
Paychex Flex was the biggest source of frustration. The reporting was genuinely poor — I could pull basic payroll reports but anything more nuanced required going through their support team, which was slow. The UI hadn't been updated in what felt like years, and the mobile experience was essentially non-functional, which matters for our workforce because we have a lot of advisors who are rarely at a desk.

On the BambooHR side, the main frustration was around compliance tracking — I couldn't easily track things like required certifications and licensing renewals for our regulated employees, which is a real need in a financial services context. It's not what BambooHR is built for, so I'm not really blaming the tool, but it meant I was managing that in a separate spreadsheet.
v.Q10: We looked seriously at Paylocity, Paycor, and Rippling. I also did a preliminary review of Isolved but it didn't make it past the initial screen — the interface looked very dated and the sales process was pushy in a way that put me off early.
v.Q11: A few things were non-negotiable for us. Native payroll with strong multi-state compliance was the top requirement given our audit context. I also needed the platform to support document management and e-signatures natively, because we have a lot of compliance-driven document workflows. SOC 2 certification was required — our IT security team wouldn't allow a vendor that couldn't produce it. And I needed a credible implementation track record with financial services firms specifically, because our data handling requirements are more stringent than a typical company.
v.Q12: I was the primary recommender and drove the evaluation entirely. Our COO had final budget sign-off — we were looking at roughly a $40,000 to $60,000 annual spend so it needed his approval. Our CFO weighed in on the payroll side since she owns financial controls, and she had specific questions about audit trail functionality. IT was involved for security review. So I'd say it was me as the primary driver with three stakeholders who each had specific veto points.
v.Q13: We stayed with BambooHR but switched our payroll from Paychex Flex to Paylocity. So it was a partial switch — we replaced one component of the stack but kept the anchor system.
v.Q14:
Paylocity won for a few reasons. Their compliance tracking for multi-state payroll was demonstrably stronger than Paychex, and I felt more confident in their audit trail functionality, which mattered given our compliance context. The UI was considerably more modern and I thought my team and our employees would actually use the self-service features without needing hand-holding.

And honestly, Paylocity's implementation team was responsive and specific — they'd worked with financial services firms before and they knew how to answer the compliance questions our CFO was asking without flinching. That experience credibility mattered a lot in our context.

As for keeping BambooHR — it's a good product for what we use it for. Employee records, org management, time-off tracking, and performance reviews all work well for a company our size. I didn't see a compelling reason to replace it when the payroll problem was really the main driver of the evaluation.
v.Q15:
Paycor was the closest runner-up. Their product was solid and the pricing was competitive, but their compliance story for our specific regulatory environment felt less developed. When I asked pointed questions about SEC and FINRA-adjacent recordkeeping requirements, their sales team couldn't answer them fluently and I ended up having to follow up twice to get responses. That eroded my confidence.

Rippling was interesting and I genuinely liked their IT-HR convergence story, but it felt like the right answer for a faster-growing tech company rather than a stable, compliance-heavy financial services firm. The complexity of the platform and the pricing model — which had a lot of per-module add-ons — made it harder to get to a clean total cost of ownership number, and I couldn't get a straight answer on what our annual spend would actually be. That opacity was a dealbreaker for me given I needed to present a clear budget to our COO.
v.Q16: BambooHR does a nice job with core people management for a company our size. The performance review workflows are intuitive and adoption is genuinely high, which I can't say was true with every tool I've worked with. Paylocity has been a meaningful upgrade from Paychex — the payroll accuracy is better and the audit reporting features are actually useful. And I will say that having the two systems connected via integration has reduced our data reconciliation burden noticeably.
v.Q17: The compliance-specific functionality I need for a regulated industry is still a gap in BambooHR. Tracking certifications, licenses, and required training completions for our advisors is still being managed in a spreadsheet, which I'm not happy about. I also think the compensation management capabilities in BambooHR are thin — running our annual merit cycle is more manual than it should be.
v.Q18: The regulatory certification tracking gap is my biggest frustration. In financial services, keeping track of which advisors hold which licenses, when those licenses expire, and what continuing education requirements are outstanding isn't optional — it's a compliance obligation. And the fact that I'm managing that in a spreadsheet that my team has to manually update creates real audit risk. I'd describe the frustration level as significant — it's not something I deal with every day but when audit season comes around it becomes very acute very quickly.
v.Q19: Our headcount has stayed pretty flat, so scale isn't a new variable. But our compliance obligations have gotten more complex — there have been some state-level regulatory updates affecting our industry and I need better tooling to track compliance posture across the employee base. I'm also starting to think more about succession planning and skills mapping as our workforce ages in certain practice areas, and that's a capability I don't have anywhere in my current stack.
v.Q20: Across BambooHR and Paylocity, I think we're around $45,000 to $55,000 annually. Benefits administration through our broker platform is kind of bundled into the broker relationship so it's harder to isolate that cost.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. I think Paylocity is good value — the improvement from Paychex was real and the compliance features justify the cost in our context. BambooHR is reasonable for what it does. I just wish it did a bit more for the price at our specific use case.
v.Q22: A genuine compliance and certification tracking module built into our HRIS — something that could track license expiration dates, send automated renewal reminders, log training completions, and produce a clean audit report — I'd say that's worth $8,000 to $12,000 a year to us, probably more if you factor in the risk reduction value from an audit exposure standpoint.
v.Q23: I'd say unsure, leaning somewhat unlikely. We just went through a fairly involved evaluation fourteen months ago and I'm not eager to go back into that process so soon. But if I came across a platform that genuinely solved the compliance tracking problem with real financial services industry knowledge, I'd be open to at least having that conversation.
v.Q24: I think the biggest challenge is that most tools are built for a generic company and don't account for industry-specific requirements. In financial services, in healthcare, in government contracting — there are compliance requirements that general-purpose HR tools just aren't designed to support, and that forces people like me to maintain secondary systems for the things that matter most from a regulatory standpoint. That gap between what the tool does and what the industry requires is a real problem and I don't think the vendors are closing it fast enough.

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: Sure, I'm a manager in Talent Acquisition. I oversee most of the recruiting activity for our firm.
v.Q2: Coming up on four years now, so I'd say in that three-to-five-year range.
v.Q3: We're in professional services — specifically management consulting. We have right around 180 employees at the moment, all based here in the Chicago area.
v.Q4: We use Gusto as our main platform. It handles payroll and benefits primarily. For the recruiting side, we layer in Greenhouse on top of that, so it's kind of a two-tool setup rather than one fully unified system.
v.Q5: That was roughly a year and a half ago, so within the last two years I'd say.
v.Q6: Before Gusto we were on Paychex. We had been using Paychex for payroll and benefits for a few years before we started looking around.
v.Q7: Honestly, a few things piled up at once. The biggest one was that Paychex just felt clunky for a team our size — the interface hadn't really kept pace and simple tasks took way too many steps. There was also a cost issue. We felt like we were paying a premium for a platform that wasn't delivering the value we expected, especially when we compared what was available at similar price points. And then the lack of integration with Greenhouse was a constant irritant for my team specifically. We were manually moving candidate data around, which created errors and slowed everything down.
v.Q8: We had gone through a small leadership change in HR — our former HR director left and a new one came in. New leadership tends to want to put their stamp on things and revisit vendor relationships, so that was kind of the catalyst that made the evaluation feel official rather than just something we griped about internally.
v.Q9: The reporting was genuinely painful. Paychex had some canned reports but almost nothing you could customize without calling support, and getting actual data out in a usable format felt like a project every single time. And on the TA side, the onboarding workflow was disconnected from anything I was doing in Greenhouse, so new hires had this disjointed experience right out of the gate. I think those two things — reporting and onboarding experience — were the core frustrations we wanted to solve.
v.Q10: We looked at Gusto, Rippling, and Namely. We also did a brief demo with ADP Workforce Now but kind of ruled it out pretty quickly — it felt like overkill for our size.
v.Q11: It had to integrate with Greenhouse — that was non-negotiable for me. And it needed to handle multi-state payroll cleanly because we have employees in Illinois, Michigan, and Wisconsin. Beyond that, we wanted something with a modern UI that wouldn't require a ton of training. Those were really the table stakes.
v.Q12: Our new HR director led the process. I was the primary voice from the TA side — kind of the internal advocate for whatever worked best for recruiting. Our CFO had to sign off on budget, so she was involved at the end. IT wasn't really in the room for this one, which honestly surprised me, but our setup isn't super complex so they were comfortable staying hands-off.
v.Q13: We switched. Moved to Gusto, and we've been on it since.
v.Q14: Gusto won mostly on ease of use and price. The implementation looked straightforward, and the pricing was transparent — we knew what we were paying upfront, which was a big contrast to the Paychex experience. It also had a clean integration with Greenhouse, which was my requirement. Rippling was interesting but felt more complex than what we needed right now, and the cost was higher. Namely looked solid but the support reputation we heard from peers was mixed, so that made us nervous.
v.Q15: Rippling — great product, honestly, but it was priced above where we wanted to be and felt like it had more infrastructure than a 180-person consulting firm needs. Namely — the peer feedback on support was the deal-breaker; a couple of people in my network had bad experiences with implementation delays and we didn't want to take that risk. ADP Workforce Now — just too enterprise, too much complexity, and the demo didn't inspire confidence that onboarding would be smooth.
v.Q16: Gusto does payroll really cleanly. Taxes are handled automatically, direct deposit is seamless, and the employee-facing experience is good — people can log in and see their pay stubs, benefits summaries, and PTO without bothering my team. For a company our size, that self-service piece saves us a meaningful amount of time every week.
v.Q17: The reporting is still not where I want it. I can get basic headcount and payroll reports, but anything more nuanced — like offer-acceptance trends or time-to-fill pulled alongside compensation data — requires me to go to Greenhouse and manually stitch things together. The two tools don't talk to each other as deeply as I'd hoped they would.
v.Q18: The reporting gap is my biggest frustration. I'd call it moderate — it's not breaking anything, but it costs me time every month and makes me look less prepared in leadership meetings than I'd like. I basically have to build my own dashboards in Excel to tell a coherent story about talent metrics, and that feels like something a modern platform should just handle.
v.Q19: Our headcount has been flat, so scaling isn't a pressure right now. But I think my expectations for analytics have genuinely gone up. There's more pressure from leadership to show TA data in a rigorous way, and the tools we have don't quite keep up with that expectation.
v.Q20: I think we're somewhere in the $20K to $50K range annually across Gusto and Greenhouse combined.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. I think Gusto is pretty fairly priced for what it does. Greenhouse is the one I question a bit more — it's not cheap and I'm not sure we're using enough of its capability to justify the full cost.
v.Q22: If I could get genuinely integrated TA and payroll reporting in one place, I'd say that's worth somewhere in the $5K to $10K range to us annually — both in time saved and in the quality of decisions we'd be able to make faster.
v.Q23: Probably not within six months. I'd say switching is somewhat unlikely in that window. The pain isn't severe enough to justify the disruption right now, and our headcount isn't growing in a way that forces the issue.
v.Q24: I think the most common complaint is that tools are either too simple or too complex — there's not a lot of great middle ground for companies in the 100-to-500-employee range. You either get something built for a startup that you outgrow fast, or something enterprise that requires a full implementation team. And then data fragmentation is a real issue — most of us are cobbling together two or three tools and trying to make them feel like one system, and that's just a constant source of friction.

Q4: Point Solution Layered on Core Platform

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm the VP of Human Resources. So I sit at the executive level and I'm responsible for the full people function — everything from talent strategy and compensation to employee experience and HR operations. We're a mid-size tech company, fully remote, so the scope is pretty broad even though the team isn't enormous.
v.Q2: I've been here just over six years, so I'd put myself in that five-to-ten-year band. I actually joined when the company was closer to 60 people, so I've watched a lot of the infrastructure get built from the ground up. That context matters a lot when I think about how we've made tooling decisions over the years.
v.Q3: We're a B2B SaaS company, so squarely in the technology sector. Right now we sit at about 215 employees. Headcount has been relatively flat for the past year and a half — we went through a period of hypergrowth a few years back and then pulled back and stabilized. That stabilization phase actually changed what we needed from our tools pretty significantly, which I'll probably get into as we go.
v.Q4: BambooHR is our core HRIS. It's the system of record for employee data, and we use it for performance management, time-off tracking, onboarding workflows, and org chart. For payroll specifically we actually run through a separate payroll processor — we've been using Paylocity for that. And benefits administration is handled through a benefits broker who has their own portal. So honestly it's three separate systems that we've tried to wire together, which creates its own friction. BambooHR is the gravitational center, but it's not a complete end-to-end solution for us.
v.Q5: The most recent full evaluation was about fourteen months ago, so squarely within the last twelve to eighteen months. We were re-examining our entire HR tech stack at that point — it wasn't just a single-tool purchase question, it was a broader conversation about whether we should consolidate onto one platform or continue managing the multi-tool approach we'd evolved into.
v.Q6: We were already on BambooHR at that point — we'd been on it for about four years. And we had Paylocity for payroll. So the evaluation wasn't about replacing something that was completely broken; it was more about asking whether there was a better way to do this holistically, or whether we should double down on what we had and try to optimize it.
v.Q7: There were honestly four or five things converging at once, and I want to give you the full picture because they reinforced each other. The first was data fragmentation. Having employee records in BambooHR, payroll in Paylocity, and benefits in a broker portal meant my team was constantly reconciling between systems. When someone got a promotion or a compensation change, we were making that update in multiple places and errors were creeping in. That eroded my confidence in our data integrity, which is a serious problem when you're reporting to a board or making workforce planning decisions. The second was reporting limitations. BambooHR's native reporting is fine for simple things, but I needed to pull together headcount analytics, attrition trends, and compensation equity data in a way that told a coherent story. I was essentially building that in spreadsheets every quarter, and that's just not a sustainable operating model for a people function that's supposed to be strategic. Third was a growing pressure to do more with compensation benchmarking. We were losing candidates and occasionally employees to companies who had more transparency around pay bands and equity, and I needed tooling that would support a more sophisticated comp program. Fourth was the fact that our Paylocity contract was coming up for renewal, which gave us a natural moment to ask the broader question. And fifth — and I'll be honest about this — I had a new CFO who came in with a lot of questions about HR spend and wanted to understand what we were getting for it. That created both pressure and an opportunity to rationalize the stack.
v.Q8: A few things at the macro level. The remote-first model had become permanent for us, and that changes what you need from an HRIS in subtle but important ways. Things like digital onboarding quality, asynchronous performance feedback, and making sure remote employees feel like they have the same access to HR resources as someone who could just walk to an office — those requirements had become non-negotiable. And frankly, what we'd set up in a rush during 2020 and 2021 was starting to show its age. The other thing I'd point to is that the HR tech market itself had matured a lot. Products that were early-stage or underfunded when we made our original BambooHR decision had grown up significantly, so the competitive landscape had genuinely shifted. I felt like we owed it to ourselves to take a fresh look rather than just assume the choice we made four years ago was still the right one.
v.Q9: Yes, and I'd organize them into two buckets. The first bucket is BambooHR-specific limitations. The performance management module had become a bottleneck — it's functional but not flexible. We couldn't configure the review cycles the way we wanted, goal tracking was clunky, and manager adoption was consistently low because the experience just wasn't intuitive for them. I spent a lot of time manually reminding managers to complete reviews that the system should have been driving automatically. The reporting was the other BambooHR frustration I mentioned earlier — it's limited without a significant workaround effort. The second bucket is the integration gap between BambooHR and Paylocity. Those two systems don't sync as cleanly as the vendor documentation implies. We had a payroll discrepancy that took three weeks to untangle because data had diverged between the two systems, and that incident really crystallized for me how much operational risk we were carrying by relying on a manual integration process. Benefits administration was also a constant source of open enrollment headaches — employees were confused by having to navigate a separate portal, and my team spent an enormous amount of time being the help desk for a process that should have been self-service.
v.Q10: We looked at Rippling, Lattice paired with a payroll solution, Workday — though we were pretty skeptical about fit from the beginning — HiBob, and we revisited whether staying with BambooHR and adding complementary point solutions made more sense than switching. So it was a reasonably wide evaluation.
v.Q11: Absolutely, and we were explicit about this going in. First, it had to be a credible solution for a fully remote workforce — not just technically compatible with remote but actually designed with that use case in mind. Second, it needed to have genuine payroll capability or a seamless, native integration with a payroll processor — I wasn't willing to replicate the disconnected experience we already had. Third, it needed SSO and solid security posture because our IT team had become much more rigorous about that after a company-wide security review. Fourth, compensation management functionality had to be present — at least pay band tracking and ideally some benchmarking capability. And fifth, the implementation support story had to be credible. I've seen enough bad implementations to know that a great product with a poor implementation experience is still a disaster. So those were the five gates, and anything that couldn't clear all five wasn't seriously in the running.
v.Q12: I led the evaluation and I'd characterize myself as the primary recommender — final budget authority lived with the CFO, so I needed her sign-off. IT was meaningfully involved this time, specifically around security and SSO requirements, and they had effective veto power over anything that didn't meet our security standards. I also looped in two senior HR business partners who would be day-to-day power users — their input shaped how we scored the UX and the performance management module specifically. And I brought in our head of Finance Operations because she's the one who has to reconcile payroll every month, so her perspective on the Paylocity integration pain was directly relevant. It was genuinely a cross-functional group, which added time to the process but I think led to a better decision.
v.Q13: We stayed with BambooHR. And I want to be nuanced about that — it wasn't a ringing endorsement, it was more of a pragmatic renewal. We added Lattice on top of BambooHR specifically for performance management and engagement, and we renegotiated the Paylocity contract on better terms. So we didn't switch the core HRIS, but we did restructure the stack around it.
v.Q14: The honest answer is switching costs. When I actually mapped out what a full migration off BambooHR would look like — data migration, re-training 215 employees, reconfiguring integrations, absorbing implementation time while my team was already stretched — the business case for switching had to clear a pretty high bar. Rippling was genuinely compelling and came close, but the pricing at our scale and the implementation complexity gave us pause. HiBob was interesting but felt like it skewed toward a different cultural profile than ours — a bit more consumer-y than we needed. Workday was never really a fit; it's built for much larger organizations and the total cost was disconnected from reality for us. So staying with BambooHR and patching the performance gap with Lattice was the path of least disruption that still addressed our most acute pain point. I won't pretend it was a triumphant choice — it was the most defensible one under the constraints we were working with.
v.Q15: Rippling — I think it's a genuinely strong product and if we were starting from scratch I might have chosen it. The rejection was really about implementation scope and total cost. The implementation timeline they quoted us was longer than I expected, and when I added up the full first-year cost including implementation services, it was meaningfully higher than staying. For a CFO who was already scrutinizing HR spend, that math was hard to close. Lattice as a full HRIS — we actually did choose Lattice but just for performance and engagement, not as an all-in-one solution. As an HRIS it wasn't developed enough at the time of our evaluation. Workday — honestly it shouldn't have even been in the evaluation, but I put it there because a board member mentioned it and I wanted to close that conversation definitively. The cost and complexity for 215 employees is just disconnected from our reality. HiBob — the product itself was fine, but the payroll story wasn't clean enough for our needs, and I had concerns about how their customer support scaled as you moved past the core product into more complex configurations. The peer references we checked were mixed on that point.
v.Q16: BambooHR genuinely does the fundamentals well. Employee records are clean, time-off management is intuitive, and the employee self-service portal has strong adoption — our employees actually use it, which is not something I take for granted. Onboarding workflows are solid. The org chart and directory features are things that remote employees rely on heavily to understand who's who, and BambooHR handles that well. Lattice has been a real improvement for performance — the goal-tracking structure and the continuous feedback features have noticeably improved manager engagement with the review process. So the stack, imperfect as it is, has improved materially since we restructured it.
v.Q17: The data fragmentation problem hasn't gone away — it's just more manageable than before. I still don't have a single source of truth that spans payroll, performance, and core HR data without manual reconciliation steps. Compensation management is still a gap. I don't have the pay band visibility or equity analysis capability that I need to run a credible comp program, and I'm still doing that work in spreadsheets. And the BambooHR-to-Lattice integration, while better than BambooHR-to-Paylocity, still isn't seamless. There are field mapping gaps that require manual cleanup.
v.Q18: Compensation management being essentially a manual spreadsheet exercise is my biggest frustration right now, and I'd call the intensity significant. When I'm trying to do pay equity analysis, when I'm benchmarking roles against market data, when I'm preparing for a merit cycle — none of that has adequate tool support. It creates real risk because I'm working off data that isn't automatically updated, and it creates reputational risk if I present something to leadership or the board that has an error buried in a formula. It also means I can't move as fast as the business needs me to. Pay decisions are time-sensitive, and the fact that my operational infrastructure can't keep up with that pace is frustrating.
v.Q19: The expectation for AI-assisted workflows has become real for me in a way that it wasn't eighteen months ago. I want to see tools that can flag potential equity issues before I run a merit cycle, or surface attrition risk signals from engagement data. That capability didn't feel mature enough to factor into our last evaluation, but I think it's now a legitimate criterion. I've also become more serious about workforce planning functionality — with headcount flat, the conversation with leadership is less about hiring and more about organizational design and role-level ROI, and I need tooling that supports that kind of analysis.
v.Q20: Across BambooHR, Paylocity, Lattice, and the benefits broker portal, I'd estimate we're in the $100K to $250K range annually when you count licensing, support tiers, and the broker fees that touch technology.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes, but with real reservations. Each individual tool is arguably reasonably priced on its own. But the aggregate cost of three separate systems — plus the staff time my team spends bridging the gaps between them — starts to feel like poor value compared to what a truly integrated platform could potentially deliver at a similar or lower total cost. So I'd say it's somewhat reasonable but not efficient.
v.Q22: If I had a genuinely capable compensation management module — pay bands, equity analysis, market benchmarking, merit cycle workflow — I'd estimate that's worth $25K or more to us annually. That factors in the staff time we'd recover, the reduced risk of errors in comp decisions, and the strategic value of being able to move faster on pay-related decisions. That feels like a conservative number honestly.
v.Q23: Within six months — probably not a full switch, but I think we'll seriously re-examine the stack in the next twelve to eighteen months. The compensation management gap is the most likely trigger. If a platform can solve that problem in an integrated way and make a credible implementation case, I'm genuinely open to having that conversation. So I'd say switching is somewhat unlikely in the immediate six-month window but probably neutral to somewhat likely over the next year to year and a half.
v.Q24: I think there are three things that most VPs of HR at companies our size would agree on. First, the integration story across the HR tech ecosystem is still fundamentally broken. Vendors advertise integrations that are actually shallow data syncs with significant manual overhead, and that gap between marketing and reality costs HR teams real time and real money. Second, the mid-market is genuinely underserved. There's a well-developed SMB tier and a well-developed enterprise tier, and companies between 100 and 500 employees are constantly choosing between tools that are a bit too simple and tools that are too complex and too expensive. We need products designed specifically for that band, and I don't think the market has fully cracked that yet. Third, the promise of people analytics hasn't materialized for most teams at our scale. We hear a lot about data-driven HR, but the tooling required to actually do that work is either locked behind enterprise pricing or requires a dedicated data analyst to operate, and most HR teams our size don't have that resource. Those three things come up constantly when I talk to peers.

cat.Q5: 12 to 18 months ago (12-18 mo to 12-18 mo)
cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm a Director of HR. I sit between our CHRO and the business-facing HR partners, so I'm mostly running operations and program design for the people function.
v.Q2: About two and a half years. I came in to help build out the HR infrastructure after the company had gone through a pretty fast scaling phase without a lot of formal people ops structure.
v.Q3: We're in environmental services — kind of a niche space. We do consulting and field services work related to environmental compliance and remediation. We're at about 390 people right now, mostly remote but with field crews that are W-2 employees, which adds some complexity. So we don't fit neatly into the typical tech-company HRIS use case.
v.Q4: Rippling is our primary platform. We use it for HRIS, payroll, and benefits administration. We also use it for device management for our remote employees, which was actually a factor in why we chose it. So it's as close to a single platform as we've been able to get. We have a separate ATS — we're on Lever — but everything post-hire runs through Rippling.
v.Q5: That was right around when I joined, so about two and a half years ago. The evaluation was already partially underway when I came on, and I stepped into it and helped drive it to a close.
v.Q6: The company had been using a combination of ADP for payroll and a pretty bare-bones implementation of Zenefits for HR and benefits. Neither was serving us particularly well, especially as the company had grown past 200 people.
v.Q7: Scale was the primary driver. The company had grown from around 130 to over 250 people in roughly eighteen months, and the existing toolset just wasn't architected for that volume. Zenefits in particular had some reliability issues — there were open enrollment periods where employees couldn't access their benefits elections, and that kind of failure at a critical moment erodes trust in the HR function pretty quickly. ADP was functional but the user experience was dated and the support was genuinely difficult to work with. And the fact that the two systems had essentially no meaningful integration meant my team was doing a lot of redundant data entry. Beyond those, the company was starting to hire more remote employees across more states, and our compliance confidence in the multi-state payroll setup wasn't high.
v.Q8: The shift to a distributed workforce was a big one. We'd historically been a company where most employees were either in an office or in the field within a specific geography. When we started hiring remote knowledge workers across the country, the HR and payroll complexity jumped significantly. And there was some investor interest in seeing the company operate more efficiently from an HR infrastructure standpoint — not dramatic pressure, but the expectation that we'd modernize was definitely present.
v.Q9: The Zenefits reliability issues I mentioned were the most visible frustration because they directly impacted employees. But honestly the deeper frustration was around visibility. I didn't have a clean source of truth for headcount, employment status, or compensation data that I trusted enough to report from without first auditing it. When you're a 250-person company that wants to operate professionally, having shaky data infrastructure is a real problem. I also had field crew employees on variable schedules who needed time tracking that integrated cleanly into payroll, and neither Zenefits nor ADP handled that gracefully.
v.Q10: We seriously looked at Rippling, TriNet, Paycom, and BambooHR paired with a separate payroll solution. We did a lighter-touch review of Namely but didn't take it all the way to a formal demo stage.
v.Q11: A few hard requirements. It had to handle multi-state payroll natively — not through a third-party workaround. It needed time tracking that could handle variable schedules and sync directly to payroll without manual intervention, because our field crews made that a real operational requirement. And it needed solid benefits administration capability, not just a portal that pointed to a broker. Device management was a nice-to-have that ended up being a differentiator for Rippling specifically. And we needed implementation support that was actually substantive — we'd heard horror stories about implementations that went sideways, and we couldn't afford to have payroll disrupted during a transition.
v.Q12: I was the primary driver of the evaluation. Our CHRO gave directional guidance and had final approval authority. IT was involved specifically around the device management evaluation for Rippling — that was actually a joint decision with them in a way that the other tools didn't require. Finance had to sign off on budget. And I brought in our payroll specialist early in the process because she was going to be the one living with the system every pay cycle, and her technical input on the payroll requirements was really valuable. It was a more structured decision process than I think this company had historically run for HR tooling.
v.Q13: We switched. We moved to Rippling and migrated off both Zenefits and ADP at the same time. Doing a dual migration simultaneously was ambitious, honestly, but we wanted to be done with both legacy systems quickly.
v.Q14: Rippling won because it genuinely solved more of our requirements in one platform than anything else we evaluated. The multi-state payroll was strong, the time tracking integrated cleanly with payroll, and the device management capability was something no other HR platform offered at all. The UX was clearly more modern than Paycom or TriNet, which mattered for employee adoption. And the implementation team they assigned us was actually knowledgeable — during the sales process they were specific about how they'd handle our field crew time-tracking setup, which gave me confidence they understood our situation rather than just giving generic answers. Price was competitive but wasn't the deciding factor — we genuinely felt like Rippling was the right tool, not just the acceptable one.
v.Q15: TriNet — the PEO model felt like the wrong fit for a company that wanted to own its employer infrastructure directly. I think PEOs work well for certain companies but we wanted control over our payroll and benefits design. Paycom — strong payroll, but the platform felt designed for a more traditional in-office workforce and the UX, honestly, showed its age. I wasn't confident it would drive employee adoption for a remote team used to modern software. BambooHR paired with a separate payroll processor — I actually like BambooHR as an HRIS, but adding a third system to solve the payroll problem felt like exactly the kind of fragmentation we were trying to escape. And I'd seen enough integrations promise seamlessness and deliver friction that I wasn't willing to bet on it.
v.Q16: Rippling's payroll is genuinely excellent. Multi-state compliance is handled automatically in a way that takes real cognitive load off my team. The unified employee record means when something changes — compensation, role, location — it flows through to payroll and benefits without manual intervention. The device management piece continues to be valuable as we onboard remote employees. And the automations capability is something I use constantly — I have workflows built for onboarding, status changes, and offboarding that run without anyone having to remember to trigger them manually.
v.Q17: The reporting and analytics layer is where I feel the most friction. Rippling has improved here but I still can't easily build the kinds of ad hoc workforce reports I want without some workaround effort. Performance management is also an area where I think Rippling is developing but not yet mature — we've kind of worked around it rather than leaning into it. And the support experience has been inconsistent. When something breaks, getting to someone who can actually diagnose and fix it takes longer than it should given what we're paying.
v.Q18: Support response time is the biggest frustration and I'd rate it as significant. When there's a payroll issue or a benefits enrollment problem, those are urgent situations for employees and for my team's credibility. Getting a meaningful response through Rippling's support queue in time to actually resolve the issue before it escalates is harder than it should be. We've had a few situations where I've had to escalate through our account manager just to get traction on something that should have been resolved through normal support channels.
v.Q19: We've grown from around 260 to close to 390 employees since we implemented Rippling, so the volume and complexity has increased. I kind of need more from the analytics and reporting side now than I did at the time we selected the tool. And performance management has become a more urgent program priority — we're at a size where informal performance conversations aren't sufficient and we need more structured tooling to support that, which means Rippling's current capabilities in that area are being tested more seriously than they were initially.
v.Q20: I'd estimate somewhere in the $100K to $250K range annually for Rippling, and then Lever on top of that adds more. So it's meaningful spend.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. The payroll reliability and the automation value justify a significant chunk of it. But honestly, given the support frustrations and the gaps in reporting and performance management, I think the price-to-value ratio could be stronger. I don't feel like we're being overcharged, but I also don't feel like we're fully realizing the value we're paying for.
v.Q22: If Rippling had genuinely responsive, knowledgeable support — not chat bots and ticket queues but actual fast resolution — I'd say that's worth $10K to $25K to us annually in staff time saved and stress avoided during payroll cycles.
v.Q23: Not within six months — switching is very unlikely in that timeframe. We're in a growth phase and a platform migration would consume bandwidth I don't have right now. But if the support issues persist and the performance management gap doesn't close, I think there's a real conversation to have in the twelve-to-eighteen-month range. I'd say somewhat unlikely overall, but not locked in.
v.Q24: I think the support quality problem is genuinely widespread — a lot of HR directors I know feel like they bought a great product during the sales process and then got handed off to a support model that doesn't match the urgency of HR and payroll issues. The second thing I hear consistently is that compliance complexity is outpacing the tools — multi-state regulations, pay transparency laws, leave requirements — and most platforms are reactive to regulatory changes rather than proactive. And I think there's a real challenge around getting non-HR employees to actually use the self-service features they're supposed to use, which puts the burden back on HR teams regardless of how good the tool technically is.
