cat.Q5: 6 to 12 months ago (6-12 mo to 6-12 mo)
cat.Q21: Somewhat no / not really reasonable

v.Q1: Sure. I'm a senior manager in HR. I oversee most of the people operations side of the house, so everything from recruiting coordination to benefits administration kind of falls under my umbrella.
v.Q2: I've been here just over three years now, so I'd put myself in that three-to-five-year band.
v.Q3: We're in financial services — specifically we're a registered investment advisory firm, so we sit at the intersection of wealth management and compliance-heavy operations. Headcount-wise, I think we're sitting at around eighty-five people right now, though honestly that number has been moving pretty fast over the last couple of years. We were closer to fifty-five when I joined, so we've grown quite a bit.
v.Q4: We primarily use BambooHR as our core HRIS. Payroll is actually run through a separate ADP integration at the moment, and benefits administration goes through a broker portal that isn't really connected to anything. So I guess technically it's a bit of a patchwork, but BambooHR is the main hub where employee data lives.
v.Q5: That was roughly fourteen or fifteen months ago, so well within the last twelve to eighteen months. We did a fairly structured evaluation and it took maybe two months from start to finish.
v.Q6: We were on a combination of Namely for the HRIS functions and then a bunch of spreadsheets, honestly. Namely was kind of limping along for us. We also had a separate payroll vendor we were unhappy with.
v.Q7: There were really a few things stacking on top of each other. The most immediate trigger was that we were hiring aggressively — we added about twenty people in a twelve-month window — and our existing setup just was not built to support that kind of pace. Onboarding was taking forever because so much was manual. We'd send new hires a packet of PDFs and then chase them down for signatures, which is just not a great experience when you're trying to attract financial services talent. The second thing was compliance. In our industry you really can't afford loose record-keeping on employee data, and Namely had some reporting limitations that made our compliance team nervous. And honestly a third factor was that our contract with Namely was coming up for renewal and leadership used that moment as a natural forcing function to ask whether we should be looking at other options.
v.Q8: Yeah, I think the broader growth story was really the backdrop for everything. Our firm had closed a new funding round and there was explicit board-level pressure to get our infrastructure in order before we scaled further. So HR technology was one of three or four operational areas that got a hard look at the same time. There was also just a general shift in what candidates in financial services expect — people are comparing their employer experience to their consumer apps, and our old onboarding process felt really dated by comparison.
v.Q9: Definitely. The biggest one was the manual onboarding workflow. Every new hire packet was assembled by hand, and we had no automated task assignments for things like IT provisioning or benefits enrollment reminders. My team was spending hours every week just tracking down paperwork status. The second frustration was reporting — Namely's out-of-the-box reports were pretty thin, and pulling anything custom required exporting to Excel and doing the work ourselves. And then the integration situation was a real pain point. We had our payroll system, Namely, and our benefits portal all siloed from each other, which meant data entry was happening in multiple places and we had sync errors constantly.
v.Q10: We looked at BambooHR, Rippling, and Paylocity. We also had a pretty brief look at Paychex Flex but that fell off fairly quickly.
v.Q11: A few things were non-negotiable. First, electronic onboarding with customizable workflows — that was table stakes after what we'd been dealing with. Second, we needed a clean integration path with our payroll provider or we needed payroll to be native. Third, given our compliance obligations, the system had to have solid audit trail capabilities and role-based access controls. And I think the fourth one was implementation support — we didn't have bandwidth to do a fully self-serve implementation, so we needed a real onboarding team on their side.
v.Q12: It was primarily me driving the evaluation day-to-day. I put together the requirements, ran the demos, and built out the scoring matrix. Our CFO had final sign-off because it crossed a budget threshold that required executive approval, and our Chief Compliance Officer was a key stakeholder who weighed in specifically on the data security and audit trail questions. So I was the primary recommender and they were approvers — I don't think either of them would have overridden a strong recommendation from me, but I needed their alignment to move forward.
v.Q13: We switched. We moved to BambooHR. We moved off Namely completely and BambooHR became our core system.
v.Q14: BambooHR won primarily on a combination of usability and fit for our size. The employee self-service experience was genuinely intuitive, and when we ran it past a few managers during the evaluation they responded really positively to how clean the interface was. The onboarding workflow builder was exactly what we needed — you could set up task lists, assign owners, and the system would send reminders automatically. Honestly, it also felt like it was built for a company our size, whereas Rippling sometimes felt like it was pulling us toward feature complexity that we didn't actually need. Price was also a factor — BambooHR came in at a noticeably lower total cost, and we felt the value trade-off was clear. The implementation experience was also smooth, which mattered given the timeline pressure we were under.
v.Q15: Rippling was interesting and I think it could be the right fit for a different kind of company, but for us it felt overbuilt. The IT device management features and the full workforce platform positioning were things we didn't have an immediate need for, and the pricing reflected all of that bundled functionality which pushed the cost higher than we wanted. There was also a sense that the implementation lift would be significant. Paylocity we basically ruled out early — it felt very much like a mid-market payroll company that had bolted on some HR features, and the UX was noticeably clunkier than the others. Their sales process also wasn't particularly responsive, which honestly didn't build a lot of confidence. Paychex Flex was similar — it felt too transactional and not really designed around the modern HR experience we were trying to build.
v.Q16: BambooHR does a really solid job on the core HRIS stuff. Employee records are clean and easy to maintain, the onboarding workflows have genuinely saved my team a meaningful amount of time, and the reporting — while not perfect — is much better than what we had before. The time-off tracking module works well for us too, and managers have actually adopted it without a lot of hand-holding, which I consider a win.
v.Q17: The biggest gap for us right now is on the payroll side. We're still running ADP separately and the integration between the two is okay but it's not seamless — there's still some manual reconciliation happening each pay period. I'd love a more tightly integrated payroll solution. The performance management module in BambooHR is also pretty basic, and as we've grown we've started to feel the limits there. We're kind of outgrowing the out-of-the-box performance review templates.
v.Q18: The payroll integration gap is definitely the biggest frustration and I'd call it moderate to significant. Every payroll cycle my team is doing a manual check between what BambooHR shows and what ADP processed, and occasionally we catch discrepancies that take time to trace. It's not a crisis-level situation but it's a consistent drag on my team's bandwidth and it introduces a risk surface that I'd rather eliminate entirely. As we continue to grow, I think that friction is only going to get worse.
v.Q19: We've added nearly thirty people since we implemented BambooHR, so scale is a real consideration now. The performance management need has become much more acute — when we were sixty people we could kind of manage review cycles informally, but at eighty-five and growing that's not sustainable. I'm also thinking more about compensation benchmarking and total rewards visibility, which BambooHR doesn't really do in a meaningful way. And honestly, the compliance complexity has increased as we've added people in additional states.
v.Q20: Across BambooHR and our ADP contract, I think we're probably in the range of twenty-five to thirty-five thousand dollars annually when you add it all up.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. I think BambooHR itself is reasonably priced for what it delivers. The combined spend feels a bit high when I consider that we're still running two systems and doing manual work between them — if it were all integrated I'd feel better about the value story.
v.Q22: If I think about the time my team spends on payroll reconciliation and the risk it introduces, I'd probably say solving that cleanly is worth somewhere in the ten-to-twenty-five-thousand-dollar range annually. That's the kind of figure that would make a business case pretty straightforward.
v.Q23: I'd say it's something we'll probably discuss, yes. I don't think a full switch is imminent but I'd put switching likelihood at somewhat likely over the next twelve months, maybe less certain in the six-month window specifically. The payroll situation is the thing that will eventually force a harder conversation.
v.Q24: I think the number one thing people in my position talk about is integration — tools that don't talk to each other create so much duplicated effort and data risk. The second is that a lot of platforms make promises about scalability and then the reality of growing into them is painful. And then I think there's a real tension right now between wanting modern AI-driven features and not having the budget or the IT support to implement them responsibly. Compliance complexity is also something that comes up constantly, especially for companies in regulated industries like mine.

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm a manager in HR. My role is pretty generalist — I handle everything from employee relations to open enrollment to working with our recruiting coordinator on hiring. It's a small team so we all wear a lot of hats.
v.Q2: I've been with the company for about four years, so I'd put that in the three-to-five-year range.
v.Q3: We're in professional services — specifically management consulting. We advise mid-market companies on operational strategy, so our workforce is mostly consultants and project managers with a relatively lean support staff. Headcount right now is around three hundred and twenty people. We've been pretty stable for the last couple of years — maybe a net gain of five or ten people since I've been tracking it closely.
v.Q4: Our main platform is Gusto. We use it for payroll and some of the HR basics — employee profiles, time-off tracking, that kind of thing. Benefits administration actually runs through a separate broker, and we use a point solution for our applicant tracking. So Gusto is the backbone but it's not really handling everything end-to-end.
v.Q5: That evaluation happened about a year and a half ago, so I'd put it in the one-to-two-year range. We spent a few months on it before landing where we landed.
v.Q6: We were using TriNet at that point — the full PEO arrangement. So we were essentially renting HR infrastructure through them rather than owning our own stack.
v.Q7: The primary driver was honestly cost. TriNet's per-employee pricing at our headcount had gotten to a point where leadership was asking hard questions about what we were actually getting for the spend. The math just didn't feel right anymore. Beyond cost, there was a capability concern — TriNet's reporting was really limited from our perspective, and when I needed data to present to leadership, I was constantly having to pull things manually or request it from a TriNet account manager and wait. The third factor was that exiting a PEO structure gives you a lot more control over your benefits design, and our benefits had felt kind of cookie-cutter for a while. Leadership wanted to use benefits as a talent differentiator and felt constrained by what TriNet offered in terms of plan choices.
v.Q8: There was a broader push toward operational autonomy at the company level. Our firm had been going through a period of maturing its internal functions and HR was specifically identified as an area where we should be building our own capability rather than outsourcing it. The consulting industry is also pretty competitive for talent, and there was a real strategic conversation about whether our HR experience — onboarding, benefits, the general employee experience — was keeping pace with what our competitors were offering their people.
v.Q9: Yeah, TriNet specifically was frustrating on a few dimensions. Getting any kind of customized reporting was a real ordeal — you'd have to work through their support team and sometimes wait days for something that should be instant. The employee-facing portal was also pretty clunky and we got a lot of complaints from staff about it being hard to find information. And the co-employment model itself was a source of confusion for employees who didn't understand why their W-2 said TriNet instead of our company name. Those are all things I was hoping a direct-ownership model with a modern platform would solve.
v.Q10: We looked at Gusto, Justworks, and we had a demo with Zenefits — which I think they've rebranded since then. We also briefly looked at ADP Run but it felt pretty dated and didn't make the serious consideration cut.
v.Q11: The first requirement was multi-state payroll capability — we have employees in about eight states so single-state tools were a non-starter. Second was a genuine self-service employee portal, because one of our goals was reducing the number of basic HR questions that came to my team. Third was reporting that I could actually run myself without submitting a ticket. And I think the fourth minimum was a clear, transparent pricing model — after the opacity of PEO pricing we were really attuned to understanding exactly what we'd be paying and why.
v.Q12: It was me and our Head of HR — she's my direct manager — working together through the evaluation. I handled the heavy lifting on research, demo scheduling, and building the comparison summary. She was the decision-maker who presented the recommendation to our CFO for final budget approval. The CFO's involvement was really just a financial review — she wasn't evaluating features. So I'd describe my role as primary recommender and my manager as decision-maker with CFO sign-off required.
v.Q13: We switched. We moved from TriNet to Gusto, which was a significant change because we were going from a full PEO to managing payroll and HR directly for the first time in the company's history.
v.Q14: Gusto won primarily because of how straightforward the implementation and ongoing operations felt for a team our size. We're a three-person HR team and we needed something we could actually manage without dedicated ops resources. Gusto's interface is genuinely approachable — my Head of HR described it as feeling like it was designed for people who aren't payroll specialists, which is kind of accurate for us. The pricing was also very transparent compared to what we'd been dealing with, and the per-employee-per-month model was easy to model out and defend to the CFO. The employee self-service experience tested really well too — we did a soft review with a few employees and they found it intuitive. Justworks was close, honestly, but Gusto's payroll capabilities felt a bit more robust for what we needed and the integrations with our benefits broker were a cleaner story.
v.Q15: Justworks was a close second but ultimately felt more PEO-adjacent than we wanted — we were intentionally moving away from that model and Justworks still operates in a co-employment structure, which made some of the same concerns from TriNet still relevant. Zenefits had a good feature set on paper but during the demo the product felt a bit unstable — there were a couple of moments where things didn't work as expected, and that eroded confidence. I think their support reputation at the time was also not great based on what I'd read. ADP Run we essentially ruled out in the first round because the interface felt like it hadn't been meaningfully updated in years and I just couldn't imagine my team enjoying using it day to day.
v.Q16: Gusto genuinely does payroll well — it's reliable, the tax filings happen automatically, and I can't remember the last time we had a payroll error that wasn't a data entry mistake on our end. The employee portal is clean and employees actually use it to find their pay stubs and benefits info, which means fewer basic questions to my team. Onboarding paperwork being electronic has also been a real quality-of-life improvement for us.
v.Q17: The biggest gap is on the HRIS side. For a company our size, Gusto's employee data and HR management features feel a bit thin — it's really built around payroll and the HR functionality feels somewhat bolted on. Performance management is essentially nonexistent in Gusto, so we're using a separate tool for that. And reporting is still limited in ways that frustrate me — I want to be able to build custom reports without workarounds.
v.Q18: Honestly, the reporting limitations are my biggest ongoing frustration and I'd describe it as moderate. When I need headcount analytics or turnover data sliced in specific ways, I end up exporting CSVs and doing the work in spreadsheets. That's not the end of the world, but when I'm trying to prep for a leadership meeting and I need something quickly, it's annoying and a bit embarrassing when I can't produce a clean report straight from the system. I think for a company with three hundred people, I'd expect more flexibility there.
v.Q19: The biggest shift is that leadership has become much more data-driven about workforce decisions. Two years ago, headcount planning was pretty intuitive — people knew the business. Now we're being asked for workforce analytics, tenure distributions, and cost-per-hire benchmarks, and I need a tool that can actually surface that stuff. Performance management has also become more of a priority as we've made a push toward a more structured feedback culture.
v.Q20: Between Gusto and the separate ATS and performance tool we're running, I'd estimate we're somewhere in the thirty-thousand-to-fifty-thousand-dollar range annually. That's a rough number but I think it's in the right ballpark.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes for Gusto specifically. The payroll reliability alone is worth a lot to us. But when I add in the cost of the supplemental tools we need because Gusto doesn't cover everything, the overall picture feels a bit fragmented and I start to wonder if a more comprehensive platform would be a better investment.
v.Q22: For reporting — if Gusto had a genuinely flexible reporting engine that let me build what I needed without exporting — I'd say that's probably worth five to ten thousand dollars a year to us in saved time and the value of better decisions. Maybe toward the higher end if I think about the hours my team spends on workarounds.
v.Q23: I'd say we'll probably have the conversation in the next six months, but I'd put actual switching likelihood as somewhat unlikely in that window. Gusto is working well enough that there's no burning platform moment. The more realistic scenario is that we evaluate more seriously in the next twelve to eighteen months as the reporting and performance gaps continue to be felt.
v.Q24: I think most HR managers at companies our size would say the biggest challenge is finding a tool that grows with you without blowing up your budget or requiring a full IT implementation team. There's a real gap between the lightweight SMB tools and the enterprise platforms, and a lot of us are sitting in the middle wondering which direction to move. Data and analytics expectations have also gone up significantly — HR is being asked to be more strategic and the tools need to enable that. And benefits cost management is a persistent challenge that most platforms don't really help you solve.

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: Sure, I'm a manager in HR. My focus is mostly on people operations — workforce systems, compliance, onboarding and offboarding processes — though I collaborate pretty closely with our talent acquisition function since they sit adjacent to our team.
v.Q2: Just over two years. I came in specifically to help the company get its HR operations onto a more scalable foundation, so system evaluation has been a big part of my role from the start.
v.Q3: We're in professional services — specifically an architecture and engineering firm. So our workforce is a mix of licensed architects, structural engineers, project managers, and then administrative and business development staff. We're currently at around three hundred and forty people. It's been pretty stable — we had a small dip during a project slowdown last year and then a modest recovery, but we're roughly flat over the two-year view.
v.Q4: We run Rippling as our primary platform and it covers quite a bit — HRIS, payroll, benefits administration, and we have the device management module turned on as well since IT sits under the same operational umbrella. We also use Greenhouse for applicant tracking, which integrates into Rippling. So it's fairly consolidated compared to what I see at a lot of companies my size.
v.Q5: That was right around when I joined, so about two and a half years ago. The evaluation was already partially underway when I came onboard and I stepped into it and helped drive it to a conclusion.
v.Q6: The company had been on Paychex for payroll and was using a combination of spreadsheets and a pretty old version of Sage HRMS for employee records. It was a pretty fragmented setup with limited automation.
v.Q7: There were several things happening at once. The most foundational issue was that the existing systems were genuinely holding the HR function back — Sage HRMS had very limited self-service capabilities and the version they were on was aging out of active support, which was a real concern. Paychex was functional but the service experience had been frustrating — slow to respond, and there had been a couple of payroll tax filing errors that required correction. The combination of an unsupported system and a payroll provider with service issues was a risk that leadership couldn't ignore. There was also a new HR leadership hire — my predecessor had left — and the company used that moment as a natural opportunity to reconsider the whole stack rather than just patch the existing setup.
v.Q8: The firm had made a commitment to a broader digital transformation initiative the year before. It wasn't just HR — project management, finance, and client delivery tools were all getting reviewed. HR was specifically flagged because the manual processes were creating delays in getting people licensed and credentialed properly when they joined, which actually affected project staffing timelines. In architecture and engineering you need licensed staff on projects for compliance reasons, so any inefficiency in the onboarding and credentialing process has direct business impact. That gave the HR system evaluation a higher priority than it might have had otherwise.
v.Q9: The manual onboarding process was a significant pain point — new hires had to physically come into the office on day one to complete paperwork, which was already an anachronism even before hybrid work became the norm. Employee data was duplicated across Sage and Paychex and neither talked to the other, so any change — a pay adjustment, an address update, a title change — had to be entered in two places. And the reporting situation was pretty dire. The operations director had tried to pull a headcount-by-department report before I arrived and ended up having to do it manually from an org chart. That kind of thing is just not acceptable at our size.
v.Q10: We seriously evaluated Rippling, BambooHR, and UKG Ready. We had an initial conversation with Paycom as well but they were reaching toward the higher end of our budget ceiling and the product felt sized for a larger company, so they didn't progress past the first demo.
v.Q11: There were a few firm requirements. First was a true single system of record — we were done with data existing in two places. Second was electronic onboarding that could be completed remotely before day one, which was non-negotiable given our hybrid posture. Third was payroll that was either native or tightly integrated enough to eliminate manual sync. And fourth was multi-state compliance support, because we have staff in seven states and our prior experience with filing errors made that a real focus area. Anything that couldn't confidently check those four boxes didn't advance.
v.Q12: The evaluation committee was me, our VP of Finance, and our IT director. I led the HR evaluation track — requirements, demos, and the functional scoring. Our IT director was specifically involved because of the device management and security considerations, and his sign-off was important for anything that would touch employee devices or SSO. Finance held the budget and was evaluating total cost of ownership. The final recommendation went to our COO who approved it. So I was a primary recommender alongside IT, with Finance and the COO as approvers. It wasn't a solo decision but I had significant influence over the direction.
v.Q13: We switched completely. We moved to Rippling, which replaced both Sage HRMS and Paychex simultaneously. The implementation was a pretty substantial lift but it was the right call.
v.Q14: Rippling won because of the breadth of the platform and how tightly everything was connected. The fact that a single system could handle HRIS, payroll, benefits, and IT device management was genuinely compelling for us because of where IT and HR overlap in our firm. The workflow automation capabilities were also a differentiator — the ability to trigger a sequence of actions across HR and IT when someone is onboarded or offboarded was something neither BambooHR nor UKG Ready could really match in terms of configurability. The IT director was particularly enthusiastic about the device management piece, which I think gave us additional internal alignment that made the approval process smoother. Honestly, the demo experience was strong too — the Rippling rep understood our specific use case pretty quickly and showed us exactly the workflows we'd described as pain points, which built a lot of confidence.
v.Q15: BambooHR was a genuine contender and had a really clean user experience, but the payroll integration story was less native than we wanted and the IT management capabilities were essentially nonexistent — it's really an HRIS tool with some payroll bolted on, which didn't fit our cross-functional requirements. UKG Ready had strong payroll and compliance features and honestly was a solid product, but it felt like it was built for a more traditional workforce — the UX had a slightly older feel and some of the implementation requirements were heavier than we wanted to take on. The implementation timeline they quoted was also significantly longer than Rippling's, which was a practical factor. Paycom, as I mentioned, felt too enterprise-sized for where we were and the pricing reflected that.
v.Q16: Rippling excels at automation and integration. The onboarding workflow we've built means a new hire can complete all their paperwork, get added to payroll, have their benefits enrollment triggered, and have their laptop provisioned essentially without my team manually touching anything after the initial setup. That automation has genuinely changed what my team is able to focus on. Payroll is also rock solid — we haven't had a tax filing issue since we moved off Paychex, which tells you something.
v.Q17: The learning curve is real and it never fully goes away — Rippling is a powerful platform but it's also complex, and when you want to configure something new it can take a meaningful amount of time to figure out the right approach. Customer support responsiveness has also been inconsistent in my experience. For straightforward questions the help center is good, but for anything nuanced you can wait longer than you'd want. I'd also say the performance management module is functional but not exceptional — it works but it's not what I'd call best-in-class.
v.Q18: Support responsiveness is the one that frustrates me the most on a day-to-day basis and I'd call it a moderate frustration that occasionally spikes to significant. When something breaks or a configuration isn't behaving as expected, getting a timely and knowledgeable response from their support team can be a real challenge. We have a dedicated customer success contact but availability varies. For a platform this central to our operations, I want to feel like I have a reliable lifeline when something goes wrong.
v.Q19: I think our expectations around analytics have matured quite a bit. When we implemented Rippling we were primarily focused on operational reliability — getting payroll right, getting onboarding automated. Now that those things are working, leadership is asking for more strategic workforce data and I want the system to help me build those stories. I'm also thinking more about employee experience as a retention tool, which puts more focus on things like total compensation visibility and the mobile experience for our field-based staff.
v.Q20: With Rippling covering the full platform plus Greenhouse for ATS, I'd estimate we're somewhere in the seventy-five-thousand-to-one-hundred-thousand-dollar range annually. Rippling is not a cheap platform at our headcount, especially with the additional modules we have active.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. The automation value is genuinely real and I can quantify it in terms of time my team gets back. But at that spend level I expect a higher tier of support than we're consistently getting, and that's a gap between the value promise and the delivered experience.
v.Q22: If dedicated, responsive support were genuinely solved — like a real SLA with a knowledgeable person — I'd say that's worth ten to twenty-five thousand dollars a year to us. When support failures create delays on payroll or compliance questions, the downstream cost is significant.
v.Q23: I don't think we'll switch in the next six months — the switching cost from Rippling would be substantial at this point and the platform is embedded pretty deeply into our operations. I'd put switching likelihood as very unlikely in that window. That said, if the support situation doesn't improve I think we'd be having a harder conversation in the twelve-to-eighteen-month range.
v.Q24: I think the most common complaint is that platforms promise a lot in the sales process and the reality of implementation and ongoing support tells a different story. There's a trust gap between what vendors demonstrate and what customers actually experience. Beyond that, I think HR managers at mid-sized companies are really struggling with the complexity-versus-capability tradeoff — you want a powerful system but you also need your team to be able to use it without becoming a full-time administrator. And multi-state compliance keeps getting more complicated, especially with remote and hybrid work — the regulatory landscape changes constantly and most people feel like their tools are always a step behind.

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: Sure. I'm VP of People Operations. I've been in this seat for a few years now and I oversee everything from HR policy to comp and benefits to the day-to-day people infrastructure of the company.
v.Q2: I've been with this company right around six years, I think. Started as a director-level role and moved into the VP seat about three years in.
v.Q3: We're in manufacturing — precision component manufacturing, specifically. We have about 185 employees right now, mostly plant floor and operations staff, with a smaller corporate and administrative team. We're headquartered in the Cincinnati area, so kind of classic Midwest industrial company.
v.Q4: We're primarily on BambooHR. That handles our core HRIS functions — employee records, time off tracking, onboarding workflows, and performance reviews. For payroll we actually run a separate integration with a regional payroll processor, and benefits administration goes through our broker's portal. So it's BambooHR as the hub, but honestly it's not a fully unified stack.
v.Q5: That was roughly a year and a half ago, so I'd say within the last 12 to 18 months. We went through a fairly structured evaluation process over the course of about two quarters.
v.Q6: We were using a legacy HRIS called Paychex Flex at the time. It handled payroll and had some basic HR record-keeping, but it was not designed with modern people operations workflows in mind. It was very much a payroll system that bolted HR onto it as an afterthought.
v.Q7: There were really two main drivers. The first was manual process pain — I mean, the amount of time my team was spending on things like paper-based new hire paperwork, manually updating records, chasing down managers for performance review completions, it was just not sustainable for a team our size. We were a team of three doing the work of five because the tools weren't doing any of the heavy lifting. The second driver was honestly a capability gap around self-service. Our employees — most of whom are on the plant floor — had no easy way to check their own pay stubs, request time off, or update their personal information without coming directly to HR. That was creating bottlenecks and, frankly, some frustration on both sides. We also had a contract renewal coming up with Paychex and that served as a forcing function to at least ask whether we were in the right place.
v.Q8: Manufacturing has had a real challenge holding onto workers, especially in the skilled trades. So there was some board-level conversation about improving the employee experience as a retention lever, and that included looking at whether our HR technology was contributing to a positive or a negative experience for people. I think when leadership starts talking about retention strategy, it naturally flows down into what tools support the employee lifecycle. That gave my evaluation a little more executive visibility and, honestly, a bit more budget flexibility than I might have had otherwise.
v.Q9: Yes, several. Reporting was a big one — Paychex Flex's reporting capabilities were pretty minimal. If I needed anything beyond canned reports, I was exporting to Excel and building things manually, which is not a good use of my time or my team's time. Onboarding was another pain point — there was basically no structured digital onboarding workflow, so every new hire was a manual process of printing packets, collecting signatures, scanning things back in. And the integration story was poor. We use Outlook and a few other Microsoft tools, and Paychex had essentially no native connectors, so everything was siloed. Those three things — reporting, onboarding, and integrations — were the clearest gaps.
v.Q10: We seriously looked at BambooHR, Paylocity, and Paycor. We also had a preliminary conversation with ADP Workforce Now but ruled them out early because they felt much more oriented toward companies in the 500-plus range and the pricing reflected that.
v.Q11: A few non-negotiables. First, it had to have a mobile-accessible employee self-service component — that was critical given our plant floor workforce, because not everyone is sitting at a desktop. Second, it had to have configurable onboarding workflows with e-signature built in, not as an add-on. Third, I wanted to see a clear integration path or native connector with our payroll processor, or native payroll capability itself. And honestly, implementation support was a factor — I didn't want to be handed a help center and told good luck. We needed actual onboarding assistance.
v.Q12: It was primarily me driving the evaluation, but I needed sign-off from our CFO on the budget and from our CEO just as a courtesy given the scope of the change. IT was looped in briefly to review the integration and security questions, but they weren't deeply involved in the feature evaluation. So I would say I was the primary recommender — I built the business case, ran the demos, and made the final recommendation — but I needed financial approval above me.
v.Q13: We switched. We moved to BambooHR, and we went live about fourteen months ago.
v.Q14: BambooHR stood out for a few reasons. The UX was genuinely the most intuitive of the three we evaluated seriously — and that mattered because I knew I'd be rolling this out to managers who are not particularly tech-forward. I didn't want to spend six months on change management just to get adoption. The self-service mobile experience was solid. And the onboarding workflow configurability was exactly what we needed — I could build out the new hire packet process end to end without needing developer help. Price-to-value was also favorable. Paylocity had some features I liked but it was priced higher and felt like it was built for a company with a larger HR team than mine. Paycor had a strong payroll story but the HRIS side felt a little thin. BambooHR was the best overall balance for a company our size and complexity.
v.Q15: Paylocity — honestly, the product itself was good, but the price point was higher and the sales process felt like it was designed for a much larger company. There was a lot of pressure to commit quickly and the contract structure was less flexible. For a stable, not-growing organization like ours, it felt like we'd be paying for capacity we'd never use. Paycor — the payroll module was impressive, I'll give them that, but the HRIS and people management side felt secondary to them. The reporting was limited compared to BambooHR and the onboarding workflow builder wasn't as configurable. ADP we ruled out early, as I said — they came in with a proposal that didn't feel like it was calibrated to our size at all, and the implementation fees alone were a signal that we weren't their target customer.
v.Q16: BambooHR does the core HRIS stuff really well. Employee records are clean and easy to maintain. The onboarding workflows have genuinely cut our new hire processing time significantly — I'd estimate we've reduced the administrative time per new hire by close to 40 percent. The performance review module is easy enough that managers actually use it without a lot of hand-holding. And the reporting, while not the most advanced thing in the world, is a massive step up from what we had before. Self-service adoption on the plant floor has been better than I expected, honestly.
v.Q17: The payroll integration is the biggest structural gap. Because we're not using BambooHR's payroll — we're using a third-party processor — we're doing a manual sync every pay period, which defeats part of the purpose of having an integrated platform. I'd also say the benefits administration piece is weak. BambooHR has basic benefits tracking but our benefits complexity — we have a few different plan tiers and some union-adjacent classifications — is more than it handles gracefully. And the analytics capabilities cap out pretty quickly if you want anything more sophisticated than headcount summaries.
v.Q18: The manual payroll sync, without question. Every other week, someone on my team is exporting data from BambooHR, reformatting it, and uploading it to our payroll processor. That is time we are spending on data transfer, not on anything that adds value. And when there are discrepancies — which happens — it's a reconciliation headache. I'd call it a significant frustration. It's not going to make me switch tomorrow, but it's the thing I think about most when I consider whether we have the right setup.
v.Q19: I think the compliance landscape has gotten more complex, particularly around leave management — Ohio has seen some changes in state-level leave requirements and tracking those accurately matters more than it did. And I've started to think more seriously about whether we need more robust workforce analytics, not just headcount reports but things like turnover predictors or time-to-fill trends. Those weren't really on my radar during the last evaluation.
v.Q20: Across BambooHR and our payroll processor, I think we're somewhere in the range of $30,000 to $40,000 annually. Give or take — I'd have to pull the exact contracts to be precise.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes, I'd say. BambooHR itself is good value. The overall spend feels reasonable when I consider what we were paying before and what we've eliminated in manual labor costs. I just think we could get more value if the payroll integration were native rather than bolted on.
v.Q22: If native payroll integration eliminated that bi-weekly sync entirely, I think it's worth somewhere in the $10,000 to $15,000 range annually when you account for staff time saved and the error correction overhead we currently deal with. So I'd say the $10K to $25K band feels right.
v.Q23: Not in the next six months, no. I'd say very unlikely. We've only been live for a bit over a year and the change management cost of another platform switch would be hard to justify to leadership right now. That said, I'm not closing the door entirely on a 12-to-24 month horizon if the payroll situation doesn't improve.
v.Q24: I think the fragmentation problem is universal — most HR leaders I talk to are stitching together three or four tools that don't talk to each other, and that creates data integrity issues and manual work that nobody has time for. The promise of an all-in-one platform is real but the execution rarely fully delivers at the mid-market level. And I think there's a growing expectation from employees for consumer-grade experiences — people compare their self-service HR portal to their banking app or Amazon, and most HR tools are not winning that comparison. That gap between employee expectation and platform reality is something I hear about constantly.

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm an HR manager. I'm the only HR person at my company, so I kind of do everything — hiring, onboarding, benefits, employee relations, you name it.
v.Q2: About three years now.
v.Q3: Healthcare — we're an outpatient behavioral health group with a mix of clinical and administrative staff. Right around 140 employees total. We're based in the Atlanta metro area.
v.Q4: We use Gusto for payroll and some HR basics. Benefits administration is handled separately through our insurance broker's system. So it's not fully unified — Gusto is the primary tool but it doesn't cover everything.
v.Q5: That was about a year ago, I think. Maybe a little over — closer to 14 or 15 months ago.
v.Q6: We were using ADP Run. It was honestly fine for basic payroll, but it wasn't doing much beyond that for us.
v.Q7: The biggest thing was that I was drowning in manual work. As a solo HR person supporting 140 employees, I needed tools that would do more of the lifting for me. ADP Run was basically just cutting checks — it wasn't helping me with anything like onboarding checklists, offer letters, or time-off tracking. The contract renewal was also coming up, and I used that as an opportunity to push leadership to let me evaluate other options. Cost was a secondary factor — I thought we might be able to get more features for a similar or lower price point somewhere else.
v.Q8: Healthcare has a lot of credentialing and compliance requirements, and I was feeling the pressure to have better documentation and audit trails. We had a state licensing review come up and pulling together employee records was more painful than it should have been. That experience made leadership more open to investing in better HR infrastructure.
v.Q9: Definitely. The lack of any self-service for employees was a constant source of friction — I was fielding questions about pay stubs and PTO balances all day because there was no easy employee portal. And onboarding was entirely paper-based, which in healthcare is a real problem because we have a lot of compliance documents that need signatures and tracking. I also had no reliable way to run even basic HR reports out of ADP Run without calling their support line, which was its own frustration.
v.Q10: I looked at Gusto, Rippling, and Paychex Flex. I also briefly looked at BambooHR but ruled them out fairly early.
v.Q11: Employee self-service was non-negotiable. Digital onboarding with e-signature was required. And I needed it to be something I could actually implement and manage myself without a dedicated IT resource, so ease of setup mattered a lot. Price was also a real factor — leadership gave me a rough budget ceiling and I had to stay within it.
v.Q12: Our CFO had to approve the budget, and our CEO was looped in because it touched payroll. But I was honestly the one running the evaluation from start to finish. I presented a recommendation and they approved it. I'd call myself the primary recommender with financial sign-off required from above.
v.Q13: We switched to Gusto.
v.Q14: Gusto was the easiest to set up and the pricing was transparent — I knew exactly what I was getting into. The UI felt modern and approachable, which mattered because I was going to be rolling it out to clinical staff who are not particularly interested in learning new software. The employee self-service portal was clean. And honestly, their support during implementation was better than I expected. Rippling had more features but felt like overkill for where we are, and the pricing was harder to pin down.
v.Q15: Rippling was interesting but it felt like a lot more than I needed, and the pricing conversation was more complex than I had time for. BambooHR — I just couldn't justify the price for a company our size given that payroll was a separate add-on situation. Paychex Flex I ruled out because it felt too similar to ADP Run — same category of tool, same limitations, just a different logo.
v.Q16: Payroll runs smoothly and I barely have to touch it after setup. The employee onboarding flow has saved me a lot of time — new hires complete their own paperwork before day one, which is great. And the employee portal reduces the number of repetitive questions I get each week by a lot. Tax filing is also handled automatically, which was a headache with ADP.
v.Q17: Benefits administration is the weak point. Gusto has some benefits features but they don't integrate well with our broker's system, so I'm still doing a lot of manual cross-referencing during open enrollment. The reporting is also fairly basic — I can get headcount and payroll summaries but not much beyond that.
v.Q18: Open enrollment is genuinely painful. Every year I'm exporting data from Gusto, reformatting it, and sending it to our broker manually. Employees are confused about the process because nothing is fully integrated. I'd rate the frustration as significant — it's a concentrated period of high effort every fall and it feels like the tool is working against me during one of the most critical HR periods of the year.
v.Q19: I'm more focused on compliance documentation now than I was before. Healthcare regulations don't sit still and I need better audit trails. I've also started thinking about whether I need a more integrated benefits platform, not just a payroll tool with benefits features bolted on.
v.Q20: I'd estimate somewhere in the range of $12,000 to $18,000 a year, including Gusto and the broker portal fees.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. For payroll specifically, the value is there. But when I factor in the benefits gap and the manual work I still do around open enrollment, it feels like we're not getting the full return we should be.
v.Q22: If open enrollment were fully automated and integrated with our broker, I'd say that's worth maybe $5,000 to $8,000 a year in my time savings alone. So somewhere in the $5K to $10K range.
v.Q23: I'd say somewhat unlikely in the next six months — switching is a big lift when you're a solo HR team. But I'm not locked in forever. If open enrollment is as painful next fall as it was last year, I'll probably start a more serious evaluation.
v.Q24: I think the biggest issue is that most tools are good at one thing and mediocre at everything else. You get a great payroll tool that has weak HR. Or a great HRIS that doesn't touch payroll. And for solo HR practitioners especially, that fragmentation means we're always doing manual work to fill the gaps. The integration problem hasn't really been solved at the price point that small-to-mid-size companies can actually afford.

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm a senior manager in HR. I handle the full HR function for our company — which is a lot, given that I'm a team of one supporting close to 400 people.
v.Q2: Just under two years. I came in as the company was scaling fast and they needed someone to build out the HR infrastructure.
v.Q3: We're in retail — specifically direct-to-consumer e-commerce. No physical storefronts. We have about 390 employees right now, spread across about 30 states since everyone is remote. We're headquartered in Austin, Texas, though most of the team is distributed.
v.Q4: We use Rippling as our main platform. It handles payroll, benefits administration, device management, and a lot of the HRIS basics. It's the most unified stack I've personally worked with — still not perfect, but it's a single pane of glass for most of what I do.
v.Q5: That evaluation happened before I joined, but I was brought in right at the tail end of it and was part of the final vendor selection. I'd say it was about 18 to 20 months ago.
v.Q6: The company was on a combination of Justworks for PEO services and a separate ATS — Greenhouse, I believe. As they crossed the threshold where a PEO model stopped making financial sense, they needed to build their own HR stack.
v.Q7: The primary trigger was a scaling event — the company had grown from around 150 to 300 people in about 18 months, and the PEO model with Justworks was getting very expensive at that headcount. The per-employee cost of a PEO doesn't scale well when you're adding 10 or 15 people a month. So cost reduction was a real driver. But alongside that, there was also a capability gap — leadership wanted more direct control over benefits design, comp structures, and HR data, which you give up to some degree under a PEO arrangement. And with a fully remote, multi-state workforce, multi-state payroll compliance was a requirement that Justworks wasn't handling as cleanly as we needed.
v.Q8: The company had just closed a Series B, so there was investor pressure to get unit economics in order — and HR vendor costs were part of that conversation. There was also a push from the CFO to move away from the PEO model because it obscured some of the employment-related cost visibility that finance wanted. So digital transformation and financial discipline were both in the picture.
v.Q9: Multi-state compliance was the biggest technical gap — tracking different state leave requirements, tax registrations, and benefits eligibility rules across 30 states is genuinely complex and the PEO handled it opaquely. I also think there was frustration with the lack of integration between Justworks and Greenhouse — the hiring-to-onboarding handoff was entirely manual. And the analytics coming out of the PEO were limited — you got what they gave you, not what you actually needed.
v.Q10: Rippling, Deel, Gusto, and Paylocity. Workday was briefly mentioned but immediately ruled out as too enterprise for where we were at the time.
v.Q11: Multi-state payroll capability across at least 40 states — that was table stakes given our footprint. Benefits administration had to be native, not a broker referral. Integration with Greenhouse for the ATS handoff was required. And device management or IT provisioning was a strong preference because we were onboarding remote employees and shipping laptops — that whole workflow needed to be tied in.
v.Q12: The CFO was heavily involved because this was fundamentally a financial decision — moving off a PEO changes your cost structure significantly. The COO was looped in because operations touches onboarding and equipment provisioning. IT was consulted on the device management piece. I came in as the HR subject matter expert in the final stages and helped evaluate the functional capabilities. The CFO had final sign-off. So it was a cross-functional group with finance holding the most authority.
v.Q13: We switched — moved to Rippling and fully exited the PEO model.
v.Q14: Rippling won on breadth. It was the only tool that genuinely unified HR, payroll, benefits, and device management under one roof in a way that actually worked. For a remote company scaling fast, that unified view of an employee — who they are, what they're paid, what benefits they have, what device they're using — was compelling. The integration with Greenhouse was also cleaner than the alternatives. And the multi-state compliance tooling felt more mature than what Gusto or Paylocity showed us. The price was higher, but the CFO could see the cost comparison against PEO fees and it made sense.
v.Q15: Gusto — I think it's a genuinely good product for smaller companies, but at 300-plus employees with 30-state complexity, it started to feel like we were at the edge of what it's built for. The benefits administration piece was less sophisticated than we needed. Paylocity had strong payroll but the platform felt more traditional — the UX wasn't as modern and the device management piece didn't exist. Deel was interesting for international hiring, which we weren't doing yet, so it felt like a future-state tool rather than a present-state one. It didn't have the domestic HR depth we needed.
v.Q16: The unified employee record is genuinely useful — I can look at one profile and see everything from comp to benefits elections to the device they were provisioned. Onboarding automation is strong. Multi-state payroll compliance has been reliable. And the app ecosystem — the way Rippling connects to other tools — means I've been able to build out workflows without needing an IT person sitting next to me.
v.Q17: The performance management module is pretty thin — I've supplemented it with a separate tool. And customer support has been inconsistent. When something breaks, getting a fast, knowledgeable response is harder than it should be for the price we're paying. The learning curve is also steeper than I expected — there's a lot of capability in the platform but it's not always intuitive to find.
v.Q18: Support responsiveness, honestly. When I have a payroll issue that needs to be resolved before a pay run, waiting 24 to 48 hours for a useful response from support is not acceptable. It's happened more than once. I'd call it a significant frustration — not severe enough to make me start shopping again tomorrow, but significant because payroll errors have real consequences for employees and I need to be able to resolve them quickly.
v.Q19: Our headcount growth has plateaued a bit, so I'm less focused on scaling speed and more focused on depth and reliability. I also need better performance management tooling than what Rippling currently gives me — that's become a priority as the organization matures. And leadership is starting to ask for workforce analytics that go beyond what I can pull out of Rippling today.
v.Q20: I believe we're somewhere in the range of $80,000 to $100,000 annually for Rippling at our employee count and the module tier we're on.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes — the value is real, but the support experience makes me feel like we're not getting everything we're paying for. If the support were consistently strong, I'd say strongly yes without hesitation.
v.Q22: Dedicated support with a guaranteed response SLA for payroll-critical issues? I'd say that's worth $10,000 to $15,000 a year to us, easy. The risk cost of a payroll error at 400 employees is significant, so I'd put it in the $10K to $25K range.
v.Q23: Somewhat unlikely in the next six months — the switching cost at our size is real and I don't have a team to help manage a migration. But if support doesn't improve before our next renewal conversation, I'll push leadership to at least open up an evaluation.
v.Q24: I think the gap between what platforms promise in the sales process and what they actually deliver at scale is a real and persistent problem. Every platform demos beautifully. But when you're running payroll for 400 people across 30 states and something goes wrong, you find out pretty quickly whether the vendor relationship is real or not. I also think the expectation that one solo HR person can manage an enterprise-grade platform without meaningful support is a structural mismatch — the tools are getting more complex but the HR team sizes aren't growing proportionally.

cat.Q5: 18 to 24 months ago (18-24 mo to 18-24 mo)
cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: Sure. I'm a manager in Talent Acquisition. I oversee recruiting for a mid-size healthcare organization, and I work pretty closely with our broader HR team on things like onboarding and headcount planning.
v.Q2: I've been here a little over four years now, so I guess I'd fall in that three-to-five-year band.
v.Q3: We're in healthcare — specifically outpatient behavioral health services. And right now we're sitting at around one hundred and sixty employees, though honestly that number has been coming down over the last year or so as we've gone through some restructuring.
v.Q4: We primarily use Gusto. It handles payroll and benefits administration for us, and we use it alongside a separate ATS — we're on Breezy HR for recruiting. So it's kind of a two-platform setup rather than a single integrated system.
v.Q5: That was roughly twelve to fourteen months ago. So within the last year, pretty recent actually. It was tied to some leadership changes we were going through at the time.
v.Q6: We were already on Gusto at that point, and we had been using it for a couple of years. The evaluation wasn't necessarily to replace Gusto entirely — it was more about whether we needed to add something on top of it or consolidate into something more comprehensive. We were also still on Breezy at the time.
v.Q7:
There were a few things happening at once. First, we had brought in a new VP of Operations who wanted to take a hard look at all of our people systems and figure out whether we were getting enough value out of them. That was probably the main trigger — new leadership wanting to validate or change how things were being done.

Beyond that, we were starting to feel real pain around the fact that Gusto and Breezy weren't talking to each other. When someone was hired in Breezy, we had to manually re-enter all of that data into Gusto to set up payroll and benefits. That was time-consuming and error-prone, and with a team our size, errors in onboarding are a real problem, especially in healthcare where you've got compliance requirements to think about.

And then the third factor was honestly cost. We were paying for two separate tools, and the question came up of whether there was something that bundled everything together for less than what we were spending combined.
v.Q8: Honestly, the broader context was that we were already starting to see some signs of the restructuring that would come later. We had lost a couple of major payer contracts, and leadership was in cost-reduction mode. So any vendor evaluation was really happening under that umbrella of tightening budgets and trying to do more with less. There was also some pressure around compliance documentation in behavioral health specifically — state licensing requirements and credentialing stuff — and we were trying to figure out whether our tools were helping or hurting us on that front.
v.Q9:
Yes, definitely. The biggest one was that manual data re-entry I mentioned between Breezy and Gusto. It was taking one of my coordinators a meaningful chunk of time every week, and it felt like something a modern platform just shouldn't require us to do.

Beyond that, Gusto's reporting capabilities were pretty limited for what we needed. We wanted to be able to pull headcount reports, track turnover by department, and get some visibility into time-to-fill and offer acceptance rates. Gusto just didn't give us that. We were building those reports manually in spreadsheets, which is kind of embarrassing to admit but it's the reality.

And then on the benefits side, open enrollment in Gusto was clunky. Employees had a hard time comparing plan options, and we'd get a flood of questions every November that really should have been answerable through the platform itself.
v.Q10: We looked at Rippling, BambooHR, and Paycor. Those were the three we got to demo stage. We also briefly looked at Paylocity but didn't end up requesting a demo.
v.Q11: Yes, we were pretty clear about a few things. It had to handle both payroll and benefits natively — we didn't want another two-tool setup. It needed to have either a built-in ATS or a solid integration with Breezy or a comparable ATS, because we weren't ready to rip out recruiting entirely. And it had to be able to handle healthcare-specific compliance requirements, at least at a basic level — things like I-9 management and document storage for credentialing. Price was also a real constraint given where the company was heading.
v.Q12: So it was me, the VP of Operations who had triggered the evaluation, our CFO, and our HR Director. I was the primary recommender — I did most of the research, coordinated the demos, and put together a comparison summary. But the CFO had final sign-off on any contract, and the VP of Ops was really the executive champion who could have pushed things through or shut them down. The HR Director was involved throughout as a co-evaluator, especially on the benefits administration side, which is more her area than mine.
v.Q13: We ended up staying with Gusto. We didn't switch. The evaluation concluded that switching costs were too high given everything else going on with the restructuring, and the CFO wasn't comfortable committing to a new contract in that environment.
v.Q14: I mean, it wasn't really that Gusto stood out positively — it was more that the alternatives didn't clear the bar we needed them to clear given the timing and the cost environment. Gusto was familiar, it was already implemented, and switching would have meant migration costs and staff retraining during a period when we were already stretched thin. There was also a real concern that going through an implementation while simultaneously managing layoffs and restructuring was just too much risk. So it was more of a status quo decision than an enthusiastic choice.
v.Q15:
Rippling was actually the most impressive in the demo, but it came in too expensive for where we were budget-wise. The pricing model also felt a little complex — lots of add-ons — and we couldn't get a clean number out of them quickly, which frustrated the CFO.

BambooHR felt more like an HRIS than a full payroll solution. We got the sense that payroll was kind of bolted on rather than native, and we'd heard mixed things from peers about their payroll reliability. So that raised a flag.

Paycor we didn't demo, so I can't say much about them specifically. They seemed oriented toward larger organizations and I wasn't sure they'd give us the attention a company our size would need.

So really, cost and implementation timing killed Rippling, and product concerns killed BambooHR.
v.Q16: Gusto is genuinely easy to use, and I think that matters more than people give it credit for. Our employees can log in and find their pay stubs, update their direct deposit, or look at their benefits without needing to call HR. That self-service aspect reduces a non-trivial amount of inbound questions. Payroll runs reliably — I'll give it that. And their support, while not lightning fast, has generally been helpful when we've had issues.
v.Q17: Reporting is still the biggest gap. We're still building a lot of our workforce analytics in spreadsheets because Gusto just doesn't give us the depth we need. And the ATS integration situation hasn't improved — we're still doing manual transfers between Breezy and Gusto. I also think the benefits experience during open enrollment could be a lot better. Those same issues from before the evaluation are still sitting there unresolved.
v.Q18: The manual data transfer between our ATS and Gusto is my biggest frustration, and I'd call the level significant. It creates real operational risk — if someone makes a data entry error, we could have a new hire set up incorrectly for payroll or benefits, which in healthcare can cause compliance issues on top of the obvious employee experience problem. And it just shouldn't be a manual process in 2024. Every time I onboard someone, I'm thinking about the fact that we're doing something that should be automated and isn't.
v.Q19: Honestly, the restructuring has changed things in an unexpected way. We're not growing, so recruiting volume is down, but the compliance and documentation demands have actually gone up — terminations, severance, COBRA administration. Those workflows are areas where Gusto isn't particularly strong, and that's become more visible to us as we've worked through the restructuring. I think if we were to evaluate again today, we'd be weighing offboarding capability much more heavily than we did last time.
v.Q20: Between Gusto and Breezy together, I think we're somewhere in the twenty to thirty thousand dollar range annually. I don't have the exact figure in front of me but that feels about right.
v.Q21: Somewhat, I guess. Gusto is reasonably priced on its own. But when I factor in the hidden cost of manual processes and the time my team spends doing things the platform should be doing for us, I'm less confident the overall value equation is strong.
v.Q22: If someone could give me a seamless, automated integration between our ATS and Gusto — real-time, no manual re-entry — I'd say that's worth somewhere in the five to ten thousand dollar range to us annually when you factor in the time savings and reduced error risk.
v.Q23: I'd say we're unlikely to switch in the next six months. The restructuring has us in a kind of holding pattern — leadership doesn't want to take on any new vendor commitments while we're still working through the headcount situation. Maybe once we're on the other side of that, the conversation will open back up. But right now, I'd say very unlikely.
v.Q24: I think the top challenge is fragmentation — most tools do one or two things well and the rest poorly, and you end up stitching together multiple platforms that don't talk to each other. And then you're paying for all of them. I also think reporting and analytics is a universal pain point, especially for smaller HR teams who don't have a dedicated data person. And in healthcare specifically, compliance documentation is a constant headache that most general-purpose HR tools handle pretty superficially. Those would be my three big ones.
