cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm an HR Manager. I handle pretty much all things people-related at a small consulting firm — everything from recruiting to onboarding to benefits to employee relations.
v.Q2: Just over two years. I came in when the company was around forty-five people and we've grown a lot since then.
v.Q3: We're a management consulting firm — professional services. We're at about eighty-five employees right now. It's been a busy couple of years growth-wise.
v.Q4: We're on Gusto for payroll and benefits, and we use Lever for applicant tracking. So two separate tools. There's been some conversation about consolidating, but we haven't done it yet.
v.Q5: That was about eight or nine months ago. So within the last year.
v.Q6: We were already using Gusto. The evaluation was specifically about whether to add a proper HRIS on top of it, or whether to move to something that bundled HRIS plus payroll so we could simplify.
v.Q7: Growth was the main driver, honestly. When you go from forty-five to eighty-plus employees in under two years, the tools that worked fine at the smaller size start to show their limits. Gusto is a great payroll tool, but it doesn't have much in the way of performance management, org charting, or employee self-service beyond pay stubs and benefits. We were also getting more complex on the benefits side — adding new plan options — and managing that in Gusto was getting unwieldy. And I was essentially a one-person HR team for most of that growth period, so anything that created manual work was genuinely hurting me.
v.Q8: Our leadership team was professionalizating the business generally — bringing in more formal processes across finance, sales, operations. HR was kind of the last function to get that treatment. So there was pressure from the partners to have an HR infrastructure that matched where the company was heading, not where it had been.
v.Q9: Gusto's limitations on the HRIS side were the big frustration. I had no good place to store employee documents, no org chart, no way to run headcount or turnover reports without exporting to Excel. And onboarding was mostly manual — I was emailing paperwork back and forth with new hires. For a company growing as fast as we were, that was kind of untenable.
v.Q10: We looked at BambooHR, Rippling, and Namely. Those were the three we actually demoed.
v.Q11: It needed to have native onboarding workflows — actual e-signature and task routing, not just a checklist. It needed document management. And it had to integrate with Gusto or replace it entirely. I wasn't going to run payroll in two places.
v.Q12: It was mostly me doing the legwork, but our COO had final approval on the spend. I presented a summary comparison to her and she signed off. Our office manager also weighed in because she touches onboarding a lot. So I was the primary recommender, COO had final authority.
v.Q13: We stayed with Gusto. We didn't end up adding anything new either. The evaluation kind of stalled when our COO pushed back on the price points for the options we were looking at.
v.Q14: It was really a cost decision more than anything else. Gusto's pricing was already baked into our budget and the alternatives would have added meaningful cost on top of what we were paying or required us to migrate payroll, which felt risky. I think if the budget had been there, we probably would have moved to something with stronger HRIS capabilities. But the timing wasn't right.
v.Q15: BambooHR was appealing and the demo went well, but the payroll integration with Gusto felt like it added complexity rather than reducing it. Rippling was impressive but priced at the high end for our size — felt like we were paying for capabilities we wouldn't use for a couple more years. Namely felt a bit dated in the UI, and honestly the sales process was slower and less organized than I expected, which made me a little nervous about their support.
v.Q16: Gusto runs payroll really reliably. Employees trust it, direct deposit works, W-2s go out on time — the core payroll stuff just works. And benefits enrollment is reasonably straightforward. For a two-person HR team, those are things I genuinely can't afford to have be broken.
v.Q17: Everything outside payroll and benefits, honestly. We still have no real HRIS layer. Documents live in a shared drive, org charts are in a slide deck someone updates occasionally, and performance reviews happen in Word documents. It's not sustainable as we keep growing.
v.Q18: The lack of a structured onboarding workflow is my biggest frustration. Every new hire is kind of a manual scramble — I'm coordinating across email, Slack, and a shared folder. It causes me significant frustration, and I think new hires notice when the process feels ad hoc. At our growth rate, I'm onboarding someone almost every other week right now.
v.Q19: We just added a second HR person to the team, which is great, but it also means I now need to coordinate work between us in a way that's more structured. And leadership is starting to ask for workforce data — turnover rates, headcount forecasts — that I can't easily produce right now. Those needs are sharper than they were a year ago.
v.Q20: Between Gusto and Lever I think we're somewhere around fifteen thousand dollars a year. Maybe a bit more depending on the Lever tier.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes for Gusto on payroll. Less sure about the overall picture when I think about what we're not getting.
v.Q22: If Gusto had a real onboarding workflow module — e-signatures, task assignments, the whole thing — I'd say that's worth somewhere between five and ten thousand dollars a year to us in saved time and reduced errors.
v.Q23: I think we'll consider it again, yeah. I'd say somewhat likely to actually switch this time. We've kept growing and the pain is getting harder to ignore. I think I have better ammunition now to make the business case to our COO than I did a year ago.
v.Q24: I think most HR managers at companies our size would say the same thing — the tools that are affordable don't do enough, and the tools that do enough aren't affordable at your stage. There's a gap in the market around that fifty-to-one-fifty employee range where you've outgrown the basics but you're not ready for enterprise pricing. And then integration headaches are universal — nobody's tools really talk to each other cleanly.

Q4: Point Solution Layered on Core Platform

cat.Q5: 6 to 12 months ago (6-12 mo to 6-12 mo)
cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm a Director of HR. I've been in this role for about three years and I sit at the intersection of all things people — workforce planning, compliance, employee relations, the full scope. At a company our size, the Director title means you're also doing a lot of the hands-on work yourself rather than just overseeing it.
v.Q2: I've been here just under five years. So I was here before I moved into the Director role, which gives me some useful context on how the company has evolved — and honestly, how dramatically things have changed in the last eighteen months or so.
v.Q3: We're in light manufacturing — specifically, we produce precision components for aerospace and defense applications. It's a pretty specialized niche. As for headcount, we're sitting at around seventy-five employees right now. We were closer to a hundred and ten eighteen months ago, so we've gone through a meaningful reduction in force tied to a contract loss. That context matters a lot for understanding everything that's happened with our systems over the past year and a half.
v.Q4: We're on Rippling as our primary platform. It handles payroll, benefits administration, and the core HRIS functions. We have a separate time and attendance system — we use Replicon for that because of how our shop floor tracking works — and those two talk to each other through an integration. But Rippling is the central hub for everything people-related. It's been in place for about two and a half years.
v.Q5: The evaluation that led to where we are now happened about two and a half years ago, so I'd put that in the two-to-three-year range. That said, I want to be upfront that we have informally revisited the question more recently — maybe eight or nine months ago — in the context of the restructuring, just to make sure we were on the right platform given how much the company had changed. But the formal evaluation that resulted in a purchase was the one from two-plus years ago.
v.Q6: We were on a combination of ADP Workforce Now for payroll and an older version of Paycom that we'd inherited from previous ownership. It was a messy setup — the two didn't integrate cleanly, there was duplicate data entry happening regularly, and neither one was particularly well-suited for a manufacturing environment where you have a mix of salaried and hourly workers with complex overtime and shift differential calculations. So we were coming from a fragmented, legacy-ish stack that had accumulated over years of ownership changes.
v.Q7:
There were honestly quite a few things converging at the same time, which is usually how these evaluations get enough momentum to actually happen.

The most immediate trigger was that our ADP contract was coming up for renewal and the renewal pricing they quoted us was significantly higher than what we'd been paying. That created a natural forcing function — suddenly we had a reason to look at alternatives rather than just auto-renewing.

Beyond the contract trigger, we had significant manual process pain. We were running payroll across two systems, doing manual reconciliation every pay period, and it was eating up way too much time for a two-person HR team. I had one HR generalist at the time and she was spending a full day every two weeks just on payroll-related data cleanup. That's not sustainable.

We also had a compliance issue that got our attention — we had an audit finding related to I-9 documentation storage that wasn't exactly catastrophic but was a wake-up call about the fact that our document management processes were not where they needed to be for a company with federal defense contracts. So compliance and documentation capability became a genuine must-have.

And finally, we had new private equity ownership come in about six months before the evaluation started, and they had expectations around HR data and workforce reporting that our old systems genuinely couldn't support. They wanted to see turnover metrics, labor cost ratios, time-to-fill data — all stuff that would have required us to build everything manually from exports. That made a strong internal case for investing in better tooling.
v.Q8:
The PE ownership change was probably the biggest contextual factor. When private equity comes in, they often bring expectations about operational infrastructure that a founder-led company of our size wouldn't have prioritized the same way. There was a real expectation that we would professionalize our back-office systems, and HR was on that list alongside finance and ERP.

Beyond that, there was broader pressure in aerospace and defense manufacturing around ITAR compliance and government contractor requirements. Some of our workforce has security clearance implications and there are documentation standards we have to meet for government contracts. So the regulatory environment in our specific slice of manufacturing was becoming more demanding, and we needed to be on a platform that could at least support our documentation and audit trail requirements, even if it wasn't specifically designed for aerospace.

And honestly, I think the broader market shift toward more integrated platforms was just becoming visible to us. We were attending a SHRM conference around that time and it was hard not to notice how far the SMB HR tech market had moved. The idea that a company our size could be on a fully integrated HRIS, payroll, and benefits platform for a reasonable cost — that wasn't as obvious a few years earlier.
v.Q9:
Yes, quite specifically. The payroll complexity for a manufacturing workforce was the most acute pain point. We have hourly workers on multiple shifts, overtime rules, shift differentials, and at the time we had a union subset of the workforce as well. ADP handled this but required a lot of manual configuration to get right, and any time we made a change — a new shift, a new pay code — it was a significant configuration exercise that often required calling ADP support.

The Paycom piece was theoretically our HRIS but in practice it was barely used. Nobody had been trained on it properly, data was stale and incomplete, and it had essentially become a system of record that nobody trusted. So we had phantom HRIS capabilities that weren't delivering any value.

Reporting was a mess. We had data in two systems that didn't agree with each other, and producing anything meaningful for leadership required exporting from both, reconciling in Excel, and hoping nothing had changed since the last export. It was kind of a disaster from a data integrity standpoint.

And then the employee experience during open enrollment was poor. Employees were filling out paper forms, we were re-entering everything manually, and errors happened every year. For a workforce that skews toward production workers who aren't particularly tech-savvy, a better benefits experience felt important — but it also had to be simple enough for those employees to actually use it.
v.Q10: We seriously evaluated Rippling, Paylocity, and Paychex Flex. We also had a brief look at ADP's TotalSource PEO option, which was their pitch to retain us, but we took it off the table pretty quickly once we understood what a PEO model would mean for our autonomy on benefits design. Those were the four we engaged with meaningfully.
v.Q11: We were quite specific about table stakes. First, it had to handle complex payroll natively — shift differentials, overtime calculations for hourly manufacturing workers, multiple pay codes. We'd been burned by platforms that marketed payroll capability but really meant simple salaried payroll. Second, it needed robust document management with audit trail capability, specifically because of our government contractor obligations. Third, the benefits administration had to support multiple carrier integrations — we had three carriers at the time and we needed data flowing to all of them without manual re-entry. And fourth, we needed the time and attendance system to be able to feed data into payroll cleanly, either natively or through a tested integration. If a vendor couldn't demonstrate that their system handled those four things credibly, we didn't go further.
v.Q12: It was a small committee, which honestly made the process move faster than I expected. I led the evaluation — I set the criteria, coordinated the demos, did the reference checks, and built the recommendation memo. Our CFO was involved on the financial side and had final approval authority on the contract. Our Controller also participated in the payroll-specific demo sessions because she cared a lot about the GL integration and how the payroll journal entries would flow into our accounting system. And our CEO was looped in at the final stage — he reviewed the recommendation and signed off conceptually before the CFO executed the contract. So I was the primary recommender with real influence, the CFO had financial sign-off authority, and the CEO had executive endorsement authority. IT wasn't formally involved, which in retrospect is interesting given how much Rippling touches the IT infrastructure side of things.
v.Q13: We switched. We moved to Rippling and fully decommissioned both ADP Workforce Now and the old Paycom instance. The migration took about three months end to end, which was longer than Rippling initially projected, but we got there.
v.Q14:
Rippling stood out on a few dimensions that mattered specifically to us. The platform architecture was genuinely unified — not just loosely integrated modules, but a single data model underlying everything. That meant employee data entered once flowed everywhere, which directly addressed our data integrity problems with the old two-system setup.

The automation capability was impressive. Rippling had workflow automation that could do things like automatically trigger benefits enrollment when a new hire was set up in payroll, or automatically update access permissions when someone changed roles. For a two-person HR team, that kind of automation had real operational value.

Their sales team was also responsive and organized, which sounds like a small thing but it actually gave us some confidence in what their support experience would be like post-purchase. Paylocity's sales process was slower and felt more bureaucratic.

And honestly, the PE ownership of our company had some familiarity with Rippling from portfolio companies they'd worked with previously, which gave us an informal reference point that mattered to the CFO. I think that peer validation through the PE network carried some real weight in the final decision.
v.Q15:
Paylocity was the closest runner-up. Their HRIS and reporting capabilities were solid, and they had experience with manufacturing clients, which was reassuring. But their payroll configuration for complex hourly scenarios required a lot of professional services engagement to set up correctly, and the cost of that implementation, on top of the licensing fees, made the total cost of ownership uncomfortable. They also felt slightly more oriented toward larger mid-market companies — the support model felt like it was designed for companies with three hundred or more employees, not seventy-five.

Paychex Flex came in and honestly the demo was not impressive. The interface felt dated, the reporting was limited, and the integration story with third-party tools was weak. I think Paychex is probably fine for a very simple payroll-only use case, but we needed more than that and they couldn't demonstrate it convincingly.

The ADP TotalSource PEO option we dismissed fairly quickly. Moving to a PEO model would have meant giving up control over our benefits design, which was a non-starter because our benefits package is genuinely one of our retention tools in a competitive labor market for skilled manufacturing workers. We didn't want to be constrained to whatever the PEO's carrier relationships were.
v.Q16: Rippling does the unified data model exceptionally well — I genuinely cannot overstate how much better life is when employee data is in one place and flows correctly across payroll, benefits, and the directory without anyone having to manually sync anything. The automation capabilities are strong and we've built out a number of workflows that run without my team having to touch them. Payroll runs reliably for our complex hourly workforce, which was the thing I was most worried about during the evaluation and which has held up well. And the employee self-service is good — employees can access pay stubs, update their information, and work through benefits enrollment without calling HR. For a manufacturing workforce that is not particularly tech-forward, the mobile app is actually intuitive enough that adoption has been reasonable.
v.Q17:
The reporting module is honestly the most consistent disappointment. The standard reports are fine, but building custom reports requires more technical comfort than I'd like, and the visualizations are pretty limited. When our PE owners ask for workforce dashboards, I'm still often exporting data and building things in Google Sheets or Excel because the in-platform reporting doesn't produce what they want in a visually digestible format.

The customer support has also gotten noticeably slower over the last twelve months. I think Rippling has scaled really fast and I get the sense their support staffing hasn't kept pace with their customer growth. Response times on tickets have stretched and I've had a few situations where I needed a quick answer on a payroll-impacting issue and the response came hours later than I needed it.
v.Q18: The support responsiveness is my biggest frustration right now, and I'd rate it as significant — bordering on severe in certain moments. When you're running payroll for a manufacturing workforce and something behaves unexpectedly, every hour of uncertainty matters. I've had situations during the restructuring — processing terminations, handling severance, coordinating COBRA notifications — where I needed timely answers from Rippling support and the response times were not what I needed them to be. It creates real anxiety when you're doing something consequential and you're not sure you've done it correctly and you can't get confirmation quickly. I understand they're a growing company, but at the price point we're paying, I expect better responsiveness on time-sensitive issues.
v.Q19:
The restructuring has fundamentally changed what I need from the platform in the near term. We went from being in growth mode — thinking about onboarding automation and scaling recruiting — to being in reduction mode, where I needed robust offboarding workflows, COBRA administration support, severance documentation management, and audit trails for terminations. Rippling handles some of this reasonably well but it wasn't really designed with the reduction-in-force use case as a primary workflow. I've had to piece together processes that I'd expect to be more standardized.

I also think I need stronger analytics now than I did two years ago. v.Q24:
I think there are a few themes that I'd expect resonate pretty broadly across HR directors at companies our size. The first is the gap between what platforms promise and what they actually deliver at scale — a lot of these tools sell you on a vision of integration and automation and then the reality of support, configuration complexity, and edge cases is more friction than you expected. That's not unique to any one vendor.

The second is that the analytics expectations from leadership have outpaced what most SMB HR platforms can natively deliver. The business wants real-time workforce intelligence, and the tools give you canned reports that require a lot of manipulation to be useful. That gap is getting more frustrating as data literacy improves in the C-suite.

And then for manufacturing specifically — and I'd guess this applies to other industries with complex hourly workforces — most HR platforms are still really designed for the knowledge worker, salaried employee use case. The complexity of shift work, overtime, multi-rate pay, union agreements — those things are afterthoughts in most platforms, and you feel it.

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: Sure. I'm a VP of HR — technically my title is Vice President of People, but the function is traditional HR. I oversee everything from recruiting and onboarding through total rewards, HR business partnering, and HR technology. It's a fairly broad scope.
v.Q2: I've been here just over five years. I joined when the company was around two hundred and fifty people, so I've lived through a pretty significant growth phase and then the more recent stabilization. That context shapes a lot of how I think about tooling, honestly.
v.Q3: We're a B2B SaaS company — we sell data infrastructure tooling to enterprise customers. Headquartered in Austin, Texas, with a significant presence in New York and a few smaller hubs in Seattle and Denver. We're at about eight hundred and forty employees right now. Headcount has been relatively flat for the past eighteen months or so after a period of very aggressive growth — we grew from around four hundred to close to nine hundred in roughly two and a half years, which was a wild ride on the HR side, and then we pulled back and have been in more of a steady-state mode.
v.Q4: Rippling is our core platform and it's doing a lot of heavy lifting. We run payroll through Rippling, benefits administration, HRIS, and device management. We use Greenhouse separately for ATS — Rippling's recruiting module wasn't at the maturity level we needed when we made that call — and we have Culture Amp sitting alongside for engagement and performance. So it's Rippling as the anchor, but we're not purely consolidated. I'd say we have three or four meaningful HR tools in the stack depending on how you count it.
v.Q5: The most recent significant evaluation was about a year and a half ago. We did a fairly structured process — probably four months of active evaluation — and that resulted in us expanding our use of Rippling. Before that, we had evaluated and switched to Rippling about two and a half years ago from a previous setup, so I've been through two meaningful evaluations in the last three years or so. The one I'll mostly speak to is the more recent one, since that's fresher.
v.Q6: When we started the most recent evaluation, we were already partially on Rippling — we had originally implemented it for payroll and basic HRIS when we first switched — but we were still running benefits through a broker-managed platform, and our IT device management was completely separate. So it was kind of a partial implementation and we were evaluating whether to go deeper into Rippling, bring in a dedicated benefits administration platform, or potentially look at a different consolidated solution altogether.
v.Q7:
There were several distinct forces converging at the same time. The first was a pure capability gap — our broker-managed benefits platform was essentially a manual workflow dressed up as software. It couldn't produce the kind of real-time enrollment visibility that we needed to manage open enrollment at our scale, and reconciliation against payroll deductions was still a spreadsheet exercise every month. That was unsustainable.

The second motivator was that we had brought in a new Chief Financial Officer who came from a larger tech company background and had much higher expectations for HR data quality and HRIS reporting than we were delivering. She was asking for workforce planning outputs and headcount scenario modeling that our current setup simply couldn't generate, and that became a top-of-mind initiative fairly quickly.

The third factor was the IT and HR intersection. We'd gone through a period where managing device provisioning and deprovisioning for new hires and terminations was done entirely by our IT team independent of HR, and there were enough incidents — delayed access, late laptop shipments, access credentials lingering after termination — that we had both a security concern and an operational one. Someone at the C-level flagged that as a risk, and it got elevated.

And honestly the fourth thing was just contract timing. Our broker arrangement was coming up for renewal and it created a natural forcing function to ask whether there was a better way to structure the whole thing rather than just auto-renewing.
v.Q8:
The macro context was interesting. We were coming out of a hypergrowth period and entering what leadership was calling an efficiency phase — there was real pressure from the board to demonstrate that we could maintain HR service quality with a more optimized headcount rather than just throwing bodies at problems. That shifted the conversation toward automation and tooling in a way it hadn't been before. When you're growing fast, you just hire to keep up — when you're in efficiency mode, you start asking whether technology can absorb some of that labor cost.

There was also a broader moment in our industry around security and SOC 2 compliance — we were in the middle of a SOC 2 Type II audit cycle, and the auditors had flagged our access provisioning and deprovisioning workflows as areas of concern. So there was external audit pressure pointing directly at the HR-IT integration problem I mentioned. That elevated the priority.

And I think honestly there was some peer benchmarking happening too. I'm part of a VP HR peer community — mostly other late-stage SaaS companies — and Rippling's unified IT-HR workflow kept coming up as something other companies were leveraging that we weren't fully using yet, even though we were paying for it. That social proof reinforced the internal conversation.
v.Q9:
Yes, quite a few. The benefits reconciliation problem was probably the most operationally painful — I mentioned it earlier, but to put a finer point on it: we had a dedicated person spending roughly a third of her time every month just reconciling benefits deductions between the carrier invoices, the broker platform, and what Rippling was processing for payroll. That's an enormous amount of manual labor for something that should be automated.

Reporting was a constant frustration. We could pull basic headcount and payroll reports from Rippling, but anything that required cross-referencing HR data with financial data — headcount by cost center, fully-loaded comp modeling, attrition rate by department — required an analyst pulling exports and doing the work in Excel or Sheets. For a data-driven SaaS company, that felt embarrassing, frankly.

And on the benefits experience side, our employees were getting a pretty underwhelming enrollment experience. The platform they were enrolling through looked outdated, the decision support tools were minimal, and our benefits team was fielding a high volume of questions that a better self-service experience could have deflected. That has real cost implications and it affects how employees perceive total comp.
v.Q10: In the most recent evaluation we looked seriously at expanding with Rippling — going deeper into their benefits and IT modules — versus alternatives including Workday, Namely, and a point solution for benefits called Benefitfocus. We also had early conversations with TriNet PEO as a way to offload some of the benefits management complexity, but we ruled that out pretty quickly.
v.Q11:
We had a fairly explicit set of gates. First, native payroll integration was non-negotiable — I wasn't willing to manage a payroll-benefits integration that depended on file feeds and manual reconciliation, because that was exactly the problem we were trying to solve. Second, the platform had to support our multi-state complexity — we have employees in over twenty states and a few international contractors, so the compliance engine needed to be genuinely robust, not bolted-on.

Third, SSO and role-based access controls were required — our security team was involved and they had a short list of identity management requirements. Fourth — and this one narrowed the field significantly — we needed a credible IT asset management and provisioning workflow, because the HR-IT integration problem was one of our primary drivers. Most pure-play HRIS platforms couldn't touch that.

And finally, implementation timeline was a soft gate. We had a hard deadline tied to our next open enrollment cycle, which was about five months out, and anything that couldn't realistically be implemented and stable within that window was a non-starter regardless of how good the features were.
v.Q12: The decision committee was me, our CFO, our CTO, and our VP of IT. I was the primary recommender and project lead — I owned the evaluation process, managed vendor relationships, and put together the business case. The CFO had final budget authority and was particularly focused on the total cost of ownership and the ROI framing around automation savings. The CTO and VP of IT cared mostly about the IT provisioning and security aspects and had veto power over anything that didn't clear their technical requirements. We also ran a pilot group of about twenty employees through a proof of concept with the top two finalists before making the final call, so there was some end-user feedback incorporated as well. It was a real committee decision, not just me making a call.
v.Q13: We deepened our commitment to Rippling — so it was less of a switch and more of a significant expansion. We went from using a narrow slice of the platform to running payroll, benefits, IT, and HRIS workflows through it in a much more integrated way. We also renegotiated our contract in the process, so there was a meaningful commercial change alongside the scope expansion.
v.Q14:
The honest answer is that Rippling won on the IT-HR integration story, which was the most differentiated part of our requirements. No other platform we evaluated could genuinely do device management, app provisioning, and HRIS in a single unified workflow the way Rippling does — Workday obviously has depth on the HRIS side but the IT asset story is not really there in the same way, and the smaller players just couldn't match it.

The second factor was total cost. Going deeper into Rippling was meaningfully cheaper than licensing Workday at our scale, even accounting for the fact that Rippling isn't free. Workday at around eight hundred employees is a serious investment and the implementation costs alone were prohibitive without a larger internal IT team to support it.

And I think the third factor was momentum — our team already knew Rippling, our payroll was running cleanly on it, and our employees had logins. The switching cost of a full platform migration versus going deeper on something that was already in production was a real consideration. Rippling's team was also quite good during the evaluation process — responsive, technically knowledgeable, willing to do a real proof of concept rather than just sales theater. That built confidence.
v.Q15:
Workday was eliminated primarily on cost and implementation complexity. The licensing cost at our size was roughly two to two-and-a-half times what we were going to pay for expanded Rippling, and the implementation timeline was quoted at nine to twelve months with a required implementation partner — we don't have that kind of bandwidth or budget, and the timeline blew past our open enrollment deadline. Workday is a genuinely excellent platform, but it's built for organizations with a full-time HRIS team, which we don't have.

Namely was interesting and much more competitively priced, but their IT integration story was essentially nonexistent. They kept trying to reframe our IT requirements as out of scope or address them with third-party integrations, which was exactly the fragmentation we were trying to get away from. Their implementation reputation in our peer network was also a concern — I heard a few stories about rocky go-lives that gave me pause.

Benefitfocus was a solid point solution for benefits administration specifically, but it would have added another integration to maintain and wouldn't have addressed the IT-HR workflow problem at all. At a certain point you have to weigh point-solution depth against integration overhead, and for our particular mix of requirements, Benefitfocus couldn't win that trade-off.

And TriNet, as I mentioned, we ruled out early — the PEO model isn't right for a company at our scale and maturity. We need to own our HR infrastructure, not co-employ through a PEO.
v.Q16: The IT-HR workflow is genuinely excellent now — new hire onboarding is almost entirely automated from offer acceptance through device shipment, app provisioning, and first-day access. That has had a measurable impact on new hire experience scores and significantly reduced the coordination overhead between HR and IT. Payroll reliability is strong — we run multi-state payroll for over eight hundred people and I can count the number of meaningful issues in the last two years on one hand. And the unified employee record is valuable — having one source of truth that flows to payroll, IT, and benefits without manual data entry has been a real improvement from where we were.
v.Q17: Reporting and analytics is still the place where I feel the most friction. Rippling has improved — their dashboards have gotten better — but I still find myself exporting to build the deeper workforce analytics views that our CFO and the board want to see. The advanced analytics story requires their separate analytics add-on, which we haven't licensed yet, and I'm skeptical it fully solves the problem based on what I've seen in demos. The performance management module is also not something we use — Culture Amp is significantly better for our needs — but that means we're running a separate integration and a separate employee experience for performance, which adds some friction.
v.Q18: The reporting gap is my biggest frustration and I'd characterize it as moderate to significant. It's not a daily pain — the core operations run smoothly — but every time I need to prepare a board deck or a workforce planning presentation, the process of building the underlying data requires more manual effort than it should for a platform at this price point. I'm a VP at a data company — the irony of hand-building HR analytics in a spreadsheet every quarter is not lost on me or my CEO.
v.Q19:
Two things have shifted meaningfully. First, the expectation around AI capabilities has changed pretty dramatically in the last twelve months. When we did our evaluation eighteen months ago, AI in HR software was mostly marketing language. Now I'm seeing genuinely useful AI features in some platforms — things like automated job description generation, AI-assisted compensation benchmarking, anomaly detection in payroll — and I'm starting to benchmark our current stack against those capabilities more actively. Rippling has been shipping some AI features but I don't think they're leading the market there.

The second thing is that our workforce planning needs have gotten more sophisticated. In a flat-headcount environment, the story isn't about hiring velocity anymore — it's about retention, internal mobility, skills mapping, and total compensation competitiveness. Those are much more analytically demanding than what most HRIS platforms were designed for.
v.Q20: When I aggregate Rippling, Greenhouse, and Culture Amp, I think we're somewhere in the one hundred to one hundred and fifty thousand dollar range annually. Rippling is the largest piece of that, followed by Greenhouse. That's excluding the broker and carrier costs on the benefits side, which are a separate budget line.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes — I think the operational automation we've gotten from Rippling genuinely justifies most of the spend, especially when I mentally translate the IT-HR workflow efficiency into FTE cost savings. But I think the reporting and analytics gap means we're not fully capturing the ROI that the platform theoretically promises. We're paying for a sophisticated platform and still building some pretty fundamental outputs by hand.
v.Q22: For genuinely usable workforce analytics — headcount by cost center, attrition modeling, comp benchmarking, scenario planning — I think that's worth twenty-five thousand dollars or more annually in saved analyst time and better decision quality. Honestly maybe higher. The time my team and I spend manually assembling that data has real cost, and the decisions we'd make better with clean real-time data have strategic value that's harder to quantify but probably larger than the direct labor savings.
v.Q23: I would say yes, we'll consider it — but switching likelihood within six months is somewhat unlikely. The reality is that we're in a stable operating period and a full platform migration is a significant disruption I wouldn't take on without a compelling reason. What's more likely is that within the next twelve to eighteen months we re-evaluate the analytics layer specifically — whether that means licensing Rippling's analytics add-on, building something on top of our data warehouse, or bringing in a dedicated workforce analytics tool. I'm watching what a few other platforms are doing in this space pretty closely.
v.Q24:
I think there are a few challenges that come up consistently when I talk to peers. The first is the gap between what vendors promise and what's actually production-ready. Most enterprise HR platforms have a slide for every capability — AI, analytics, skills mapping, whatever the current trend is — but when you actually dig into what those features do in production, you often find they're early or limited. That credibility gap makes evaluation really hard because it's difficult to separate genuine capability from sales positioning without extensive hands-on testing.

The second challenge is integration fragmentation. Even when you buy an all-in-one platform, you still end up with specialty tools for recruiting, performance, engagement, or compensation benchmarking — and those integrations require maintenance and create data consistency issues. I haven't seen a single platform that genuinely covers every need at the level of quality that best-of-breed point solutions offer. That tension between consolidation and quality is something I think every VP HR at a mid-sized company is navigating right now.

And the third thing — and this is maybe more specific to technology companies — is the expectation gap around AI. Leadership teams increasingly expect HR to be using AI in meaningful ways, whether for talent analytics, compensation modeling, or workforce planning. The tools are getting there but the honest answer is that most of what's being called AI in HR software today is not yet transformationally useful. Setting realistic expectations internally while still pushing vendors to ship meaningful capabilities is a constant balancing act.

v.Q2: Just under two years — I'd say in the one-to-three band.

v.Q5: Our last real evaluation was about a year ago — within the past twelve months. It was a pretty focused process, maybe six to eight weeks of active evaluation.
v.Q6: We were already on Rippling for payroll, but we were using Lever for ATS and didn't yet have a formal performance tool. So the evaluation was specifically about performance management and whether Lever was still the right recruiting solution for us.
v.Q7: Lever had become a frustration point — it felt dated compared to what we'd seen in demos from newer ATS platforms, and the reporting was honestly pretty weak. We were also moving more toward structured hiring processes and panel interviews, and Lever's scorecard and feedback workflow was clunky to manage. On the performance side, it was a pure capability gap — we had nothing, and people managers were asking for a more structured way to run reviews and track development goals. So it was a combination of one tool underperforming and a missing capability we needed to add.
v.Q8: We had recently gone through a Series B close and there was some expectation from leadership that People Ops would level up the infrastructure to match the company's maturity. That created an opening for budget conversations that wouldn't have happened six months earlier. There was also just a general push toward more data-driven decision-making across the company — our CEO had brought that culture from his previous company and People Ops was expected to participate in that shift.
v.Q9: Lever's feedback collection during interviews was the main operational pain. Interviewers would forget to submit scorecards, follow-up reminders were manual, and it was hard to see a complete picture of where a candidate stood without chasing people. The lack of any performance tool meant that our six-month and annual review processes were entirely managed in Google Docs and Sheets, which was messy and hard to track completion on. I think there was also some frustration that Lever's integrations with Rippling required more manual maintenance than I expected.
v.Q10: For ATS we looked at Ashby, Greenhouse, and Workable. For performance management we looked at Lattice, Leapsome, and 15Five.
v.Q11: For ATS, it had to have a clean Rippling integration — that was the hard line. It also needed strong structured interview tooling, specifically customizable scorecards and automated interviewer reminders. For performance, it had to support both structured review cycles and ongoing goal-tracking, not just one or the other. Price was a factor — I had a budget ceiling of around forty thousand dollars total for both tools combined, so anything that blew past that was out regardless of feature quality.
v.Q12: I was the primary decision-maker and recommender. Our CEO had final sign-off given the budget involved, but he was largely deferring to my recommendation as long as the business case was clear. Our Head of Engineering weighed in specifically on Ashby versus Greenhouse — he had strong opinions about the technical recruiting workflow. So I'd say I had real decision authority, with light sign-off required from above and one key stakeholder input on the ATS side.
v.Q13: We switched on both fronts — moved from Lever to Ashby, and launched Lattice as our first performance tool. Both were new purchases.
v.Q14: Ashby stood out because the structured interviewing workflow was genuinely best-in-class — automated scorecard reminders, really flexible interview plan builder, and the analytics on pipeline health were much more sophisticated than what Lever had offered. The Rippling integration was also native and well-documented, which mattered a lot given our multi-state payroll complexity. Lattice won mostly on breadth — it could do performance reviews, goals, and engagement surveys in one place, and the interface was intuitive enough that I felt confident rolling it out without heavy change management. Leapsome was actually functionally comparable, but Lattice's sales process was smoother and their implementation support was stronger.
v.Q15: Greenhouse was more expensive than Ashby for what felt like comparable structured hiring functionality, and I think it carries more complexity than we needed at our stage — it felt like a tool built for a recruiting team of ten, not a team of two. Workable was actually affordable but the candidate experience felt a bit generic and the analytics were limited. For performance, 15Five felt more focused on OKR tracking and manager check-ins than on formal review cycles, which wasn't the right balance for where we were. Leapsome, as I mentioned, was close — ultimately just lost out on the sales and implementation experience, not really on features.
v.Q16: Rippling handles multi-state payroll complexity really well — we have employees across thirty states and I've never had a meaningful compliance issue since we've been on it. Ashby has been great for our recruiting workflows and the hiring manager experience has genuinely improved. Lattice has made performance cycles much more structured and trackable, which was a big improvement over our Google Docs era.
v.Q17: Rippling's reporting is okay but not great for benefits cost analysis — I'd like to be able to model benefits cost per employee by tier without exporting data. Lattice's goal-tracking feature is kind of underused by our team because it requires too much manual input to stay current. And the three-tool stack means I'm maintaining three separate integrations and three separate employee data sets that need to stay in sync, which creates occasional inconsistencies.
v.Q18: Integration maintenance between Rippling, Ashby, and Lattice is my biggest frustration — specifically keeping employee status and department data consistent across all three when we have org changes. I'd rate it as moderate frustration. It's not a daily crisis but every time we have a reorganization or a wave of terminations, I spend a couple of hours cleaning up data inconsistencies that shouldn't exist if the integrations were tighter.
v.Q19: We've been adding headcount steadily and are getting closer to the point where a three-person People Ops team managing three separate tools starts to feel like a real constraint. I think our next evolution is probably consolidation — whether that means pushing Rippling to cover more of what Lattice does, or finding a more integrated platform. I've also started thinking more seriously about compensation benchmarking tooling, which we don't currently have in a systematic way.
v.Q20: I think we're in the fifty to one hundred thousand dollar range when you combine Rippling, Ashby, and Lattice.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. I think each individual tool is reasonably priced for what it does. The friction is more about the integration overhead than about any single tool being overpriced.
v.Q22: If someone solved the cross-tool data sync problem cleanly — like genuinely automated bi-directional employee record sync — I think that's worth ten to twenty-five thousand dollars a year to us in saved time and reduced error risk.
v.Q23: Yes, I'll likely kick off a light evaluation within six months — specifically around whether to consolidate performance and HRIS into a single platform. Switching likelihood I'd call somewhat likely, not very likely. It depends on whether Rippling's performance module has gotten good enough to replace Lattice, which I'm honestly not sure about yet.
v.Q24: I think the biggest challenge for most people in my position is the consolidation-versus-quality trade-off. All-in-one platforms rarely do everything at a best-in-class level, so you end up choosing between operational simplicity and functional depth. And honestly, the integration tax — the hidden cost of maintaining connections between tools and cleaning up data inconsistencies — is something I don't think gets talked about enough in vendor conversations. It's real and it compounds as your stack grows.

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q5: That evaluation was about two years ago, so I'd say roughly in the one-to-two-year range. We wrapped up the decision and went live on Rippling about eighteen months back.
v.Q6: We were on a combination of ADP Workforce Now for payroll and then a pretty cobbled-together setup for HR — we had BambooHR for the HRIS side and we were manually managing benefits enrollment through a broker portal. v.Q7: Honestly there were a few things converging at once. The biggest trigger was that we had grown from around 400 to 600 people in about eighteen months, and the manual process burden was becoming completely unsustainable for a team our size. Factor two was that we were adding benefits complexity — we'd expanded our benefits package and our broker was pushing us toward a platform that could handle open enrollment more elegantly, and neither ADP nor BambooHR felt like the right answer for that. And then honestly, I think the third thing was that our CFO had done a cost analysis and realized we were paying for two platforms that together were more expensive than a unified solution probably needed to be. v.Q8: We were in kind of a hyper-growth phase — we'd won a couple of large client contracts that required rapid hiring, and the business was really pushing HR to operationalize faster. There was also pressure coming from our leadership team around digital transformation broadly. They wanted to modernize our internal systems, and HR was one of the areas where we were obviously behind. I think there was also some implicit pressure around talent competition — professional services is a pretty competitive hiring market, and the feeling was that a more modern HR infrastructure would help us move faster on offers and give new hires a better onboarding experience.

Anything that couldn't check all three was off the table before we even did a demo.
v.Q12: The core decision group was me, my HR director who I report into, our CFO, and our IT director. My director and I drove the evaluation — we built the RFP, we ran the demos, we put together the recommendation. The CFO had final sign-off authority because of the contract value, and IT weighed in specifically on the device management capabilities and the SSO setup. So I'd describe my role as primary recommender — I did the most legwork and put the final recommendation together, but I needed sign-off from above me.
v.Q13: We switched. We went with Rippling and moved off of both ADP and BambooHR entirely.
v.Q14: Rippling stood out for a few reasons. The unified platform story was genuinely compelling — the idea that HR, payroll, and IT device management could all sit in one system was something Paylocity couldn't match. The Greenhouse integration was cleaner in the demo, and I think our IT director was pretty sold on the device management piece. Honestly, the product felt more modern — the UX was better than Paylocity, and that matters when you're trying to get employees to self-serve. And the implementation team gave us confidence during the sales process that they'd been through this kind of migration before at our scale. The price was also competitive once we factored in eliminating two existing subscriptions.
v.Q15: Paylocity was the hardest to say no to because it was a solid product. But the integration story with Greenhouse was weaker — it felt more like a workaround than a native connection — and the UX felt a bit dated in certain modules. The implementation process also sounded more heavy-handed, like there would be more back-and-forth with a dedicated implementation firm versus doing it more internally. Workday we ruled out almost immediately — it felt like a tool built for companies with 5,000-plus employees, the pricing reflected that, and the implementation timeline was quoted at something like nine months, which was just not viable for us. Namely had a decent pitch but the company's stability was something we'd heard mixed things about from peers, and at our size and growth rate we couldn't afford to bet on a platform that might have roadmap uncertainty.
v.Q16: Rippling does payroll really well — it's consistently accurate and the run process is fast. The employee self-service experience is genuinely good; employees use it, which was not the case with BambooHR for us. And I think the automation capabilities, particularly around onboarding workflows, have saved my team real hours. Connecting a new hire's account setup with their benefits enrollment and device provisioning in one flow is something we couldn't do before.
v.Q17: Reporting is still not where I need it to be. I can pull basic headcount reports but building custom people analytics is clunky — I end up in spreadsheets more than I'd like. And support has become a frustration as we've grown; it feels like the responsiveness has gotten slower and we sometimes get passed between teams before someone who can actually help us picks it up.
v.Q18: The reporting and analytics gap is my biggest frustration right now, and I'd say it's moderate-to-significant in terms of impact. When I'm trying to pull together a headcount analysis for leadership or track turnover by department or tenure band, I'm building that in Excel because Rippling's custom report builder doesn't give me the flexibility I need without a lot of workarounds. For a team our size, with the pace of growth we're managing, I should be able to answer headcount questions in five minutes and I can't always do that.
v.Q19: We've kept growing, so scale is an even bigger factor now. I think we also have higher expectations around analytics — when we bought Rippling, I was willing to accept some reporting limitations, but now leadership wants more data-driven HR conversations and I need tools that can support that. There's also been more conversation internally about compensation benchmarking and total rewards visibility, which wasn't really on our radar two years ago.
v.Q20: I believe we're somewhere in the range of $100,000 to $150,000 annually when you include all the modules we're using. I don't own the contract directly — that sits with finance — so I'm estimating based on what I've seen in budget conversations.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. I think the core payroll and HRIS value is there, but the reporting gaps make me feel like we're not getting full value for what we're paying. If the analytics were stronger I'd say it was a clear yes.
v.Q22: For genuinely strong people analytics — the kind where I could build dashboards, run turnover cohort analyses, and pull compensation equity reports without needing to go to Excel — I'd estimate that's worth somewhere in the $10,000 to $25,000 range to us annually, just in time savings and the quality of decisions we could make faster.
v.Q23: Probably not within six months — I'd say somewhat unlikely. We're mid-growth and a platform migration right now would be disruptive. But I wouldn't say we're completely locked in long-term. If the analytics piece doesn't improve and we keep hitting the same walls, that conversation will happen eventually.
v.Q24: I think the number one thing is that most tools are still not great at connecting the dots across data. You've got payroll data over here, headcount data over there, and performance data somewhere else, and getting a unified picture of your workforce is harder than it should be. Beyond that, I think the gap between what a tool promises in a demo and what it actually delivers at scale is a persistent problem — and for HR managers like me who are doing the day-to-day in the system, that gap is felt every week.

v.Q1: I'm the Director of People Operations. I'm kind of a team of one, so I cover everything from recruiting and onboarding to payroll and benefits and culture programming — basically anything people-related runs through me.
v.Q2: Just under two years. I joined right as the company was starting to scale pretty rapidly, so it's been a busy stretch.
v.Q3: We're a professional services company — specifically a boutique PR and communications firm based in Chicago. We're at about 85 people right now, but we were closer to 55 when I came on board, so we've added a significant chunk of headcount in a short window.
v.Q4: We run on Gusto as our primary platform — payroll, benefits administration, and our HR records all live there. I also have a separate ATS that I use, which is Breezy HR, and I use a simple performance check-in tool that we're kind of trialing. But Gusto is really the center of gravity for everything operational.
v.Q5: That was roughly a year and a half ago — so within the last two years. I came into the role and pretty quickly initiated a review because what was in place at the time wasn't set up to scale with us.
v.Q6: When I joined, they were using a mix of QuickBooks for payroll — run by our bookkeeper — and basically Google Sheets and email for everything else. There was no HRIS to speak of. Benefits were managed through a broker with paper enrollment. So I was essentially starting from scratch in terms of building out a real infrastructure.
v.Q7: Honestly the hiring itself was the forcing function. When I came on board, the founders were already talking about doubling the team within eighteen months, and it was immediately obvious that running payroll out of QuickBooks and tracking employee data in spreadsheets was not going to hold up. I had a new hire start and we were manually emailing them their onboarding paperwork — that was a signal that things needed to change immediately. Beyond the tactical pain, I also had a compliance concern. We were adding employees in multiple states and I wasn't confident that our payroll setup was handling multi-state withholding correctly. That scared me more than anything else. And then there was also a benefits issue — our broker was great but the enrollment process was entirely manual, and I knew that even adding ten more employees would make it significantly harder to manage. So it was a mix of scaling pressure, compliance risk, and just the manual burden being unsustainable for one person doing it all.
v.Q8: The firm had just closed a new business deal that required us to staff up quickly, and the founders were very focused on being able to hire fast and hire well. There was a real sense that our internal operations needed to be more professional — not just for us but because our clients notice how buttoned-up you are. In PR and communications, reputation matters even internally. I think there was also a broader recognition from the partners that if they wanted to attract mid-career talent away from larger agencies, they needed to look like a real company with real HR infrastructure, not a startup using Google Sheets.
v.Q9: The multi-state payroll concern was the biggest thing keeping me up at night — I genuinely wasn't sure we were compliant. The manual onboarding process was also a real problem because we were hiring fast and first impressions matter. I had a new hire tell me she felt like she'd joined a disorganized company because her first week involved a lot of chasing down paperwork and waiting for IT access. That stung. And benefits administration was just a mess — I was coordinating between the broker, employees, and the carrier manually, and errors happened. We had one employee enrolled in the wrong plan and it took weeks to fix. So I'd say compliance risk, onboarding experience, and benefits accuracy were the three big pain points.
v.Q10: I looked at Gusto, Rippling, and Justworks. I also briefly looked at TriNet but their model felt more like a PEO arrangement than a platform, and that wasn't the direction I wanted to go.
v.Q11: A few firm requirements. First, it had to handle multi-state payroll natively — that was non-negotiable given our compliance concern. Second, it needed to include benefits administration, not just point me toward a third-party broker portal. Third, I needed it to be something I could genuinely implement and manage by myself without needing a dedicated HRIS admin or implementation consultant. I was one person with a tight timeline. So ease of setup and ease of ongoing use were essentially table stakes for me. Anything that required months of implementation or a team to manage it was automatically out.
v.Q12: It was primarily my decision. I presented my recommendation to the two managing partners and they asked some questions about cost and about the implementation timeline, but they trusted me to make the call. I think one partner poked around the Gusto demo recording I shared with them, but functionally I was the sole decision-maker. There was no IT team to loop in, no finance committee — it was really just me bringing a recommendation and them saying yes.
v.Q13: We switched — moved completely off QuickBooks for payroll and off the spreadsheet system. We went with Gusto.
v.Q14: Gusto won for a few interconnected reasons. The onboarding experience for employees was genuinely the best of the three — new hires can complete everything digitally before their first day, which directly addressed the feedback I'd gotten about our disorganized first-week experience. The multi-state payroll handling gave me confidence from a compliance standpoint, and the built-in benefits administration meant I could actually consolidate everything in one place. Honestly, the pricing was also very relevant — at 85 people, we're not spending enterprise money, and Gusto's pricing model made sense for our scale. Justworks had some appeal as a PEO-adjacent option but I felt like it gave me less control and visibility than I wanted. And Rippling, while impressive, felt like a lot of platform for where we are right now — I didn't need device management or all the IT workflow pieces.
v.Q15: Rippling was genuinely impressive and I can see why larger companies love it, but for a solo operator at a company our size, it felt overbuilt. The implementation process sounded more involved, and the pricing was higher than I could justify to the partners at our headcount. There were also more modules than I needed and I worried I'd be paying for things we'd never use. Justworks I liked conceptually — their customer support reputation is strong — but the co-employment PEO model made the partners uncomfortable. They didn't love the idea of a third party technically being the employer of record. TriNet had the same issue and I never got past that conceptual hurdle with leadership. So in the end Gusto was the clearest fit for the size of company we are and the solo-operator structure I'm working within.
v.Q16: Gusto does payroll really reliably — I run it, it runs, employees get paid accurately and on time, and the multi-state handling has been solid. The new hire onboarding flow is still one of the things I value most. The employee-facing experience is clean and simple, which matters a lot when you're trying to make a good first impression with new hires. Benefits administration is also reasonably smooth — open enrollment last fall was so much better than what I inherited. And honestly the support team has been responsive when I've needed them, which as a solo HR person is genuinely meaningful.
v.Q17: The reporting capabilities are limited — not as bad as a spreadsheet, but not where I'd want them as we push toward 100 people. I also find that the performance management side is basically nonexistent in Gusto, so I've had to bolt on a separate tool for that. And as we've grown, I'm starting to feel like we might be outgrowing some of Gusto's more basic HRIS capabilities — org chart, compensation history tracking, and things like that are pretty thin.
v.Q18: The HRIS depth is my biggest frustration, and I'd call it moderate heading toward significant. As we've grown to 85 people and we're planning to keep hiring, I need compensation history, more robust employee records, and better org management, and Gusto is just kind of thin on all of that. I find myself maintaining a separate spreadsheet to track compensation history, which feels like exactly the kind of thing I should be able to do in my HR platform. It's not a crisis, but it's a gap I bump into regularly.
v.Q19: When I evaluated tools, I was trying to solve for compliance and onboarding chaos — those were the urgent needs. Now that those are under control, I'm thinking more about people analytics and performance infrastructure. I need to have more data-driven conversations with the partners about the workforce, and I'm also dealing with more complex compensation questions as we bring in more senior hires. So the needs have matured from fixing broken basics to actually building out a real people ops function.
v.Q20: I'd estimate we're spending somewhere in the range of $10,000 to $20,000 annually on Gusto, depending on headcount fluctuation. That's a rough number but I think it's in the right ballpark.
v.Q21: Yes, I think so — I'd say somewhat yes. For what it delivers on payroll and onboarding, the value is there. I start to question it a little when I think about the pieces it doesn't do well, but on net it's still reasonable for us.
v.Q22: For richer HRIS capabilities — compensation history, better org management, stronger employee records — I'd probably say that's worth somewhere in the $5,000 to $10,000 range annually to us. It would eliminate the spreadsheet workarounds and honestly let me spend less time on data management and more time on actual people strategy.
v.Q23: I've actually started having that conversation with myself. I'd say I'm somewhere between neutral and somewhat likely to consider it, especially if we cross 100 people. Six months feels aggressive, but within the next year I could see us doing a real evaluation. The HRIS depth issue is the thing that would push me to look.
v.Q24: I think the fundamental challenge is that most tools are optimized for either small companies or large ones, and there's a really awkward middle ground — the 75 to 300 person range — where you need more than an SMB tool but you can't justify or staff an enterprise platform. A lot of us are cobbling things together and spending real time maintaining the glue between systems. I also think the lack of true people analytics at the mid-market level is a persistent gap — most of us are still making workforce decisions with less data than we should have.

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm a VP of Talent Acquisition. My scope is everything related to recruiting and hiring — sourcing strategy, employer brand, the recruiting tech stack, and I partner closely with HR on onboarding. We're a fairly lean org so I also touch some of the broader people operations decisions, even though technically talent acquisition is my lane.
v.Q2: Four years this past spring.
v.Q3: We're a specialty retail company — we operate physical stores plus a growing e-commerce channel. Headquartered in Austin. We're right around 380 employees currently, a mix of corporate and field-based store staff, which creates some interesting complexity from an HR and benefits standpoint because we've got pretty different populations under one umbrella.
v.Q4: Rippling is our primary platform — that's where payroll, benefits, and HR records live. For recruiting specifically, I use Lever as our ATS, which sits alongside Rippling and we have an integration between the two. So it's kind of a Rippling-plus-Lever setup, with Rippling as the system of record.
v.Q5: We went through a full evaluation about fourteen months ago, so within the last two years. It resulted in us moving to Rippling, which we went live on about a year back.
v.Q6: We were on Paychex Flex for payroll and had a pretty outdated HRIS — I think it was UltiPro, which is now UKG, but we were on an older version that hadn't been updated in a while and honestly felt pretty stale. Benefits administration was kind of orphaned between the broker and a clunky portal that nobody liked using.
v.Q7: There were a few overlapping things. From my side — talent acquisition — the friction between our ATS and the HRIS was a significant operational problem. When a candidate converted to an employee, the handoff was essentially manual. Someone on my team was re-entering data that already existed in Lever into UltiPro, and that introduced errors and delays on day one for new hires. That drove me to push for a conversation about replacing the HR infrastructure. On the broader HR side, the leadership team had been frustrated with Paychex support for a while — responsiveness was slow and there were a couple of payroll error incidents that eroded trust. And then there was a contract renewal conversation coming up with UltiPro that was the practical forcing event — nobody wanted to just auto-renew without looking at what else was out there. So it was a combination of integration pain from talent acquisition, reliability and support frustration from HR, and a contract renewal window that gave us the opening to go look.
v.Q8: Retail has had a rough few years around talent — hourly turnover is a real challenge for us, and we were under pressure from our CEO to reduce time-to-fill and improve the quality of the hiring experience for store-level candidates. There was also a push from our CFO to look at total HR technology spend and see if there were consolidation opportunities. And I think genuinely the hybrid shift changed things for us — our corporate team went hybrid post-pandemic, which meant we needed better self-service and digital workflows than we'd built for an in-office environment. Those macro pressures made the case for modernizing stronger than it would have been otherwise.
v.Q9: The biggest one from my vantage point was the broken handoff between recruiting and HR. I had candidates who accepted offers and then had a rough first week because their system access was delayed or their benefits enrollment was incomplete, and that kind of thing damages your employer brand. UltiPro's interface was also genuinely hard to use — employees didn't like it, managers didn't like it, and it led to a lot of HR help tickets that should have been self-service. Paychex support was a known frustration — you'd call in with a payroll question and the resolution time was unpredictable. And honestly the reporting in UltiPro was complex in a way that required specialized knowledge to use, and we didn't have dedicated HRIS admin resources, so a lot of it just sat unused.
v.Q10: We looked at Rippling, Paycom, Dayforce — which is Ceridian — and we did a brief look at BambooHR, though that one came off the list pretty quickly. So the real contenders were Rippling, Paycom, and Dayforce.
v.Q11: From my side, a clean integration with Lever was essentially required — I wasn't going to blow up our ATS in the middle of a recruiting push. Beyond that, we needed robust payroll for a mixed workforce of salaried corporate employees and hourly retail staff, which is actually more complex than it sounds. And we needed employee self-service that was genuinely usable on a mobile device because a significant portion of our store workforce doesn't sit at a desk. Those were the hard requirements. Anything that couldn't demonstrate those three things confidently in a demo was out of consideration.
v.Q12: It was a cross-functional group. Our CHRO led the evaluation formally, I was deeply involved from a talent acquisition and integration perspective, our CFO weighed in on commercial terms and total cost of ownership, and our head of IT had to sign off on the security and SSO architecture. I'd describe myself as one of several equal stakeholders — I had a strong voice because of the ATS integration requirement, but I didn't have unilateral authority. The CHRO made the final call with CFO sign-off.
v.Q13: We switched. We moved off both Paychex and UltiPro and went to Rippling as our unified platform.
v.Q14: Rippling won for a few reasons that were pretty concrete for us. The Lever integration was native and well-documented — it wasn't a workaround, it was an actual supported connection, and that mattered a lot to me personally. The mobile experience for employees was demonstrably better than Paycom or Dayforce in the demos, which was important for our store staff population. And Rippling's onboarding workflow automation — where you can trigger IT provisioning and benefits enrollment from a single new hire record — addressed the exact broken handoff problem we'd been dealing with. The implementation timeline was also more reasonable than Dayforce quoted us. Honestly, it felt like a platform that had been designed with some intentionality around the user experience, not just built to check compliance boxes.
v.Q15: Paycom was a legitimate contender and the payroll capability was solid, but the Lever integration story was weak — their recommendation was essentially to use a middleware solution, and I didn't want to introduce another layer of complexity. The UX also felt more HR-centric in a way that made it less intuitive for managers doing things like approving time-off requests. Dayforce was the most feature-rich option but the implementation was quoted at nine-plus months and the total cost was meaningfully higher — it felt right-sized for a company two or three times our size. And when we got into the demo, the configurability that Dayforce prides itself on actually felt like complexity to us given our team's capacity. BambooHR we ruled out early because it doesn't have native payroll in the same way — you'd still be stitching together payroll separately — and we wanted to consolidate, not add another vendor relationship.
v.Q16: The new hire workflow has been the biggest win — from accepted offer in Lever to active employee in Rippling, the experience is so much cleaner than what we had before. Employee self-service adoption is high, which has reduced the volume of basic HR tickets. And payroll has been accurate and consistent, which sounds like a low bar but after some of the Paychex incidents we had, consistent and accurate is genuinely meaningful.
v.Q17: Talent analytics is the gap I feel most acutely. Rippling gives me HR analytics, but the recruiting and talent pipeline analytics I need for executive reporting aren't really there — that lives mostly in Lever. I'd love tighter data flow between the two. I also find that Rippling's compensation management capabilities are fairly basic, and as we've gotten more sophisticated about total rewards, that's becoming a more visible gap.
v.Q18: The analytics fragmentation is my biggest frustration. I have recruiting data in Lever, workforce data in Rippling, and when I need to tell a cohesive talent story to the executive team — things like source-of-hire to retention correlation, or time-to-productivity for new hires by recruiting channel — I'm assembling that picture manually. I'd call it a moderate frustration that spikes to significant when I'm on a deadline for a board or exec presentation. It's the kind of thing that makes me feel like my tech stack isn't working for me as strategically as it should.
v.Q19: The expectation for data-driven talent decisions has gone up significantly. When we bought Rippling, I was focused on operational fixes — the broken handoff, the bad mobile experience. Those are solved. Now the conversation with leadership is more strategic and they want to see analytics that connect recruiting investment to business outcomes. I also think AI-assisted sourcing and screening has gone from a nice-to-have to something I actively need to evaluate, and that lens wasn't really part of my toolkit thinking a year ago.
v.Q20: Between Rippling and Lever, I'd estimate we're in the $75,000 to $100,000 range annually. I don't own the full budget — our CHRO does — but that's my rough understanding based on what I've seen in planning conversations.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. The operational value is real and I think we'd be hard-pressed to replicate what Rippling does at a lower price point. But the analytics gap makes me feel like we're leaving value on the table relative to what we're paying.
v.Q22: If I could get unified talent analytics that connected Lever recruiting data with Rippling workforce data in one place — real cross-system reporting — I'd put that value somewhere in the $10,000 to $25,000 range. It would save me meaningful time on executive reporting prep and frankly enable better decisions that could have real ROI in terms of hiring quality.
v.Q23: I'd say very unlikely to switch in the next six months. We just went through a migration and nobody has the appetite for another one anytime soon. But I'll be honest — if a platform emerged that genuinely solved the analytics fragmentation problem in a compelling way, I'd at least be paying attention. I'm not locked in emotionally.
v.Q24: I think the biggest challenge is that our tool ecosystems are still quite siloed — recruiting lives in one place, workforce management in another, compensation in a third — and getting a unified talent picture requires either expensive enterprise platforms or a lot of manual assembly. For talent acquisition leaders specifically, I think the pressure to demonstrate ROI on recruiting investment is intensifying and most of our tools aren't built to help us answer that question cleanly. And I think the AI conversation is creating real confusion right now — there are a lot of vendors making claims and it's genuinely hard to evaluate what's substance versus what's just good marketing.
