cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm a Director of HR at a mid-size retail company based out of Atlanta.
v.Q2: Just about four years now, so I'd say in that three-to-five range.
v.Q3: We're in retail — mostly e-commerce with some physical locations scattered across the Southeast. We're right around 700 employees at this point, though that number fluctuates a bit seasonally.
v.Q4: We're primarily on Rippling. It handles payroll, benefits administration, and a good chunk of our HR workflows. We do use a separate LMS for training, but for core HR and payroll it's Rippling.
v.Q5: That was roughly a year and a half ago, so I'd put it in the one-to-two-year bucket.
v.Q6: We were on ADP Workforce Now for payroll and had a separate BambooHR instance for the HRIS side of things. So we were running two systems that weren't really talking to each other cleanly.
v.Q7: Honestly, the biggest driver was the integration failure between ADP and BambooHR. We were doing a lot of manual data reconciliation every pay period, and as we grew past 600 employees that became genuinely unsustainable. The HR team was spending probably six to eight hours every two weeks just reconciling headcount data. On top of that, we had a compliance gap — our benefits carrier integrations were brittle, and we had a couple of instances where enrollment data didn't sync correctly, which created real exposure for us. Cost was also a factor; we were paying for two platforms and neither one was doing the job we needed individually.
v.Q8: We had just gone through a pretty significant push to consolidate our tech stack across the whole company — not just HR, but finance and ops too. The CTO had basically said that every department needed to evaluate whether they were running redundant systems and eliminate where possible. That initiative created the window for us to go out and do a real evaluation rather than just renew on autopilot.
v.Q9: The reporting was a real pain point in BambooHR at the scale we were at. I kind of felt like we had outgrown the analytics capabilities — building custom reports was clunky, and getting headcount and turnover data into a format leadership could actually consume required a lot of manual work in Excel. The ADP side had better reporting for payroll, but it wasn't connected to our HR data. So I'd say limited reporting and the integration gap were the two core frustrations we were trying to solve.
v.Q10: We looked at Rippling, Paylocity, UKG Ready, and we had an initial conversation with Workday but ruled it out pretty quickly as too enterprise for our size.
v.Q11: Unified payroll and HRIS in a single platform — that was non-negotiable. We also required native benefits administration, not just a broker integration. And it had to have an open API or pre-built connectors to Shopify and our warehouse management system. If it couldn't connect to those two systems, it wasn't even in the running.
v.Q12: It was HR, IT, and Finance. I was the primary recommender — I owned the evaluation and built the recommendation deck. Our CFO had final sign-off authority on the contract because it crossed a dollar threshold that required C-suite approval. IT was involved specifically to evaluate the security posture and API capabilities. So I'd say I was the primary driver but needed CFO sign-off to close it.
v.Q13: We switched — moved to Rippling and sunset both ADP and BambooHR over about a three-month implementation window.
v.Q14: Rippling won primarily on integration depth and the unified data model. The fact that payroll, benefits, and HR records all live in one place and actually reflect the same employee record in real time was the core value proposition for us. Paylocity was close, but the API story wasn't as strong for our specific Shopify use case. The implementation support Rippling offered was also better than what Paylocity was proposing — they had a more structured onboarding process that gave us more confidence we could actually get it live without a major disruption to payroll cycles.
v.Q15: Workday we ruled out immediately — it was priced for a company three times our size and the implementation timeline alone was nine to twelve months, which wasn't viable. UKG Ready had a fine product but the demo felt dated and the support model was heavily partner-dependent, which added cost and a layer of risk we didn't want. Paylocity was genuinely competitive, but their Shopify connector was a third-party add-on, not native, and that added integration risk we weren't comfortable with.
v.Q16: Rippling does the unified data model really well in practice — it lives up to what they promise. Payroll accuracy has been solid, onboarding workflows are genuinely efficient, and the device management integration is something we didn't have before that's actually been useful for our remote workforce. The reporting is meaningfully better than what we had before.
v.Q17: The benefits administration module is honestly a bit thin compared to what I'd want. Open enrollment is functional but the employee-facing experience feels clunky, and we've had some complaints from employees about the interface. I'd also say the performance management features are pretty bare-bones — we've had to layer in Lattice separately because Rippling's native performance tools just aren't there yet.
v.Q18: The open enrollment experience is probably the biggest one right now. The employee-facing flow is confusing enough that we get a high volume of support tickets during enrollment periods, and my team ends up doing a lot of hand-holding. I'd call it a moderate-to-significant frustration — it's not threatening to make us leave, but it's a real time cost every fall.
v.Q19: We've grown a bit and the workforce is more complex now — more part-time and seasonal workers, more state-specific compliance requirements as we've expanded into new markets. And honestly, leadership is now asking for more predictive workforce analytics than they were before, which is something Rippling doesn't fully deliver on today.
v.Q20: I think we're in the $100,000 to $250,000 range annually when you factor in all the modules we have active.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes — I think we're getting value, but I feel like we're paying for capabilities in the benefits module that aren't quite delivering at the level we'd expect for the price.
v.Q22: If someone could genuinely solve the open enrollment UX problem and cut our support ticket volume in half during that period, I'd say that's probably worth somewhere in the $10,000 to $25,000 range to us in recovered HR team time alone.
v.Q23: I don't think we'll be evaluating in the next six months — we're still in the middle of optimizing our Rippling setup. I'd call switching somewhat unlikely in that timeframe.
v.Q24: I think the biggest challenge is that most platforms are either built for companies much smaller than us or much larger — the 500-to-1,000-employee range is kind of an awkward middle ground where SMB tools start to strain and enterprise tools are over-engineered. The other thing I hear consistently from peers is that data fragmentation is still a huge problem — payroll, benefits, and talent data living in different systems and never quite reconciling cleanly.

Q16: Unified Platform as System of Record

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: Sure. I'm a VP of Talent Acquisition at a financial services firm headquartered in Chicago. I oversee our full recruiting function, from sourcing strategy all the way through offer and onboarding handoff.
v.Q2: I've been here just under three years — I came in as a senior director and was promoted to VP about eighteen months ago. So I'd say in the one-to-three-year band.
v.Q3: We're in financial services — specifically wealth management and registered investment advisory. We're right around 190 employees right now, but that number has moved pretty substantially since I joined. We were closer to 130 when I started, so we've grown meaningfully in a fairly short window.
v.Q4: Our main platform is BambooHR — that's where we manage employee records, onboarding, and a good portion of the recruiting workflow through their ATS module. Payroll runs through a separate provider, Paychex, and benefits administration is handled through our broker's portal. So technically it's three separate systems, though BambooHR is the center of gravity for my team.
v.Q5: That would have been roughly fourteen months ago, so within the last twelve-to-twenty-four-month window. We did a fairly structured evaluation that ran over about two months.
v.Q6: At that point we were using Greenhouse as our ATS — it was a legacy choice made before my time — and BambooHR for HRIS. So we had those two plus Paychex for payroll. The evaluation was really about whether to replace Greenhouse, potentially consolidate into a single platform, or do something else entirely.
v.Q7: There were honestly several things converging at once. The most immediate trigger was that our Greenhouse contract was coming up for renewal and the renewal price had increased substantially — I think something like 30 percent over the prior year — and the CFO pushed back hard and said we needed to justify that spend or find an alternative. That created the opening for a broader evaluation rather than just a straight renewal. But beyond the cost trigger, we had genuine capability gaps that were becoming more painful as we scaled. Greenhouse is a strong product, but the integration with BambooHR was not seamless — we were manually pushing candidate data into BambooHR after offers were accepted, and with the volume of hiring we were doing, that was becoming a real bottleneck. And the third factor was that my team had grown — I had hired two additional recruiters — and the candidate experience reporting in Greenhouse wasn't giving me what I needed to manage team performance effectively. I want to be able to see offer acceptance rates, time-to-fill by requisition type, and source quality, and getting clean data on all of those things required too much manual work.
v.Q8: The growth rate was probably the biggest contextual factor. We were in a hiring sprint — we needed to add roughly 50 people in about 12 months — and the inefficiency of our tooling was starting to create real drag on that. Our CEO was also paying close attention to time-to-hire numbers because we were competing with much larger firms for certain advisory talent, and we couldn't afford to have a slow or clunky process. There was also a broader theme in financial services at the time around data security and compliance — SEC and FINRA have specific expectations around record-keeping and data handling, and there was some internal pressure to make sure any tool we used could document a clear compliance posture. That raised the bar for what we were willing to consider.
v.Q9: The candidate experience piece was a real frustration. Greenhouse's application and interview scheduling flow is functional, but the self-scheduling capability for candidates was limited at our tier, and we were getting feedback from candidates that the process felt dated compared to what they were experiencing at other firms they were interviewing with. In financial services, perception matters — we're asking people to trust us with their careers and with client assets, so if our hiring process feels sloppy, that creates a real impression problem. Beyond that, the lack of a unified data model between Greenhouse and BambooHR meant I was often presenting leadership with headcount and pipeline data that had a two-to-three-day lag built in, because someone had to reconcile the two systems manually. That's not a position I want to be in when the CEO asks for an update on open headcount.
v.Q10: We seriously looked at Lever, Ashby, the BambooHR native ATS as a consolidation option, Rippling as a full platform play, and we also had a brief conversation with Gem, though that was more of an exploratory CRM conversation than a full evaluation.
v.Q11: A few things were genuinely non-negotiable. First, it had to have a clear integration story with BambooHR or be able to replace it — we weren't going to add a third HRIS layer on top of what we already had. Second, given our regulatory environment, the tool needed to be able to demonstrate SOC 2 Type II compliance and have clear data residency documentation — our Chief Compliance Officer reviewed that before we would even schedule a demo. Third, we needed built-in interview scheduling with candidate self-scheduling at no additional per-seat cost, because that was a core frustration we were trying to solve. And honestly, price ceiling was a factor too — our CFO had made it clear that total ATS spend needed to come down, not go up, so anything that was going to be more expensive than our Greenhouse contract was fighting uphill.
v.Q12: I drove the evaluation — I built the RFP, ran the demos, and put together the final recommendation. Our Chief Compliance Officer had a veto on any tool that didn't meet our compliance documentation requirements, so she was a real stakeholder, not just a reviewer. The CFO had sign-off authority on the contract value. And our Head of HR was involved as a peer — she had strong opinions about whether we consolidated into a single platform or stayed with BambooHR plus a best-in-class ATS, and we needed to agree on direction before I could finalize the recommendation. So it was HR plus Compliance plus Finance, with me as the primary driver.
v.Q13: We switched — we moved from Greenhouse to Lever as our ATS and kept BambooHR as the HRIS. So a partial switch rather than a full platform consolidation.
v.Q14: Lever won for a few reasons. The native BambooHR integration was tighter than what Ashby was offering at the time — it was a listed partnership with documented field mapping, not a Zapier workaround. The candidate-facing experience was genuinely better — the scheduling flow and the application interface felt more polished, which mattered to us for the reasons I mentioned earlier about perception. And the pricing was meaningfully lower than what Greenhouse had been charging us, which made the CFO conversation much easier. I think the Lever team also did a better job during the sales process of understanding our specific compliance context — they came prepared with their SOC 2 documentation without me having to chase it, which honestly signaled something about how they operate. Ashby was a close second and I think they have a strong product, but the BambooHR integration story at that point was less mature and I couldn't take that risk mid-hiring-sprint.
v.Q15: BambooHR's native ATS was the consolidation option, and I wanted to like it more than I did, but honestly it's not built for the kind of structured interview process and pipeline analytics that a dedicated talent team needs. It's fine for a smaller company with lighter recruiting volume, but at our pace it felt underpowered. Ashby is a genuinely great product and I'd consider them again, but the BambooHR integration gap was disqualifying at that moment. Rippling was interesting as a full platform play, but the ask was essentially rip-and-replace everything — BambooHR, Paychex, and Greenhouse all at once — and that implementation risk was too high during an active hiring sprint. Gem we ruled out because they're really a sourcing CRM layer, not a full ATS replacement, so it was solving a different problem.
v.Q16: BambooHR does the core HRIS fundamentals well — employee records are clean, the onboarding workflow builder is solid, and our HR team finds it genuinely usable day-to-day. Lever has been a meaningful upgrade from Greenhouse for us in terms of candidate experience and recruiter workflow. The pipeline visibility and the way Lever handles collaborative hiring notes has been well received by our hiring managers, which matters because getting managers to actually engage in the ATS is a real challenge in any company.
v.Q17: The biggest gap today is that we still have three systems — BambooHR, Lever, and Paychex — and they don't create a genuinely unified view of employee data. The Lever-to-BambooHR handoff is better than Greenhouse was, but it's not seamless. I also think BambooHR's compensation management and offer letter workflow is clunky for our use case, where offers often have variable comp components that need custom fields. And Paychex honestly feels like the weakest link — it's functional but the reporting is not good and the support has been inconsistent.
v.Q18: The Paychex reporting situation is my biggest frustration right now. I need headcount-by-department and compensation-band data to build workforce planning models, and getting clean data out of Paychex is genuinely painful — it requires either a manual export and reformat or working through their support team to pull custom reports, and their support response times are slow. I'd rate that as significant frustration. It's not a daily thing, but every time I need to build a board presentation or a workforce plan, I lose several hours to data wrangling that should be automated.
v.Q19: The growth we've experienced has increased our complexity in ways I didn't fully anticipate. We now have employees in seven states, and multi-state payroll compliance — particularly around state-specific deductions and reporting requirements — is a lot more demanding than it was when we were concentrated in Illinois. I've also started to think more seriously about AI-assisted sourcing tools, which wasn't really on my radar eighteen months ago. And honestly, as we've scaled, the expectation from leadership for real-time workforce analytics has gone up significantly.
v.Q20: Across BambooHR, Lever, and Paychex, I think we're probably in the $50,000 to $100,000 range annually. Paychex pricing is a bit opaque to me because it's managed through Finance, so I'm estimating on that piece.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes for BambooHR and Lever — I think we're getting fair value from both of those. For Paychex, I'd say somewhat no. The functionality doesn't justify the cost given what I know is available in the market at a similar price point.
v.Q22: If I had genuinely clean, real-time payroll and compensation reporting without manual intervention, I think that's probably worth $10,000 to $25,000 annually in recovered time across my team and the finance team that also gets pulled into these data pulls. That's probably a conservative estimate, honestly.
v.Q23: I think it's somewhat likely that we evaluate a Paychex replacement within the next six months — that conversation has already started internally. Whether we land on a full platform consolidation or just swap out payroll is still an open question. I wouldn't say we're definitely switching, but I'd call it more likely than not that we're at least in evaluation mode before the end of the year.
v.Q24: I think the common theme I hear from peers in talent acquisition is that the tool landscape is fragmented and expensive, and the promise of consolidation keeps not quite delivering. Everyone's been told they can get one platform that does everything, but in practice there's always a capability compromise somewhere — the ATS is great but the payroll is weak, or the HRIS is solid but the recruiting module is an afterthought. And I think there's also a growing challenge around AI — vendors are all claiming AI capabilities but it's genuinely hard to evaluate which of those claims are real and which are marketing. People don't want to overbuy on AI features they won't actually use, but they also don't want to get caught flat-footed if AI-assisted sourcing becomes a real competitive differentiator in two years.

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm a Director of People Operations. I oversee the full people function for an education company based in Texas.
v.Q2: I've been here a little over two years — so in the one-to-three-year band.
v.Q3: We're in education — specifically workforce training and professional development, so a mix of corporate clients and direct-to-consumer programs. We're at about 780 employees today, though we've grown pretty substantially over the last 24 months. We were around 580 when I joined.
v.Q4: We're on Rippling as our primary platform — payroll, benefits admin, and core HR all live there. We have a separate LMS for curriculum delivery and use Greenhouse for recruiting, which connects back to Rippling through an integration. So Rippling is the system of record.
v.Q5: About 18 months ago — so within the last one-to-two-year window.
v.Q6: We were on Paycom. That was the incumbent when I joined, and it had been in place for several years before me.
v.Q7: The growth rate was the primary trigger. We had scaled from roughly 450 to 580 employees in about 14 months, and Paycom was starting to show its limits in terms of how we managed org structures and workflow automation. Every time we added a new cost center or updated a job ladder, it was a manual configuration effort that took days and required opening support tickets. The support quality from Paycom had also declined noticeably — we were waiting five to seven business days for responses on basic configuration questions, which was not sustainable at our pace. And I had a new CPO who came in with a clear mandate to modernize our people tech stack, so there was executive sponsorship for actually doing the evaluation rather than just complaining about Paycom.
v.Q8: We had just closed a Series B round, and with that came pressure from investors to build out operational infrastructure that could support continued scaling. The board wanted to see that we had people systems capable of handling double our current headcount without a proportional increase in HR headcount. That framing — can your tools scale without adding more people to run them — became a real lens for how we evaluated everything.
v.Q9: Manual workflows were the central pain. In Paycom, so much of what should have been automated — offer approvals, onboarding task routing, PTO policy enforcement — required human intervention at every step. We also had a real problem with multi-state compliance. We had employees in 11 states and Paycom's handling of state-specific payroll tax configurations was not reliable — we had had a small but real compliance issue in Colorado around FAMLI that had rattled the CFO. And the analytics were genuinely poor. Getting turnover data or headcount-by-department required a custom report build every single time.
v.Q10: We seriously evaluated Rippling, Paylocity, and Namely. We also had an exploratory call with Lattice when they still had a payroll product, but that didn't go far.
v.Q11: Three things were non-negotiable. Automated workflow engine — we needed to be able to build multi-step approval flows without writing code or opening support tickets. Reliable multi-state payroll with built-in compliance updates, not manual patches. And a modern employee self-service experience — our workforce is mostly in-office and reasonably tech-savvy, and they were frustrated by Paycom's clunky mobile app. If a tool couldn't demonstrate those three things in a live demo, it was out.
v.Q12: I was the primary evaluator and owned the recommendation. Our CPO was the executive sponsor and had final approval authority — she had strong opinions and I needed her alignment before I could bring anything to the CFO. Finance reviewed the commercial terms. IT had a brief security review but wasn't deeply involved because Rippling and Paylocity both had clean SOC 2 documentation. So it was mostly People Ops plus CPO plus Finance.
v.Q13: We switched — moved from Paycom to Rippling. Implementation took about ten weeks.
v.Q14: Rippling's workflow automation was genuinely more powerful than anything else we saw — you can build conditional logic into onboarding flows, approval chains, and off-boarding in a way that felt like it was designed for an ops-minded person, not just an HR generalist. The multi-state payroll reliability gave us confidence, especially after the Colorado situation. And the overall platform velocity — the sense that they were shipping new features constantly — was a real differentiator. Paylocity felt more static. The Rippling team also had a stronger understanding of what a post-Series-B people ops function actually needs, which came through in the demo and the discovery process.
v.Q15: Paylocity was a credible option but the workflow automation was more limited — it felt more HR-administrator-centric than ops-centric, and I could tell it would still require a lot of manual process management on my team's part. Namely was eliminated early because the implementation timeline they quoted — sixteen to twenty weeks — was too long given our growth pace, and a few of their reference customers we spoke to had mentioned support quality issues post-implementation, which was already our core frustration with Paycom. Lattice's payroll product at the time was still pretty new and we didn't feel confident in its multi-state maturity.
v.Q16: The workflow engine is as good as advertised — it's genuinely transformed how we handle onboarding and off-boarding. Payroll accuracy has been solid across all our states. The employee self-service experience is clean and our workforce actually uses it without prompting, which was not the case with Paycom.
v.Q17: The performance management module is thin — we've ended up running performance reviews in a Google Form setup, which is embarrassing for a team that's supposed to be running a modern people ops function. And the customer success model has shifted — we got a lot of attention during implementation and in the first six months, but the ongoing support responsiveness has declined as I think they've scaled their customer base faster than their CS team.
v.Q18: The support issue is honestly the most frustrating thing right now. When we have a payroll configuration question that needs to be resolved before a close cycle, waiting 48 hours for a response is a real problem. I'd call it significant — it's not daily friction but when it hits, it hits at exactly the wrong moment.
v.Q19: Performance management has become a real gap that didn't feel as urgent during the evaluation. We also need better compensation benchmarking integration now — our talent team is asking for market data in context, not as a separate subscription they have to tab out of the system to access. And we're starting to think about succession planning, which requires a kind of org analytics depth that Rippling doesn't really have today.
v.Q20: For Rippling specifically I think we're in the $100,000 to $250,000 range when you add up all the active modules.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes — the core platform value is there. But I think we're paying for some modules we're not fully utilizing, and the support quality doesn't match the price point at the tier we're on.
v.Q22: Dedicated support with a guaranteed response SLA for payroll-critical questions? I'd say that's worth somewhere in the $10,000 to $25,000 range to us annually in avoided scramble time and risk mitigation.
v.Q23: I don't think we'll be switching in the next six months — we're still getting full value out of the core platform. I'd call it somewhat unlikely. But I think within 12 to 18 months we'll probably be evaluating performance management solutions, and whether that ends up being an add-on or a reason to reconsider the broader stack is an open question.
v.Q24: I think the biggest frustration I hear from people in people ops roles is that vendor support quality degrades after you sign. Everyone gets a great implementation experience and then the attention drops off. The other thing I hear constantly is that the market is good at selling integration but the actual integrations between even certified partners are often brittle or limited in what data they pass back and forth. You buy the promise of a connected system and you end up with three systems that mostly work together but still require a human to babysit the edges.

Q4: Point Solution Layered on Core Platform
Unified Platform as System of Record

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: Sure. I'm a senior manager in Talent Acquisition. I basically own all of recruiting for our organization, which is a solo situation on the HR side.
v.Q2: I've been here just about three years now.
v.Q3: We're in healthcare — specifically outpatient rehabilitation clinics, so a pretty regulated environment. We have right around 320 employees across multiple clinic locations, mostly in the Southeast.
v.Q4: We use Rippling as our main platform. It handles HR records, payroll, and some benefits administration. We do also use an ATS separately — that's Greenhouse — but Rippling is the core system.
v.Q5: That was about a year and a half ago, so kind of right at the edge of that twelve-to-eighteen month window.
v.Q6: We were on ADP Workforce Now for payroll and had a pretty basic BambooHR setup for HR records. They weren't really talking to each other in any meaningful way.
v.Q7: Honestly, the biggest driver was the integration mess. ADP and BambooHR weren't syncing properly, so I was manually reconciling employee data way more than I should have been as a solo HR person. We also had a compliance push — healthcare has a lot of credentialing and licensure tracking requirements, and neither tool was helping us with that. And then we were hitting a growth point where onboarding was just taking too long and we were losing candidates to faster-moving competitors because our process was so manual. Those three things together made it pretty undeniable that we needed to change.
v.Q8: The healthcare staffing market was brutal at that point. Competition for physical therapists and occupational therapists was intense, and we knew our onboarding experience was hurting us. There was also some pressure from ownership to get more efficient operationally, so there was a cost-consciousness element to it too.
v.Q9: The reporting in BambooHR was really limited for what I needed. I couldn't get clean time-to-hire data or offer acceptance rates without exporting to Excel and building things manually. ADP's support was also a constant headache — long hold times, inconsistent answers. And the employee self-service in both tools was clunky enough that staff were calling me directly for things they should have been able to do themselves, which was eating up a lot of my time given that I'm a team of one.
v.Q10: We looked at Rippling, Paylocity, and Paychex Flex. We also had a brief conversation with Gusto but ruled them out pretty early.
v.Q11: It had to do payroll natively — no bolt-on integrations for that core function. It needed solid employee self-service so I could get time back. And it had to have real reporting, not just canned dashboards. Those were the hard requirements.
v.Q12: Our CFO had final budget sign-off, and our COO was loosely involved because the clinics are ops-heavy. I was the primary recommender — I did all the demos, built the comparison, and essentially said here's what I think we should do. The CFO approved the spend based on my recommendation.
v.Q13: We switched. We moved to Rippling and fully replaced both ADP and BambooHR.
v.Q14: Rippling's device and app management piece was something the others just didn't have, and for us with staff across multiple sites that mattered. The automation around onboarding — you can set up a workflow and it actually fires correctly — was a big deal for me. The reporting was also meaningfully better than what I'd seen in BambooHR. Honestly the implementation support during the sales process felt more credible than what Paylocity showed us. I had a sense Rippling was built for companies that were growing and wanted to consolidate, which fit us well.
v.Q15: Gusto felt too small for us — it seemed oriented toward companies well under a hundred people and I wasn't confident it could handle multi-location healthcare complexity. Paychex Flex honestly felt dated; the UX was rough and the demo didn't inspire a lot of confidence that the product was moving forward. Paylocity was actually a close second, but the pricing came in higher and the implementation timeline they quoted was longer. I also felt like Paylocity was optimized for companies bigger than us, so some of the features we'd be paying for weren't really relevant at our size.
v.Q16: The onboarding automation is genuinely good. I can get a new hire from offer to day-one ready in a way that used to take me hours and now takes maybe twenty minutes of actual work. Payroll runs cleanly. And the self-service has absolutely reduced the number of people calling or emailing me for basic requests.
v.Q17: The recruiting module inside Rippling is weak — it's pretty much unusable for serious talent acquisition, which is why I'm still paying separately for Greenhouse. I'd love a tighter native ATS or a much cleaner integration. Benefits administration also gets complicated with our carrier mix and I find myself doing more manual reconciliation there than I expected.
v.Q18: The biggest one is honestly the cost of running Rippling alongside Greenhouse. I'm paying for two platforms and the integration, while better than what I had before, still isn't seamless enough to justify the combined spend forever. It's a moderate frustration right now — not critical, but it's the thing I think about most when I consider whether we got the right setup.
v.Q19: We've added about forty people in the last year, so scale is becoming more of a factor. I'm also thinking more about AI-assisted screening tools now — that wasn't really on my radar eighteen months ago but the market has moved quickly. Compliance tracking for licensed clinical staff has also gotten more complex as we've expanded into a new state.
v.Q20: I think we're in the range of fifty to seventy-five thousand dollars annually when you add up Rippling and Greenhouse together.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. Rippling alone feels like good value. The combined spend including Greenhouse is where I start to feel like there's room to rationalize.
v.Q22: If Rippling had a genuinely capable ATS built in — something that could actually replace Greenhouse — I'd estimate that's worth ten to fifteen thousand dollars a year to us just in consolidated licensing, plus real time savings for me.
v.Q23: Probably not within six months. I'd say very unlikely to switch in that timeframe. We're still in the stabilization phase from the last migration and I don't have appetite to go through that again soon.
v.Q24: I think the biggest thing is that most of these platforms are still built for either very small companies or very large ones, and the mid-market — where a lot of healthcare organizations sit — ends up cobbling together solutions that don't fully work together. Compliance complexity in healthcare doesn't get enough attention from vendors. And for solo HR people especially, the time investment to manage and maintain these tools is significant and often underestimated when you're buying.

Q4: Point Solution Layered on Core Platform

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: Yeah, so I'm a manager in People Operations. I oversee the day-to-day HR function for our company, and I work closely with our Head of People who sits above me and handles more of the strategic stuff.
v.Q2: I've been with this company for a little over two years. Coming up on my two-and-a-half-year mark actually.
v.Q3: We're kind of in a niche that doesn't fit neatly into standard categories — we're a membership-based professional association that also has a events and media arm. So I usually say other when those dropdowns come up. We have about 175 employees, mostly full-time with a handful of part-time staff, and we're based in Chicago.
v.Q4: We use Gusto as our main platform for payroll and HR records, and we have a separate tool — Lattice — for performance management and engagement. Benefits are administered through Gusto but we work through a broker for the actual plan selection. So Gusto is the core, and Lattice sits on top of it for the people-development side.
v.Q5: That was roughly eighteen months ago, maybe slightly more. It was part of a broader systems review that my Head of People kicked off shortly after I joined.
v.Q6: We were on a combination of QuickBooks Payroll and a pretty old version of ADP Run. HR records were honestly just a set of spreadsheets and a shared Google Drive. There was no real HRIS in place — just payroll software.
v.Q7: There were a few things all hitting at once. The most immediate trigger was that we were onboarding new employees and the process was completely disjointed — payroll was in one place, new hire paperwork was in email threads, benefits enrollment was being done manually by our broker. It was taking two to three weeks to fully get someone set up, which felt embarrassing. Beyond that, our Head of People had just joined and she wanted to build a real People Ops function rather than just a payroll-admin situation. So there was new leadership energy driving the change. We also had a compliance concern — our employee handbook hadn't been updated in years and we had no audit trail for things like signed acknowledgments or policy updates. That was a real risk area. And honestly the cost picture was murky — we weren't totally sure what we were spending across the different tools and we suspected there was waste.
v.Q8: We had shifted to a hybrid model after spending most of the pandemic fully remote, so there was a re-onboarding of people to physical office life happening at the same time. That actually surfaced a lot of gaps because suddenly managers were asking for things like org charts, updated job descriptions, and team directories — and we just didn't have good infrastructure to support those requests. There was also a broader push from our executive team to get more data-driven about the organization, and HR was kind of the last function to go through that kind of modernization.
v.Q9: The biggest frustration was how disconnected everything was. Running payroll required pulling data from multiple places and then manually entering it into QuickBooks, and there was always at least one error per cycle that had to be fixed after the fact. The employee experience was also poor — people couldn't self-serve anything. If someone needed a pay stub or wanted to update their direct deposit, they had to contact me directly. And for a team of three in People Ops serving a hundred-and-some employees, that kind of volume of manual requests adds up fast. Reporting was another issue. We had no way to run a simple headcount report or look at turnover trends without exporting data and building it ourselves. Our Head of People was regularly asking me for data that I simply couldn't produce efficiently.
v.Q10: We seriously looked at Gusto, Rippling, and Namely. We also did a quick look at BambooHR but it didn't make it to the full demo stage for us.
v.Q11: Yes, we were pretty clear on this. First, it had to include payroll processing natively — we weren't interested in a system that relied on a third-party payroll integration. Second, it needed a real employee self-service portal, not just a static directory. Third, it needed to be able to handle our mix of full-time and part-time employees without charging us per-contractor-tier rates that would spike our cost. And fourth — this was my Head of People's requirement — it had to have some level of onboarding workflow automation, not just document storage.
v.Q12: My Head of People was the decision-maker with final authority. I was doing most of the ground-level evaluation — running demos, comparing features, building out the comparison matrix. Our CFO was looped in specifically for the pricing review and had a soft veto on anything over a certain budget threshold. IT wasn't formally involved, though our Head of People did check with them informally about security requirements. So it was essentially a three-person decision with my Head of People holding the final call.
v.Q13: We switched. We moved entirely to Gusto, decommissioned QuickBooks Payroll and ADP Run, and consolidated onto a single platform.
v.Q14: Gusto won primarily on ease of use and implementation simplicity. The demo was genuinely approachable — when we showed it to our CFO and to a couple of managers who would be using it for time-off approvals, everyone came away feeling like they could actually figure it out without training. Rippling had more features overall, but the implementation looked significantly more complex, and given that I'm not a technical person and our team is small, that complexity felt like a real risk. Gusto's pricing was also more transparent — you could see exactly what you were going to pay, whereas Rippling's pricing conversation felt more like a negotiation. Namely felt enterprise-sized for us, honestly — it seemed like it was built for companies of four or five hundred with a dedicated HRIS admin, which we didn't have.
v.Q15: Rippling was close, but the implementation complexity and the overall pricing opacity were the main reasons we passed. I also had some concern that we'd end up paying for a lot of modules we didn't need yet and couldn't easily turn off. BambooHR didn't make it to full demo, mostly because early in our research it became clear their payroll was only available in certain tiers and the integration with their own HR system had a reputation for being clunky based on things I read in user reviews. Namely was knocked out mostly on size fit — it felt like a tool designed for an HR department, not an HR team of three that needed something we could run without a dedicated admin. The pricing also came in at the top of our range.
v.Q16: Gusto does payroll really well for our situation. It's reliable, it runs on time, and the employee-facing experience for things like viewing pay stubs, updating W-4s, and managing direct deposit is genuinely smooth. Our employees almost never contact us for payroll-related questions anymore, which was a real win. Onboarding is also much better — we have a workflow that sends new hires through paperwork digitally before day one, and the completion tracking is helpful for us on the back end. Benefits enrollment is cleaner than it used to be, even though our broker still does a lot of the heavy lifting there.
v.Q17: Reporting is still a gap, honestly. I can run basic reports but anything more nuanced requires a data export and then I'm back in spreadsheets anyway. We've also grown to a point where we're doing more performance cycle work and compensation planning, and Gusto has basically nothing for that — which is why we added Lattice. But the two don't integrate as cleanly as I'd like, so there's still some manual work bridging data between them. Q4: Point Solution Layered on Core Platform

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm a senior manager in People Operations. I think my title formally says Senior Manager of People but I oversee everything from recruiting coordination to compensation to benefits — basically the full HR lifecycle for our company.
v.Q2: Just over two years. I came in as the first dedicated People Ops hire when we were about forty-five people, and I've kind of built the function from the ground up since then.

Right now we're at about eighty-five employees, and that number has moved pretty fast — we were sixty people at the start of last year and closer to forty the year before that, so we've roughly doubled in two years. Which, honestly, is a big part of why we've been thinking hard about our infrastructure.
v.Q4: We use Gusto as our primary platform — it covers payroll, basic HR records, and benefits administration. We also use Lever as our ATS, which sits outside of Gusto, and we've got a homegrown Notion-based onboarding tracker that we've been using as a stopgap because Gusto's onboarding capabilities don't fully meet our needs. So technically it's Gusto as the system of record, Lever for recruiting, and Notion duct-taped to the side for new hire process management. It's not ideal and we know it.
v.Q5: The most recent formal evaluation was about eight months ago. We didn't end up switching at that point, which I can get into, but we went through a pretty thorough process.
v.Q6: Same as now, actually — we were on Gusto. So this was an evaluation of whether to stay with Gusto or move to something that could scale with us better. We were not coming from a previous tool; Gusto was already in place when I joined and had been there since the company was maybe twenty people.
v.Q7: So there were honestly several things converging at once. The most tangible trigger was headcount growth. When you're doubling in size, the manual burden of using a payroll-centric tool like Gusto for everything HR-related starts to become really visible really fast. We were adding ten to fifteen people a quarter and the onboarding process was just not scaling — I was building individual Notion pages for every new hire, coordinating with IT over Slack, chasing managers for their part of the onboarding checklist over email. It was not a sustainable system. The second driver was compensation and equity management. We'd started doing more structured compensation reviews and we had a growing number of employees with equity, and Gusto just has no infrastructure for any of that. We were trying to manage comp bands in spreadsheets and it was getting messy. Third, I think I was starting to feel pressure from our engineering and product team — who use very polished internal tools — about the HR experience feeling dated. Our employees are pretty tech-forward, and when the onboarding portal looks like it was built in 2014, it reflects on the People team. And then there was also a Series B conversation happening, and I knew that investors would want to see more mature people infrastructure, so there was a little bit of anticipatory pressure there too.
v.Q8: The broader context was really about the maturity moment the company was at. We were coming out of early startup mode and trying to operate more like a real company — better processes, more documentation, clearer accountability structures. That kind of organizational maturation puts pressure on every function to upgrade its infrastructure, and People Ops felt that acutely. I'd also say the hiring market at that time was still competitive enough that candidate experience was top of mind for me. Our offer-to-start process was longer than I wanted it to be and I knew that some candidates had dropped off during that window, even though I couldn't prove it definitively. So candidate experience and speed-to-onboard were very much in my head. And I'll be honest — I'd been to a couple of HR technology conferences and seen what other tools could do, and I came back feeling like we were meaningfully behind where we could be.
v.Q9: Gusto's onboarding is probably what frustrated me most. You can send an offer letter and collect some paperwork, but there's no real workflow engine behind it — you can't assign tasks to managers, you can't set up IT provisioning triggers, you can't build a structured thirty-sixty-ninety-day check-in cadence. For an eighty-five person tech company, that's a real gap. Reporting was also a significant frustration. Gusto gives you payroll reports and some basic headcount data, but it's not a people analytics tool at all. I couldn't answer questions like what's our average tenure by department, where are we seeing attrition risk signals, or what's our offer acceptance rate trend without building that manually. And every time a founder asked me for data I should have been able to pull in thirty seconds, I felt that gap. The third frustration was the lack of a proper org management layer — there's no dynamic org chart, no headcount planning view, no way to model out what the org looks like in six months if we execute our hiring plan. For a company growing at our pace, that matters.
v.Q10: We seriously considered Rippling, HiBob, and Lattice — though Lattice was more of a complementary evaluation than a full HRIS replacement candidate. We also looked briefly at Workday, mostly because one of our board members mentioned it, but we ruled it out almost immediately as too enterprise for our size. And we revisited whether a heavier Gusto plan could close the gaps, which it couldn't.
v.Q11: Yes, I had a pretty defined list going into it. Native payroll was the first requirement — we weren't going to add a separate payroll system given we'd just gotten payroll running smoothly on Gusto. The second was onboarding workflow automation with task assignment — not just document collection, but actual process orchestration across multiple stakeholders. Third was some form of people analytics or reporting that went beyond payroll data — headcount trends, retention signals, that kind of thing. Fourth was integration with Lever, which we had invested in and weren't planning to replace. And fifth was scalability — I needed to know this tool could work for us at two hundred employees, not just eighty-five, because switching again in a year wasn't something I wanted to do. I also kind of loosely required that the employee experience had to feel modern, because that mattered to our team culture.
v.Q12: Our CFO was involved pretty significantly — more than I expected, honestly. He wanted to own the total cost of ownership conversation and was particularly focused on whether we'd be paying for features we wouldn't use for another year or two. Our CEO was looped in because one of the tools we were evaluating would touch a lot of employee-facing workflows and she wanted visibility into that. Our Head of Engineering had a soft influence on the decision because he cared about IT provisioning and device management capabilities, which is a real need for us as we've been scaling the engineering team. I was the primary evaluator and recommender — I ran all the demos, built the comparison framework, and made the final recommendation. My CEO said yes to the recommendation, CFO negotiated the contract terms. So I had real decision weight, but it wasn't solely mine.
v.Q13: We ended up staying with Gusto, which was genuinely a hard call and not a decision I was fully satisfied with. The short version is that the timing wasn't right — we had a board meeting coming up and the CFO didn't want to absorb a migration during that window, and I didn't feel like I had enough internal momentum to push it through. So we renewed with Gusto and I've been living with that decision since.
v.Q14: I want to be clear that staying with Gusto wasn't really a choice based on Gusto being the best fit — it was a choice based on timing and internal constraints. What kept us there was really inertia and the CFO's appetite for risk at a sensitive moment for the company. Payroll continuity was a genuine concern — our CFO was worried about a payroll error during a migration and that was a meaningful deterrent. And to be fair, Gusto handles payroll reliably, which is the most mission-critical piece. But the honest answer is that if the internal timing had been different, I think we would have moved to HiBob. It had the most thoughtful employee experience layer of anything we evaluated, the onboarding workflows were genuinely impressive, and the people analytics capability was well ahead of Gusto. Rippling was also compelling, especially for the IT management side, but I found the pricing model harder to predict as we scaled and the implementation scope felt heavy.
v.Q15: So starting with Rippling — it was the other finalist alongside HiBob and I genuinely liked a lot of it. The IT and device management piece would have been valuable, and the automation capability was strong. But the pricing conversation was complicated. The modular pricing meant the final number kept moving as we scoped it out, and by the time we had a real quote it was meaningfully above what we'd budgeted. I also felt like Rippling was optimized for companies that had an IT operations team or at least someone who was technical, and our IT function is pretty lean. The implementation timeline was also longer than I wanted. HiBob was actually my preferred choice, and the only reason it wasn't selected was the internal timing issue I mentioned — not a product problem. The employee experience design was excellent, the Lever integration looked solid, and the analytics layer was what I'd been looking for. If we re-evaluate in the next year, HiBob is going to be on the shortlist again. Workday was knocked out almost immediately — it was built for companies at five-hundred-plus with a dedicated HRIS team, and the implementation cost alone was out of our range. And a heavier Gusto tier didn't close the gaps — the capability ceiling is just structurally different from what I needed.
v.Q16: Payroll is genuinely reliable in Gusto. I've run payroll on it for two years and I've had maybe one issue that required a correction, and Gusto's support resolved it the same day. For a function where getting it wrong has real consequences for employees, that consistency matters a lot. Benefits administration is also reasonably smooth — the open enrollment flow in Gusto is clean enough that employees can navigate it without a lot of hand-holding from my team, which saves us meaningful time every fall. The employee self-service for pay stubs, W-2s, and basic profile updates works well and has reduced a category of inbound requests to my team almost entirely. And the direct deposit and contractor payment workflow is clean, which matters for us because we have about fifteen contractors in addition to full-time employees.
v.Q17: The onboarding gap is still the most visible one day-to-day. I'm still using Notion to bridge the workflow orchestration piece and it's still not elegant. There's no way to assign tasks across stakeholders, track completion in real time, or give new hires a coherent single-entry-point experience. Every time we bring someone new on, I feel the friction. Reporting is the other persistent gap. I've tried to work around it with data exports to a Google Sheet that I've built out over time, but that's maintenance burden I shouldn't have. And I still can't give leadership a clean dashboard view of people metrics without manually refreshing my exports. Headcount planning and org management are also missing — as we keep growing, those gaps are becoming harder to work around informally.
v.Q18: The onboarding workflow limitation is my biggest frustration and I'd call it significant rather than just moderate. Every single hire we make involves me going into at least three different tools — Gusto for paperwork, Lever for the transition from candidate to employee, Notion to build and assign the onboarding checklist, and Slack to ping IT and the hiring manager. That's four systems to onboard one person. At forty hires a year and growing, the cumulative time cost is real. But more than the time, it just doesn't represent the experience I want people to have joining our company. We talk a lot about culture and employee experience, and then the onboarding feels like it was built for a much smaller, less intentional company. That dissonance bothers me professionally.
v.Q19: Quite a bit has evolved, honestly. We're starting to build out a manager layer that didn't really exist a year ago, which means I now need tools that support managers in doing things like running check-ins, tracking development goals, and giving structured feedback — none of which Gusto touches. We've also just done our first formal compensation benchmarking cycle and it made really clear that we need dedicated comp management tooling, because trying to do it in spreadsheets at eighty-five people is already unwieldy. I'm also thinking more about retention analytics now — we've had a few unexpected departures in the last six months and I want earlier signals. And I'd say AI capability has become more of an expectation from our founder team, even if they can't always articulate exactly what they want from it. There's an expectation that our tools should be getting smarter, not just storing data.
v.Q20: For Gusto and Lever combined, I think we're in the thirty to fifty thousand dollar range annually. Gusto's per-employee pricing scales with headcount so it's been creeping up as we've grown, and Lever is a fixed annual contract. So combined it's probably closer to forty thousand at our current size.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes for Lever — I think the ATS is well-matched to what we're getting. For Gusto specifically, I'm increasingly neutral on the value equation because the per-employee cost has grown as we've scaled but the capability ceiling hasn't moved. So I'm paying more for the same product, and the gaps are more visible now than they were when we were smaller. That's not a great value trajectory.
v.Q22: If Gusto had a genuinely functional onboarding workflow engine — task assignment across stakeholders, automated triggers, a new hire portal that felt like a real product — I'd estimate that's worth somewhere in the ten to twenty-five thousand dollar range annually for us. That's a combination of my time savings across forty-plus hires a year, the reduced risk of onboarding errors that create downstream problems, and the improvement in early employee experience that I believe has some retention value even if it's hard to quantify precisely. The time savings alone, if I'm honest, is probably the most defensible part of that estimate.
v.Q23: I'd say I'm somewhat likely to at least re-open the evaluation within six months, and if I did, I think there's a reasonable chance we'd actually switch this time. The internal timing issue that blocked us last year is less of a factor now — the board meeting has passed, we're in a steadier operational moment, and I think the CFO has seen enough of the manual workarounds to understand that the status quo has a real cost too. I'd call switching likelihood somewhere between somewhat likely and neutral. It really depends on whether I can carve out the time to run a proper evaluation given everything else on my plate.
v.Q24: I think the most consistent challenge I hear from peers in similar roles is the gap between what these tools promise in a demo and what they actually deliver at implementation and in ongoing use. There's a lot of polish at the sales stage and then you get into the tool and you find that the feature you most cared about is partially built or requires a workaround. Related to that, I think the integration story across the HR tech stack is still genuinely hard — most of us are running four or five tools that nominally integrate but require ongoing maintenance to stay functional. The second big challenge is the expectation gap between what founders and executives think HR tools can do and what they actually do at our company sizes. There's a perception that we should have real-time people analytics and AI-driven retention predictions, and the reality is that most SMB-oriented tools aren't there yet in a way that works reliably at scale. And honestly, for People Ops leaders at fast-growing companies, the biggest operational challenge is just that the tools don't grow with you gracefully — you either start too small and outgrow your platform, or you buy too much too early and can't get value from it. The market hasn't fully solved that problem.

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: Sure. I'm a VP of HR. I lead the entire people function here, which honestly covers everything from recruiting and onboarding through compliance, compensation, and benefits — all of it. And I do it largely on my own, which is its own kind of adventure at a company this size.
v.Q2: I've been here just under five years. I came in when we were around 180 people and have grown with the organization since then.
v.Q3: We're in education — specifically, we're a private K-12 school network with campuses in three states. We're sitting at about 340 employees right now, which is a meaningful jump from where we started, and we expect to keep adding staff at a measured pace as we open a fourth campus over the next couple of years.
v.Q4: We use BambooHR as our primary HRIS. It handles employee records, onboarding, performance management, and some reporting. For payroll specifically, we actually process through a separate payroll provider — we use Paylocity for that — and benefits are administered through our broker's portal. So it's not a fully unified stack, which is something I think about often.
v.Q5: That was about two years ago, give or take a few months. We went through a fairly thorough evaluation and landed on BambooHR, which is where we are now.
v.Q6: We had been limping along on a combination of Paychex Flex for payroll and a lot of shared Google Drive folders and spreadsheets for everything else. There was no real HRIS in place. It was very much held together with institutional knowledge and manual effort.
v.Q7: The honest answer is that we had simply outgrown what we were doing. When you're 180 people and growing, managing employee records in shared spreadsheets is not sustainable. Onboarding new hires was an embarrassment — it was a stack of PDFs emailed to people before their first day, and then a pile of paperwork when they arrived. We were also running into compliance issues because nothing was centralized. I couldn't pull a clean headcount report without rebuilding it from scratch every time. And I think there was a new campus opening on the horizon, which meant we were going to be hiring a cohort of teachers and administrators, and I knew our process couldn't handle that volume. So the triggers were really: scale pressure, manual process pain, compliance risk, and a hiring surge on the horizon.
v.Q8: In the education sector specifically, there's been a lot of pressure around staff retention over the last few years — particularly for teachers. The market got very competitive post-pandemic, and that pushed us to think harder about the employee experience from day one. A clunky onboarding process doesn't set the right tone when candidates have options. So there was an industry-level retention dynamic that made investing in a proper HRIS feel more urgent. Our board was also asking more questions about workforce data — things like turnover rates by campus and compensation benchmarking — and I simply could not answer those questions with the tools I had.
v.Q9: So many. Paychex Flex was honestly the biggest pain point. The user interface was dated, the support model was frustrating — you'd get a different person every time you called and have to re-explain your situation from scratch. Running reports out of Paychex was painful, and anything multi-state added a layer of complexity that the tool didn't handle gracefully. The broader issue was that there was no single source of truth for employee data. I'd have payroll data in one place, PTO tracking in a spreadsheet, and performance notes in someone's email. The fragmentation was costing me a significant amount of time every week.
v.Q10: We looked at BambooHR, Paycor, Namely, and we had a brief look at Rippling as well. Those were the four we got to a real evaluation stage.
v.Q11: Multi-state payroll handling was non-negotiable given our three-campus structure. We also needed strong onboarding workflows — not just e-signature, but actual configurable onboarding checklists and task assignment. And because I'm a solo HR team, implementation had to be manageable without needing a dedicated IT resource or a six-month rollout. I also had a soft price ceiling — anything that was going to push us above a certain threshold per employee per month was going to face a very hard conversation with our CFO, and I didn't want to go into that fight unless I was certain the value was there.
v.Q12: I drove the entire evaluation. I built the comparison matrix, ran the demos, collected feedback from a couple of campus principals who were going to be end users of some of the onboarding features. Our CFO had final approval authority on the budget, so I presented my recommendation to him with a full cost-benefit summary. But in terms of the actual decision-making process, it was essentially me recommending and the CFO approving. Our COO also had a brief opinion, mostly on whether the implementation timeline worked with our calendar, since schools have very specific busy seasons.
v.Q13: We switched. We moved to BambooHR for the HRIS layer and kept a separate payroll solution, which is actually one of my ongoing regrets — I wish we had gone fully unified, but the timing and budget didn't allow it at the time.
v.Q14: BambooHR won primarily because of the onboarding module and the overall ease of implementation. The UI is also genuinely user-friendly — I knew my campus principals were not going to read a training guide, so the tool needed to be intuitive enough that people would figure it out on their own. I think honestly the UX and the implementation simplicity were the two things that pushed it ahead of Paycor, which had more features on paper but felt significantly more complex to stand up.

v.Q16: BambooHR does onboarding really well.
