cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: Sure. I'm a Director of HR. I oversee the full people function — everything from talent acquisition and onboarding through comp and benefits, employee relations, and a lot of the HR operations and systems work. So it's a pretty broad remit, and I'm involved in most of the vendor decisions that touch the people side of the house.
v.Q2: I've been here about two and a half years. I came in when we were around 300 employees, and we've grown pretty substantially since then, so it's been quite a ride in terms of building infrastructure that can actually keep pace with the hiring.
v.Q3: We're a B2B SaaS company — kind of developer tooling and infrastructure. So firmly in technology. And we're currently sitting at around 680 employees. We've been growing fast — I think we added something like 200 people in the last 18 months alone, which is honestly what's driving a lot of the conversations we're having about our systems.
v.Q4: We're on Gusto as our core payroll and benefits platform. We run Greenhouse on top of that for recruiting and ATS, and then we have Lattice for performance and engagement. So it's not a fully unified stack — we've got three distinct systems that we're stitching together with integrations of varying quality. Gusto handles payroll, benefits administration, and some basic employee records. But the HRIS functionality in Gusto is, honestly, not where it needs to be for a company our size.
v.Q5: We went through a pretty serious evaluation about eight months ago. So that's within the last twelve months. We actually came close to switching, and the fact that we didn't is kind of its own story.
v.Q6: Same as now — Gusto plus Greenhouse plus Lattice. We were already on that stack. The evaluation was specifically about whether to replace Gusto with something that had stronger HRIS capabilities and could potentially consolidate some of what Lattice does.
v.Q7: There were honestly several things converging at once. The most immediate one was that our headcount growth had exposed some real scalability limits in Gusto. When we were 300 people it was fine, but as we pushed past 500, the reporting got painful, the org chart tooling became basically unusable, and we started hitting limits on how we could segment employees for different policies — things like PTO accrual rules for different employee classifications, or managing multiple state compliance requirements as we expanded into new states. That was a capability gap issue that was becoming a real operational problem. The second driver was that we'd just hired a new VP of People above me, and she came from a company that had used Workday and then HiBob, so she had a clear perspective on what a more mature HRIS should look like. That new leadership factor definitely accelerated the evaluation. And third, we were heading into a contract renewal with Gusto in about four months, and it felt like the right forcing function to actually do the work of evaluating alternatives rather than just rolling over on the renewal.
v.Q8: A couple of things. We had just closed a Series C, so there was investor-level interest in making sure our people infrastructure could scale to where we wanted to go — there was actually some explicit board-level conversation about operational readiness. That created budget availability that we wouldn't have had otherwise. And I think there was also a broader digital transformation mindset in the company at that point. Our CTO had been pushing for consolidating and upgrading a lot of the internal tooling, and HR was part of that conversation. So it wasn't just an HR-driven initiative — it had cross-functional momentum behind it.
v.Q9: Yes, and I can be pretty specific here. The reporting in Gusto is genuinely limited. You can get basic headcount data, but the moment you want to slice by department, location, tenure band, comp range — you're exporting to a spreadsheet and building it yourself. For a company our size running weekly leadership reviews, that's just not sustainable. My team was spending hours every month on data wrangling that should have been automated. The second big frustration was multi-state compliance. We operate in eleven states now, and keeping up with the variation in leave laws, local tax rules, and benefits requirements is complex. Gusto handles some of it, but we were relying heavily on manual tracking and our broker to fill gaps, which introduced real compliance risk. Third — and this one's more about the employee experience — the self-service capabilities in Gusto are pretty basic. Employees couldn't update certain things on their own, managers couldn't run basic reports on their own teams without coming to HR. It created unnecessary bottlenecks for us.
v.Q10: We looked seriously at Rippling, HiBob, Namely, and we had one exploratory conversation with Paylocity. HiBob and Rippling got the furthest — we did full demos, reference checks, and I think we got to a pricing proposal stage with both of them.
v.Q11: We were pretty clear on a few things. One was native integration with Greenhouse — that was a hard requirement because we weren't going to replace our ATS at the same time. Two was robust multi-state compliance support, meaning built-in policy management for different state leave laws, not just manual workarounds. Three was a self-service manager experience that actually worked — dashboards, headcount reporting, org visualization. And four, honestly, was implementation support that didn't require us to hire a consultant. We'd heard enough horror stories about HRIS implementations going sideways that we wanted a vendor with a dedicated implementation team, not just documentation and a ticketing system.
v.Q12: It was a cross-functional group. The VP of People was the executive sponsor and had final approval authority. I was the primary evaluator — I ran the process, did the demos, managed the reference checks, and put together the recommendation. We also had our CFO involved because of the budget implications, and he wanted to see a business case, not just a feature comparison. IT security was looped in for the single sign-on and data security review — our CTO requires a security review on any new vendor that touches employee data. And then I had two members of my HR ops team participating in demos specifically so they could evaluate the day-to-day usability. So it was a pretty involved committee, which honestly made the decision take longer than I wanted.
v.Q13: We stayed with Gusto. I know that's maybe surprising given everything I just said, but we renewed. The short version is that the implementation risk and the timing didn't work in our favor — we were heading into Q4 and open enrollment simultaneously, and both HiBob and Rippling had implementation timelines that would have landed us in a really bad spot. The CFO also pushed back on the switching cost analysis. So we negotiated better pricing on the Gusto renewal and got a few feature commitments on their roadmap, and we agreed to revisit the evaluation in the second half of this year.
v.Q14: Staying with Gusto wasn't really a vote of confidence — I want to be clear about that. It was primarily a timing and risk decision. That said, Gusto's payroll reliability is genuinely strong. We've never had a payroll error in two and a half years, which is not nothing. The benefits administration experience for employees is clean and relatively easy to use. And the existing integrations we'd built with Greenhouse and our equity platform were working without much maintenance overhead. Those were the things that gave me enough confidence to say okay, we can live with this for another cycle without it being a disaster. But I wouldn't say Gusto won on merit against what we saw from HiBob and Rippling — it won on timing and switching cost.
v.Q15: HiBob was actually really compelling on the people experience side — the UI is excellent, the engagement and performance modules are genuinely well-designed, and the manager self-service was exactly what we wanted. The reason we didn't go with it came down to two things: their payroll solution is third-party in the US, which meant we'd still have a separate payroll vendor, and that partially defeated the consolidation goal. And their implementation timeline in our region was quoted at four to five months, which took us past open enrollment. Rippling was the other serious contender. The IT management angle was interesting since our IT team liked the idea of unified device and app management. But the platform felt more complex than what my team was ready to operationalize — there's a lot of configurability, which is great in theory, but I was worried about our ability to actually maintain it without a dedicated HRIS admin. The sales process also felt a little aggressive, which wasn't a dealbreaker but didn't help. Namely we kind of deprioritized early — the product felt a bit dated in the demo, and their customer references were mixed when I did some informal peer network checks. Paylocity was never really in the running; it felt more mid-market and the demo wasn't compelling enough for us to invest more time.
v.Q16: Payroll is consistently accurate and runs smoothly — I genuinely can't complain about that. Benefits open enrollment, while not perfect, is functional enough that employees can navigate it without a lot of hand-holding from HR. The onboarding workflow for new hires has some good automation for document collection and I-9 handling. And the employee self-service for things like address changes and direct deposit updates works reliably. For a company that was under 400 people, Gusto was a really solid choice. The issue is that we've grown past the point where its limitations are just minor inconveniences.
v.Q17: The reporting gaps I mentioned earlier haven't gotten better — that's still a daily frustration for my team. The org chart and people directory functionality is too basic for a 680-person company that has a pretty complex matrix structure. We don't have a good way to model org changes or run scenario planning in the system. And the multi-state compliance tooling still requires a lot of manual oversight, which is a real risk exposure. I also think the product has been slow to adopt anything AI-adjacent — I'm not expecting miracles there, but the contrast with what some competitors are showing is becoming more noticeable.
v.Q18: Honestly, the reporting situation is the biggest ongoing frustration, and I'd call it significant — not quite severe because we've built workarounds, but it burns real time every week. My HR ops team runs a weekly people metrics dashboard for the leadership team, and building that report still requires exporting raw data from Gusto into a Google Sheet and then doing a bunch of manipulation. That process takes three to four hours every week. Over a year that's something like 150 to 200 hours of my team's time just on data assembly that the system should be doing for us. When I frame it that way for my CFO it gets attention, but it still hasn't been enough to force the switch.
v.Q19: A few things have shifted. We're now in eleven states and adding more, so the compliance complexity has increased. We've also started having conversations about global expansion — Canada first, probably — and that's going to require a vendor that has international payroll or at least a clear path to it. I'm also thinking more about the manager experience than I was before. As we've scaled, I've realized how much of HR's bottleneck comes from managers not having the data and tools to self-serve, so the manager dashboard and reporting capabilities have moved up in priority for me. And I'd say expectations around AI-assisted features have come up — not as a top priority but as a tie-breaker.
v.Q20: Across Gusto, Greenhouse, and Lattice, I think we're in the $250K-plus range annually. Gusto itself is probably $100K to $150K of that when you factor in all the per-employee fees.
v.Q21: Somewhat no, honestly. The payroll reliability is worth something, but at this scale I think we're paying for a platform that is visibly under-delivering on the HRIS side. I think a more capable platform at a similar or modestly higher price point would deliver better ROI — especially when I factor in the staff hours we're spending on manual reporting and compliance tracking.
v.Q22: If Gusto actually had robust, configurable reporting and analytics — the kind where I can build the views I need without exporting to spreadsheets — I think that's worth $25K or more annually to us just in staff time recovered, not even accounting for the decision quality that better data enables. So I'd say the $25K-plus band is where I'd put that.
v.Q23: Yes, I think we'll actively consider switching. We made a commitment to revisit this in the second half of the year, and I fully expect to run a formal evaluation again. How likely is it that we actually switch? I'd say somewhat likely. The business case is stronger now than it was eight months ago, the international expansion question is going to force a more urgent timeline, and I think the CFO is more open to it than before now that he's seen the reporting burden accumulate. The main risk is timing again — it always comes down to when you can safely absorb an implementation.
v.Q24: I think the number one challenge most directors and VPs of HR would name is that the market is still pretty fragmented — you end up building a stack of three or four tools that each do one thing reasonably well, but the integrations are brittle and the employee experience is inconsistent across them. People want a unified platform but the ones that offer true unification either feel too enterprise and expensive for where most growth-stage companies are, or they're too lightweight to grow into. The second challenge I hear a lot is implementation risk — everyone has a horror story about a payroll migration or an HRIS launch that went sideways, and that fear of change is actually keeping a lot of companies on systems that don't fit them anymore. And I'd add that AI expectations are starting to create a new kind of pressure — there's a growing expectation that your HRIS should be surfacing insights, not just storing data, and very few platforms are actually delivering on that in a meaningful way yet.

Q4: Point Solution Layered on Core Platform

cat.Q21: Somewhat no / not really reasonable

v.Q1: I'm a VP of People Operations. I oversee everything on the people side — recruiting, HR, comp, culture, the whole picture. It's a broad role and I essentially function as the CHRO for our company even though we don't use that title.
v.Q2: Coming up on five years. I was one of the earlier people ops hires, so I've kind of grown with the company as it's scaled.
v.Q3: We're a fintech company — specifically payments and financial infrastructure software. And we're at about 85 employees right now. We've been growing steadily, maybe 10 to 15 percent per year, which is healthy but not the kind of hypergrowth that creates chaos.
v.Q4: BambooHR is our core HRIS and handles a lot of the employee data management, onboarding workflows, and time-off tracking. For payroll we actually still use a separate payroll processor — we're on ADP Run for that — and benefits administration goes through our broker's portal. So it's genuinely fragmented, which is something I think about a lot.
v.Q5: We did a review about fourteen months ago, so I'd call it within the last twelve to eighteen months — closer to the twelve-to-twenty-four range.
v.Q6: At the start of that evaluation we were on Zenefits for HR and benefits, and ADP for payroll. Zenefits had gone through a rough period and we'd lost confidence in the platform and the company, so that was really the starting point of the whole thing.
v.Q7: Zenefits was the primary driver. The reliability had degraded — we were seeing sync errors between their HRIS and our payroll feed with enough frequency that I didn't trust the data integrity anymore. There were also some benefit enrollment issues where employee elections weren't being transmitted to carriers correctly, which is a serious problem. Beyond the reliability issues, the platform had started to feel like it was in maintenance mode — no meaningful product updates, support was getting slower. And we'd grown past 70 people, which is where Zenefits starts to feel a little thin on the reporting side.
v.Q8: We'd just come through a period of building out more formal HR processes — things like structured performance reviews, a compensation framework, a more deliberate onboarding program. And as we built those processes, it became clear that our tooling wasn't going to support them well. So there was an internal maturation happening on the people ops side that the tools needed to catch up to. I think that's a pretty common pattern at companies our size.
v.Q9: The data integrity issue was the most urgent — I couldn't have incomplete or incorrect benefits data flowing to carriers, and that was genuinely keeping me up at night. Beyond that, reporting was a real gap. I wanted to be able to pull workforce analytics for my leadership team without having to manually build spreadsheets. And the employee self-service experience in Zenefits was clunky enough that we were getting a lot of inbound tickets from employees who couldn't figure out basic tasks. Those three things — data reliability, reporting, and self-service usability — were the core frustrations.
v.Q10: We looked at BambooHR, Rippling, and Gusto. I also briefly looked at Justworks but ruled it out early because we weren't interested in a PEO model. So it was really BambooHR, Rippling, and Gusto that got serious consideration.
v.Q11: A few firm requirements. The HRIS and benefits administration had to be genuinely integrated — not just a partnership where they pass data via file transfer. We needed strong document management for offer letters, NDAs, and compliance documents because we'd been doing that manually. And the employee onboarding experience had to be configurable, because our onboarding process has some specific sequences that a rigid system can't accommodate. Price ceiling mattered too — I wasn't going to go above roughly $25 to $30 per employee per month all-in.
v.Q12: It was primarily me and our CEO. At 85 employees, the CEO is still in the room for any significant software purchase. I was the primary evaluator and the formal recommender — I ran demos, did reference calls, built the comparison matrix. The CEO had final approval authority and his main lens was cost and simplicity. Our finance lead gave input on contract terms. I'd say I was the primary driver and recommender with sign-off required from the CEO.
v.Q13: We switched to BambooHR and moved away from Zenefits. We kept ADP Run for payroll rather than consolidating payroll into a single platform, which in hindsight I'm somewhat ambivalent about.
v.Q14: BambooHR's reputation for reliability and data integrity was the biggest factor. After Zenefits, I needed to trust the platform, and BambooHR has a very solid track record there. The onboarding workflow builder was genuinely the best of the three — I could configure it in a way that matched how we actually run onboarding, with department-specific task lists and conditional logic. The UI was also the most intuitive of the options, which mattered because I wanted my small HR team to be productive without a steep learning curve. And the implementation process was well-documented and felt manageable for a team our size.
v.Q15: Rippling was impressive in terms of breadth — the IT management and device provisioning capabilities are things I genuinely wish BambooHR had. But honestly it felt more complex than what we needed, and the pricing once you add all the modules together pushed past our ceiling. I also felt like Rippling is optimized for companies where IT and HR are tightly integrated, and at 85 people our IT function is pretty lean, so some of that value proposition wasn't going to materialize for us. Gusto was appealing from a simplicity standpoint — the UI is clean, the payroll experience is really strong, and the price is competitive. But the HRIS capabilities were thin enough that I felt like I'd be buying a payroll product with some HR features bolted on, rather than a proper HRIS. The reporting and workforce analytics story in Gusto didn't meet our bar, and the onboarding workflow configurability wasn't there.
v.Q16: BambooHR is genuinely solid on the employee record and document management side — I trust the data, which was my top priority. The onboarding workflows have worked well and my team likes using them. The time-off tracking is clean and self-service for employees is good enough that we rarely get support tickets for basic things. The analytics module has improved and I can pull most of the standard reports I need without a lot of wrangling.
v.Q17: The payroll integration with ADP is still more manual than I'd like. I think if I'd consolidated everything onto one platform I'd save meaningful time every pay cycle. BambooHR's compensation management features are pretty basic — I've been building our compensation framework in a Google Sheet because the system doesn't support the kind of banding and range modeling I need. And as we think about performance management, the performance module in BambooHR is functional but not especially sophisticated.
v.Q18: The payroll separation is the one that creates the most recurring friction. Every pay period I'm reconciling between BambooHR and ADP to make sure changes to employee records — new hires, terminations, compensation changes — have been accurately reflected in payroll. It's not catastrophically broken, but it's a moderate frustration that costs time every two weeks and introduces avoidable risk.
v.Q19: We've become more serious about compensation strategy — we're doing more structured salary reviews, thinking about pay equity more formally, and I need a system that can actually support that work rather than making me do it all in a spreadsheet. I also think about the total experience more holistically now — I want employees to have one place they go for everything people-related, and right now we're still asking them to navigate multiple systems.
v.Q20: Across BambooHR and ADP Run together, I think we're in the $20K to $50K range annually. It's probably closer to $30K to $35K when I add it all up.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. BambooHR specifically I think is fair value. ADP Run I'm less sure about — I think we could get equivalent payroll functionality for less if we consolidated, so the combined spend feels slightly above where I'd want it to be.
v.Q22: If BambooHR had genuinely native, reliable payroll built in — so I could eliminate the ADP integration entirely — I think that's worth somewhere in the $10K to $25K range in combined time savings and reduced risk. I'd probably put it at the lower end of that band, around $10K to $15K.
v.Q23: I think there's a real possibility we revisit things in the next six to twelve months, especially if we cross 100 employees — that feels like a natural trigger point. Within the next six months specifically, I'd say somewhat unlikely to actually switch, but I wouldn't rule out starting to evaluate. I'm more in early-research mode than active-evaluation mode right now.
v.Q24: I think the core challenge is that no single platform does everything well at the size most of us are operating at. You're always making tradeoffs. The tools that are great at payroll are often thin on HRIS, and vice versa. And then the consolidation platforms that promise to do everything tend to be either priced for companies twice our size or are complex enough that you need a dedicated admin to operate them effectively. I'd also say implementation anxiety is real — switching systems is genuinely disruptive, and the fear of getting it wrong keeps a lot of people on platforms that no longer fit.

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm the VP of HR here, so I oversee the whole people function — recruiting, comp, benefits, compliance, the works.
v.Q2: Coming up on four years now, so I'd put myself in that three-to-five band.
v.Q3: We're in manufacturing — precision components, primarily for aerospace and industrial clients. We're sitting at around 210 employees right now, though that number has moved quite a bit in the last couple of years.
v.Q4: We're on Gusto as our main platform. It handles payroll and benefits enrollment. We use a separate ATS on top of it, but Gusto is the core system of record.
v.Q5: That was about a year ago, honestly. We went through a fairly structured evaluation process around mid-last year.
v.Q6: We were using a combination of ADP Workforce Now for payroll and a really basic HRIS that I'd describe generously as a spreadsheet with a login. The two systems didn't talk to each other at all.
v.Q7: The biggest driver was scale. We had grown from about 130 employees to over 180 in under 18 months, and our processes were breaking under the weight of that growth. Manual payroll corrections were happening almost every cycle. Benefits administration was a nightmare at open enrollment. We also had a new compliance requirement around OSHA recordkeeping and state-level paid leave that our old tools genuinely couldn't support. And frankly, I think I was the one pushing hardest because the team I had inherited just couldn't keep up using the tools that were in place.
v.Q8: We had a private equity firm take a minority stake in us about two years ago, and they started asking for workforce reporting and headcount forecasting data that we just couldn't produce quickly. There was real board pressure to modernize the HR function. That accelerated everything.
v.Q9: ADP was feature-rich but enormously overcomplicated for our size. Support was slow and expensive. Every configuration change felt like it required a consultant. The reporting module was honestly just bad — I couldn't get a simple headcount-by-department export without building a custom report. And benefits enrollment had zero employee self-service. People were emailing my team PDF forms in 2023, which is just not acceptable.
v.Q10: We looked at Gusto, Rippling, Paychex Flex, and briefly at Paylocity. Those were the four we put through any kind of real evaluation.
v.Q11: It had to handle multi-state payroll natively — we operate in Ohio, Texas, and Pennsylvania. It had to have integrated benefits administration with a carrier connection, not just a form-filing system. And it needed to support salaried and hourly workers in the same platform, because we have both office staff and floor workers.
v.Q12: I led the evaluation and made the recommendation. Our CFO had final sign-off on budget, and our IT director reviewed the security posture of each vendor. But I'd say I was the primary recommender — the CFO trusted my assessment as long as I could defend the cost.
v.Q13: We switched. We moved to Gusto and went live about eight months ago.
v.Q14: Gusto's implementation experience was genuinely better than anything else we saw. The demo was clean, the onboarding team was responsive, and the price-to-value at our size was hard to argue with. It also had the best employee self-service experience of the group, which I knew would reduce ticket volume to my team. Rippling was a close second, but it felt a bit more like an IT platform that also does HR, and we didn't need device management or that level of complexity.
v.Q15: Paychex Flex felt outdated — the interface reminded me of ADP, and I didn't want to trade one legacy system for another. Paylocity was honestly a decent product, but their implementation timeline was too long and their mid-market sales motion felt really pushy. Rippling, as I said, was strong but overcomplicated for our current state. Maybe if we were 400 employees it would've been the right call.
v.Q16: Payroll runs cleanly. Benefits enrollment this past fall was the smoothest we've ever had — employees actually completed it themselves. The dashboard is intuitive enough that my managers can pull basic reports without calling my team. Those three things alone are a massive quality-of-life improvement.
v.Q17: Reporting is still limited for what I need at the VP level. I want workforce analytics — turnover by department, time-to-fill trends, compensation bands — and Gusto's reporting layer isn't built for that kind of analysis. I'm still exporting to Excel more than I'd like.
v.Q18: The analytics gap is my biggest frustration, and I'd call it moderate to significant. I can live with it for now, but as we keep growing and the PE firm keeps asking for data, it's going to become a real problem. I kind of expected Gusto to have grown that capability more by now.
v.Q19: We've added about 25 people since we implemented Gusto, which is faster than I anticipated. I'm also starting to think more seriously about succession planning and compensation benchmarking, neither of which Gusto does well. Those needs didn't feel urgent a year ago — they do now.
v.Q20: I think we're in the $50K to $100K range annually when you include the per-employee fees and the benefits administration piece.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes. It's a fair deal for what we get today, but if we're paying that much and still exporting to Excel for real analysis, I start to wonder whether we're outgrowing the platform.
v.Q22: If Gusto could genuinely solve the analytics and workforce reporting gap, I think that's worth $10K to $25K a year to us, easy — just in time saved and better decisions.
v.Q23: Probably not within six months — we just finished an implementation. But I'd say within 18 to 24 months, it's somewhat likely if the analytics situation doesn't improve. I'm keeping an eye on Rippling and a couple of others.
v.Q24: I think the biggest theme is that most tools are built for one size of company and struggle when you grow out of that bucket. And the analytics gap is industry-wide — everyone I talk to is still living in spreadsheets for anything meaningful. Integration fragmentation is the other one; payroll, benefits, and recruiting almost never live in a single system that actually works end to end.

Q4: Point Solution Layered on Core Platform

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q1: I'm the VP of People Operations. So my scope is essentially everything from the moment a candidate enters our pipeline through their entire tenure at the company — onboarding, performance, engagement, comp, offboarding, all of it.
v.Q2: I've been here six years, which puts me comfortably in the five-to-ten band. I've seen this company go through a couple of pretty significant growth phases, which honestly shapes how I think about our tooling.
v.Q3: We're a professional services firm — management consulting, primarily focused on financial services clients. We have around 380 employees right now, almost entirely distributed across the U.S., with a small team in London.
v.Q4: We use BambooHR as our core HRIS — it's our employee record system and handles performance management, time-off tracking, and org chart. We run payroll through a separate vendor, and benefits administration is handled through a benefits broker platform. So it's honestly a bit of a patchwork, but BambooHR is the central hub.
v.Q5: We went through a fairly thorough evaluation about 14 months ago, so I'd say within the last 12 months is close, but technically just over that. Call it the 1-to-2-year range to be accurate.
v.Q6: We were on Namely at the time. We had been using it for a few years, and it was struggling to keep up with where we were as an organization.
v.Q7: There were honestly several things converging at once. The most immediate trigger was that Namely had become increasingly unreliable — we were seeing data sync errors, payroll discrepancies that required manual corrections, and their support response times had gotten quite poor. But beyond the reliability issue, we had also grown from roughly 280 to 350 employees over the prior two years, and the workflows Namely supported just weren't keeping pace. Performance review cycles were nearly impossible to administer at scale through the tool. We also had a new Chief People Officer join about 18 months before the evaluation, and she came in with a clear mandate to modernize the People function — she had strong opinions about what a modern HRIS should look like and was willing to invest in getting there. And finally, our contract renewal was coming up, and we felt like it was the right moment to pause and actually evaluate rather than just default-renew.
v.Q8: The shift to primarily remote work had been a significant operational change for us. Managing a fully distributed workforce in a consulting context introduced compliance complexity we hadn't anticipated — multi-state tax obligations, varying PTO laws, that sort of thing. Our previous tool wasn't built for that level of geographic distribution. I think there was also a broader moment in our industry where people operations was getting elevated from an administrative function to a strategic one, and the tools we were using just didn't reflect that shift.
v.Q9: The performance management piece was particularly painful. Namely's review cycle tools were clunky and not configurable enough for how we run reviews — we do 360s with weighted competency scoring, and getting that to work properly was a constant battle with the system. Reporting was also a consistent frustration; pulling a simple tenure report or a compensation analysis took way more effort than it should have. And employee self-service was weak — people were still submitting requests via email for things that should've been a simple workflow in the system. Those were the three areas I most wanted another tool to improve.
v.Q10: We evaluated BambooHR, Lattice, Rippling, and we took a fairly serious look at Workday for a moment — though we pretty quickly concluded it was too much platform for our size. So realistically it came down to BambooHR and Rippling.
v.Q11: We had a few non-negotiables. It had to support configurable performance review workflows — not just basic annual reviews but the 360-style process we use. It needed strong employee self-service, including a mobile experience, because our consultants are often at client sites. And it had to integrate cleanly with our payroll vendor and our Slack environment. Those were the hard filters going in.
v.Q12: Our CPO was the executive sponsor — she shaped the initial requirements and had final approval authority. I ran the day-to-day evaluation, managed the vendor relationships, and made the formal recommendation. We also brought in our Head of Finance to review contract terms and pricing, and we had our IT Security lead review vendor SOC 2 documentation. So it was a cross-functional group, but the People team drove it entirely. I'd describe my role as primary recommender with C-suite sign-off required.
v.Q13: We switched to BambooHR. We went live about 11 months ago and I think the transition went reasonably well, all things considered.
v.Q14: BambooHR honestly won on a combination of implementation simplicity and user experience. Our team had done demos with both BambooHR and Rippling, and while Rippling had more raw capability, the configuration burden was significantly higher. We knew that with a mid-size People Ops team, we didn't have the bandwidth to spend months implementing a platform that required that level of setup. BambooHR's implementation timeline was realistic, the onboarding support was structured and responsive, and the interface was clean enough that we felt confident employees would actually use it without requiring training. The performance management module wasn't perfect, but it was configurable enough to meet our core requirements. And the price point made it much easier to get CPO approval without a long budget fight.
v.Q15: Workday was eliminated quickly — it's built for enterprises with dedicated HRIS teams, and we simply don't have that. The cost alone was disqualifying. Lattice is excellent as a performance and engagement platform, but it's not really an HRIS — we would've still needed a separate system of record, and managing two platforms wasn't something we wanted to do. Rippling was genuinely a close call. The reason it lost was implementation complexity and the sense that we'd be paying for a lot of capability — device management, IT provisioning — that we didn't need and didn't want to manage. It felt like the right tool if you're a tech company that wants to consolidate HR and IT, but that's not our profile.
v.Q16: Employee self-service is genuinely good — the adoption rate we've seen since launch has been much higher than with Namely. The org chart and people directory features are used constantly in a remote environment. Time-off management is clean and the approvals workflow works well. And the onboarding workflow module has saved my team meaningful hours per new hire.
v.Q17: The analytics and reporting layer is the most significant gap. I can pull standard reports, but any kind of custom workforce analysis still requires exporting data and manipulating it externally. I also think the performance management module, while adequate, is not as sophisticated as tools like Lattice or Culture Amp — we've had to make some compromises on how we run reviews. And the payroll integration, while functional, requires manual reconciliation steps that I'd rather not have.
v.Q18: I'd say the reporting limitation is the biggest one, and the frustration is significant for me personally — maybe moderate for the broader team. I'm regularly asked by our CPO and leadership team for workforce insights that should take me 20 minutes to pull and instead take two hours because I'm working around the tool's limitations. That gap between what leadership expects and what the tool enables is honestly the most frustrating thing I deal with.
v.Q19: The expectation around people analytics has accelerated faster than I anticipated. When we evaluated tools 14 months ago, good reporting was important but not urgent. Today, our leadership team wants real-time workforce dashboards, attrition risk modeling, DEI tracking — that's a meaningfully higher bar than what we scoped for. I also think the AI conversation has shifted expectations. I'm getting asked regularly what our tools are doing with AI, and honestly the answer right now is not much.
v.Q20: Across BambooHR, our payroll vendor, and the benefits administration platform, I'd estimate we're in the $100K to $250K range annually when you add it all up.
v.Q21: Somewhat yes — BambooHR itself feels reasonably priced for what it does. But when I think about the total stack and the gaps that still exist, I'm less confident we're getting full value out of the combined spend.
v.Q22: If BambooHR solved the analytics gap with a genuinely capable reporting and dashboarding layer, I think that's worth $25K or more annually to us — between the time savings for my team and the strategic value of being able to answer leadership questions quickly and credibly.
v.Q23: Not within six months — we're too recently implemented to consider another switch. But I'd say within 12 to 18 months, if the analytics situation doesn't meaningfully improve and if the AI gap keeps widening, it becomes a real conversation. I'd call switching likelihood neutral to somewhat likely on a longer horizon.
v.Q24: I think the number one challenge is the fragmentation problem — most companies in our size range are running three or four tools that don't integrate cleanly, and the reconciliation burden falls on HR teams that are already stretched. The second thing is the gap between what AI is being marketed as capable of and what actually exists in production in these platforms — there's a lot of vaporware in that space right now. And I'd say the third challenge is that most tools are still built around administrative workflows rather than strategic insight, and that doesn't match how the People Operations function is evolving.

cat.Q21: Somewhat yes / mostly reasonable with caveats

v.Q2: I've been here just under three years, so I'd put that in the one-to-three range. I joined when we were still pretty small and I've been part of the build-out of the HR function from something fairly informal into what we have today.

We have about 85 employees right now. Most of them are either consultants out in the field or project managers working hybrid, so we've got a pretty distributed population even though we're small.

It was actually my first major tool evaluation since joining the company, and I'll be honest, it was a bigger process than I expected for a company of our size.
v.Q6: We were using a combination of things that had just sort of accumulated over time rather than been deliberately chosen. The employee records were mostly in an old version of ADP — I think it was ADP Run — and beyond that it was honestly a lot of spreadsheets and shared Google Drive folders. There was no real HRIS. Time-off requests came in through email. Offer letters were Word documents passed around by email. It was kind of the classic small-company situation where HR infrastructure just hadn't kept up with the headcount.

But the longer-standing motivation was just the manual process pain that my team and I were dealing with every single day. Tracking PTO in a spreadsheet works until it doesn't, and we were past the point where it was working. I was also personally frustrated because I had come from a slightly larger company where I had used an actual HRIS and I knew what good looked like. I was spending time on administrative busywork that a system should have been handling. The CEO and our COO had been in conversations with a few peer companies and I think some of those conversations surfaced the idea that we needed real infrastructure before we could grow responsibly. There was also a moment where we had a near-miss on an I-9 audit — nothing came of it, but it scared people into realizing that manual processes carry real compliance risk. I think that fear was actually a useful motivator for getting budget approved.
v.Q9: So many things, honestly. The biggest one for me personally was the absence of any kind of employee self-service. Every single thing required someone on my team to manually intervene — whether that was a PTO balance question, an address update, a request for a pay stub, it all came to us. That constant volume of small administrative requests was killing our capacity to do anything more strategic. The second major frustration was onboarding — or the lack of it. We had no automated workflow, no task checklist, no way to track whether a new hire had completed their paperwork. Everything was manual follow-up. The third thing was reporting. If our COO asked me how many employees we had in each state, or what our average tenure was, I was going to spend an afternoon pulling that together from different places rather than just running a report. That's not a good use of anyone's time. And then there was just the reliability issue with ADP Run — for a relatively small payroll, we were having more errors than we should have been, and the customer support experience was poor.
v.Q10: We looked at BambooHR, Gusto, and Zenefits — or I guess Zenefits had rebranded to TriNet Zenefits by that point. v.Q13: We switched and went with BambooHR. We migrated off ADP Run and launched BambooHR about 14 months ago. We kept Paychex for payroll, which I sometimes regret, but at the time it felt like the lower-risk path to not change both systems simultaneously.
v.Q14: BambooHR stood out for a few reasons.
